CHAPTER I

What is Faith in this place, and what is its need for salvation. But since in the divine Scriptures the meaning of Faith is multiple, here we are dealing with that by virtue of which we completely assent to the things that have been transmitted by God. That this is necessary to achieve salvation, no one will rightly doubt, especially when it is written: Without faith it is impossible to please God. For since the end proposed to man for blessedness is higher than what the acuity of the human mind can reach, it was necessary for him to receive his knowledge from God Himself. And this knowledge is nothing other than faith: the virtue of which makes us hold for certain what the authority of the most holy Mother Church has proven to have been transmitted by God. For no doubt can come to the faithful in the things of which God is the author, who is the same truth. From which we understand how much difference there is between this faith that we have in God and that which we lend to the writers of human history. But although faith extends widely and differs in magnitude and dignity (for so it is in the sacred Letters: O man of little faith, why did you doubt? and: Great is your faith; and: Increase our faith; likewise: Faith without works is dead; and: Faith that works through charity), nevertheless it is the same in kind, and the different degrees of faith are appropriated by the same force and reason of definition. How fruitful it is and how much use we get from it will be said in the explanation of the articles.

The Catholic faith, although it is one, nevertheless has different degrees according to the quality of the people. The Christian must believe above all that God is One and Triune. The three parts of the Apostles' Creed are adapted to the three divine Persons. First. Second. Third. Why are the different sentences of the Symbol called articles, which are like the decree of the apostolic faith. What an article.

When and for what reason were these twelve chapters of faith transmitted by the Apostles. Those things, then, that Christian men must first have are the things that the holy Apostles, guides and doctors of the faith, inspired by the divine Spirit, distinguished in twelve articles of the Symbol. For having received from the Lord the mandate to go throughout the world as his ambassadors and preach the Gospel to every creature, they judged that a formula of the Christian faith should be composed, so that everyone would feel and say the same thing, and there would be no schisms among those who called to the unity of the faith, but that they would be perfect in the same feeling and in the same sentence.

Where do you say Symbol from? This profession of Christian faith and hope, composed by them, was called the Apostles Symbol: because it was formed from several sentences that each one contributed in common; because they used it as a sign and password with which they could easily distinguish the deserters and the false brothers introduced secretly, who adulterated the Gospel, from those who were truly obligated with the sacrament of the militia of Christ. 4. What need does this Symbol have and how many parts it is divided into. There are many things that are proposed to the faithful in the Christian religion, of which one must have a certain and firm faith, either in each one by itself, or in a group, first of all and necessarily everyone must believe that which (as the foundation and sum of the truth) about the unity of the divine essence and the distinction of the three Persons, and the actions that are primarily rightly attributed to them, God himself taught us. The parish priest will teach that the doctrine of this mystery is briefly included in the Apostles' Creed. For, as our elders observed, who with piety and exactness treated this argument, it seems to be distributed mainly in three parts: so that in one the first Person of the divine nature and the wonderful work of creation are described; in another, the second Person and the mystery of human redemption; In the third, the third Person also, head and source of our holiness, concludes with several and very apt sentences. We call these sentences, due to a certain similarity frequently used by our Fathers, articles. For just as the members of the body are distinguished by their joints, so also in this confession of faith, everything that we are to believe in a distinct and separate way from the rest, we rightly and properly call an article.

CHAPTER I

I believe in God the Father almighty, Creator of heaven and earth.

The first article is briefly explained. To these words is subject this sentence: I believe with certainty and without a doubt I confess God the Father, that is, the first Person of the Trinity, who by his omnipotent power created out of nothing the very heaven and earth and all things that are contained in the realm of heaven and earth, and preserves and governs them once they were created: and I not only believe it with my heart and confess it with my mouth, but with utmost study and piety I tend towards Him as towards the supreme and most perfect good. So, this is a brief understanding of this first article. But since great mysteries are hidden in almost every word, the parish priest must now ponder them with greater diligence, so that, as soon as the Lord allows it, the faithful people may come to contemplate the glory of his majesty with fear and trembling.

What does the word "believe" mean? Thus, the word "Believe" in this place does not mean to give an opinion, estimate or conjecture, but rather, as the Sacred Letters teach, it has the force of a very certain assent, by which the mind assents firmly and constantly to God who opens his mysteries to it. Therefore he believes (as regards the explanation of this place) to whom something is true and persuaded without any hesitation. And no one should consider that the knowledge of faith is less certain because we do not see the things that faith proposes to us to believe: since the divine light with which we perceive them, although it does not give things transparency, does not, however, allow us to doubt them. For God, who said, "Let light shine out of darkness," has himself shone in our hearts, so that the gospel may not be hidden from us, as it is from those who are lost.

What is proposed in the Symbol must not be scrutinized with curiosity, but rather stated with simplicity. From what has been said, it follows that he who is endowed with this heavenly knowledge of faith is free from the curiosity of inquiring. Because God, when he commanded us to believe, did not propose to us to scrutinize divine judgments or to inquire into their reason and cause, but rather he commanded us to have an immutable faith, which makes the spirit rest in the knowledge of the eternal truth. And in truth, when the Apostle testifies: God is truthful, and every man is a liar, if it is typical of the arrogant and impudent man not to give faith to a grave and wise man who affirms something, and also to urge him to prove what he said with reasons or witnesses, what rashness and even what foolishness would it be, hearing the voices of God, to ask for the reasons of the heavenly and healthy doctrine? Thus, faith must exclude not only all ambiguity, but also the desire to demonstrate.

It is not enough for salvation to believe, but it is also necessary to profess faith. Let the parish priest also teach that he who says "I believe", in addition to declaring the intimate assent of his mind (which is the interior act of faith), must reveal with an open profession of faith what he has locked up in his soul, and confess it and preach it publicly with great joy. For it is necessary that the faithful have that spirit with which, confidently, the Prophet said: I believed, therefore I spoke; imitate the Apostles, who responded to the princes of the people: We cannot stop speaking what we have seen and heard; be excited by that illustrious voice of Saint Paul: I am not ashamed of the Gospel, because it is the power of God for the salvation of everyone who believes. Likewise, with what the truth of this sentence is most confirmed: With the heart one believes for righteousness, but with the mouth one confesses for salvation. 5. Excellence of the Christian faith. In God. Here we can already know the dignity and preeminence of Christian wisdom, and how much we owe to divine goodness, to whom it has been given to rise immediately, as if by degrees of faith, to the knowledge of the most excellent and most desirable thing.

How much Christian wisdom about God differs from philosophical knowledge of divine things. In this, Christian philosophy and the wisdom of this century differ greatly from each other: because it, guided only by natural light, advancing little by little from the effects and from the things that are perceived by the senses, only after long labors does it finally contemplate the invisible things of God, and recognizes and understands the first cause and author of all things; but the former, on the contrary, sharpens the acuity of the human mind in such a way that it can penetrate heaven without any work, and illuminated by the divine splendor, contemplates first the eternal source of light itself and then the things that are beneath it: so that we experience with the utmost depth of mind that we have been called from darkness to the admirable light, as the Prince of the Apostles says, and believing we exult with joy unspeakable Rightly, then, the faithful profess first that they believe in God, whose majesty, according to the sentence of Jeremiah, we say is incomprehensible: for there dwells, as the Apostle says, an inaccessible light, which no man has seen, nor can see; for when he spoke to Moses, "Man shall not see me," he said, "and live." For in order for our mind to reach God, of whom there is nothing more sublime, it is necessary that it be completely abstracted from the senses: a faculty of which we do not naturally have in this life. But even if this were the case, God did not leave himself without witness, as the Apostle says, doing good from heaven, giving rain and fruitful times, filling the hearts of men with food and joy. This was the reason why the philosophers did not feel anything abject about God and kept from Him the further away everything corporeal, everything concrete and mixed: to whom they also attributed the perfect strength and abundance of all good things, so that from Him, as from a perpetual and inexhaustible source of goodness and benignity, flow all perfect good things to all created things and natures: whom they called wise, author and lover of truth, just, most beneficent, and by other names in which the supreme and absolute perfection is contained: whose immense and infinite virtue they said fills every place and extends through all things. This is stated much better and more clearly by the divine Letters, as in that place: God is spirit; Likewise: Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect; then: All things are naked and open to his eyes; and that: Oh depth of the riches of the wisdom and science of God!; then: God is true; and: I am the way, and the truth, and the life; Furthermore: Your right hand is full of justice; Finally: You open your hand and fill every animal with blessing.

Lastly: Where shall I go from your spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? And: If I ascend to heaven, there you are; If I descend into hell, there you are; if I take my wings at dawn and live at the ends of the sea, etc. And: Do I not fill heaven and earth, says the Lord? Great and illustrious are these things of the nature of God, in accordance and consistent with the authority of the sacred books, that the philosophers learned through the investigation of things done: although in this we also know the necessity of the celestial doctrine, if we notice that faith not only provides this, as has been said above, that what only wise men attained with long study is immediately opened and is at hand also to the rude and inexperienced, but also that the news of things that is acquired with the discipline of faith settles in our minds much more certain and purer from all error than if the mind understood those same things understood with the reasons of human science.

But how much more excellent must be esteemed the knowledge of the divine Majesty, to which the contemplation of nature does not enter in a way common to all, but the light of faith specifically for those who believe. This is contained in the articles of the Symbol, which open to us the unity of the divine essence and the distinction of the three Persons, and that God himself is the ultimate end of man, from whom the possession of celestial and eternal blessedness is to be expected: for from Saint Paul we learned that God is a rewarder of those who seek Him. How great these things are, and whether they are goods of that kind to which human knowledge could aspire, was shown long before by the Apostle Isaiah the Prophet himself in these words: Since the ages they have not heard, nor perceived with their ears: no eye has seen, O God, apart from you, what you have prepared for those who await you. 7. It must be confessed that there is only one God, not many gods. But from what we have said it must also be confessed that there is only one God, not many gods. For attributing to God the supreme goodness and perfection, it cannot be that what is supreme and most absolute is found in many. And if anyone lacks anything for the utmost, for that very reason he is imperfect: for this reason the nature of God is not suitable for him. This is proven in many places in the sacred Letters; for it is written: Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God is one God. Furthermore there is the command of the Lord: You shall have no other gods before me. Afterwards the Prophet often admonishes: I am the first and I am the last, and besides me there is no God. The Apostle also testifies openly: One Lord, one faith, one baptism. 8. The name of God is sometimes attributed to created natures, but improperly. Nor does it bother us that sometimes the sacred Letters impose the name of God also on created natures. For the fact that they called the prophets and judges gods was not done in the manner of the Gentiles, for many foolishly and impiously pretended to be gods, but with a certain habit of speaking they wanted to signify some excellent virtue or function that was granted to them by the gift of God. Thus, then, the Christian faith believes and confesses God as one by nature, substance and essence, as was said in the Symbol of the Council of Nicaea to confirm the truth: but ascending still higher, one understands Him in such a way that he venerates the Unity in the Trinity and the Trinity in the Unity: of which mystery we must now begin to speak.

God calls himself the Father of all men for a general reason, and of Christians for a peculiar reason. It continues, in effect, in the Symbol: Father. But since the word Father is attributed to God not in just one way, it must first be declared what the most appropriate meaning of this place is. Some, to whose darkness faith did not bring light, also understood that God is an eternal substance from which things were born and by whose providence all things are governed and preserve their order and state. Thus, having drawn a resemblance from human things, just as they called father the one from whom the family was propagated and by whose council and empire it is governed, in this way it became that they wanted to call God Father, whom they recognized as the architect and ruler of all things. The Sacred Letters also used the same name when, speaking of God, they indicated that the creation of all things, the power and the admirable providence should be attributed to him. For we read: Is he not your Father, who possessed you, and made you, and created you? And elsewhere: Is he not one Father of us all? Did not only one God create us? But much more frequently, and with a somewhat peculiar name, especially in the books of the New Testament, God is said to be the Father of Christians, who did not receive the spirit of bondage to fear, but received the spirit of adoption as children of God, in which we cry: Abba, Father! because the Father gave us such charity that we should be called and be children of God: and if children, then heirs, heirs certainly of God, joint heirs of Christ, who is the firstborn among many brothers; nor is he ashamed to call us brothers. So, whether you look at the common cause of creation and providence, or the main cause of spiritual adoption, it is no wonder that the faithful profess to believe in God the Father.

What mysteries are to be gathered from this voice "Father"; and of the distinction of Persons in the divine. But in addition to the notions that we will explain, upon hearing the name of Father, the parish priest will teach that the mind must be lifted to higher mysteries. Well, what in that inaccessible light that God inhabits is most hidden and abstruse, and that human reason and intelligence could not reach or even suspect, that is what the divine oracles begin to open to us with the word Father. In effect, this name indicates that not only one Person, but the distinction of Persons must be believed in a single essence of divinity. For there are three Persons in one divinity: of the Father, who is begotten of no one; of the Son, who before all ages was begotten of the Father; of the Holy Spirit, who also from eternity proceeds from the Father and the Son. And the Father is in one substance of the divinity the first Person, who with his only begotten Son and with the Holy Spirit is one God, one Lord, not in the singularity of a single Person, but in the Trinity of a single substance. And these three Persons, since it is unlawful to think of anything dissimilar or unequal about them, are understood to be different only because of their properties. Because the Father is unbegotten; the Son begotten of the Father; the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. And thus we confess the same essence and the same substance of the three Persons; so that in the confession of the true and everlasting Deity we believe that property in the Persons, unity in the essence and equality in the Trinity must be piously and holyly cultivated.

For when we say that the Father is the first Person, it is not to be understood as if we thought that in the Trinity there is something before or after, greater or less; Such impiety is absurd in the minds of the faithful, since the Christian religion preaches the same eternity and the same majesty of glory in the three Persons. But we affirm truly and without a doubt that the Father, being a principle without a beginning, is the first Person: which, as he is distinguished by the property of the Father, so it is primarily appropriate for this one to have begotten the Son from eternity: for we are signified that God was always both and Father, when we pronounce together in this confession the names of God and Father. But since in the knowledge and explanation of nothing we can move with more danger or err more seriously than in this, the highest and most difficult of all, let the parish priest teach that the very words of essence and person with which this mystery is meant must be religiously retained, and let the faithful know that there is unity in the essence and distinction in the Persons. But it is not advisable to investigate this with more subtlety, remembering that voice: He who searches the majesty will be oppressed by the glory: for it is enough to have it as certain and explored by faith that we have been thus taught by God (to whose oracles not to assent is extreme folly and misery): Teach, he says, all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. And again: There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one and the same. Pray, however, assiduously and entreat God and Father, who created all things from nothing and arranges them gently, who gave us the power to be children of God, who opened to the human mind the mystery of the Trinity; Let him pray, I say, without intermission who for divine benefit believes these things, so that someday, received into the eternal tabernacles, he may be worthy of seeing how great is the fruitfulness of God the Father, so that, looking at and understanding himself, he begets a Son equal and similar to himself; and in what way the same and equal love of charity of both, which is the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and the Son, unites the genitor and the begotten to each other with an eternal and indissoluble bond, and thus the essence of the divine Trinity is one and the distinction of the three Persons is perfect. 11. What do we understand here by the name of Omnipotent. Omnipotent. Sacred Letters usually explain with many names the supreme strength and immense majesty of God, to show how much religion and piety his most holy name must be cultivated; But first of all let the parish priest teach that omnipotent force is very frequently attributed to him. For He Himself says of Himself: I am the Lord omnipotent. And again Jacob, when he sent his sons to Joseph, thus besought them: May my almighty God make it favorable to you. Later in the Apocalypse it is written: The Lord God, who is and who was and who is to come, the Omnipotent; and elsewhere it is called the great day of Almighty God.

Sometimes the same thing is usually meant by several words. And to this belongs what is said: Not every word will be impossible for God; and: Is the hand of the Lord weak? Likewise: You have power when you want. And others of the same kind: from whose various ways of saying one perceives what is clearly understood in a single word of Omnipotent. We understand, therefore, with this name that there is nothing, nothing can be pretended with the spirit and the thought, that God cannot do; because not only does it have the power to effect these things that, although they are very great, somehow fall into our thoughts—namely, that all things are reduced to nothing, and that many worlds suddenly exist out of nothing—but there are also much greater things in its power, which the human mind and intelligence cannot suspect.

Although God is omnipotent, he cannot sin or deceive himself. But no, because God can do all things, he can lie, or deceive, or be deceived, or sin, or perish, or ignore something. These things fall into that nature whose action is imperfect: but God, whose action is always most perfect, is why it is said that he cannot these things, because being able to do them is a matter of weakness, not of the sum and infinite power of all the things that He has. Thus, we believe that God is omnipotent in such a way that, nevertheless, we think that all things are very far from Him that are not maximally and conveniently united to His perfect essence.

Why, omitting the other names said of God, mention is made only of Omnipotence in the Symbol; and what are the benefits of this faith. Let the priest show that it was rightly and wisely that, omitting the other names that are said of God, this one was proposed to us only to believe in the Symbol. For in recognizing God omnipotent, it is necessary that we confess at the same time that he has knowledge of all things and that all things are subject to his dominion and empire. And when we do not doubt that all things can be done through Him, it is entirely consequential that we also have explored the others about Him; which if they are missing, we cannot in any way understand how he is omnipotent. Furthermore, nothing is worth as much to confirm our faith and hope as if we have fixed in our minds that there is nothing that God cannot do: because everything that is later to be believed, however great and admirable it may be and surpasses the order and mode of things, human reason, once perceiving the news of the omnipotent God, assents to it without any hesitation; and rather, the greater the things that the divine oracles teach, the more gladly it is estimated that faith should be given to them. And if some good is to be expected, the spirit is never depressed by the magnitude of the thing it desires, but rather it rises and is confirmed, often thinking that there is nothing that the omnipotent God cannot accomplish. Therefore it is necessary that we be armed mainly with this faith, both when we are forced to do some admirable works for the use and benefit of our neighbor, and when we want to ask for something from God with prayers. The first thing was taught by the Lord himself when, reproaching the disciples for their unbelief, he said: If you have faith like a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain: Move from here to there, and it will pass, and nothing will be impossible for you. Saint James testified about the second: Ask with faith, doubting nothing; because he who doubts is like the wave of the sea, which is moved by the wind and agitated; Let this man therefore not think that he will receive anything from the Lord. This faith provides us with many other comforts and benefits; First of all, it instructs us for all modesty and humility of mind; Thus says, in effect, the Prince of the Apostles: Humble yourselves under the powerful hand of God: he also warns that we are not to fear where there is no fear, but we are to fear God alone, in whose power we are and all our things: for our Savior says: I will show you whom you should fear. Fear him who, after killing, has the power to cast into Gehenna. We also use this faith to know and celebrate the immense benefits of God for us. For he who thinks of the omnipotent God cannot be of such an ungrateful spirit that he does not often exclaim: He who is powerful has done great things for me.

The voice of Omnipotence is not attributed here to the Father in such a way that it is not also said of the Son or the Holy Spirit. But the fact that in this Article we call the Father omnipotent, no one should be misled into judging that this name was attributed to him in such a way that it is not also common to the Son and the Holy Spirit. For just as we say God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit, and not yet three gods, but one God: so we confess equally omnipotent the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and not, however, three omnipotents, but one Omnipotent One. But with a certain main reason we call the Father by this name, because he is the source of all origin; just as we also attribute wisdom to the Son, who is the eternal Word of the Father, and goodness to the Holy Spirit, who is the love of both, although these and other names of this kind are commonly said of the three Persons, according to the rule of the Catholic faith.

How and for what reason God created heaven and earth. Creator of heaven and earth. How necessary it was to transmit the knowledge of the omnipotent God to the faithful shortly before can be seen from what is now to be explained about the creation of all things. Well, such a wonderful work is more easily believed because there is no room to doubt the immense power of the Creator.

He did not manufacture the world from some matter, but created it from nothing, and established it not forced by any force or necessity, but of his own will and spontaneously. Nor was there any other cause that impelled Him to the work of creation except to communicate His goodness to the things that were to be made of Him: because the nature of God, most blessed in itself, needs nothing, as David says: I said to the Lord: You are my God, because you do not need my goods. And just as, induced by His goodness, He did everything He wanted, so He did not follow any example or form that was outside Him when He created the universe: but, because the exemplar of all things is contained in the divine intelligence, the supreme artificer, looking at it in Himself and as if imitating It, with supreme wisdom and infinite virtue, which is His own, procreated at the beginning the universality of things: Because He said it, and they were made; He commanded it, and they were created.

What is to be understood in this place by heaven and earth. But with the name of heaven and earth we must understand everything that heaven and earth embrace. For in addition to the heavens, which the Prophet called the works of his fingers, he also added the radiance of the sun and the ornamentation of the moon and the other stars, and so that they would be for signs and for times and for days and for years, he so tempered the orbs of the heavens with a certain and constant course, that nothing can seem more mobile than their perpetual revolution, nor anything more certain than that mobility.

Of the creation of the spiritual heavens, that is, of the Angels. Furthermore, He created from nothing spiritual nature and innumerable Angels, to minister and assist God, whom He then increased and adorned with the admirable gift of His grace and power. For since it is clear from the divine Letters that the devil did not remain in the truth, it is clear that he and the other deserting Angels were endowed with grace from the beginning of their origin: of which Saint Augustine says thus: He created the Angels with good will, that is, with chaste love with which they adhered to Him, at the same time giving them nature and granting them grace. Hence it must be believed that the holy Angels never existed without good will, that is, without the love of God. And as far as science is concerned, there is that testimony of the sacred Letters: You, Lord my king, are wise as an angel of God to understand all things on earth. Finally the divine David gave them power with these words: Powerful in virtue, who do his word; and for the same reason they are often called virtues and armies of the Lord in sacred Letters. But although all of them were adorned with heavenly gifts, many, however, for having deserted God their father and creator, were cast down from those highest seats and locked up in the darkest prison on earth, and paid the eternal penalties of their pride: of whom the Prince of the Apostles writes in this way: He did not spare the angels who sinned, but, throwing those held in chains of Gehenna, handed them over to be tormented, reserved for judgment.

Of the creation of the earth. But God also commanded by his word that the earth, founded on its stability, should be established in the middle of the world, and he made the mountains go up and the fields go down to the place where he founded them: and, so that the force of the waters would not flood it, he set a boundary that they will not pass through or cover the earth again. Afterwards he not only clothed and adorned it with trees and every variety of herbs and flowers, but, like the waters and air before, he also filled the earth with innumerable kinds of animals.

Of the creation of man. Finally he formed man from the slime of the earth, constituted in the body in such a way that not by the force of nature itself, but by divine benefit, he would be immortal and impassive. And as for the soul, he formed it in his image and likeness, and gave it free will: he also tempered in it all the movements of the spirit and desires in such a way that they never ceased to obey the rule of reason. He also added the admirable gift of original justice, and then wanted it to preside over the other animals: which will be easy for parish priests to learn about the sacred story of Genesis for the instruction of the faithful.

With the name of heaven and earth all things visible and invisible are understood. This, then, is to be understood of the creation of all things by the words heaven and earth: which the Prophet briefly embraced in these words: Yours are the heavens and yours is the earth; You founded the orb of the earth and its fullness: but the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea meant it much more briefly, adding in the Symbol those two words: of the visible and of the invisible. For all things that are understood in the universality of things and we confess that they were created by God, either fall under sense and are called visible, or they can be perceived by us with the mind and intelligence, which are signified by the name of invisible.

The things created by the virtue of God cannot subsist without his government and providence. Nor should God be believed to be the creator and effector of all things in such a way that we consider that, once the work was perfected and absolved, the things made by Him could later exist without His infinite virtue. For just as it was brought about by the supreme power, wisdom and goodness of the Creator that all things existed, so also, if his perpetual providence did not assist created things and did not preserve them with the same force with which they were originally constituted, they would immediately be reduced to nothing. And the Scripture declares it when it says: How could anything remain if you did not want it? Or how would what was not called by you be preserved?

God with his government does not destroy the force of secondary causes. And not only does God with his providence guard and administer all things that are, but he also impels with intimate virtue those that move and do something towards movement and action in such a way that, although he does not prevent the efficiency of the secondary causes, he prevents them; for its most virtuous strength extends to each one, and as the Wise One testifies: It reaches from one end to the other with strength and arranges all things smoothly. Therefore the Apostle said, when he announced to the Athenians the God whom they worshiped without knowing Him: He is not far from each one of us: for in Him we live and move and have our being.

Creation is not to be attributed to the Father alone. And this is enough about the explanation of the first article, if we also admonish that the work of creation is common to all the Persons of the holy and undivided Trinity. Because in this place, according to the doctrine of the Apostles, we confess the Father Creator of heaven and earth; In the sacred Scriptures we read of the Son: All things were made through Him; and of the Holy Spirit: The Spirit of God moved over the waters; and elsewhere: By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all his power.

CHAPTER III

And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord. 1. Of the second article, and of the usefulness of his profession. How great and abundant the usefulness that has flowed to the human race from the faith and confession of this article is shown by that testimony of Saint John: Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him and he in God; and it is declared by the proclamation of beatitude that Christ the Lord granted to the Prince of the Apostles: Blessed are you, Simon, son of Jonah, because flesh and blood did not reveal it to you, but my Father who is in heaven. Because this is the very firm foundation of our salvation and redemption.

Where is the magnitude of the benefit proposed in this article better known? But since the fruit of this admirable usefulness is understood mainly from the ruin of that most happy state in which God placed the first men, let the parish priest undertake this diligence: that the faithful know the cause of the common miseries and hardships. Because when Adam departed from the obedience of God and violated the interdict: He eats from every tree in paradise; but do not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil: for in the day that you eat of it, you will die of death: he fell into that supreme calamity of losing the holiness and justice in which he had been constituted, and of suffering the other evils that the holy Council of Trent explained more abundantly. He will remember, furthermore, that sin and the penalty of sin did not stop at Adam alone, but that from him, as a seed and cause, they passed by right to all posterity.
No one outside of Christ could restore the human race. Having therefore fallen from the highest degree of dignity,

the original justice lost only by the Son of God was recovered. Here is placed the occasional and accessory cause of the Incarnation of the Son of God, so that he would come mortal and passible; but at the beginning the cause is placed first and for itself. Adam's sin spread to his descendants. The human race could not be restored by the forces of any creature.

Without the faith of redemption no one could ever be saved, and that is why Christ was often announced from the beginning of the world. What does the third article of faith propose to the faithful to believe? Why is it attributed to the Holy Spirit. In the Incarnation of Christ some things are made according to nature and others above nature.

Through the temporal nativity there was no confusion of natures in Christ. Only the Holy Spirit did not perfect the work of the Incarnation. But not omitting the explanation of the words, let the parish priest teach that when we say that the Son of God was conceived by the virtue of the Holy Spirit, not only one Person of the divine Trinity created the mystery of the Incarnation. For although only the Son assumed human nature, nevertheless all the Persons of the divine Trinity, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, were authors of this mystery, since that rule of the Christian faith must be held: All the things that God works outside of himself in created things are common to the three Persons, and one does not work more than another, nor one without the other. But that one Person proceeds from another, this alone cannot be common to all: because the Son is begotten from the Father alone, the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son; but everything that is outside of them proceeds from them, the three Persons work without any difference: and of this kind the Incarnation of the Son of God must be esteemed. And even if this is so, the sacred Letters nevertheless tend to attribute to some what is common to all Persons, in another way to others: as they attribute to the Father the supreme power of all things, to the Son wisdom, to the Holy Spirit love. And since the mystery of the divine Incarnation declares the singular and immense kindness of God towards us, for this reason this work is attributed with a certain peculiar reason to the Holy Spirit.

Not all things were made above the order of nature at the conception of Christ, but very many. In this mystery we notice that some things were carried out above the order of nature, and others by the force of nature. Because we believe that the body of Christ was formed from the most pure blood of the Virgin Mother, in this we recognize human nature; for it is common to the bodies of all men to be formed from the blood of the mother. But what surpasses the order of nature and human intelligence is this: as the blessed Virgin, assenting to the words of the Angel, said: Behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord, let it be done to me according to your word; Immediately the most holy Body of Christ was formed, and the soul endowed with reason was united to it, and thus in the same instant of time God was perfect and perfect Man. And that this was a new and admirable work of the Holy Spirit, no one can doubt, since, the order of nature being preserved, no body can be informed by the soul of man except within the prescribed space of time. Then was added that worthy of maximum admiration: that as soon as the soul was united to the body, the same divinity was also united to the body and the soul; Therefore, the body was immediately formed and animated, the divinity was united to the body and the soul, from which it follows that at the same point in time God was perfect and perfect Man, and the holy Virgin was truly and properly called Mother of God and Man, because at the same moment she conceived God and Man. This was signified to her by the Angel when he said: Behold, you will conceive in the womb and bear a son, and you will call his name Jesus: He will be great, and will be called the Son of the Most High. And what Isaiah predicted was confirmed by the event: Behold, the Virgin will conceive and give birth to a son. Likewise Elizabeth, when, filled with the Holy Spirit, she understood the conception of the Son of God, declared it with these words: Whence does this come to me, that the Mother of my Lord should come to me? But just as the body of Christ was formed from the most pure blood of the most intact Virgin, without any work of man, as we said before, but only by the virtue of the Holy Spirit: so also, as soon as he was conceived, his soul received the abundant copy of the Spirit of God and all the abundance of the charisms: because not, like other men who adorn themselves with holiness and grace, God gives him the Spirit in measure, as Saint John testifies; but he infuses his soul with all grace so abundantly that we all receive from its fullness.

What does this clause mean to believe: Dead and buried. Dead and buried. With these words the priest will explain with certainty that Jesus Christ, after being crucified, truly died and was buried. Furthermore, since Christ was true and perfect man, he could also truly die: and man dies when the soul is separated from the body. It was fitting, then, that the Son of God should die, in order to destroy by death him who had the power of death, that is, the devil, and to free those who, through fear of death, were subject to slavery for life.

Christ did not suffer death reluctantly or forcefully. Why did Christ want to suffer the extreme, and what must be felt by those who, professing Christianity, stain themselves in sins. Although if we remember the sweat of the Lord made like drops of blood that ran to the ground, when He perceived with the spirit the torments and cruciates with which shortly after He was to be afflicted, each one will easily understand that nothing could be added to that pain. For if the thought of impending evils was so bitter, which the sweat of blood declared, what is to be estimated that the same suffering was? But, nevertheless, it is clear that Christ the Lord was afflicted with extreme pains both of mind and body. And in the first place there was no part of his body that did not feel very serious pain: because his feet and hands were nailed to the cross, his head was crowned with thorns, and his entire body was scourged with scourges. Furthermore, men of all genders and orders gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ. Because the people and the Jews were persuaders, authors and ministers of the passion: Judas betrayed him, Peter denied him, the rest abandoned him.

Already on the same cross, will we seek acerbity, or ignominy, or both at the same time? And in truth no kind of death could be thought more clumsy or more bitter, with which only the most harmful and most rapid men were usually afflicted, and in which the diuturnity of death made the sense of the utmost pain and cruciate more vehement. Furthermore, the magnitude of the penalties was increased by the very constitution and habit of the Body of Christ Jesus; which, having been formed by the virtue of the Holy Spirit, was much more perfect and tempered than the bodies of other men can be; and for that reason he also had a more acute force of feeling, and he endured all those torments more severely. And as far as the intimate pain of the soul is concerned, no one can doubt that it was supreme in Christ. For the holy men who endured any tortures and cruciates did not lack the consolation of the divinely given spirit, with which they were refreshed and able to endure with equal courage the force of the torments: what's more, in the cruciates many were elevated with intimate joy: for the Apostle says: I rejoice in the passions for your sakes: and I fulfill in my flesh what is lacking in the passions of Christ for his body, which is the Church; and elsewhere: I am full of consolation, overflowing with joy in all our tribulation. But Christ the Lord did not mildly temper any mixture of the bitterest chalice of the passion that he drank. Because the human nature that he had assumed allowed him to feel all the torments, no differently than if he had been a man and not also God.

What comforts and goods primarily engendered the Christian race by the passion of Christ. It now remains for the parish priest to also explain exactly the comforts and goods that we perceive from the passion of the Lord. Firstly, then, the passion of the Lord was deliverance from sin: because, as it is in Saint John: He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood. And the Apostle says: He made you alive with Him, forgiving you all your crimes, erasing the document of the decree that was against us, that was contrary to us, and removed it from the way, nailing it to the cross. Then he snatched us from the tyranny of the Devil; for the Lord Himself says, Now is the judgment of the world: now the prince of this world will be cast out: and I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself. He also paid the penalty due to our sins. Then, because no sacrifice more pleasing and acceptable could be offered to God, he reconciled us to the Father and made him propitious and favorable toward us. Finally, since he took away sins, he also opened to us the little gate of heaven, closed by the common sin of the human race. And this the Apostle meant with these words: Having confidence for the entry of the Saints in the blood of Christ. Nor was there lacking in the old law a certain figure and image of this mystery: for those who were interdicted not to return to their country before the death of the high priest, meant this: that to no one, even if he had lived justly and piously, the access to the heavenly country was opened before that high and eternal Priest Christ Jesus died: which once dead, the doors of heaven were immediately opened to those who, atoned by the sacraments and endowed with faith, hope and charity, become participants in his passion. 15. Where did the passion of Christ have the strength to deserve such great goods for us? The parish priest will teach that all these maximum and divine goods came to us from the passion of the Lord: firstly because it is an integral and perfect satisfaction in all numbers, which with a certain admirable reason Jesus Christ paid God the Father for our sins. Nor was the price he paid for us only equal to our debts, but far exceeded them. Afterwards it was a most acceptable sacrifice to God; which, when the Son offered it to him on the altar of the cross, completely mitigated the wrath and indignation of the Father: and the Apostle used this name when he says: Christ loved us and gave himself for us as an offering and host to God in a sweet odor. Furthermore it was redemption, of which it is in the Prince of the Apostles: Not with corruptible gold or silver were you redeemed from your vain conversation of the paternal tradition, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb spotless and undefiled; and the Apostle teaches: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, becoming a curse for us.
Sixth fruit of the passion of Christ. His tomb will be glorious. Triumph of Christ over hell. Sentence of the first part of the fifth article.

How to understand the first part of this article. Certainly it is very important to know the glory of the burial of our Lord Jesus Christ, of which little has been said: but it is more important for the faithful people to know the illustrious triumphs that the victory over the Devil and the dispossession of the seats of hell brought about: of which, and at the same time of the resurrection, we must speak: which place, although in itself separately can be treated with reason; We, however, following the authority of the holy Fathers, judge that it must be combined with the descent into hell. In its first part, then, we are proposed to believe this: that, once Christ was dead, his soul descended into hell, and remained there as long as his body was in the tomb. And with these words we confess at the same time that the very person of Christ at that time was in hell and lay in the tomb. Which when we say, should not seem wonderful to anyone, because, as we have often taught, although the soul was separated from the body, never, however, was the divinity separated from either the soul or the body. 2. What is to be understood here by the word hell. But since it can shed a lot of light on the explanation of the article if the parish priest first teaches what is to be understood in this place by the word hell, it is necessary to warn that hell in this place is not taken as a tomb, as some no less impious ones who impetuously judged. Because in the article above we were taught that Christ the Lord was buried: and there was no reason why in the transmission of the faith the holy Apostles repeated the same thing with another and certainly more obscure genre of speech. But the name hell means those hidden receptacles in which souls who did not reach heavenly bliss are detained. Thus, in effect, they used the sacred Letters of this voice in many places. Because in the Apostle we read: So that in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those in hell: and in the Acts of the Apostles Saint Peter testifies: That Christ the Lord was raised up, the pains of hell released.

How many are the places where souls constituted outside of beatitude stop after death. Nor, however, are all those receptacles of one and the same kind. Because there is a very dark and terrifying prison where with perpetual and inextinguishable fire the souls of the condemned are tormented at the same time as the unclean spirits; which is also called gehenna, abyss, and with its own meaning hell. Furthermore, there is the fire of purgatory, with which the souls of the pious, cruciated for a defined time, atone, so that entry can be opened to them to the eternal homeland, into which nothing enters stained. And the truth of this doctrine, which the holy Councils declare confirmed both by the testimonies of the Scriptures and by apostolic tradition, must be discussed by the parish priest with all the more diligence and frequency since we have fallen into times in which men do not hold sound doctrine. There is, finally, a third type of receptacle, in which the souls of the Saints were received before the coming of Christ the Lord, and there, without any feeling of pain, sustained by the hope of the blessed redemption, they enjoyed quiet habitation. The souls, then, of these pious ones, who were waiting for the Savior in the bosom of Abraham, Christ the Lord, descending into hell, freed them.

The soul of Christ descended into hell not only with power, but actually. Nor should it be considered that he descended into hell in such a way that only his strength and virtue, and not also his soul, reached there. But it must be completely believed that the same soul descended into hell in reality and with presence; of which there is that very firm testimony of David: You will not leave my soul in hell.

Nothing was detracted from the dignity of Christ by his descent into hell. But although Christ descended into hell, nothing was detracted from his supreme power: nor was the splendor of his holiness stained with any stain, but with this fact it was clearly proven that all the things that had been celebrated about his holiness are very true, and that he is the Son of God, as he had previously declared with so many prodigies: which we will easily understand if we compare with each other the causes by which Christ and the other men came to those places. Because all the others had gone down as captives: He, on the other hand, among the dead, free and victorious, came down to defeat the Demons, by whom those, through guilt, were confined and constrained. Furthermore, all the others who descended, some were tormented with the most bitter sorrows, some, although they lacked any other feeling of pain, nevertheless, deprived of the aspect of God and suspended from the hope of the blessed glory that they expected, they were tormented. But Christ the Lord descended not to suffer something, but to free the holy and just men from the miserable annoyance of that custody, and to communicate to them the fruit of his passion. Thus, when he descended into hell, his supreme dignity and power were in no way diminished.

For what reasons did Christ want to descend to hell. Having stated this, it must be taught that Christ the Lord descended into hell to, having snatched away the spoils of the Demons, free those holy Fathers and the other pious ones from prison and lead them to blessedness, which through Him was perfected admirably and with utmost glory; because immediately his appearance brought very clear light to the captives, and filled their souls with immense joy and joy: to whom he also communicated the most desired blessedness, which consists of the vision of God, with which what he had promised to the thief was confirmed with these words: Today you will be with me in paradise. This deliverance of the pious was predicted by Hosea long before in this way: I will be your death, O death; I will be your bite, oh hell. The prophet Zechariah also meant this when he says: You also, in the blood of your testament, released your captives from the cistern where there is no water. The Apostle finally expressed this same thing in these words: Having stripped away the principalities and powers, he led them boldly, triumphing over them openly in himself. But, to better understand the force of this mystery, we must often repeat in memory that not only the pious men who were born to the light after the coming of the Lord, but also those who preceded him after Adam, or those who will be until the end of the age, achieved salvation by the benefit of his passion. Therefore, before He died and rose again, the gates of heaven were never opened to anyone: but the souls of the pious, when they came out from the living, were either carried into the bosom of Abraham, or, what also now happens to those to whom something must be diluted and paid, were atoned for by the fire of purgatory. There is also that reason why Christ the Lord descended into hell: to declare there also, as in heaven and on earth, his strength and power, and completely so that in his name every knee of the heavenly, the terrestrial and the infernal might bow. Who in this place will not admire and be astonished at the extreme kindness of God towards the human race, who not only wanted to suffer the most bitter death for us, but also penetrate the lowest parts of the earth, in order to snatch from there the souls dearest to Him, leading them to blessedness? 7. Sentence of the other part of the fifth article. The other part of the article follows: in whose explanation how much the parish priest must work is declared by those words of the Apostle: Remember that the Lord Jesus Christ rose from the dead. Because what he commands Timothy, there is no doubt that it is also commanded to the other healers of souls. And the sentence of the article is this: after Christ the Lord on Friday, at the ninth hour of the day, gave up the spirit on the cross, and on the same day at sunset he was buried by his disciples, who, with the permission of President Pilate, deposited the body of the Lord from the cross, introduced it into a new monument in the nearby garden: on the third day of death, which was Sunday,

How the promised blessedness was fulfilled to the thief on the same day. The fruit of Christ's passion was spread to the faithful of all times. That the fire of purgatory was persuaded to the Jews before the death of Christ is gathered from several places in Scripture.

At dawn his soul was united again to his body: and thus he who had been dead that triduum returned to the life from which he had departed when he died, and was resurrected. Christ was raised from hell by his own power.

Christ was resurrected not by someone else's virtue, like other men, but by his own strength. But with the voice of resurrection it is not only to be understood that Christ was raised from the dead, which was common to many others; but he rose again by his own strength and virtue, which was peculiar and unique in him. For neither nature tolerates it, nor was it granted to any man that he could by his own virtue revoke himself from death to life. But this is reserved only to the supreme power of God, as we understand from those words of the Apostle: Although he was crucified for weakness, yet he lives by the virtue of God. Which, since it was never separated from either the body of Christ in the tomb or the soul when he descended into hell, the divine force was both in the body, with which it could be united again to the soul, and in the soul, with which it could return again to the body, by which it was lawful for it to revive by its virtue and rise from the dead. This was predicted by David, full of the spirit of God, with these words: His right hand saved him, and his holy arm. Then the Lord himself confirmed it with the divine testimony of his mouth: I lay down my soul to take it again, and I have the power to lay it down and the power to take it again. Also to the Jews, to confirm the truth of the doctrine, he said: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. Which, although they understood of the magnificent temple built of stones, He, however, as is declared in the same place with the words of Scripture, spoke of the temple of His body. And although we sometimes read in the Scriptures that Christ the Lord was raised up by the Father, this must refer to Him as a man: just as those others address Him as God, by which it is meant that He rose again by His own virtue.

How Christ is called the firstborn of the dead, when it is known that others were resurrected before Him. But it was also peculiar to Christ that He was the first of all to be favored with this divine benefit of the resurrection. Because in the Scriptures he is called the firstborn from the dead and the firstborn of the dead. And as it is in the Apostle: Christ was raised from the dead, the first fruits of those who sleep, for through one man death, and through one man the resurrection of the dead: and as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive. But each one in his order: the firstfruits, Christ; then those who belong to Christ. Which words are to be interpreted of the perfect resurrection, by which we are excited to immortal life, completely removing all need of dying. And in this kind Christ the Lord obtains the first place: because if we speak of resurrection, that is, of the return to life to which is attached again the necessity of dying, before Christ many others were raised from the dead; who, however, all revived on condition that they were to die again; but Christ the Lord was resurrected in such a way, subjugated and oppressed by death, that he could no longer die, which is confirmed by that very clear testimony: Christ, rising from the dead, no longer dies: death will no longer rule over Him.

How and why Christ delayed his resurrection until the third day. But what is added to the article, On the third day, the parish priest must explain, so that the faithful do not judge that the Lord was in the tomb for three whole days: because, as He was in the tomb for a full calendar day and part of the preceding day and the following day, for this reason it is said with great truth that He lay in the tomb for a triduum, and on the third day He rose from the dead; and to declare his divinity, he did not want to defer the resurrection until the end of the centuries: and again, so that we would believe that he was truly man and truly dead, he did not revive immediately after death, but on the third day, a space of time that seemed sufficient to prove true death. 11. Why the Fathers of the Synod of Constantinople added to this article the clause: According to the Scriptures. The Fathers of the Synod of Constantinople added in this place: According to the Scriptures: which, taken from the Apostle, they transferred to the Symbol of Faith because the Apostle himself taught that the mystery of the resurrection is maximally necessary with these words: If Christ is not resurrected, then our preaching is vain, your faith is also vain; and if Christ has not been raised, your faith is in vain: for you are still in your sins. Therefore Saint Augustine, admiring the faith of this article, wrote thus: It is not a great thing to believe that Christ died: this is also believed by the pagans, and the Jews, and all the wicked; everyone thinks he died. The faith of Christians is the resurrection of Christ: we consider this great, because we believe that He was resurrected.
On the third day not simply, but according to the Scriptures. First cause.

Second. Third. Quarter. From which the Lord frequently spoke of his resurrection, and almost never spoke with the disciples of his passion without also speaking of the resurrection; Therefore, when he said, The Son of Man will be handed over to the Gentiles, and will be mocked, and scourged, and spit upon, and after scourging he will be put to death; Finally he added: And on the third day he will rise again. And when the Jews asked him to prove his doctrine with some sign and miracle, he answered: No other sign will be given to them except that of the prophet Jonah: for just as Jonah was in the belly of the cetacean three days and three nights, so he affirmed that the Son of Man would be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights. But to better perceive the force and meaning of this article, we must investigate and know three things: first, why it was necessary for Christ to rise from the dead; then, what is the end and purpose of the resurrection; and what benefits and comforts have come from it for us.

For what reasons it was necessary for Christ to resurrect. Regarding the first, it was necessary for Him to resurrect so that the justice of God could be shown, by which it was most appropriate that he who, in order to obey Him, had been dejected and affected by all ignominy, be exalted. This cause was adduced by the Apostle when he said to the Philippians: He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross: for which God also exalted him. Furthermore, so that our faith could be confirmed, without which the justice of man cannot be established; because it must be the maximum argument that Christ was the Son of God who by his own virtue rose from the dead. Then, so that our hope could be nourished and sustained. Because Christ being resurrected, we rely on a certain hope that we too will be resurrected: for the members must follow the condition of their head; This is how the Apostle seems to conclude the argument when he writes to the Corinthians and the Thessalonians; and the Prince of the Apostles Peter said: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy has regenerated us to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, to an incorruptible inheritance. Finally, it must be taught that also for this reason the resurrection of the Lord was necessary: ​​so that the mystery of our salvation and redemption could be absolved. Because Christ with his death freed us from sins; but by resurrecting he restored to us the main goods that we had lost by sinning. Therefore it is said in the Apostle: Christ was delivered for our crimes, and was raised for our justification. So that nothing would be lacking for the salvation of the human race, just as it was necessary for Him to die, so it was also necessary for Him to rise again. 13. What comforts return to men from the resurrection of Christ. From what has been said up to this point we can perceive how much usefulness the resurrection of Christ the Lord has brought to the faithful: because in the resurrection we recognize that God is immortal, full of glory, conqueror of death and the Devil; which of Christ Jesus must be believed and confessed without a doubt. Afterwards, the resurrection of Christ also engendered for us the resurrection of the body: both because it was the efficient cause of this mystery, and because we must all be resurrected after the example of the Lord. For as regards the resurrection of the body, the Apostle thus testifies: Through one man death, and through one man the resurrection of the dead; because everything that God worked in the mystery of our redemption, he used with the humanity of Christ as an efficient instrument. Therefore his resurrection was a certain instrument to effect our resurrection. And it can truly be called exemplary, because the resurrection of Christ the Lord is the most perfect of all: and just as the body of Christ when resurrected was transformed to immortal glory, so also our bodies, which were before weak and mortal, will be restored adorned with glory and immortality.

Because as the Apostle teaches: We wait for the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will reform the body of our humility configured to the body of his clarity. This can also be said of the soul dead in sins; To which way the resurrection of Christ is proposed as an example, the Apostle himself shows in these words: As Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so let us also walk in newness of life. For if we were planted together in the likeness of his death, we will also be planted together in the resurrection. And a few verses later he says: Knowing that Christ, being raised from the dead, dies no more: death will no longer rule over Him. For inasmuch as he died to sin, he died once: but insofar as he lives, he lives for God. So you also consider yourselves dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord.

What examples are to be taken from the resurrection of Christ. Two examples, then, we must ask for of the resurrection of Christ. One is that, after washing away the stains of sin, we institute a new kind of life, in which integrity of customs, innocence, holiness, modesty, justice, beneficence, and humility shine. The other is that in this institute of life we ​​persevere in such a way that, with the Lord helping us, we do not fall from the path of justice that we once had entered. Nor do the Apostle's words alone demonstrate that the resurrection of Christ is proposed to us as an example of resurrection; but they also declare that it gives us the virtue of resurrection, and grants us strength and spirit to remain in holiness and justice and keep the precepts of God. For just as from his death we not only take the example of dying to sins, but we also drink the virtue with which we die to sins: so his resurrection gives us strength to achieve justice, so that later, worshiping God piously and holy, we walk in newness of life, to which we resurrect. For this is what the Lord primarily accomplished with his resurrection: that we who were previously dead with Him to sins and to this world, may also rise with Him to a new institution of life.

What are the signs that someone has been resurrected according to the spirit with Christ? The Apostle admonishes us about the indications that are mainly to be observed of this resurrection; for when he says, If you have been raised with Christ, seek those things above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God; It clearly shows that those who desire to have life, honors, leisure and riches primarily where Christ is, have truly been resurrected with Christ; and when he adds: Taste things above, not things on earth; He also put this other one as a note, with which we can perceive if we have truly been resurrected with Christ. Because just as taste usually indicates the condition and health of the body, so if someone knows any things to be true, any modest, any just, any holy, and perceives with an intimate sense of the mind the youth of heavenly things, this can be the maximum argument that he who is thus affected has been resurrected to a new and spiritual life together with Jesus Christ.

Excellence of this article, and sentence of the first part. The prophet David, when, filled with the spirit of God, he contemplated the blessed and glorious Ascension of the Lord, exhorts everyone to celebrate that triumph with utmost joy and joy with these words: All peoples, clap your hands, praise God with a voice of exultation: God has ascended with acclamations. From which the priest will understand that this mystery must be explained with maximum study; and that he must diligently ensure that the faithful not only perceive it with faith and mind, but that, as far as possible, with the Lord helping them, they also strive to express it with works and life. As regards, therefore, the explanation of the sixth article, which mainly deals with this divine mystery, we must begin with its first part, and reveal what its force and sentence are. Because the faithful must also believe in Christ Jesus without a doubt that, having already perfected and absolved the mystery of our redemption, as a man he ascended to heaven with body and soul, because like God he was never absent from him, like the one who fills all places with his divinity. 2. Christ did not ascend only by virtue of divinity, but also of humanity. Teach that he ascended by his own virtue, not lifted up by another's force, like Elijah, who was taken to heaven in a chariot of fire, or the prophet Habakkuk, or the deacon Philip, who, carried through the air by divine virtue, crossed long spaces of land. Not only as God he ascended to heaven with the prepotent virtue of divinity, but also as a man; for although by the force of nature it could not be done, yet the virtue with which the blessed soul of Christ was endowed was able to move the body as it pleased: and the body, which had already achieved glory, easily obeyed the empire of the soul that moved it. And for this reason we believe that Christ, as God and as man, ascended to heaven by his own virtue.

In what sense does it say in the back of the article that Christ sits at the right hand of the Father. In the other part of the article are these words: He sits at the right hand of God the Father, in whose place it is permissible to notice a trope, that is, a change of word, frequent in the divine Letters, when, accommodating human affections and members to our intelligence, we attribute them to God; because, being a spirit, nothing corporeal can be thought of in Him. But since in human things we consider that greater honor is paid to him who is placed at the right hand, also transferring this thing to the heavenly, to explain the glory of Christ, which as a man he achieved above all others, we confess that He is at the right hand of the Father. But sitting in this place does not signify the situation and figure of the body, but declares that firm and stable possession of the royal and supreme power and glory which he received from the Father: of which the Apostle says: Raising him from the dead, and establishing him at his right hand in heaven, over all principality and power, virtue and dominion, and over every name that is named not only in this age, but also in the future. And you put all things under his feet. From whose words it appears that this glory is so unique and unique to the Lord that it cannot suit any other created nature. Therefore in another place he testifies: To which of the Angels did he ever say: Sit at my right hand?

Why the story of the Ascension of Christ must be repeated frequently to the people. But the parish priest will explain the meaning of the article more fully, following the story of the Ascension, which the holy evangelist Luke described in the Acts of the Apostles with admirable order. In which explanation it must be observed first that all the other mysteries refer to the Ascension as to its end, and in it the perfection and absolution of all is contained; because just as all the mysteries of our religion begin from the Incarnation of the Lord, so with His Ascension the pilgrimage concludes. Furthermore, the other chapters of the Symbol that belong to Christ the Lord show the sum of his humility and despondency, because nothing more abject or humble can be thought of than the fact that the Son of God for us assumed human nature and weakness, and wanted to suffer and die. But the confession that in the upper article he rose from the dead, and now that he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father, nothing more magnificent or admirable can be said to declare his supreme glory and divine majesty.

Why Christ ascended to heaven, and did not rather establish his kingdom on earth. Having already stated this, it must be taught exactly why Christ the Lord ascended to heaven. First he ascended because his body, to which the glory of immortality had been given in the resurrection, was not suited to the place of this earthly and dark habitation, but rather the highest and most splendid domicile of heaven. And not only to possess the throne of his glory and kingdom, which he had deserved with his blood, but also to take care of the things that belonged to our salvation. Then, to prove for himself that his kingdom is not of this world; because the kingdoms of the world are earthly and obsolete, and are based on great riches and the power of the flesh; but the kingdom of Christ is not earthly, as the Jews expected, but spiritual and eternal: and he likewise showed that his riches and goods are spiritual when he placed his seat in heaven: in which kingdom those who most diligently seek the things of God are to be esteemed richer and more abundant in copy of all goods; because Saint James also testifies that God chose the poor in this world, rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom that God promised to those who love him. But our Lord also wanted, by ascending to heaven, to make us follow him with the mind and desire to which he ascended; because just as with his death and resurrection he had left us an example of the spirit of dying and rising, so with the ascension he teaches us to confess that we are pilgrims and guests on earth, and that we seek the homeland, that we are fellow citizens of the saints and domestics of God: because our conversation, as the Apostle himself says, is in heaven.

What benefits have been conferred upon us from the Ascension of Christ. And in truth the strength and inestimable copy of the inexplicable benefits that the kindness of God pours into us, the divine Prophet had long before sung with these words: Going up on high, he took captivity captive, he gave gifts to men; because on the tenth day he gave the Holy Spirit, with whose virtue and abundance he filled that present multitude of the faithful, and truly fulfilled those magnificent promises; It is better for you that I go away: because if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go away, I will send it to you. He also ascended to heaven, according to the Apostle's sentence, to now appear before the face of God for us, and perform before the Father the office of lawyer. My little children, says Saint John, I write this to you so that you do not sin; But if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and He is a propitiation for our sins. Nor is there anything from which the faithful should draw greater joy and youthfulness of spirit than that Jesus Christ has been constituted patron of the cause and preacher of our salvation, who has supreme grace and authority before the eternal Father.

Finally he prepared a place for us, which he also promised he would do, and in the name of us all the head himself, Jesus Christ, came to possess heavenly glory; because by going to heaven he opened the doors that had been closed due to Adam's sin, and opened the way for us to reach heavenly bliss; as He Himself at the supper foretold to the disciples what was to be: which, to also openly verify it with the event of the thing, brought with Him into the abode of eternal blessedness the souls of the pious whom He had snatched from hell.

Comforts that Christ brought us with his Ascension. This admirable copy of heavenly gifts was followed by that healthy series of comforts: first, the maximum accumulation was added to the merit of our faith; because faith is one of those things that do not fall under sight and are remote from the reason and intelligence of men. Therefore, if the Lord had not departed from us, the merit of our faith would be diminished: for by Christ the Lord those who have not seen and have believed are preached blessed. Furthermore, Christ's ascent to heaven has a great moment to confirm hope in our hearts; for, as we believe that the man Christ ascended into heaven and placed human nature at the right hand of God the Father, we are in great hope that we also, his members, may ascend there and be united there with our head: which the Lord himself testified in these words: Father, I will that where I am, those also whom thou hast given me may be with me. Afterwards we also achieved this most great benefit: that snatched our love from heaven and inflamed it with divine spirit: because it is said with great truth that our heart is where our treasure is.

It was not useful to us that Christ remained on earth. And in truth, if Christ the Lord were on earth, all our thoughts would be fixed on the same appearance and conversation of the man, and we would only look at that man who affected us with such great benefits, and we would follow him with a certain earthly benevolence: but ascending to heaven, he made our love spiritual, and made him whom we now think absent we venerate and love as God. After the Ascension of Christ the Church was maximally amplified.
