Three distinguished benefits of Christ to his Church, and sentence of the seventh article. There are three distinguished offices and munera of our Lord Jesus Christ to adorn and illustrate his Church: redemption, patronage and judgment. And since it is clear from the articles above that by Him the human race was redeemed with passion and death, and also with the ascension to heaven our cause and patronage was taken up in perpetuity, it follows that in this article His judgment is declared: the force and reason of the article is that on that high day Christ the Lord will judge the entire race of men.

Double is the coming of Christ. Because the sacred Letters testify that there are two comings of the Son of God; one when for the sake of our salvation he assumed flesh and became man in the womb of the Virgin; another, when at the end of the century he will come to judge all men. This coming in the sacred Letters is called the day of the Lord; of which the Apostle says: The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night; and the Savior himself: Of that day and hour no one knows. And that authority of the Apostle is sufficient for the supreme judgment: It is necessary that all of us appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what belongs to the body, according to what he has done, whether good or bad. Because the sacred Scripture is full of testimonies that will often occur to parish priests, not only to prove the thing, but also to put it before the eyes of the faithful: so that, just as from the beginning of the world that day of the Lord in which he put on human flesh was always highly desired by all, because in that mystery they had placed the hope of their liberation: so from now on, after the death of the Son of God and his ascension to heaven, we desire with the most vehement study the other day of the Lord, waiting for the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God.

How many times must each man suffer in person the sentence of Christ the judge. But parish priests must observe two times for the explanation of the thing, in which it is necessary for each one to come to the presence of the Lord, and give an account of each of the thoughts, the actions, the words and finally of all things, and at the end suffer the present sentence of the Judge. The first is when each one of us emigrates from this life: because he is immediately presented to the tribunal of God, and there a most just inquisition is made of all the things that he has ever done, or said, or thought: and this is called private judgment. The other is when on a single day and in a single place all men at the same time will be before the court of the Judge, so that, seeing and hearing all the men of all the centuries, each one will know what has been decreed and judged of him: whose pronouncement of the sentence will not be for the impious and scelerated the least part of the penalties and tortures, and again the pious and just will receive from it no small reward and fruit, when it will appear what each has been. one in this life. And this is called general judgment.

Why was it necessary to subject the general to private trial. From which it is necessary to show what was the cause why, in addition to the private judgment of each one, another judgment was also exercised by all men. Because, as sometimes even dead men themselves are survived by children who imitate their parents, and there remain books, disciples, lovers and defenders of examples, prayers and actions, with whose things it is necessary to increase the rewards and penalties of the dead themselves; and since this usefulness or calamity, belonging to many, must have no end before the last day of the world comes: it was fair that a perfect inquisition should be made of this whole reason for things well or badly done and said: which could not be done except with a common judgment of all men. It is also added that, as the fame of the pious is often injured, and the impious are praised with praise of innocence, the reason of divine justice requires that the pious recover in the public convent and judgment of all men the esteem taken away by injury before men.

Fourth, so that everyone knows the reason for divine providence. Fifth, so that the good would persevere and the bad would repent. Then, since good and bad men did not do anything in life without bodies, it follows that the benefits or evils also belong to the bodies, which were the instrument of the same actions. It was therefore most appropriate that the due rewards of eternal glory or torture be imparted to the bodies together with their souls: which certainly could not be done without the resurrection of all men nor without the general judgment. Finally, since in the adverse and prosperous things of men, which sometimes happen promiscuously to good and evil, it had to be proven that nothing is done and governed except with the infinite wisdom and justice of God; It was necessary that in the future century not only would rewards be established for the good and punishments for the bad, but also that they would be decreed with a public and general judgment; with which they would become more known and illustrious to all, and the praise of justice and providence would be given to God by all, instead of that unjust quarrel with which also the holy men used sometimes, as men, to deplore when they warned of the impious brave in riches and flourishing in honors: because the Prophet: My feet were almost moved, he says, my steps were almost spilled, because I was jealous of the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners. According to both natures, the power to judge the race of men was attributed to Christ.

I believe in the Holy Spirit. 1. How great is the need of faith in the Holy Spirit, and the fruit. Up to this point, the things that belonged to the first and second Person of the Holy Trinity have been explained, as the reason for the proposed argument seemed to postulate: it now follows that those things that are transmitted in the Symbol are transmitted from the third Person, that is, from the Holy Spirit, should also be explained. In which declaration the Pastors will put all study and diligence, since it is no more licit for the Christian man to ignore this part, or to feel less correctly about it, than what must be considered of the other higher articles. Therefore the Apostle did not allow some Ephesians to be ignorant of the Person of the Holy Spirit; To whom, when he asked if they had received the Holy Spirit, and they answered that they did not even know if there was a Holy Spirit, he immediately asked: Into what, then, were you baptized? With whose words he meant that the different knowledge of this article is maximally necessary for the faithful: from which they mainly capture that fruit: that when they think carefully that everything they have has been achieved by munere and benefit of the Holy Spirit, then they begin to feel about themselves with more modesty and humility, and to put all their hope in the help of God; which should be the first degree of the Christian man towards supreme wisdom and happiness.

The word Holy Spirit does not suit the third Person of the Trinity in such a way that it cannot also be attributed to the others. The explanation of this article must, therefore, begin with the force and notion that in this place is subject to the word Holy Spirit: because, as with equal rightness it is also said of the Father and the Son (since both are Spirit, and Holy, since we confess that God is spirit), and then with this word the Angels and the souls of the pious are also meant, care must be taken that the people are not led into error by the ambiguity of the word. Therefore it must be taught that in this article the third Person of the Trinity is understood by the name of the Holy Spirit: as is frequently taken in the sacred Letters of both the Old and New Testaments. For David prays: And do not take away your Holy Spirit from me; and in the book of Wisdom we read: Who will know your meaning, except you give wisdom and send your Holy Spirit from above? and elsewhere: He created it in the Holy Spirit. But in the New Testament we are commanded to be baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit; and we read that the blessed Virgin conceived of the Holy Spirit: and again we are sent by Saint John to Christ, who baptizes us in the Holy Spirit: and also in many other places this voice occurs.

Why was the third Person of the Trinity not attributed, like the other two, a proper name. But no one should be surprised that a proper name has not been attributed to the third Person, like the first and the second. Because the second person has his own name and is called Son, because his eternal origin from the Father is properly called generation, as explained in the articles above. Thus, then, as that origin is signified by the name of generation, so we properly call the Person who emanates Son, and the One from whom He emanates, Father. Now, since the production of the third Person was not given a proper name, but is called spiration and procession, it follows that the Person who is produced also lacks his name. But no proper name has its emanation, because we are forced to take the names attributed to God from created things: in which, as we recognize no other reason for communicating nature and essence except by the virtue of generating, for this reason we cannot express with our own words the reason with which God communicates everything to himself by the force of love. Therefore the third Person was called by the common name of the Holy Spirit: which we understand to be most suitable for him because he infuses spiritual life into us, and without the breath of his most holy majesty we can accomplish nothing worthy of eternal life.

The Holy Spirit is God, of the same power and nature of the whole as the Father and the Son. But, once the meaning of the word has been explained, the people must first of all be taught that the Holy Spirit, equally with the Father and the Son, is God, equal to them, equally omnipotent, eternal and infinitely perfect, supremely good and most wise, and of the same nature as the Father and the Son.

It does not matter whether that people were worshipers of the true God or of a false religion: because in the Acts it is written of the people of Ephesus that, when the scribe quieted the mobs, he said: And if you seek something else, in the legitimate Church it will be possible to absolve it. This communication is often demonstrated in the sacred Letters with the most suitable similarity of the members of the human body: because in the body there are many members, but although they are many, they constitute a single body; in which each one exercises his own office, and not all the same. The free graces given and the other gifts of God to the Church are common.

CHAPTER XI

The remission of sins.

1. How it is necessary to believe that the remission of sins is in the Church.

There is no one who, seeing this article of the remission of sins numbered among the other articles of faith, can doubt that it not only contains some divine mystery, but also something maximally necessary to obtain salvation; because it has previously been declared that without a certain faith in those things that are proposed to be believed in the Symbol, no one is open to Christian piety. But if what in itself must be known to all seems to also have to be confirmed by some testimony, it will be enough that shortly before his ascension to heaven our Savior testified of this thing, when he opened the meaning to the disciples so that they could understand the Scriptures: It was fitting, he says, that Christ should suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and the remission of sins should be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. Whose words, if the parish priests notice them, they will easily understand that, just as the other things that belong to religion must be transmitted to the faithful, so the need has also been imposed on them by the Lord to diligently explain this article. PART I

The office, then, of the parish priest will be, as far as this place is concerned, to teach not only that the remission of sins is found in the Catholic Church, of which Isaiah had predicted: The people who dwell in it, iniquity will be taken away; but also that in it is the power to remit sins: which, if the Priests use it correctly and according to the laws prescribed by Christ the Lord, it must be believed with certainty that sins are truly remitted.

For what reason are sins remitted in the Church.

This permission, as soon as we confess our faith and are washed with sacred Baptism, is given to us so cumulatively that nothing remains to be erased from guilt—whether that incurred by origin, whether that which is omitted or committed of our own free will—nor to pay the penalty. But by the grace of Baptism, however, no one is freed from all the weakness of nature; On the contrary, (since it is necessary for each of us to fight against the movements of concupiscence, which never ceases to incite us to sin), you will hardly find anyone who resists so bitterly or who guards his salvation so vigilantly that he can avoid all wounds.

In addition to Baptism, it is shown that sins are remitted in the Church by the virtue of the keys.

In the sacrament he was entrusted with the keys to the kingdom of heaven, with which any penitent's crimes can be condoned, even if he has sinned until the last day of his life. We have very clear testimonies of this thing in the sacred Letters; because in Saint Matthew the Lord speaks thus to Peter: I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever is bound on earth will also be bound in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven. Likewise: Whatever you bind on earth will also be bound in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth will also be loosed in heaven. Then Saint John testifies that the Lord, when he breathed on the Apostles, said: Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; and from whom you retain them, they are retained. Breadth of the power to remit sins.

The power to remit sins is not limited to certain sins or certain times.

This power should not be considered to be defined to certain kinds of sins; because no crime so heinous can be admitted or thought that the Holy Church does not have the power to refer it: just as no one will have been so dishonorable and hasty to whom, if he truly repents of his errors, a certain hope of forgiveness should not be offered to him. Nor is this same power circumscribed in such a way that it is lawful to use it only at a predetermined time: for at whatever time the sinner wishes to return to health, our Savior taught that he should not be rejected, when to the Prince of the Apostles who asked how many times sinners were to be forgiven, if up to seven times, he answered: Not up to seven, but up to seventy times seven.

6. Not all Christians have been granted the power to remit sins.

But if we look at the ministers of this divine power, it will appear to extend less widely. Because the Lord did not give it to everyone, but only to the Bishops and Priests, such holy power of the munus. The same must be judged about the reason for exercising this power; because only through the Sacraments, if their form is kept, can sins be remitted; Otherwise no right has been given to the Church to release sins: from which it follows that both the Priests and the Sacraments are valid as instruments for condoning sins, with which Christ the Lord, the very author and giver of salvation, effects in us the remission of sins and justice.

How great the munus of remitting sins granted to the Church.

And so that the faithful look with greater esteem on this celestial munus, which by God's singular mercy towards us has been donated to the Church, and approach its use and treatment with a more ardent study of piety, the parish priest will strive to demonstrate the dignity and breadth of this grace. Which is best perceived if it has been diligently explained what virtue it is to remit sins and make unjust men just. Because it is clear that this is carried out with the infinite and immense strength of God: the same that we believe is necessary to resurrect the dead and for the creation of the world. And if also, as is confirmed by the sentence of Augustine, it is to be considered a greater work to make someone pious than to be impious than to create heaven and earth from nothing—since the creation itself cannot exist except by infinite virtue—it follows that the remission of sins must be attributed much more to the infinite power of God. The justification of sinners is the work of the infinite power of God.

St. Augustine, tract. 72 in Ioann., and it is also gathered from Ps 144, 9. Only God remits sins, which is stated in a similar way. Augustine, lib. 1 of Pecc. mer. chap. 28 and Hom. 23. Ambrose, lib. 2 of Abel et Cain, chap. 4. Is 43, 25; Mt 9, 6; Mk 2, 10. Mt 6, 12; Luke 11, 4. Christ as a man excellently had the power to remit sins. See St. Thomas 3 p. q. 64 art. 3; Mt 9, 6; Mark 2, 10; Jn 20, 22. Through the blood of Christ sins are remitted. Rom 5, 9; Eph 1, 7; Rev 1, 5; 1 Pet 3, 18; 1 Pe 1, 18-19.

No one except God alone remits sins by his own authority.

For this reason we recognize that the voices of the ancient Fathers are very true, with which they confess that only through a God are men's sins forgiven: and that such a wonderful work must not refer to another author but to his supreme goodness and power: I am, says the same Lord through the Prophet, I myself am the one who erases your iniquities. Because the reason for remitting crimes seems to be the same as keeping the money owed. Just as, therefore, through no one but the creditor the money owed can be remitted, so, since we are obligated to God alone for sins (since we daily pray: Forgive us our debts), it is perspicuous that through no one other than Him can our debts be forgiven.

The power to remit sins before the birth of Christ was not granted to any mortal.

This admirable and divine munus, before God became man, was not imparted to any created nature. The first of all, Christ, our Savior, as a man, being the same true God, received this munus transmitted from the heavenly Father. That you may know, he says, that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins, he says to the paralytic: Get up, take up your bed, and go to your house. Since, then, He had become a man to deliver to men this blessing of sins, before ascending to heaven to sit there at the right hand of God forever, He granted this power to the Bishops and Priests in the Church, although, as we previously taught, Christ remits sins by His authority, and the others as His ministers. Therefore, if we must maximally admire and esteem things done with infinite virtue, we sufficiently understand how precious this munus is, which through the benignity of Christ the Lord has been donated to the Church.

By what virtue do men obtain forgiveness for their sins.

But also the same reason why God, the most merciful Father, wanted to erase the sins of the world, will vehemently excite the spirits of the faithful to contemplate the magnitude of this benefit. Because he wanted our crimes to be atoned for with the blood of his only begotten Son, so that the penalty that we deserved for our sins would be paid voluntarily by Him, and the just would be condemned by the unjust, the innocent would be affected by the most bitter death by the guilty. Therefore, when we will think in the spirit that we were not redeemed with corruptible gold or silver, but with the precious Blood as of an immaculate and undefiled lamb of Christ, we will easily establish that nothing more salutary could befall us than this power to remit sins, which shows the inexplicable providence of God and the utmost charity towards us: and from this thought it is necessary that the maximum fruit should come to all.

By what agreement the breadth of the benefit offered in the power of the keys is maximally perceived.

Because whoever offends God with any mortal sin, immediately loses any merits that he may have obtained from the death and cross of Christ, and is completely prohibited from entering Paradise, which our Savior opened with his passion to all before being included. Which, when it comes to mind, we cannot but be vehemently solicitous for the consideration of human misery. But if we refer our minds to this admirable power that has been attributed divinitus to the Church, and confirmed by the faith of this article, we believe the faculty offered to each one of power, aided by divine help, to be restored to the pristine state of dignity: then we are truly compelled to exult with utmost joy and gladness, and to give immortal thanks to God. And in truth, if the medicines that are prepared for us with the art and industry of doctors when we suffer from a serious illness usually seem pleasant and jucund: how much more jucund must those remedies be that the wisdom of God instituted for the healing of souls and to repair life? especially when they do not bring, like those medicines that are applied to the bodies, a doubtful hope of salvation, but rather a very certain salvation to those who wish to be healed.

Why and in what way should Christians use the remedies provided by the power of the keys of the Church.

The faithful will, therefore, be exhorted, after knowing the dignity of such a broad and illustrious munus, to also strive to religiously convert it to their advantage. Because it can hardly happen that he who does not use a useful and necessary thing is not considered to despise it; especially when the Lord gave the Church this power to remit sins precisely so that everyone could use this healthy remedy. Because just as no one can be expiated without Baptism, so anyone who wants to recover the grace of Baptism lost through deadly accelerations must take refuge in another type of atonement, namely the Sacrament of Penance. But in this place the faithful must be admonished so that, given such a broad power of permission (which, as we declare, is not defined by any term of time), they do not become easier to sin or slower to respond; because in the one, being manifestly slanderous and contumelious against this divine power, they are unworthy of God imparting his mercy to them.

…and in the other case it is greatly to be feared that, prevented by death, they will confess in vain the remission of the sins, which they deservedly lost due to delay and procrastination.

OF THE ELEVENTH ARTICLE.
CHAPTER XII
The resurrection of the flesh.

1. How important it is to have explored knowledge of this article.

How much force this article has to establish the truth of our faith is shown maximally by the fact that in the divine Letters it is not only proposed to the faithful to believe it, but is also confirmed with many reasons: which, as in the other articles of the Symbol we hardly see it done, it can be understood that the hope of our salvation rests on this as a very firm foundation; because, as the Apostle reasons: If there is no resurrection of the dead, neither has Christ been raised: and if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is vain, your faith is also vain. In explaining it, then, the parish priest will put no less work and study than the impiety of many has worked to destroy: because it will be demonstrated shortly after that great and illustrious benefits will come from this knowledge for the fruit of the faithful.

Why the Apostles here called the resurrection of men the resurrection of the flesh.

But first of all it will be necessary to pay attention to the fact that the resurrection of men is called in this article the resurrection of the flesh. Which was not done without cause. Because the Apostles wanted to teach what must necessarily be established: that the soul is immortal; Therefore, lest anyone consider by chance that it perished together with the body and that both are revoked to life, as in many places in the sacred Letters it is openly stated that the soul is immortal, for this reason mention was made in the article only of the flesh that is to be raised: and although often also in the sacred Scriptures the flesh means the whole man, as in Isaiah: All flesh is hay; and in Saint John: And the Word became flesh; However, in this place the voice flesh declares the body, so that we understand that of the two parts, soul and body, of which man consists, only one, namely the body, is corrupted and returns to the dust of the earth from which it was compacted; but the soul remains uncorrupted. And since no one, unless he or she has died, returns to life, the soul is not properly said to be resurrected. Mention was also made of the flesh to refute that heresy that, while the Apostle was alive, was that of Hymenaeus and Philetus, who affirmed that when the sacred Scriptures deal with the resurrection, it should not be taken from the corporeal, but from the spiritual, by which one is resurrected from the death of sin to innocent life. Thus, with these words it is clear that that error is removed and the true resurrection of the body is confirmed.

With what Scriptures the doctrine of the true resurrection of the body is to be established primarily.

But it will be the office of the parish priest to illustrate this truth with examples taken from the Old and New Testaments and from all ecclesiastical history. Because some were recalled to life by Elijah and Elisha in the Old Testament; others, besides those whom Christ the Lord raised up from death, by the holy Apostles and by many others: whose resurrection of many confirms the doctrine of this article. For just as we believe that many were awakened from death, so it is to be believed that all are to be recalled to life. Furthermore, the main fruit that we must draw from such miracles is that we have great faith in this article. There are many testimonies that will occur easily to parish priests moderately versed in sacred Letters. More illustrious are those in the Old Testament that are read in Job, when he says that in his flesh he will see his God; and in Daniel about those who sleep in the dust of the earth, that some will awaken to eternal life, others to everlasting reproach. In the New Testament, what Saint Matthew tells of the dispute that the Lord had with the Sadducees; in addition to what the Evangelists narrate about the extreme judgment. And here we must also refer to the things that the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians and the Thessalonians, discussed with careful prayer.

With what similarities the same truth can be established.

But although this is most certain by faith... Is 40, 6. Jn 1, 14. At whose coming all men etc. Athanasius in the Symbol. Gen 3, 19. Only the body is corrupted. Damascene, lib. 4, c. 13. The soul, since it does not perish, is not resurrected. 2 Tim 2, 17-18. This error followed Basilides, according to Iren. 1, 1.

…it will be of much benefit to show with examples or reasons that what faith proposes to believe does not abhor nature or the intelligence of the human mind. Thus the Apostle, to whom he asked how the dead would be resurrected, replied: Fool! What you sow does not come to life if it does not first die; and what you sow is not the body that is to be, but naked grain, for example wheat or one of the others; but God gives it body as he wants; and shortly after he says: It is sown in corruption, it will rise in incorruption. To this similarity many others can be added, as Saint Gregory shows: For the light, he says, is withdrawn from the eyes every day as if dying, and is revoked again as if resurrected; and the bushes lose their greenery and repair themselves again as if resurrected; and the seeds die rotting and rise again germinating.

Reasons with which this same truth is verified.

Furthermore, those reasons adduced by ecclesiastical writers may seem quite adequate to prove this thing. And firstly, since souls are immortal and as part of man they have a natural propensity for human bodies, it must be considered that the fact that they remain perpetually separated from bodies is against nature. And since what is adverse to nature and violent cannot be diuturnal, it seems acceptable that they should once again be united to the bodies: from which it also follows that there must be resurrection of the bodies. Our Savior himself used this type of argument when, disputing against the Sadducees, he concluded the resurrection of bodies from the immortality of souls.

Then, as punishments and good rewards are offered to the wicked by the most just God; and of those, very many die before paying the due penalties, and of these a large part leave life without being affected by the rewards of virtue: it is necessary that the souls be united to the bodies again, so that for crimes or for righteous works the bodies, which men use as partners in sin, together with the soul are affected by punishment or reward: a place that Saint Chrysostom treated with great care in his homily to the Antiochene people. Therefore the Apostle, when he spoke of the resurrection: If in this life, he says, we only hope in Christ, we are the most miserable of all men. Whose words no one will consider to refer to the misery of the soul; which, being immortal, although the bodies were not resurrected, could nevertheless enjoy blessedness in the future life: but they are to be understood of the whole man: because if due rewards for labors are not given to the body, it is necessary that those who, like the Apostles, suffered so many afflictions and calamities in life should be the most miserable of all. And he teaches the same thing much more openly to the Thessalonians in these words: We glory in the Churches of God for your patience and faith, and for all your persecutions and tribulations which you suffer, as an example of the righteous judgment of God, so that you may be counted worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you also suffer: if, however, it is right with God to repay tribulation to those who trouble you, and to you who are troubled, rest with us in the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven with the Angels of his virtue, in a flame of fire giving revenge to those who did not know God and to those who do not obey the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ. It should also be added that men cannot, while the soul is separated from the body, achieve full happiness and the accumulation of all goods. For just as any part separated from the whole is imperfect, so also is the soul that is not united to the body.

From which it follows that, so that nothing is lacking in the highest happiness, the resurrection of the bodies is necessary. With these, then, and other reasons of this kind, the parish priest will be able to instruct the faithful in this article.

No man will then be found who does not experience death and resurrection.

It will also be necessary to diligently explain, according to the Apostle's doctrine, who is to be raised to life: for writing to the Corinthians: As in Adam, he says, all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive. Removed, then, all distinction between bad and good, all...

…from the dead, although the condition of all will not be the same, they will be resurrected: those who did good, to the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment. And when we say all, we understand both those who will already be dead when the judgment arrives, and those who will die. Because to this sentence, which affirms that everyone must die, without exception of anyone, the Church assents; and that the same sentence is more appropriate to the truth, Saint Jerome wrote: Saint Augustine also feels the same. Nor are the words of the Apostle written to the Thessalonians repugnant to this sentence: The dead who are in Christ will rise first: then we who are alive, who remain, will be caught up with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air. Because Saint Ambrose, when explaining them, says this: in the same rapture death will come, and as if by a dream, so that the soul leaves and in a moment returns; because when they are raised up, they will die, so that, coming to the Lord, the presence of the Lord may give life to the souls, because with the Lord they cannot be dead. And the same sentence is verified with the authority of Saint Augustine in the book of the City of God.

7. The same body of the whole will receive the human soul in the extreme judgment.

And as much as it is important that we be persuaded with certainty that this same and identical body that was proper to each one, although corrupted and reduced to dust, must nevertheless be raised to life: this also the parish priest will undertake to explain exactly. This is the sentence of the Apostle when he says: It is necessary that this corruptible put on incorruption: with that voice "this" openly demonstrating one's own body. Job also prophesied of this very clearly: And in my flesh, he says, I will see God my Savior, whom I myself will see, and my eyes will behold him, and no other. This can be gleaned from the very definition of the resurrection. Because the resurrection is, according to Damascene, the revocation to that state from which you fell.

Finally, if we consider why it was demonstrated shortly before that there must be a resurrection, there will be nothing that can make the spirit in this matter doubtful.

For what reason the resurrection of the bodies was instituted divinitus.

Because it is taught that bodies must be excited so that each one receives what is proper to the body, according to what it has done, whether good or bad. It is necessary, therefore, that man be resurrected in the same body with whose works he served God or the Devil; so that with the same body he can achieve triumphs, crowns and prizes, or suffer pain and miserable torture.

Bodies will not resume the deformity contracted in this life.

Not only will the body be resurrected, but everything that belongs to the truth of its nature and the decorum and ornament of man must be restored. We read the illustrious testimony of Saint Augustine about this: Nothing then, he says, of vice will exist in the bodies: if some have been more obese and thick due to fatness, they will not assume the entire mass of the body, but what exceeds that complexion will be considered superfluous; and what illness or old age wrought in the body will be repaired by Christ with divine virtue: so that if some through macilence have been graceful, because Christ will not only repair our body, but also whatever has been taken from us through the misery of this life. Likewise in another place: A man will not resume the hair that he has had, but those that suit him; according to that: Everyone…

CHAPTER

…the hairs of your head are numbered, which according to divine wisdom must be repaired. First of all, since the members belong to the truth of human nature, they will all be restored at the same time. Because those who, either from the very birth, were deprived of eyes, or due to some illness lost their light, those who are lame and completely lame and weak in any of their limbs, will be resurrected with an entire and perfect body: otherwise the desire of the soul, which is prone to the conjunction of the body, would not have been satisfied in the slightest; whose cupidity we undoubtedly believe must be fulfilled in the resurrection. Furthermore, it is sufficiently established that the resurrection is numbered among the main works of God, along with creation. Just as all things were perfect by God at the beginning of creation, so it must be fully affirmed that this is how it will be in the resurrection.

The martyrs rising with whole bodies will carry the scars of their wounds.

Not only should this be confessed of the martyrs, of whom Saint Augustine testifies thus: They will not be without those members: because that mutilation could not but be a vice of the body; Otherwise, those who were cut off at the head should be resurrected without a head; but, however, there will be in the joints of the same members the scars of the sword, shining above all gold and precious stone, as well as the scars of the wounds of Christ.

Also the bodies of the unbelievers mutilated here will be resurrected whole.

This is also most truthfully said of the unbelievers, even if their members have been amputated because of them: because the more members they have, the more bitter cruciate pain they will consume. Therefore that restitution of members will not result in their happiness, but in calamity and misery: because they are deservedly not assigned to the members themselves, but to the person to whose body they are united: because to those who did penance they will be restored as a reward; but to those who despised her, to punishment.

And if the parish priests carefully consider these things, they will never lack a copy of things and sentences to excite and inflame the spirits of the faithful with the study of piety; so that, considering the troubles and afflictions of this life, they may eagerly await that blessed glory of the resurrection which is proposed to the just and pious.

What will the bodies of men be after resurrecting?

It now follows that the faithful understand that, if we look at what constitutes the substance of the body, although it is necessary that that same and identical body that had previously been extinct be recalled from the dead: nevertheless its condition will be very different and diverse. Because, omitting the rest, in this will all the bodies of the resurrected differ from themselves maximally: that, as before they were subject to the laws of death, after being raised to life, the distinction of good and evil being removed, they will achieve immortality. This admirable restitution of nature was deserved by the distinguished victory of Christ, who reported death, as the testimonies of the sacred Letters admonish us: because it is written: He will precipitate death forever; and elsewhere: I will be your death, oh death!; which, explaining the Apostle, says: The last enemy that will be destroyed is death. And in Saint John we read: Death will be no more. It was most fitting to the merit of Christ the Lord, by whom the empire of death was overthrown, that the sin of Adam should be overcome with a long interval. It was also consensual to divine justice that the good perpetually enjoyed the blessed life, and that the wicked, paying eternal penalties, sought death and did not find it, desired to die and death fled from them. And this immortality will be common to good and bad.

13. With what endowments will the bodies of the Blessed be adorned after the resurrection.

The revived bodies of the Saints will also have certain distinguished and illustrious ornaments, with which they will be much more noble than they ever were before. The main ones are four, those called dowries, observed by the Fathers according to the doctrine of the Apostle. The first of them is impassibility, munus and endowment that will mean that they cannot suffer anything annoying or be affected by any pain or discomfort: because nothing, neither the force of the cold, nor the burning of the flames, nor the impetus of the waters can harm them. It is sown, says the Apostle, in corruption, it will be raised in incorruption. And that the scholastics called it impassibility rather than incorruption was for this reason: to signify what is proper to the glorious body: because impassibility is not common to them with the damned, whose bodies, although incorruptible, can nevertheless burn and freeze and be affected by various cruciates. This is followed by clarity, with which the bodies of the Saints will shine like the sun; thus in effect our Savior testifies in Saint Matthew: The righteous, he says, will shine like the sun in their Father's kingdom. And so that no one would doubt it, he declared it with the example of his transfiguration.

The Apostle sometimes calls this glory clarity: He will reform, he says, the body of our humility configured to the body of his clarity; and again: It is sown in ignominy, it will rise in glory. The people of Israel also saw a certain image of this glory in the desert, when the face of Moses shone so brightly through the conversation and the presence of God that the children of Israel could not fix their eyes on it. And this clarity is a certain radiance that flows from the supreme happiness of the soul to the body, so that it is a certain communication of that blessedness that the soul enjoys: just as the soul itself becomes blessed because part of the divine happiness is derived from it. And it should not be believed that all are adorned equally with this munus, unlike the first: certainly all the bodies of the Saints will be equally impassive, but they will not have the same splendor; because, as the Apostle testifies: One is the brightness of the sun, another is the brightness of the moon, and another is the brightness of the stars: for star from star differs in brightness; so also the resurrection of the dead.

With this endowment is united that which they call agility, by which the body will be freed from the burden with which it is now oppressed; and it can easily move anywhere the soul wants, so that nothing can be more famous than that movement: as Saint Augustine openly taught in the book of the City of God and Jerome in Isaiah. Therefore the Apostle said: It is sown in weakness, it will rise in virtue. To these is added what is called subtlety; By virtue of which the body will be completely subject to the empire of the soul, will serve it and will be ready for its nutum; which is shown by those words of the Apostle…

… It is sown, he says, an animal body, a spiritual body will be resurrected. These are almost the main chapters that have to be conveyed in the explanation of this article.

14. What fruit will the faithful draw from such great mysteries of the resurrection.

And so that the faithful may know what fruit they can draw from the knowledge of so many great mysteries, it will first be necessary to declare that maximum thanks must be given to God, who hid these things from the wise and revealed them to the little ones. Because how many men or experts, due to the praise of prudence or endowed with singular doctrine, were completely blind to this very certain truth? That, then, he had revealed them to us, to whom it was not lawful to aspire to such intelligence, is a reason to celebrate with perpetual praise his utmost benignity and clemency. Also after the meditation of this article follows that great fruit: that in the death of those who are united to us by kinship or benevolence we will easily console others as well as ourselves: which type of consolation is known to have been used by the Apostle when he wrote to the Thessalonians about those who sleep. But also in all other afflictions and calamities the thought of the future resurrection will bring us supreme relief from pain: as we learned from the example of Saint Job, who with this single hope sustained the afflicted and suffering spirit, that sometime in the resurrection he would contemplate his Lord God. Furthermore, this will be very valuable in persuading the faithful people to strive diligently to lead a life that is upright, upright, and completely pure of all stains of sin. Because if they think that those enormous riches that follow the resurrection are proposed to them, they will easily be attracted to the studies of virtue and piety. On the contrary, nothing will have greater force to compress the cupidities of the spirit and separate men from crimes than that they are often warned with what evils and cruciates the unbelievers must be affected, who on that extreme day will emerge to the resurrection of judgment.

OF THE TWELFTH ARTICLE. CHAPTER XIII. Eternal life.

Why was the article of faith put last, and how important it is to explain it frequently to the people.

The holy Apostles, our guides, wanted the symbol, in which the sum of our faith is contained, to be closed and ended with the article of eternal life: both because after the resurrection of the body the faithful have nothing more to expect but the prize of eternal life: and also so that that perfect happiness, accumulated from all goods, would always be placed before our eyes, and we would be taught that our minds and all our thoughts must be fixed on it. For this reason, the parish priests, when instructing the faithful, will never cease to inflame their spirits with the proposed rewards of eternal life: so that whatever things, although very difficult, which they teach must be undertaken for the sake of the Christian name, they may consider them easy and even fruitful, and they may become quicker and more encouraged to obey God.

2. What is meant here by eternal life.

But since under these words, which are usurped in this place to declare our blessedness, many mysteries lie hidden, they must be opened in such a way that, as much as the ingenuity of each one allows, they can be patent to all. The faithful must therefore be warned that with these words, Eternal Life, what is meant is not so much the perpetuity of life, to which demons and accelerated men are also addicted, but rather the blessedness in perpetuity, which fulfills the desire of the blessed. And this is how that little law expert understood it who asked our Lord Savior in the Gospel what he had to do to possess eternal life; as if to say: What things must be given to me to reach that place where it is lawful to enjoy perfect happiness? And in this sense the sacred Letters receive these words, as it is legal to note in many places. To the faithful, with the intuition of eternal life, all the most difficult things become easy.

St. Thomas 1. 2. q. 2 art. 3. 1 Jn 2, 15. 1 Pe 2, 11. With hope our blessedness can begin in this life. Tit 2, 13. Rom 1, 22. That blessedness must be eternal. Augustine, from Civ. Dei, lib. 12 chap. 20. Happiness is the continuous possession of all goods without any admixture of evil.

Why is that supreme blessedness designated by the name of eternal life?

And by this name that supreme blessedness has mainly been called, lest anyone should consider that it consists of corporeal and expired things, which cannot be eternal. Because not even this same voice of blessedness could sufficiently explain what was sought, especially when there were no shortage of men inflated with opinions of a certain vain wisdom, who placed the greatest good in those things that are perceived with the senses. These perish and grow old; but blessedness is not to be defined by any term of time: rather these earthly things are very far from true happiness, from which he who is detained by the love and desire of the world distances himself maximally: because it is written: Do not love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the charity of the Father is not in him; and shortly after: The world passes away, and its lust. These things, then, the parish priests will diligently take care to impress upon the minds of the faithful, so that they may be induced to despise what is mortal and that no happiness can be obtained in this life, in which we are not citizens, but upstarts. Although here also we are deservedly called blessed by hope, if, denying ungodliness and secular desires, we live soberly, justly, and piously in this age, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ. And since many, who thought themselves wise, did not understand this and thought that happiness had to be sought in this life, they became fools and fell into greatest calamities. But also by the force of this name Eternal Life we ​​perceive that happiness once achieved can never be lost, as some falsely suspected. Because happiness, which accumulates from all good things without any mixture of evil, and which fulfills man's desire, necessarily consists in eternal life...

… because the blessed person cannot but greatly desire that it be lawful for him to perpetually enjoy those goods that he has achieved. Therefore, if that possession is not stable and certain, it is necessary that it be anguished by the maximum cruciate of fear.

Eternal bliss cannot be understood with words or with the human mind.

But how great the happiness of the blessed who live in the heavenly homeland is, and that it can only be understood by themselves and by no one else, these same voices sufficiently demonstrate when we say Blessed Life: because when to signify something we use a name that is common with many others, we easily understand that the proper voice with which that thing is openly expressed is lacking. Since, then, happiness is declared with these words, which do not more rightly suit the blessed than all those who live perpetually, this can be an argument for us that it is a higher and more pertinent thing than what we can perfectly mean by the word itself: because although in the sacred Letters many other names are attributed to this heavenly beatitude, which are: Kingdom of God, of Christ, of heaven, paradise, holy city, new Jerusalem, house of the Father: without However, it is perspicuous that none of them is sufficient to explain its magnitude. Therefore the parish priests will not omit in this place the opportunity offered to them of inviting the faithful with such ample rewards, which are declared under the name of eternal life, to piety and justice and to all the offices of the Christian religion.

Because it is clear that life is usually numbered among the greatest goods that nature desires; and with this good mainly, when we say eternal life, blessedness is defined. And if this meager and calamitous life, which is subject to so many and so various miseries that it should more truly be called death, nothing is loved more, nothing can be more dear or more jucund: with what study of the spirit, with what restraint should we seek that eternal life, which, with all evils extinguished, has united the perfect and absolute reason for all goods?

Blessedness is contained in the deprivation of all evils and the attainment of all goods.

Because, as the holy Fathers transmitted, the happiness of eternal life must be defined by the liberation from all evils and the achievement of goods. The testimonies of the Holy Letters are very clear about evils: because it is written in the Apocalypse: They will no longer hunger or thirst, nor will the sun or any heat fall on them; and again: God will wipe away every tear from their eyes: and death will be no more, nor crying, nor crying, nor pain will be any more, because the first things have passed away. Now the immense glory of the blessed, and innumerable kinds of solid joy and voluptuousness, will be such that, since our soul cannot accommodate the magnitude of this glory nor it penetrate in any way into our souls, it is necessary that we enter into it, namely into the joy of the Lord, so that, surrounded by him, we may cumulatively fulfill the desire of the mind.

What kinds of goods will the blessed mainly enjoy.

Although, as Saint Augustine writes, the evils that we will lack can be more easily enumerated than the goods and voluptuousness that we must taste... Blessedness cannot be expressed in one's own words. Mt 6, 33 and 21, 31. Mk 1, 14. Lk 6, 20. Jn 18, 36. Eph 5, 5. Col 1, 13. Mt 5, 3. Ez 28, 13. Lk 23, 43.

...however, efforts must be made to briefly and lucidly explain the things that can inflame the faithful with the desire to achieve that supreme happiness. But first of all it will be necessary to use that distinction that we receive from the most serious writers of divine things. They establish that there are two kinds of goods: one of which belongs to the nature of beatitude, and the other follows the same beatitude; Therefore, for the sake of teaching, they called those goods essential and these accessories.

What is the essential and primary cause of eternal bliss?

And the solid beatitude, which with a common name it is licit to call essential, is located in our seeing God and enjoying his beauty, which is the source and principle of all goodness and perfection: This is eternal life, says Christ Lord, that they may know you, only true God, and whom you sent, Jesus Christ; whose sentence Saint John seems to interpret when he says: Dearest, now we are children of God, and what we will be has not yet appeared: we know that when it appears we will be like Him, because we will see Him as He is: because it means that beatitude consists of these two things: both that we will contemplate God as He is in His nature and substance, and that we will be made like gods. For those who enjoy Him, although they retain their own substance, nevertheless clothe themselves in a certain admirable and almost divine form, so that they seem more like gods than men.

In what way the blessed are clothed in some way with the form and nature of God.

And why this is done is perspicuous because of the following: that each thing is known either by its essence or by its similarity and species. But since nothing is similar to God whose likeness we can use as an aid to reach the perfect knowledge of Him, it is consequently that no one is allowed to see His nature and essence if this same divine essence is not united to us. And this is what those words of the Apostle mean: Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face: because what he says in an enigma is interpreted by Saint Augustine as a similarity suitable for understanding God. This is also openly shown by Saint Dionysius when he states that with no resemblance of the lower, superior things can be perceived: because not even from the resemblance of any corporeal thing can the essence and substance of that which lacks body be known, especially when it is necessary that the resemblances of things have less concreteness and be more spiritual than the same things of which the image refers: as we easily experience in the knowledge of all things. And as it cannot happen that a likeness is found of any created thing equally pure and spiritual that God himself is, so it is that from no likeness we can perfectly understand the divine essence. It is also added that all created things are limited to certain terms of perfection; but God is infinite, and no likeness of a created thing can accommodate his immensity. Therefore only that reason remains for knowing the divine substance: that it unites itself to us and in an incredible way elevates our intelligence higher, and thus we are made suitable to contemplate the species of its nature.

With the light of glory the blessed are enlightened, and everyone must move with all hope to see God.

And we will achieve this with the light of glory, when illustrated with that splendor we will see God, true light, in his light. Because the blessed always contemplate God present: with whose gift, the greatest and most persevering of all, made partakers of the divine essence, they achieve true and solid beatitude: which we must believe in such a way that in the Symbol of the Fathers it has been defined that due to the benignity of God we must await it with a certain hope; for he says: I look forward to the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come.

How man is united to God in beatitude is explained in a similar way.

These things are entirely divine, and cannot be explained in words nor understood in thought by us. But it is lawful to discern some image of this blessedness also in those things that are perceived with the sense. For just as iron brought close to fire conceives fire, and although its substance does not change, it is nevertheless made to appear to be something different, namely fire: in the same way, those who have been admitted to that heavenly glory, inflamed with the love of God, are affected in such a way that, without ceasing to be what they are, it can rightly be said that they are much further removed from those who are in this life than the red-hot iron is from one that does not contain in itself any force of heat. To embrace the thing in a few words, then, that supreme and absolute blessedness that we call essential must be constituted in the possession of God. Because what can be lacking in perfect happiness for those who possess the optimal and most perfect God?

What are the accidental goods with which the blessed will be surrounded.

But to that are nevertheless added certain ornaments, common to all the blessed: which, as they are less remote from human reason, also tend to move and excite our spirits more vehemently. Of this kind are those things of which the Apostle seems to understand to the Romans: Glory, and honour, and peace to all who do good: because the blessed will enjoy glory not only of that which we finally show to be the essential beatitude, or the one most united to their nature: but also of that which consists of the clear and open knowledge that each one must have of the eximia and prestige and dignity of the other. And how great is to be estimated that honor that the Lord gives them, when they are no longer called servants, but friends, brothers and children of God! Therefore with such loving and most honorable words our Savior will address his elect: Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you; so that it is deservedly lawful to exclaim: Your friends have been extremely honored, God; but also with praise they will be celebrated by Christ the Lord before the heavenly Father and his Angels. Furthermore, if nature has engendered in all men this common desire for the honor that is held among men who are gifted in wisdom, because they estimate that they will be abundant witnesses of their virtue: how much do we think that it will be added to the glory of the blessed that one follows another with utmost honor?

With what copies of goods the blessed will accumulate in those eternal seats.

The enumeration of all the delights with which the glory of the blessed will be accumulated would be infinite, and not even with thought can we fake them. But nevertheless the faithful must be persuaded of this: that whatever jucund things that may happen to us in this life or even be desired, whether they belong to the knowledge of the mind, or to the perfect habit of the body, the blessed life of the heavenly ones is surrounded by the copies of all those things: although this is done in a higher way than what the eye saw, or the ear heard, or ascended in the heart of man, as the Apostle affirms. Because the body, which was previously gross and concrete, when in heaven, with mortality removed, has been made tenuous and spiritual, it will no longer need any food. But the soul will be satiated with utmost voluptuousness from the eternal pasture of glory, which the author of that great banquet, passing by, will minister to all. Who can desire precious garments or royal ornaments of the body, where there will be no use for these things, and everyone will be clothed in immortality and splendor and adorned with the crown of everlasting glory? But if the possession of a large and magnificent house also belongs to human happiness, what can be thought larger or more magnificent than the sky itself, which is everywhere illuminated with the clarity of God? Therefore the Prophet, when the beauty of that domicile was before his eyes and burned with desire to reach those blessed seats: How lovely, he says, are your tabernacles, Lord of virtues! My soul lusts and faints in the courts of the Lord: my heart and my flesh exult in the living God. And for this to be the spirit of all the faithful, this is the common voice of all, just as the parish priests desire it vehemently, so they must also take care of it with all study.

13. The blessed will not be awarded the same prizes without any distinction.

For in my Father's house, says the Lord, there are many mansions: in which greater and lesser rewards will be given, according as each one has deserved. For he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly; and he who sows in blessings will also reap blessings. Therefore they will not only excite the faithful to that beatitude, but they will also frequently admonish that this is the certain reason for obtaining it: that, instructed in faith and charity, and persevering in prayer and in the healthy use of the Sacraments, they exercise themselves in all the offices of kindness towards their neighbor. Thus indeed it will be done by the mercy of God, who prepared that blessed glory for those who love Him, that someday what was said by the Prophet will be fulfilled: My people will sit in beauty of peace, and in tabernacles of trust, and in opulent rest.

CHAPTER I

Teaching the doctrine of the Sacraments is, above all, the care of the parish priest.

As every part of Christian doctrine requires science and diligence: so the discipline of the Sacraments, which by God's command is necessary and extremely useful, postulates the singular ease and industry of the parish priest, so that with its exact and frequent perception the faithful may be such that the most sacred and holy things can be imparted to them with dignity and health, and the Priests do not deviate from that divine rule of interdict: Do not give what is holy to the dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine.

2. What does the word Sacramento mean?

Firstly, then, since the entire genus of Sacraments must be treated universally, it is appropriate to begin with the force and notion of the name itself, and explain its ambiguous significance; so that it is more easily understood what the proper sentence of this word is in this place. Therefore, the faithful must be taught that the name of Sacrament (in what concerns the thing proposed) has been taken in one way by the profane and in another by the sacred Writers: because other authors wanted the name of Sacrament to mean that obligation with which, as sworns, we bind ourselves with some bond of servitude, from which the oath with which soldiers promise to render faithful work to the Republic was called a military sacrament: and this seems to have been the most frequent meaning of this word between them. But among the Latin Fathers, who transmitted divine things in writing, the name of Sacrament declares some sacred thing that lies hidden: just as the Greeks used the word mystery to mean the same thing. And in this sense we understand that the voice Sacrament must be taken when writing to the Ephesians: To make known to us the Sacrament of his will. Then to Timothy: Great is the Sacrament of piety. Also in the book of Wisdom: They did not know the Sacraments of God. In which places and in many others it is permissible to note that Sacrament does not mean anything else but a sacred, abducted and hidden thing.

The name of Sacrament, adapted by the Fathers to mean sacred signs, is very ancient.

Therefore the Latin Doctors considered that certain signs subject to the senses could comfortably be called Sacraments, which at the same time declare the grace they effect and place it as if before the eyes. Although, as Saint Gregory pleases, for this reason they can be called Sacraments: because the divine virtue under the integuments of corporeal things secretly effects salvation. Nor should anyone think that this word has been recently introduced into the Church: because whoever has read Saint Jerome and Augustine will easily perceive that the ancient writers of our religion, to demonstrate the thing of which we speak, used many times the name of Sacrament, and sometimes also the word Symbol, or mystical sign, or sacred sign. And this is enough of what has been said about the name of Sacrament: which also suits the Sacraments of the old law, of which it is not necessary for the Pastors to transmit precepts, since by the law and grace of the Gospel they have been abolished.

What do Catholic writers properly denote by the name of Sacrament?

But in addition to the notion of the name, which has been declared up to this point, the force and nature of the thing must also be diligently investigated, and what the Sacrament is must be opened to the faithful. Because no one can doubt that the Sacraments are of the kind of those things with which salvation and justice are achieved. But although there are many reasons that seem suitable and convenient to explain this thing, none of them demonstrate it more plainly and lucidly than the definition transmitted by Saint Augustine, which was later followed by all the scholastic doctors: Sacrament, he says, is a sign of a sacred thing: or, in other words, in the same sentence: Sacrament is a visible sign of invisible grace, instituted for our justification.

5. Division of sensible things, and what is to be understood by the name of sign.

And for this definition to be more evident, each of its parts will have to be explained to the Pastors; and above all it will be necessary to teach that of all the things that are perceived with the senses there are two kinds: some were invented to mean something; others not to signify anything else, but made only for its sake: in which number can be had almost all the things that consist of nature. But in the first genus we must put the words of things, writing, vexilos, images, trumpets and many others of this kind: because if you take away the power of meaning from the words, the cause for which they were instituted seems removed. These, then, are properly called signs.

Because Saint Augustine testifies that a sign is that which, in addition to the thing that it offers to the senses, also causes us to grasp the knowledge of something else, just as from the vestige printed on the earth that we contemplate, we easily know that someone whose vestige appears has passed.

In what way it is shown that the Sacraments are signs.

And this being so, it is perspicuous that the Sacrament refers to this type of things that were instituted for the sake of meaning, since with a certain kind and similarity it declares to us what God accomplishes in our souls, with his virtue that cannot be perceived with the sense. Because Baptism (so that what is taught may become more noticeable by example), when with certain and solemn words we wash ourselves outwardly with water, means this: that by the virtue of the Holy Spirit every stain and dullness of sin is washed inwardly, and our souls are increased and adorned with that illustrious gift of heavenly justice. And at the same time that ablution of the body, as will be explained later in its place, effects in the spirit what it means.

The same is also demonstrated by the Scriptures.

But it is also clear from the Scriptures that the Sacrament must be numbered among the signs. For the Apostle, concerning circumcision, the Sacrament of the ancient law, which had been given to Abraham, father of all believers, writes thus to the Romans: And he received the sign of circumcision, the seal of the righteousness of faith. And in another place, when he affirms that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death, it is lawful to know that Baptism has the significance of this thing, namely, as the Apostle himself says: That we have been buried with Him by Baptism into death. It will not be a little advantageous if the faithful people understand that the Sacraments belong to the signs: because in this way they will be more easily persuaded that what is signified, contained and carried out by them is holy and august; and knowing his holiness, he will be more excited to cultivate and venerate divine beneficence towards us.

How many are the types of signs.

It now follows that those words "of a sacred thing" be explained, which is the other part of the definition. And so that this can be done comfortably, the things that Saint Augustine disputed with acuity and subtlety about the variety of signs must be repeated a little louder. For some are called natural signs, which in addition to themselves engender in our minds the news of something else (which has been shown before to be common to all signs); like smoke, from which it is immediately understood that there is fire; and this sign for this reason must be called natural: because smoke does not mean fire by will, but the use of things means that if someone sees only the smoke, he perceives with the mind and the underlying thought at the same time the nature and force of the fire that is still latent. But some signs do not consist of nature, but have been constituted and invented by men, in order to be able to converse with each other and explain to others the meanings of their minds, and at the same time know the judgment and advice of others. And how various and multiple these are, it is permissible to notice from the following: that some belong to the sense of the eyes, the majority to that of the ears, and the rest to the other senses. Because when we make a sign to someone, and for example, raising the vexil, we declare something, it is sufficiently clear that that meaning refers only to the eyes: just as the sound of trumpets, flutes or zither, which is not only emitted for the sake of delight, but often for the sake of meaning, looks to the judgment of the ears; with whose meaning mainly the words are also received, which have maximum strength to express the intimate thoughts of the soul.

Of the signs instituted by God in both the Old and New Testaments.

But in addition to those signs that up to this point we have said were constituted by the consensus and will of men, there are other divinitus givens, of which however all agree that they are not of a single genus. Because some signs were entrusted by God to men only to mean or warn something; of which kind were the purifications of the law, the unleavened bread and many others that belonged to the ceremonies of the Mosaic cult: but God instituted others that not only had the power to signify, but also to effect: and in this later...

… type of signs is liquid that the Sacraments of the new law are to be numbered. Because they are signs transmitted divinitus, not invented by men, of which we believe with certainty that they contain within themselves the efficiency of some sacred thing that they declare. The grace of God is properly called a sacred thing. Each Sacrament means three things at the same time: Passion, Grace and Glory. Commemorative sign.

How is the sacred thing to be understood in the definition of the Sacrament.

But just as we show that signs are of multiple varieties, so too the sacred thing is not to be esteemed in a single way. And as regards the proposed definition of the Sacrament, the writers of divine things demonstrate with the name of a sacred thing the grace of God, which makes us saints and adorns us with the habit of all the divine virtues: to this grace they deservedly considered that the very name of a sacred thing should be attributed; since for its benefit it is consecrated and unites our spirit to God.

Most abundant definition of the Sacrament, and why it differs from the other sacred signs.

Therefore, in order to declare more explicitly what the Sacrament is, it must be taught that it is a thing subject to the senses, which by the institution of God has the power both to signify and to effect holiness and justice: from which it follows that anyone can easily understand that the Images of the Saints, the Crosses and others of this kind, although they are signs of sacred things, are not for that reason called Sacraments. And the doctrine of this truth will be easy to verify with the example of all the Sacraments, if what we previously admonished about Baptism, when we said that that solemn ablution of the body is a sign and has the efficiency of the sacred thing that is done internally by the power of the Holy Spirit, someone wishes to exercise it also in the other Sacraments.

12. The Sacraments do not mean just one thing, but several.

It is also primarily appropriate for these mystical signs instituted by God that by the Lord's institution they do not mean just one thing, but several at the same time. Which is lawful to know in each of the Sacraments, which not only declare our holiness and justice, but also two other things maximally united to the same holiness: namely, the passion of Christ the Redeemer, which is the cause of holiness, and eternal life and heavenly beatitude, to which our holiness must refer as an end. Which, as can be perceived in all the Sacraments, the sacred doctors deservedly transmitted that in each of the Sacraments a triple force of meaning is inherent: both because it brings the memory of something past; and because it indicates and demonstrates something present; and because it foretells something future. Nor should it be considered that this is taught by them in such a way that it is not also proven by the testimony of the holy Scriptures. For when the Apostle says: As many of us as have been baptized into Christ Jesus, we have been baptized into his death; It openly shows that Baptism must be called a sign because it warns us of the passion and death of the Lord. Then when he says: For we were buried with Him through Baptism into death, so that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life; From these words it is clear that Baptism is a sign with which the heavenly grace infused into us is declared, by whose munus we have been given that, by instituting new life, we can carry out with ease and pleasure all the offices of true piety. Finally, when he adds: Because if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we will also be planted together in the resurrection: it appears that Baptism also gives no obscure significance to the eternal life that we are to obtain through it.

The Sacrament does not designate only one present thing, but several.

But in addition to these various genres and reasons of meaning that we have commemorated, it often also happens that the Sacrament does not demonstrate and note only one present thing, but several. This is easy to understand for those who contemplate the Most Holy Sacrament of the Eucharist, which designates the presence of the true Body and Blood of the Lord, and also the grace perceived by those who do not impurely take the sacred mysteries. From what has been said, then, the Pastors will not be able to lack arguments with which to show how much power of divinity and how many arcane miracles there are in the Sacraments of the new law, in order to persuade everyone that they must be cultivated and received with utmost religion.

14. Why it was necessary for Sacraments to be instituted among Christians.

But to teach the correct use of the Sacraments nothing can seem more convenient than diligently exposing the causes for which it was necessary to institute the Sacraments. Several are usually numbered, of which the first is the imbecility of human ingenuity: since we see that by nature it is disposed in such a way that no one is allowed to aspire to the knowledge of those things that are understood with the mind and intelligence except through those that are perceived with some sense. In order, therefore, that we might more easily understand the things that are accomplished by the hidden virtue of God, the same supreme architect of all things wisely caused this same virtue, because of his kindness toward us, to be declared with some signs that fall under sense. Because, as Saint Chrysostom excellently said...
