If man lacked the concretion of the body, the goods themselves would have been offered to him naked and not wrapped in those integuments; But since the soul is united to the body, it was absolutely necessary for it to use the gadget of things to understand them. Another cause is that our spirit is not easily moved to believe the things that are promised to us. Therefore, God from the exordium of the world used to indicate with words very frequently what he had instituted to be done: but sometimes, when he instituted some work whose magnitude could abrogate the faith of the promise, he also added to the words other signs that sometimes had a kind of miracle. Because when he sent Moses to the liberation of the Israelite people, and they, not even trusting in the help of God who sent them, feared that a heavier burden would be imposed on them than they could bear, or that the people would not add faith to the oracles and divine sayings, the Lord signed his promise with a great variety of signs. Just as, then, in the Old Testament God had made signs to testify the constancy of some great promise: so also in the new law Christ, our Savior, when he promised us the forgiveness of sins, heavenly grace and the communication of the Holy Spirit, instituted certain signs subject to the eyes and senses, with which as with pledges we would bind him, and thus never doubt that he would be faithful in the promises. The third reason was so that they were ready as remedies, as Saint Ambrose writes, and as medicines of the evangelical Samaritan to recover or protect the health of souls. Because the virtue that flows from the passion of Christ, that is, the grace that He deserved for us on the altar of the Cross, must be derived to us through the Sacraments as by a certain channel; Otherwise no one can have any hope of salvation. For this reason, the most gracious Lord wanted to leave in the Church the Sacraments sanctioned with his word and promise, by which we would undoubtedly believe that the fruit of his passion was communicated to us re ipsa, if each one of us piously and religiously applied that healing to ourselves. But a fourth reason is also added for which the institution of the Sacraments may seem necessary: ​​namely, so that they were certain notes and symbols with which the faithful recognized each other...

…as has also been transmitted by Saint Augustine, no ceto of men can be coagmented as a single body, whether under the name of true or false religion, if they are not united with some foedus of visible signs. Both provide, therefore, the Sacraments of the new law, which both distinguish the cultivators of the Christian faith from the infidels, and unite the faithful themselves with a certain sacred bond.

Furthermore, that another reason for instituting the Sacraments was also very just can be shown by those words of the Apostle: With the heart one believes for righteousness, but with the mouth one confesses for salvation. Because with the Sacraments it seems that we profess and make our faith known in the sight of men. Therefore, as we approach Baptism, we openly testify that we believe that by the virtue of that water with which we are washed in the Sacrament, the spiritual purgation of the soul is carried out.

Then the Sacraments have great power not only to excite and exercise faith in our minds, but also to inflame that charity with which we should love one another; when we remember through the communion of the sacred mysteries that we are linked with the most arcane bond and made members of a single body.

Finally, what in the study of Christian piety must be highly esteemed, tame and compress the pride of the human mind and exercise us in humility, while we are compelled to subject ourselves to sensible elements in order to obey God, from whom we had previously impiously defected to serve the elements of the world. These are the things that have mainly been considered to be transmitted to the faithful people regarding the name, nature and institution of the Sacrament: which, after being exactly explained by the Pastors, it will be necessary to teach below what each of the Sacraments consist of, what their parts are, and also what rites and ceremonies have been added to them.

Parts necessary to constitute each Sacrament.

First, then, it must be explained that the sensible thing, which was put above in the definition of the Sacrament, is not a single thing, although it must be believed that it constitutes a single sign. Because there are two things from which any Sacrament is made...

…of which one is a matter and is called an element; the other has force of form and is addressed with the common word of word. Thus in effect we receive it from the Fathers; In which the testimony of Saint Augustine is notorious and widely spread: The word accesses the element, and the Sacrament is made. Thus, by the name of sensible thing, they understand both the matter or element, as in the sacrament of Baptism the water, of Confirmation the chrism, and of the Extreme Unction the oil, which all fall under the sight: as well as the words, which have a reason of form and belong to the sense of the ears. And the Apostle openly indicated one and the other when he says: Christ loved the Church and gave himself for her, to sanctify her, washing her with the washing of water in the word of life. In which place the matter and form of the Sacrament are expressed.

16. Why were words added to the element.

Words, therefore, had to be added to the matter, so that the meaning of the thing that was being created would become more open and clear. Because it is perspicuous that among all the signs the words have the greatest force: and if they are missing, it will be completely obscure what designates and demonstrates the matter of the Sacraments. Because as can be seen in Baptism, when water has the power to cool no less than to wash, and can be a symbol of one or the other, if the words are not added, with some conjecture someone will perhaps judge which of these two means in Baptism; but no one will dare to affirm anything true about it: but when the words are attached, we immediately understand that it has the force and significance of washing.

Excellence of the Sacraments of the new law.

In this, for their part, our Sacraments are very much before the Sacraments of the old law: because in the administration of the former, no defined form was kept, according to what we have received, for which reason they also became extremely uncertain and obscure; But ours have the form of the words so prescribed that if by chance they deviate from it, the reason for the Sacrament cannot be established: and for this reason they are very clear and leave no room for doubt. These, then, are the parts that belong to the nature and substance of the Sacraments, and of which each Sacrament is necessarily constituted.

What is the virtue and nature of the ceremonies in the Sacraments.

To these are added the ceremonies, which, although they cannot be preterminated without sin, if the same necessity does not force us to do something else; However, if they are ever omitted, since they do not touch the nature of the thing, it should not be believed that anything is diminished from the true reason for the Sacrament. And deservedly since the earliest times of the Church it has always been observed that the Sacraments were ministered with certain solemn ceremonies. Firstly, it was appropriate to pay to the sacred mysteries to the greatest degree that cult of religion, so that we might appear to treat holy things holily: furthermore, the same ceremonies declare more what is carried out with the Sacrament and put it before our eyes, and impress more deeply on the minds of the faithful the sanctity of those things. Then they elevate the minds of those who contemplate and diligently observe them to the cogitation of sublime things, and excite in them faith and charity; Therefore, greater care and diligence must be taken so that the faithful know and perceive the power of the ceremonies with which each of the Sacraments are made.

How many are the Sacraments of the Catholic Church.

It follows that the number of the Sacraments should also be explained, the knowledge of which brings this usefulness: that the people will with all the greater piety convert all the forces of their spirit to praise and preach the singular beneficence of God towards us, as they understand that more gadgets of salvation and blessed life have been prepared for us by divinitus. The Sacraments, then, of the Catholic Church, as proven by the Scriptures, and handed down to us by the tradition of the Fathers, and testified to the authority of the Councils, are defined in septenary number.

20. Why the Sacraments are not concluded in greater or lesser numbers.

And why they are not numbered neither more nor less, also for those things that by similarity are transferred from the natural life to the spiritual life can be shown with a certain probable reason. Because for man to live, to preserve life and to lead it for the benefit of himself and of the republic, these seven things seem necessary: ​​namely, that he be brought to the light, that he grow, that he be fed, that if he falls into illness he be healed, that the imbecility of the forces be referred to: then, as regards the republic, that there should never be a lack of magistrates by whose authority and empire it is governed; and finally, that with legitimate propagation of offspring he preserves himself and the human race. All of which things, as it sufficiently appears, respond to that life with which the soul lives God...

Seven things are necessary for the human race to lead life comfortably. [References: Eph 5; Saint 5; Acts 8; Prov 9,1; Zech 3 and 4; Conc. Trid. sess. 7, Can. 1 of the Sacraments in general; Council of Florence, Decree to the Armenians; St. Thomas 3rd p. q. 65 art. 1; Jn 3,5; Tit 3,5; Lk 24,49; Acts 1:8; Jn 6,56; Jn 20,22-23; James 5:15; Acts 13,2-3.]

Of the preeminence and difference of the Sacraments. Three are the necessary Sacraments above the others. Necessity of Baptism. Necessity of Penance. Need for Order. Dignity of the Eucharist. The number of the Sacraments will be easily gathered.

It is demonstrated by the Scriptures that there are seven Sacraments. The first is Baptism, as the door of the others, through which we are reborn of Christ. Then Confirmation, by whose virtue we are increased and strengthened with divine grace: because to the Apostles already baptized, as Saint Augustine testifies, the Lord said: Remain in the city until you are clothed with virtue from above. Then the Eucharist, with which, as with a truly heavenly delicacy, our spirit is nourished and sustained: of it the Savior said: My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. Next in fourth place is Penance, with whose help the healing lost after we receive the wounds of sin is restored. Then the Extreme Unction, with which the relics of sins are removed and the virtues of the spirit are recreated: for the divine James, when speaking of this Sacrament, testified thus: And if he is in sins, they will be forgiven. Follow the Order, by which the power to perpetually exercise in the Church the public ministries of the Sacraments and to execute all the sacred functions is transmitted. Finally, Marriage is added, so that from the legitimate and holy conjunction of man and woman, children may be created for the worship of God and the preservation of the human race, and they may be educated religiously.

The need or dignity of all the Sacraments is not the same. But it must be noted as much as possible that, although all the Sacraments contain within themselves divine and admirable virtue, not all of them, however, have the same necessity or dignity, nor the same power of meaning. And of them there are three who, although not for the same reason, are said to be necessary above the others. For that Baptism is necessary to each one without any adjunction, the Savior declared it in these words: Unless anyone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. But Penance is necessary only to those who, after Baptism, committed some mortal sin; because they will not be able to escape eternal extermination if they do not rightly repent of the sin committed. Furthermore, Order, although not necessary for each of the faithful, is absolutely necessary for the entire Church. But if we look at the dignity in the Sacraments, the Eucharist stands out by far for its sanctity and for the number and magnitude of the mysteries. All of which will be more easily understood when the things pertaining to each Sacrament are explained instead.

From whom have these sacred and divine mysteries been received, and by whom are they primarily dispensed. Then we must see from whom we have received these sacred and divine mysteries; because there is no doubt that the dignity of some munere preclear is maximally increased by the dignity and preeminence of the one from whom the same gift came. But this question cannot have a difficult explanation. Because, since God makes men just, and the Sacraments themselves are certain wonderful instruments to achieve justice, it is clear that one and the same God in Christ must be recognized as the author of justification and the Sacraments. Furthermore, the Sacraments contain that force and efficiency that penetrates to the depths of the soul. And since it is characteristic of the sole power of God to slide into the hearts and minds of men, it is also perceived from this that the Sacraments were instituted by God Himself through Christ, just as it must also be held with certain and constant faith that they are dispensed internally by Him: because this testimony Saint John affirms having received from Him, when he says: He who sent me to baptize in water, the same one said to me: On whom you see the Spirit descend and remain on him, this is the one who baptize in the Holy Spirit.

What ministers does God use in the dispensation of the Sacraments. But although God is the author and dispenser of the Sacraments, he nevertheless wanted that in the Church they should not be ministered by Angels, but by men. Because the office of the ministers is no less necessary than the material and form to prepare the Sacraments, as has been confirmed by the perpetual tradition of the holy Fathers.

The minister cannot prevent the virtue of sacramental grace with his evil. And these ministers, since in that sacred function they do not carry their own person but that of Christ, it follows that, whether they are good or bad, as long as they use that form and matter that by the institution of Christ the Catholic Church has always preserved, and they propose to do what the Church does in that administration, they truly make and confer the Sacraments; so that nothing can prevent the fruit of grace, but those who receive it want to defraud themselves of such great good and resist the Holy Spirit. That this has always been a true and explored statement in the Church was demonstrated very clearly by Saint Augustine in those disputes he wrote against the Donatists.

CHAPTER 3

How pernicious it is for the ministers themselves to administer the Sacraments of the new law with an impure conscience. If we also seek testimonies from Scripture, let us hear the same Apostle speaking in these words: I, he says, planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase: so neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase. From which place it is sufficiently understood that, just as trees are harmed by the evil of those by whose hand they were planted, so those who through the ministry of evil men were grafted into Christ cannot contract any vice through the fault of others. Therefore, as our holy Fathers taught in the Gospel of Saint John, Judas Iscariot also baptized many, of whom, however, we do not read of anyone who was rebaptized: so that Saint Augustine clearly wrote: Judas gave Baptism, and was not baptized after Judas; John gave, and he was baptized after John, because if Judas gave it, it was the Baptism of Christ: but what John gave was from John; We do not prefer Judas to John, but the Baptism of Christ, even given by the hands of Judas, to the Baptism of John even given by the hands of John.

What must be felt about those who administer the Sacraments with an impure conscience. Neither the Pastors nor the other ministers of the Sacraments, when they hear this, consider that it is enough for them if, putting aside the integrity of customs and purity of conscience, they only think about how the Sacraments are administered correctly by them. Because although this must be taken care of with diligence, not in it, however, are placed all the things that belong to that function. They must always remember that the Sacraments never lose the divine virtue that is inherent in them; but to those who administer them impurely they bring eternal perdition and death: because holy things, which again and again and often should be admonished, must be treated holy and religiously. To the sinner, as it is in the Prophet, God said: Why do you enumerate my righteousnesses and take my testament through your mouth? You hated discipline. If it is licit for a man contaminated by sins to treat less of divine things, how great must be esteemed the crime conceived by him who, conscious of many crimes, is nevertheless not afraid to concoct the sacred mysteries with an impure mouth, or to take them into profane hands, to handle them and to corrupt them, and to minister them to others? especially when in Saint Dionysius it is written that the evil ones are not even allowed to touch the symbols (that is what he calls the Sacraments). Therefore, above all, let ministers seek the sanctity of sacred things, approach with purity to minister the Sacraments, and in such a way exercise themselves in piety that from their frequent treatment and use, with God helping them, they obtain more sublime grace from day to day.

Of the two main effects of the Sacraments. But now that these things have been explained, it must be taught what the effect of the Sacraments is: because this seems to provide no little light to the definition of the Sacrament that has been transmitted above. These are mainly listed two. And the first place is deservedly obtained by that grace which, with the name used by the sacred Doctors, we call justifying: because this is what the Apostle taught us most openly when he says: Christ loved the Church and gave himself up for her, to sanctify her, cleansing her in the laver of water in the word. But how such a great and admirable thing is accomplished by the Sacrament, so that, as celebrated in the sentence of Saint Augustine, the water touches the body and washes the heart: this certainly cannot be understood with human reason and intelligence. Because it must be considered established that no sensible thing is endowed by its own nature with that force to be able to penetrate to the soul. But with the light of faith we know that in the Sacraments there is the virtue of the omnipotent God, with which they carry out what by their force natural things themselves cannot do.

How at the beginning of the nascent Church the effects of the Sacrament were wonderfully designated. Therefore, lest any doubt of this effect ever reside in the minds of the faithful, when the Sacraments began to be ministered, the most gracious God wanted to declare with meanings of miracles what they performed internally, so that we would constantly believe that the same things are perpetually done internally, even if they were very remote from our senses. Thus, let us omit that, when our Savior was baptized in the Jordan, the heavens were opened and the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove: to admonish us that his grace, when we are washed with the healthy spring, is infused into our soul; Let us omit, I say, this (because it belongs more to the sanctification of Baptism than to the administration of the Sacrament): do we not read that when on the day of Pentecost the Apostles received the Holy Spirit, with which they later became more courageous and stronger to preach the truth of the faith and face dangers for the glory of Christ, then, suddenly making a sound from heaven as of a vehement approaching wind, cloven tongues appeared to them as if of fire? From which it was understood that through the Sacrament of Confirmation the same Spirit is given to us and those forces are added to us with which we can fight and strongly resist the flesh, the world and Satan, our perpetual hosts. And these miracles, as often as the Apostles ministered those Sacraments, were seen for some time at the beginning of the nascent Church, until, once the faith was already affirmed and corroborated, they ceased to occur.

How much is the excellence of the Sacraments of the new law over the Sacraments of the old law. From what has been demonstrated, then, of the first effect of the Sacraments, namely, of justifying grace, it also clearly appears that there is in the Sacraments of the new law a more excellent and most excellent power than that which the Sacraments of the old law once had: which, being weak and poor elements, sanctified the defiled for the emundation of the flesh, not of the soul: for which reason they were instituted only as signs of those things that were to be accomplished by our mysteries. But the Sacraments of the new law, flowing from the side of Christ, who by the Holy Spirit offered himself immaculate to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God; and thus they operate with the virtue of the blood of Christ that grace which they signify. Therefore, if we compare them with the ancient Sacraments, it will be found that, in addition to being more effective, they are more magnificent in usefulness and more august in holiness.

What Sacraments print character, and what character is. The other effect of the Sacraments is not common to all, but is typical only of three: Baptism, Confirmation and Holy Orders, it is the character they impress on the soul. For when the Apostle says: God anointed us, who also sealed us and gave the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts, with that voice Sealed described not obscurely the character, the character of which is to point out and notice something. But character is like a certain insignia impressed on the soul, which can never be erased and is inherent in it in perpetuity: of which it is thus written in Saint Augustine: Can the Christian Sacraments be less than this corporal note with which the soldier is insignia? Because this one, returning to the militia that had deserted, is not given a new one, but rather the old one is recognized and approved.

What is the effect of character, and how the Sacraments that imprint character should not be reiterated. Now character lends this: both that we are made fit to receive or perform something sacred, and that by some note one is distinguished from another. And with the character of Baptism we achieve one thing and another: that we are made suitable to perceive the other Sacraments, and also that with it the faithful people are distinguished from the people who do not cultivate faith. The same is lawful to know in the character of Confirmation and of the sacred Order: of which the one arms and instructs us as soldiers of Christ for the public confession and advocacy of his name, and against the host inserted in us and the spiritual evils in the celestials, and at the same time we discern ourselves from those who, recently baptized, are like newborn children: the other has united the power to prepare and minister the Sacraments, and shows the distinction of those who are endowed with power of this kind from the rest of the body of the faithful. Therefore, the rule of the Catholic Church must be retained, by which we are taught that these three Sacraments imprint character and that they must never be reiterated at any time. These are the things that in general will have to be transmitted from the Sacraments.

With what reasons will the Pastors get the people to venerate the Sacraments and use them religiously. In the explanation of this argument, let the Pastors strive with all study to do two things mainly. The first is that the faithful understand how much honor and worship and veneration these divine and celestial munera are worthy of; The other is that, since the most merciful God proposed them for the common salvation of all, they should use them piously and religiously, and be so inflamed by the desire for Christian perfection that, if they lacked for some time the most salubrious use, especially of Penance and the Eucharist, they would consider that they had done themselves great harm. But Pastors will be able to easily achieve this if they often instill in the ears of the faithful the things that have been said above about the divinity and the fruit of the Sacraments: first, that they were instituted by the Lord our Savior, from whom nothing can proceed except the most perfect; Furthermore, when they are ministered, the very effective numen of the Holy Spirit is present, penetrating the depths of our heart; next, that they are endowed with an admirable and certain virtue of healing souls; and that through them those immense riches of the Passion of the Lord are derived to us. Finally they will show that the entire Christian building certainly begins on the very firm foundation of the cornerstone; But if it is not supported on all sides by the preaching of the word of God and the use of the Sacraments, it is greatly to be feared that, once it is largely done, it will collapse. Because just as we are received into life through the Sacraments, so with this as pabulum we nourish, preserve and increase. OF THE SACRAMENT OF BAPTISM.

CHAPTER I

Why it is convenient to frequently instill the doctrine of Baptism in faithful peoples. From what has been transmitted up to this point about the Sacraments in general, one can know how necessary it is, to perceive the doctrine of the Christian Religion or to exercise piety, to understand the things that the Catholic Church proposes about each of them in order to believe: but if someone reads the Apostle more diligently, he will undoubtedly establish that the perfect knowledge of Baptism is greatly required of the faithful: in such a way not only frequently, but with grave words and filled with the Spirit of God, he renews the memory of its mystery, he praises his divinity, and in it he places before our eyes the death, burial and resurrection of our Redeemer, both to contemplate and to imitate. For this reason, the Pastors never consider that they have put enough work and study into the treatise of this Sacrament.

When primarily the Baptism sermon is to be instituted by the Parish Priest. But in addition to those days in which, according to the custom of the elders, the divine mysteries of Baptism should mainly be explained, on the great Saturday of Easter and Pentecost, a time in which the Church used to celebrate this Sacrament with utmost religion and maximum ceremonies, also capture the opportunity on other days to discuss this argument. And that time may seem most opportune for this thing if sometimes, when Baptism is to be ministered to someone, they notice that a multitude of the faithful people have gathered. Because then it will be much easier, if it is not licit to pursue all the chapters that pertain to this Sacrament, to teach at least one or the other, when the faithful see expressed in the sacred ceremonies of Baptism at the same time the doctrine of those things that they perceive with their ears, and contemplate them with pious and attentive spirit. From which later each one, admonished with those things that he sees done in another, will remember with himself what promise he bound himself to God when he began with Baptism; and at the same time think if with life and customs he presents himself as the very profession of the Christian name promises. Therefore, in order for the things to be taught to be clearly explained, the nature and substance of Baptism must be revealed: first, however, the meaning of its very word is explained.

What does the name Baptism properly denote? And no one is unaware that Baptism is a Greek name: which, although in the sacred Letters it not only means that ablution that is linked to the Sacrament, but also every type of ablution, which sometimes was transferred to the passion; However, among the writers of the Church, it does not declare any ablution of the body, but rather that which is combined with the Sacrament and is not ministered without the prescribed form of words; with which meaning the Apostles used very frequently by institution of Christ the Lord.

By what other names did the holy Fathers also express this Sacrament? The holy Fathers also usurped other names to mean the same thing. Because Saint Augustine testifies that it is called the Sacrament of Faith, because those who receive it profess all the faith of the Christian religion. Others, because our hearts are illuminated with faith, which we profess in Baptism, called this Sacrament illumination: because the Apostle also says thus: Remember the first days, in which, enlightened, you sustained a great combat of passions; meaning, namely, the time in which they were baptized. Furthermore, Chrysostom, in the prayer he had for those who were to be baptized, calls it both expurgation, because by Baptism we expunge the old leaven to be new dough: as a burial, as a plantation, as the cross of Christ: from all of which appeals the cause of the Epistle written to the Romans can be deduced. Why Saint Dionysius called it the beginning of the most holy commandments is clear; because this Sacrament is like a door through which we enter the society of Christian life, and from it we make the beginning of obeying the divine precepts. And this will have to be briefly stated about the name.

What is the definition of Baptism. But as far as the definition of the thing is concerned, although many can be adduced from the sacred writers, that which can be understood from the words of the Lord in John and the Apostle to the Ephesians seems more suitable and comfortable. For when the Savior says: Unless anyone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God; and the Apostle when he spoke of the Church: Cleansing it in the laver of water in the word; This is how it is rightly and accurately defined that Baptism is the Sacrament of regeneration by water in the word. For by nature we are born of Adam children of wrath; but through Baptism in Christ we are reborn children of mercy; For he gave men the power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name, who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.

For what reason the Sacrament of Baptism is perfected. But whatever the final words are with which the nature of Baptism is to be explained, the people must be taught that this Sacrament is made with ablution, to which by the institution of the Lord Savior certain and solemn words are necessarily applied, as the holy Fathers always taught, which is demonstrated by that very open testimony of Saint Augustine: The word accesses the element, and the Sacrament is made. And this must be warned with more diligence, lest the faithful be led into that error of considering, as is commonly said, that the same water that is kept in the sacred fountain to prepare Baptism is the Sacrament. Because then it must be said Sacrament of Baptism when we actually use water to ablute someone, adding the words that were instituted by the Lord. Now, then, since at the beginning we said that each of the Sacraments is constituted of matter and form, when it was about all the Sacraments in general, the Pastors will have to declare which one and which one is in Baptism.

What is the actual matter of Baptism. The matter, then, or element of this Sacrament, is all kinds of natural water, whether from the sea, from the river, from the lagoon, from the well or from the fountain, which without any adjunction is usually called water. For the Savior also taught: Unless anyone be born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God: and the Apostle says that the Church has been cleansed in the laver of water: and in the epistle of Saint John we read written: There are three who bear witness on earth, the spirit, the water, and the blood; which is also verified with other testimonies of sacred Letters.

Place of Saint Matthew on the baptism of fire. But what John the Baptist said, that the Lord would come who would baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire, is in no way to be understood from the matter of Baptism; but it must either refer to the intimate effect of the Holy Spirit, or certainly to the miracle that appeared on the day of Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit descended from heaven on the Apostles in a kind of fire: which in another place Christ our Lord foretold: John certainly baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not after many of these days. 9. With what figures and Prophecies the strength of the waters of Baptism has been demonstrated. Because the Flood, with which the world was purged, because there was much malice of men on earth and every thought of the heart was inclined to evil.

First reason. Second reason. Third reason. The Prince of the Apostles in the first epistle shows that he bore the figure and likeness of this water. And that the passage of the Red Sea had the significance of the water itself, Saint Paul explained in writing to the Corinthians. Why did God want us to use water, rather than any other material, to perform Baptism. How in accordance with the nature and virtue of Baptism it was that water was instituted as its own matter, Saint Jerome demonstrated with various reasons, writing to Oceanus. But in what concerns this place, the Pastors will be able to teach first of all that, since this Sacrament was necessary for everyone without exception to obtain life, therefore the material of water, which is never lacking and can easily be prepared by everyone, was maximally suitable. Then water maximally signifies the effect of Baptism: because just as water washes away filth, so it also optimally demonstrates the power and efficiency of Baptism, with which the stains of sins are washed away. Why is Chrisma added to water, simple and natural. The people will also have to be taught that, although it may sometimes be uncertain whether this or that is true water, what the perfection of the Sacrament requires; It must be held, however, for certain that the Sacrament of Baptism can never be made from any other material than the liquid of natural water.

Why the perfect form of Baptism must be clearly explained to all the faithful without distinction. But of the two parts that Baptism must consist of, after one, that is the matter, has been diligently explained, let the Pastors endeavor with the same diligence to also transmit the form, which is the other most necessary part. In the explanation of this Sacrament you will consider that it must be worked with greater care and study, because the knowledge of such a holy mystery not only by itself can vehemently delight the faithful, which commonly happens in all science of divine things, but it is also extremely desirable for almost daily uses. Because as times often occur, as will be said more clearly in its place, in which both by others of the people and very frequently by little women it is necessary to minister Baptism, so it is made that all the faithful without distinction must be known and perceived the things that belong to the substance of this Sacrament.

What is the perfect and absolute form of this Sacrament. Therefore, with elucidated and open words that can easily be perceived by all, the Pastors will teach that this is the perfect and absolute form of Baptism: I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Because this is how it was transmitted by the Lord and our Savior, when he commanded the Apostles in Matthew: Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. But from that word Baptizers, the divinely taught Catholic Church optimally understood that in the form of this Sacrament the action of the minister must be expressed, which is certainly done when it is said: I baptize you. And since in addition to the ministers it was appropriate to signify both the person of the one who is baptized and the main cause that effects the Baptism, that is why that pronoun Te and the different names of the divine Persons are added, so that the absolute form of the Sacrament may be concluded with these words that have now been explained: I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. For not only the Person of the Son, of whom John writes: This is he who baptizes, but at the same time all the Persons of the Holy Trinity operate in the Sacrament of Baptism.
The Apostles baptized in the name of Christ, that is, with the form transmitted by Christ.

When we worship the name of Jesus, we venerate all the majesty of God. But the fact that it was said In the Name, not In the Names, this clearly declares the one nature and divinity of the Trinity. For in this place the Name does not refer to the Persons, but signifies the divine substance, virtue, and power, which is one and the same in the three Persons.

If in the form of Baptism all words are equally necessary. But in this form, which we have shown to be complete and perfect, it must be observed that some things are absolutely necessary, which if they are omitted the Sacrament cannot be made: but some are not so necessary that if they are missing the reason for the Sacrament is not evident: of which kind is that voice I, whose force is contained in the verb Baptism. What's more, in the Churches of the Greeks, for various reasons, it became customary to omit it: because they judged that no mention should be made of the minister. From which it was made that in Baptism they use everywhere in this way: Let the servant of Christ be baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit: with which, however, the Sacrament is perfectly ministered, as appears from the sentence and definition of the Florentine Council: for with these words what concerns the truth of Baptism is sufficiently explained, namely, the ablution that is then actually performed.

How the Apostles baptized in the name of Christ. If it is also to be said that there was once a time when the Apostles baptized only in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, we must consider that they did so by the breath of the Holy Spirit, so that at the beginning of the nascent Church the preaching would become more illustrious with the name of Jesus Christ, and his divine and immense power would be more celebrated. Then, looking more deeply into the thing, we will easily understand that in that form none of the parts that the Savior Himself prescribed are missing. For who says Jesus Christ also means the Person of the Father, by whom he was anointed, and the Holy Spirit, with which he was anointed.

It must be believed that the Apostles never baptized in the name of Christ, ignoring the other two Persons of the Trinity. Although it may perhaps seem doubtful whether the Apostles baptized anyone with this type of form, if we want to follow the authority of Ambrose and Basil, most holy and most serious Fathers, who thus interpreted Baptism in the name of Jesus Christ, who said that these words meant Baptism not that which was transmitted by John, but that which was transmitted by Christ the Lord: although the Apostles did not depart from the common and used form that contains the different names of the three Persons. And Paul also seems to have used this type of speech in the Epistle to the Galatians, when he says: As many of you as were baptized into Christ, you put on Christ, to signify that you were baptized in the faith of Christ, and in no other way, however, than that which our Savior and Lord Himself had commanded to be kept. Up to this point, then, it will be enough to have taught the faithful about the matter and the form, which maximally belong to the substance of Baptism. 17. In what way should ablution be performed in this mystery of regeneration. But since in the preparation of this Sacrament it is also necessary to observe the reason for the legitimate ablution, therefore the doctrine of this part must also be transmitted by the Pastors, and it must be briefly explained by them that by common way and custom of the Church it has been received that Baptism can be prepared in one of three ways. For those who are to be initiated with this Sacrament are either immersed in the water, or the water is infused, or they are colored by sprinkling of the water. But of these rites, whichever is kept, it must be believed that Baptism is truly perfected. Because water is applied in Baptism to signify the ablution of the soul, which it performs; for which reason Baptism is called by the Apostle lavish. But ablution is no longer performed when someone is immersed in water, which we note was observed from the earliest times in the Church, either with the effusion of water, which we now see put into frequent use, or with sprinkling, as it is gathered that Peter did when in a single day he translated the truth of the faith and baptized about three thousand men.

Is single or triune ablution required? But it must be considered that it matters nothing whether single or triune ablution is performed. Because in one way or another, Baptism was truly made before in the Church, as it can now be made, as appears sufficiently from the epistle of Saint Gregory the Great written to Leander. However, the faithful must retain that rite that each one notices is kept in their Church.

Why is the head mainly ablowered here? And mainly it must be admonished that not any part of the body must be abluted, but mainly the head, in which all the senses, both interior and exterior, are invigorated, and at the same time that the words of the Sacrament that contain the form must not be pronounced by the one who baptizes before or after the ablution, but at the same time that the ablution itself is performed.

The power of water was increased by Christ. The entire Trinity at the Baptism of Christ present declared his name. Baptism before the passion of Christ was certainly used, but afterwards it received its force. When the law of receiving Baptism was promulgated. When Baptism began to obligate men.

Did Christ institute Baptism before or after the passion? Having stated this, it will also be appropriate to teach and recall to the memory of the faithful that Baptism, like the other Sacraments, was instituted by Christ the Lord. This, then, the Pastors will frequently teach, and they will explain that two different times of Baptism are to be noted: one, when the Savior instituted it; another, when the law was passed to receive it. And as regards the first, it is perceived that this Sacrament was instituted by the Lord when He Himself, baptized by John, gave water the virtue of sanctifying. Because Saints Gregory of Nazianzus and Augustine testify that at that time water was given the power to generate, namely, spiritual life. And in another place he left it written like this: Since Christ is immersed in the water, from then on the water washes away all sins. And elsewhere: The Lord is baptized, not needing to be cleansed, but cleansing the waters with the touch of clean flesh, so that they have the power to ablute. And for this thing, the fact that the Holy Trinity, in whose name Baptism is carried out, declared its numen present, could have been the maximum argument. Because the voice of the Father was heard, the Person of the Son was present, and the Holy Spirit descended like a dove; Furthermore, the heavens were opened, to which it is now lawful for us to ascend through Baptism. If anyone wishes to know the reason why such a great and divine virtue was attributed by the Lord to the waters, this certainly surpasses human intelligence: but this can be sufficiently perceived by us: that, having received Baptism by the Lord, with the touch of his most holy and most pure body the water was consecrated for the salutary use of Baptism; in such a way, however, that it must be believed that this Sacrament, although it had been instituted before the Passion, nevertheless derived its strength and efficiency from the Passion, which was the end of all the actions of Christ.

When the law of Baptism began to bind men. But also about the other, namely, at what time the law of Baptism was promulgated, there is no room for doubt. Because among the sacred Writers it is agreed that, after the resurrection of the Lord, when he commanded the Apostles: Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, from that time all men who were to obtain eternal salvation began to be held by the law of Baptism. Which is certainly inferred from the authority of the Prince of the Apostles, when he says: He regenerated us to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead. And the same can be known from that place of Paul: He gave himself for her, to sanctify her (when he spoke of the Church), cleansing her in the laver of water in the word of life. For both seem to have referred the obligation of Baptism to the time that followed the death of the Lord, so that there is no way to doubt that also those words of the Savior: Unless anyone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God, looked at that same time that was to be after the passion.

How much veneration must be had for the Sacrament of Baptism. Of this, then, if it is treated accurately by the Pastors, there can be no doubt that the faithful recognize maximum dignity in this Sacrament and venerate it with utmost piety of spirit: and mainly when they think that those illustrious and very extensive munera which, when Christ the Lord was baptized, were declared to have significance of miracles, are donated and imparted to each one, when they are baptized, with the intimate virtue of the Holy Spirit. For if, as happened to the servant of Elisha, our eyes were opened so that we could look at heavenly things, no one would consider himself so lacking in common sense that the divine mysteries of Baptism would not translate him into maximum admiration: why should we not consider that the same thing would also happen when the Pastors had exposed the riches of this Sacrament in such a way that the faithful, if not with the eyes of the body, then with the acuity of the mind illuminated with the splendor of faith, can they contemplate them?

How many kinds of men can administer Baptism. Now, by what ministers is this Sacrament made, not only usefully but necessarily it seems to be transmitted; both so that those to whom this munere has mainly been committed make an effort to take care of it holy and religiously: and so that no one, as if leaving its limits, unexpectedly enters another's possession or arrogantly breaks in: for the Apostle admonishes that order must be kept in all things. Let the faithful be taught, then, that their order is threefold: and in the first are to be placed the Bishops and Priests, who have been given to exercise this munere by their own right, not by any extraordinary power. Because it was commanded by the Lord in the Apostles: Go... baptize. Although the Bishops, lest they be forced to desert that more serious care of teaching the people, used to leave the ministry of Baptism to the Priests. But that the Priests exercise this function by their own right, so that even when the Bishop is present they can minister Baptism, is consistent with the doctrine of the Fathers and the usage of the Church. Because, as they were instituted to consecrate the Eucharist, which is the Sacrament of peace and unity, it was appropriate that they were given the power to administer all those things by which anyone could necessarily become a participant in this peace and unity. If the Fathers ever said that Priests had not been allowed the right to baptize without the permission of the Bishop, it seems that it must be understood from that Baptism that on certain days of the year was customary to administer with solemn ceremony. The second place among the ministers is obtained by the Deacons, to whom it is not licit to administer this Sacrament without the consent of the Bishop or the Priest, as many decrees of the Holy Fathers testify.

Who can confer the Sacrament of Baptism in case of need. The last order is that of those who, forced by necessity, can baptize without solemn ceremonies; in which number are also all of the people, whether men or women, whatever sect they profess. Because also the Jews, and the infidels, and the heretics, when necessity compels, have been permitted this munere; if, however, it had been proposed to them to carry out what the Catholic Church carries out in that type of administration. This is confirmed by many decrees of the ancient Fathers and Councils, and truly by the sacred Tridentine Synod anathema was sanctioned against those who dare to say that Baptism that is also given by heretics in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, with the intention of doing what the Church does, is not true Baptism. In which it is certainly permissible to admire the supreme goodness and wisdom of our Lord. Because, this Sacrament being necessary that it be perceived by all, just as He instituted water as its matter, of which nothing can be more common, so He also wanted that no one be excluded from its administration. Although, as has been said, it is not licit to apply solemn ceremonies to everyone, not because the rites or ceremonies have more dignity, but because they are less necessary than the Sacrament.

What order must be kept by the faithful when baptizing. Nor should the faithful consider that this munere has been allowed to everyone so promiscuously that it is not at all convenient to institute some order of ministers. Because the woman, if there are men present, the layman also present the Clergyman, and the Clergyman before the Priest, should not take upon himself the administration of Baptism. Although the obstetricians who are used to baptizing should not be surprised: if sometimes a man is present who is minimally skilled in carrying out Baptism in this way, which otherwise would seem like a job more typical of a man, they carry it out.

Why, in addition to those who baptize, Godparents are adduced in the mysteries of regeneration. Added, however, to those ministers who, as has been declared up to this point, perform Baptism, there is also another type of minister, who is usually cited as an ancient custom of the Catholic Church to celebrate the sacred and salutary ablution; These are now called Godparents, formerly Receivers, Spouses or Trustees with a common word by the writers of divine things. Of which munere, since it belongs to almost all the laity, the Pastors will have to deal with accuracy, so that the faithful understand what things are mainly necessary to perfect it correctly. And first of all, it must be explained what was the reason why, in addition to the Ministers of the Sacrament, the Godparents and Receivers were also attached to Baptism. Which will certainly seem to everyone to be done with optimal right, if they remember that Baptism is spiritual regeneration, by which we are born children of God. Saint Peter speaks of it like this: Like newborn children, desire rational milk without deceit. Thus, then, just as after someone has been given this light he needs a nurse and teacher, with whose help and work he is educated and instructed in doctrine and good arts: so it is also necessary that those who from the spring of Baptism begin to live the spiritual life commit themselves to the faith and prudence of someone, from whom they can drink the precepts of the Christian religion and be instructed in all reason of piety, and thus little by little grow in Christ, until finally, With the Lord helping them, they become perfect men: especially when the Pastors, who are publicly placed in the care of the Parishes, do not have so much time left over that they can take that private care of instructing children in the faith. We have clear testimony of this ancient custom in the divine Dionysius, when he says: It came to mind to our divine guides (as he calls the Apostles) and it seemed good to receive the infants according to this holy way, so that the natural parents of the child would hand him over to someone learned in divine things, like a pedagogue, under whom, as a divine father and recipient of holy salvation, the child would spend the rest of his life. And the same sentence confirms the authority of Higinio.
