What recipients should teach their spiritual children.
These things are found in Consecration dist. 4 c. You before, where the same authority seems to come from.

The spiritual cognation contracted in Baptism prevents and resolves marriage. Therefore, it was wisely established by the Holy Church that not only the one who baptizes with the baptized, but also the recipient with the one whom he receives and with his true parents are linked with affinity: in such a way that these legitimate nuptial privileges cannot be initiated among all, and the initiates are settled.

What are the parts of the Godparents, and what is required of them. Furthermore, the faithful must be taught what the parts of the Receiver are. Because this munere is treated so negligently in the Church, that only the bare name of this function has remained; But what saint is contained in it, men do not even seem to suspect. This, then, let the Receivers always universally think: that with this law they are primarily obliged to have spiritual children perpetually entrusted to them, and in the things that concern the institution of the Christian life, they take diligent care that they present themselves throughout life as they promised with solemn ceremony that they would be. Let us hear what Saint Dionysius writes about this, expressing the words of the Betrothal: I promise that I will induce the child, when he has reached sacred intelligence, with my assiduous exhortations, to completely renounce contrary things, profess and carry out the divine things that he promises. Likewise the divine Augustine: You, he says, before all things, both men and women who received children in Baptism, I admonish that you know that you have been trustworthy before God for those whom you seemed to receive from the sacred spring. And the truth is that it is most convenient that he who has taken up any office should never tire himself out in executing it diligently; and whoever professed himself to be a pedagogue and guardian of another, may minimally suffer from the helplessness of the one whom he once received into his faith and clientele, until he understands that he needs his work and prison. But what must be transmitted to the spiritual children, the divine Augustine understands in a few words when he spoke of this same office of the Receivers: because he says: They must admonish them to keep chastity, love justice, retain charity, and above all things teach them the Symbol and the Sunday prayer; also the Decalogue and what are the first rudiments of the Christian religion. 29. Not everyone promiscuously should be admitted to the munere of Receiver. These things being so, we easily understand to what type of men the administration of this holy guardianship should not be committed; namely, to those who either do not want to or cannot carry it faithfully and with assiduity and accuracy. Therefore, in addition to the natural parents, to whom it is not lawful to take this care (so that it may appear more clearly how far this spiritual education is from the carnal one); The heretics above all, the Jews, the infidels, must completely prohibit themselves from this munere, as those who are always versed in that thought and care to obscure with lies the truth of the faith and to upset all Christian piety.

What should be the number of the Godparents. It has also been established by the Tridentine Council that the baptized person should not receive several baptisms, but only one, whether male or female, or at most one and one: both because the order of discipline and institution could be disturbed by the multitude of teachers: and because it was advisable to ensure that among several affinities of this kind did not combine that would prevent the society of men among men from spreading with the legitimate bond of marriage.

Baptism is necessary for everyone for salvation. But since the knowledge of the other things that have been explained up to this point must be considered very useful to the faithful; Thus nothing can seem more necessary than teaching that the law of Baptism has been prescribed by the Lord for all men, so that, if by the grace of Baptism they are not reborn to God, they are procreated by their parents, whether faithful or unfaithful, to everlasting misery and extermination. Thus, what is read in the Evangelist will often have to be explained by Pastors: Unless anyone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. All infants must be baptized. That this law must not only be understood by those who are of adult age, but also by infant children, and that the Church has received it from Apostolic tradition, is confirmed by the common sentence and authority of the Fathers. Furthermore, it must be believed that Christ the Lord did not want children to be denied the Sacrament of Baptism and grace, of which he said: Let the little ones be and do not forbid them to come to me: for such is the kingdom of heaven, whom he embraced, upon whom he laid his hands and on whom he blessed. Later, when we read that some entire family was baptized by Paul, it appears sufficiently that also the children who were among those were washed with the healthy spring. Later the Circumcision, which was a figure of Baptism, highly commends this custom.

Because no one can ignore the fact that boys used to be circumcised on the eighth day. And those who benefited from the circumcision made by hand in the stripping of the body of the flesh, it is clear that Baptism, which is the circumcision of Christ not made by hand, benefits the same. Finally, as the Apostle teaches: If through one crime death reigned through one, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and gift and righteousness reign in life through one Jesus Christ. As, then, through the sin of Adam the children originally contracted noxa; much more through Christ the Lord they can obtain grace and justice, to reign in life: which certainly in no way can be done without Baptism. Therefore the Pastors will teach that infants must be baptized, and then little by little the tender age must be informed with the precepts of the Christian religion to true piety. Because, as it was clearly said by the Wise Man: The adolescent according to his way, even when he grows old, will not depart from it.

Infants in Baptism receive spiritual grace. Nor is it lawful to doubt that they receive the Sacraments of faith when they are washed: not because they believe with the assent of their mind; but because they are united with the faith of the parents, if the parents were faithful; and if not, with the faith (to speak in the words of Saint Augustine) of the entire society of Saints. For we rightly say that they are offered at Baptism by all those to whom it pleases them to be offered, and by whose charity they are attached to the communion of the Holy Spirit.

The Baptism of infants is not to be deferred. The faithful, however, must be greatly exhorted to take care to bring their children to the Church, as soon as it is lawful to do so without danger, and to baptize them with solemn ceremonies. Because, since infant children have been left with no other reason to achieve salvation than to be granted Baptism, it is easy to understand how gravely guilty those who suffer are obliged to be that they lack the grace of the Sacrament more daily than the necessity postulates; especially when the weakness of age prevents them from almost infinite dangers of life.

How adults should be established before Baptism. But a different reason must be observed in those who are of adult age and have perfect use of reason, namely, those who are born of infidels, as the ancient custom of the Church declares. Because the Christian faith must be proposed to them, and they must be exhorted, attracted and invited with all study to subscribe to it. What if they converted to the Lord God; then it must truly be admonished not to defer the Sacrament of Baptism beyond the time prescribed by the Church. Because, since it is written: Do not delay in converting to the Lord, and do not defer it from day to day, they must be taught that perfect conversion is placed in the new generation by Baptism; Furthermore, the later they come to Baptism, the more diurnally they must lack the use and grace of the other Sacraments with which the Christian religion is cultivated, since without Baptism no addition can be opened: then they also deprive themselves of the maximum fruit that we perceive from Baptism: for not only does the water of Baptism wash away and completely remove the stain and filth of all the crimes that were previously committed, but it also adorns us with divine grace, with whose help and help in the future we can also avoid sins and maintain justice and innocence: in which everyone easily understands that the sum of the Christian life consists.

It is shown that Baptism must be deferred for adults. But even if this is so, the Church did not customarily attribute the Sacrament of Baptism immediately to this type of men, but rather established that it be deferred to a certain time. Because that delay does not have together the danger that has been said above that threatens children, since for those who are gifted with the use of reason, the purpose and advice of receiving Baptism and the penance of a life badly led will suffice for grace and justice, if some sudden case prevents them from being washed with healthy water. On the contrary, this delay seems to provide some benefits. Firstly, since the Church must diligently ensure that no one approaches this Sacrament with a feigned and simulated intention, the will of those who ask for Baptism is more explored and perceived: for this reason we read decreed in the ancient Councils that those who come to the Catholic faith from Jews, before Baptism is administered to them, spend some months among the catechumens. Then they are instructed more perfectly in the doctrine of the faith that they must profess and in the institutions of the Christian life. Furthermore, greater religious worship is given to the Sacrament if only on the established days of Easter and Pentecost they receive Baptism with a solemn ceremony.
Baptism does not always have to be deferred to adults. But sometimes, however, for some just and necessary cause the time of Baptism should not be deferred.

CHAPTER 46

When Baptism should not be postponed too much. As if the danger of life seems imminent; and especially if those who have already fully perceived the mysteries of faith are to be washed. Which certainly is sufficiently proven that Philip and the Prince of the Apostles did, when one to the eunuch of Queen Candaces, the other to Cornelius, without interposing any delay, but immediately after they professed to embrace the faith, he baptized them.

How those who are to be baptized must be affected. Furthermore, it must be taught and explained to the people how those who are to be baptized should be affected. Firstly, then, it is necessary that they want and intend to receive Baptism. Because as each one dies to sin in Baptism and assumes a new reason and discipline of life, it is equitable that Baptism is not given to anyone who is invited or refuses, but only to those who receive it spontaneously and with a free spirit. Therefore we warn that by holy tradition it has always been observed that Baptism is not ministered to anyone unless they have first been asked if they want to be baptized. Nor should it be considered that this will is also lacking in infant children, since the will of the Church, which is responsible for them, cannot be obscure. 39. When children can or cannot be baptized. Furthermore, the insane and the furious, who, having once been compotes of the mind, later fell into madness, like those who at that time have no will to receive Baptism, should not be baptized if it does not pose danger to life: but when they find themselves in the discrimination of life, if before beginning to go mad they gave the meaning of that will, they must wash; If not, he must abstain from the administration of Baptism. And the same judgment must be made of those who sleep. That if they were never in the power of the mind, so that they had no use of reason, the authority and custom of the Church sufficiently declares that they must be baptized into the faith of the Church in no other way than children, who lack reason.

What else is required to receive Baptism. But in addition to the will of Baptism, also faith, for that reason that has been said about the will, is maximally necessary to obtain the grace of the Sacrament. For our Lord and Savior taught: He who believes and is baptized will be saved. Afterwards it is necessary that he repent of any crimes committed and of the life badly led, and that he establishes from now on abstaining from all sins: otherwise, whoever asked for Baptism in such a way that, however, he did not want to amend the habit of sinning, would have to be completely rejected. Because nothing is so repugnant to the grace and virtue of Baptism as the mind and counsel of those who never consider any purpose to sin. Since, therefore, Baptism must be desired for this reason, to clothe ourselves with Christ and conjugate ourselves with Him, it is clear that with merit the sacred ablution must be rejected from those who propose to persevere in vices and sins: and mainly because nothing that belongs to Christ and the Church is to be received in vain: and we sufficiently understand that Baptism must be in vain, if we look to the grace of justice and salvation, in him who thinks walk according to the flesh, not according to the spirit: although, as regards the Sacrament, he undoubtedly achieves his perfect reason, provided that, when he is baptized rightly, he has in mind to receive what is administered by the holy Church. Therefore the Prince of the Apostles, to that great multitude of men who, as the Scripture says, were pricked at heart, had asked him and the other Apostles what they should do, answered thus: Do penance, and let each one of you be baptized. And in another place: Repent, he says, and convert, so that your sins may be blotted out. Likewise, the blessed Paul, writing to the Romans, openly shows that he who is fully baptized must die to sin: for which reason he admonishes us: Let us not present our members as weapons of iniquity to sin, but let us present ourselves to God as living from the dead.

How useful it is to have this sermon often. But if the faithful meditate often on these things, first they will be forced to vehemently admire the supreme goodness of God, who, without deserving anything of this kind, bestowed, induced only by his mercy, such a singular and divine benefit of Baptism: then, when it is proposed before their eyes how free from all crime the life of those who are adorned with so great munere must be; They will also easily understand that above all it is required of the Christian man that he strive daily to translate life as holy and religiously as if on that same day he had obtained the Sacrament and the grace of Baptism. Although nothing will do more to inflame spirits with the study of true piety than if the Pastors had explained with exact prayer what the effects of Baptism are.

What is the main effect of Baptism. Of this, then, since it must often be discussed, so that the faithful may better perceive that they are placed in the highest degree of dignity, and not suffer at any time to be overthrown by the wiles of the adversary or by some impetus, this must first be transmitted: that the sin, already contracted from the origin of the first parents, already committed by ourselves, however nefarious it may be, in such a way that it does not even seem to be possible to think about, is remitted and condoned with the admirable virtue of this Sacrament. And this was pronounced long before by Ezekiel, by whom the Lord God speaks thus: I will pour upon you clean water, and you will be cleansed from all your uncleanness. And the Apostle to the Corinthians, after a long enumeration of sins, added: And such were some of you; but you were washed, but you were sanctified. And it is clear that this doctrine was perpetually transmitted by the holy Church. Because Saint Augustine in the book he wrote on the Baptism of Little Ones testifies thus: By generating the flesh only original sin is contracted, but by regenerating the Spirit there is remission not only of original sins, but also of voluntary sins. And Saint Jerome to Oceanus: All, he says, crimes were condoned in Baptism. And lest it be lawful for anyone to doubt this thing any longer; After the definition of other Councils, the sacred Tridentine Synod also declared it, when it decreed anathema against those who dared to feel otherwise, or did not hesitate to assert that, although sins are remitted in Baptism, they are not completely removed or uprooted, but rather scraped in some way, so that the roots of sins fixed in the spirit still remain. For (to use the words of the same holy Synod) God hates nothing in those who are reborn: because there is nothing of condemnation for these who were truly buried with Christ by Baptism into death, who do not walk according to the flesh, but by putting off the old man and putting on the new man, which was created according to God, they have become innocent, immaculate, pure, innocent and beloved of God.

If lust in the baptized is a sin. And it must certainly be confessed, as it was decreed in the same place by the authority of the same Synod, that concupiscence or fomes remains in the baptized. But that truly has no reason for sin. Because also by the sentence of the divine Augustine: in the baptized little ones the crime of concupiscence is absolved, it is left for combat. And he himself testifies elsewhere: The crime of concupiscence is absolved in Baptism, but the weakness remains. Because concupiscence, which is of sin, is nothing other than the desire of the mind, by its nature repugnant to reason: whose movements, however, if they do not have united the consensus of the will or negligence, are far from the true nature of sin. And when Saint Paul says: I did not know lust, if the law had not said: Thou shalt not covet; From these words he did not want the very force of coveting to be understood, but rather the vice of the will. Saint Gregory transmits the same doctrine writing as follows: If there are those who say that sins in Baptism are renounced only on the surface, what is more unfaithful than this preaching? for by the Sacrament of faith the soul, absolved from root sins, adheres only to God. And to demonstrate this he uses the testimony of our Savior, when in Saint John he says: He who is washed needs only to wash his feet, but he is completely clean. 44. It is demonstrated again that all sins are removed with Baptism. If it pleases anyone to look at the express figure and image of this thing, let him contemplate the story of Naaman the Syrian leper, who, when he had bathed himself seven times with the water of the Jordan, testifying to the Scripture, was cleansed from leprosy in such a way that his flesh looked like the flesh of a child. Therefore, the very effect of Baptism is the remission of all sins, whether contracted through an original vice or through our fault. For this reason, since it was instituted by our Lord and Savior, the Prince of the Apostles explained it in very clear words (other testimonies omitted) when he says: Do penance, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of your sins. 45. Like guilt, so too all punishment is remitted with Baptism. Truly in Baptism not only are sins remitted, but also all the penalties of sins and crimes are benignly condoned by God. Because although it is common to all the Sacraments that through them the virtue of the passion of Christ the Lord is communicated; of Baptism alone, however, it was said by the Apostle: We for Him die and are buried with Christ. From which the holy Church has always understood that it cannot be done without maximum insult to the Sacrament that offices of piety of this kind be imposed on him who is to be atoned by Baptism, which the Holy Fathers called works of satisfaction with the name used. Not even what is transmitted in this place is contrary to the custom of the ancient Church, which once commanded the Jews, when they were baptized, to fast forty continuous days. Because that institute did not belong to satisfaction; but those who have perceived Baptism.

They were thus admonished to, venerating the dignity of the Sacrament, give themselves for some time without interruption to fasting and prayers. Second effect of Baptism is the remission of all penalties due to sins. Satisfaction should not be imposed on the newly baptized. The pains of hell are remitted in Baptism. Why after Baptism the sorrows of this life remain. First reason.

Second reason. 46. ​​The baptized person is not freed from civil penalties. But although it must be considered explored that in Baptism the penalties for sins are condoned, no one is freed from that type of penalties, however, that must be paid in civil trials for some serious crime; so that he who is worthy of death is not removed by Baptism from the penalty that is constituted by the laws. Although the religion and piety of those Princes who also remitted and condoned that animosity to the prisoners would be vehemently praised, so that the glory of God would become more illustrious in his Sacraments.

The penalties that are usually imposed after this life are remitted in Baptism. Baptism also effects, after the course of this life, the liberation from all the penalties that follow original sin. Well, through the merit of the Lord's death it was possible for us to achieve this. But with Baptism, as has been said above, we died with Him: For if, as the Apostle says, we were planted together in the likeness of His death, we will also be planted together in the resurrection.

Why is Baptism not immediately restored to the state of whole nature? If anyone asks why immediately after Baptism in this mortal life we ​​are not also devoid of these inconveniences, and are not transferred by the virtue of sacred ablution to that perfect degree of life in which Adam, the first father of the human race, had been placed before sin: it will be answered that this has been done mainly for two reasons; of which the first is that we, who by Baptism are conjugated to the body of Christ and made its members, should not be given something more dignity than would have been given to our own head. As, then, Christ the Lord, although from the beginning of his origin he had fullness of grace and truth, did not, however, give up the fragility of the human nature that he assumed, before he suffered the torments of passion and death, and then was resurrected to the glory of immortal life: who will marvel when he sees that the faithful, who already by Baptism obtained the grace of heavenly justice, still, however, put on an outdated and fragile body, in order to that, after having performed many works for Christ and suffered death, they are again recalled to life, and finally are worthy of enjoying with Christ the everlasting evo? The other reason, however, for which the weakness of the body, the illness, the sense of pain, the movements of concupiscence, are left in us after Baptism, is that: namely, so that we would have as harvest and material of virtue, from which we would later obtain more magnificent fruit of glory and more ample rewards. Because, when with patient spirit we tolerate all the inconveniences of life, and with divine help we subject the crooked affections of our spirit to the rule of reason, we must rely on a certain hope that, if with the Apostle we had fought the good fight, consummated the course, kept the faith, the Lord will also restore to us the crown of justice on that day the just judge. In the same way it seems that the Lord acted with the children of Israel, whom, although he freed them from the bondage of the Egyptians, when Pharaoh and his army were submerged in the sea, he did not, however, immediately introduce them into that blessed land of promise, but first exercised them in many and various cases, and then, when he sent them to the possession of the promised land, the other inhabitants he certainly expelled from the native seats, but some nations He left them, which they could not destroy, so that the people of God would never lack the opportunity to exercise warlike virtue and strength. It is added that, if by Baptism, in addition to the heavenly gifts with which the soul is adorned, goods of the body were also given, it could be doubted with merit that many, seeking more the comforts of the present life than the expected glory of the future, would come to Baptism: when, however, to us must always be close not these true and uncertain things that are seen, but the true and eternal goods that are not seen.

The reborn, among the miseries of this life, do not deprive themselves of solid delight of spirit. But in the meantime, however, the condition of this life, which is full of miseries, is not devoid of its voluptuousness and joys. For what can be, for us who, through Baptism, like branches, are grafted into Christ, more jucund or eligible than, having taken the cross on our shoulders, to follow that guide, and not to tire ourselves with labor or delay ourselves with the dangers of contending with every study for the prize of the supernal vocation of God, some to receive from the Lord the laurel of virginity, others the crown of doctrine and preaching, others the palm of martyrdom, others others? decorum of virtues? Which illustrious badges of praise would be given to no one if we had not first exercised ourselves in the stadium of this hazardous life, and had been undefeated in battle. 50. What is offered to man with Baptism in addition to the remission of guilt and punishment. But for prayer to return to the effects of Baptism, it must be explained that with the virtue of this Sacrament we not only free ourselves from evils, which must truly be said to be maximum, but we also increase ourselves with excellent goods and munera. Because our spirit is filled with divine grace, with which, having become righteous and children of God, we are also instituted heirs of eternal salvation. For as it is written: He who believes and is baptized will be saved: and the Apostle testifies that the Church has been cleansed in the washing of water in the word of life. But grace is, as the Tridentine Synod decreed that it must be believed by all, a proposed penalty of anathema, not only that by which the remission of sins is made, but a divine quality inherent to the soul, and as a certain splendor and light that erases all the stains of our souls and makes them more beautiful and splendid. And this is openly inferred from the sacred Letters, when they say that grace is poured out and they usually call it the earnest of the Holy Spirit.

To the divine grace that is infused in Baptism, the virtues are added like pedisecs. To this is added the most noble procession of all the virtues, which are divinely infused into the soul with grace. Therefore when the Apostle to Titus says: He made us saved by the laver of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior: Saint Augustine, explaining those words, poured out abundantly: Namely, he says, for the removal of sins. 52. Through Baptism we join Christ. Truly through Baptism we also copulate and connect to Christ the head as members. Thus, then, as from the head comes the strength with which the singular parts of the body move to aptly execute their own functions, so also from the fullness of Christ the Lord the divine virtue and grace is diffused in all who justify themselves, which makes us skillful for all the offices of Christian piety. 53. How is it that, filled with so many virtues in Baptism, they exercise piety so late. Nor should it seem wonderful to anyone if, although we are instructed and adorned with such a great copy of virtues, yet not without great difficulty and labor we initiate, or certainly absolve, pious and honest actions. For this is not overthrown for this reason: that the virtues from which the actions themselves proceed have not been given to us for the benefit of God; but because after Baptism there has been a bitter fight between cupidity and the spirit. In which conflict, however, it is not appropriate for the Christian man to be broken or weakened in spirit; Therefore, trusting in the goodness of God, we must rely on the optimal hope that with the daily exercise of living righteously: Whatever things are modest, whatever is just, whatever is holy, they also seem easy and jucund, these we will think of willingly, these we will do with a clever spirit, so that the God of peace may be with us. 54. Baptism imprints an indelible character. Furthermore, through Baptism we are sealed with the character, which can never be erased from the soul, of which there is no reason to discuss more in this place; since it is licit to transfer to this place quite a few things that belong to this argument that have been said above (when it was universally about the Sacraments).

It is shown that Baptism can never be repeated. But since by the force and nature of the character it has been defined by the Church that the Sacrament of Baptism must not be repeated for any reason, the faithful will have to be warned of this often and diligently by the Pastors, lest they should ever be led into errors. And this the Apostle taught saying: One Lord, one faith, one Baptism. Later, when he exhorts the Romans that, having died through Baptism in Christ, they should take care not to lose the life they had received from Him, when he says: For inasmuch as Christ died to sin, he died once and for all; This seems to openly mean that, just as He cannot die again, so it is not lawful for us to die again by Baptism. For this reason the holy Church also openly professes that it creates only one Baptism. Which certainly is vehemently in accordance with the nature and reason of the thing, from which it is understood that Baptism is a certain spiritual regeneration. Therefore, as by natural virtue we are only once generated and given to light; and (as Saint Augustine says) the womb cannot be reiterated; so also one is the spiritual generation, and Baptism must never be repeated at any time.
Why Baptism must be received only once. It is sometimes licit to baptize under condition.
It is sometimes licit to baptize under condition.

How much parish priests err when they baptize with condition without distinction. Those who rebaptize are irregular. The fifth effect of Baptism is the opening of heaven, which had been closed by sin.
[References: Mt 3,16; Mk 1,10; Lk 3,21.]

It is not reiterated to those who wash themselves by interposing a certain condition. Nor should anyone think that it is reiterated by the Church when, with an ascribed formula of words of this kind, it washes someone whose it is uncertain whether he had previously been baptized: If you are baptized, I do not baptize you again: but if you are not yet baptized, I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Because in this way it should not be said that it is impiously reiterated, but rather that Baptism is administered holy and cautiously.

Conditional Baptism does not always have to be usurped without any discrimination. In which, however, the Pastors must diligently provide for some things, in which sin is committed almost daily, not without maximum insult to the Sacrament. Because there is no shortage of those who believe that no crime can be admitted if anyone without delict is baptized with that adjunction. Therefore, if an infant is brought to them, they do not at all consider that they have to ask whether it has been washed before, but they immediately give him Baptism: what is more, although they consider it proven that the Sacrament has been administered at home, they do not hesitate, however, to repeat in the Church the sacred ablution, having attached the solemn ceremony, with the adjunction: which they certainly cannot do without sacrilege, and they raise that stain that the writers of divine things they call irregularity. Because that form of Baptism by the authority of Pope Alexander is only permitted in those of whom, after diligent investigation, doubt remains as to whether they have received Baptism correctly; Otherwise it is never licit, even with the adjunction, to administer Baptism again to someone.

What is the last fruit that by virtue of Baptism is conferred on men. In addition to the other things that we get from Baptism, that is as an extreme to which all the others seem to refer: namely, that to each of us the little gate of heaven is opened, which had previously been closed by sin. But these things which are effected in us by virtue of Baptism can be clearly understood from those which the Evangelical authority confirmed to have taken place in the Baptism of the Savior. Because the heavens were opened, and the Holy Spirit appeared descending like a dove on Christ the Lord. From which it was meant that those who are baptized are imparted the charismas of the divine numen, and the door of heaven is opened; not certainly so that they are baptized immediately, but so that at a more opportune time they may enter into that glory, when, exempt from all the miseries that cannot fall into the blessed life, through the mortal condition they will attain immortality. And these are certainly the fruits of Baptism, of which, if we look at the power of the Sacrament, it cannot be doubted that they belong equally to all: but if we consider with what spirit each one has approached to receive it, it is altogether necessary to confess that more or less of the heavenly grace and fruit comes to one than to another. 59. What is the strength and usefulness of the ceremonies of Baptism. It now remains for the things that will be transmitted from the prayers, rites and ceremonies of this Sacrament to be explained openly and briefly. Because what the Apostle admonished about the gift of tongues, when he says that it is fruitless if what someone speaks is not understood by the faithful: the same thing can almost be transferred to rites and ceremonies; because they present the image and significance of those things that are done in the Sacrament. If the faithful people ignore the force and power of those signs, it will not seem that the usefulness of the ceremonies will be great. Work must therefore be done by the Pastors so that the faithful understand them, and are convinced with certainty that, if they are less necessary, a great deal of them must nevertheless be done, and it is appropriate that they be in great honor. Which certainly sufficiently teaches both the authority of the instituents, who without controversy were the holy Apostles, and the end for which they wanted the ceremonies to be adduced. Because in this way it is clear that the Sacrament is administered with greater religion and holiness, and those illustrious and excellent gifts that are contained in it are placed before the eyes, and the immense benefits of God are more impressed on the minds of the faithful. 60. How many types of Baptism rites are there. But all the ceremonies and prayers used by the Church in the administration of Baptism must be reduced to three chapters, so that a certain order can be observed by the Pastors in their explanation, and the things that have been transmitted by them are more easily retained in the memory of the listeners. And the first type of them is that of those that, before the source of Baptism is accessed.
are saved; the second, that of those that, when the same source has already been reached, are adduced; the third, that of those that, once Baptism has been perfected, are usually added.

At what time must the water necessary for Baptism be consecrated. First, then, the water that must be used for Baptism must be prepared. Because the fountain of Baptism is consecrated, adding the oil of the mystical anointing. Nor is this allowed to be done at all times; but, according to the custom of the elders, certain festival days are expected that with optimal right must be considered the most famous and holiest of all: on whose vigils the water for the sacred ablution is made; in which also only days, if necessity did not force it to be done otherwise, it was established in the custom of the ancient Church that Baptism be administered. But although the Church at this time, due to the dangers of common life, had not judged that that custom should be retained; However, he still observes with great religion those solemn days of Easter and Pentecost, in which the water of Baptism must be consecrated.
The fruits of Baptism, although common to all men, do not reach everyone equally.

Why those who are to be baptized are not immediately admitted into the Church. After the consecration of the water, the other things that precede Baptism must be explained immediately. Because those who are to be initiated with Baptism are brought, or also alleged, to the doors of the Church, and their entry is completely prohibited; because they are unworthy to enter the house of God before they have repelled from themselves the yoke of the most torpid servitude, and have become completely addicted to Christ the Lord and to his most just empire.

Why are those who are to be baptized asked questioned and instructed? The Priest now truly inquires from them what they ask of the Church, which, once known, first instructs them in the doctrine of the Christian faith that they must profess in Baptism: which is carried out with the Catechism. From whose customary institution no one can doubt that it flowed from the precept of the Lord Savior; when He Himself commanded the Apostles: Go into all the world and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit: teaching them to observe all things that I have commanded you. From which it is lawful to know that Baptism must not be administered before at least the highest chapters of our religion are explained.

In what way, according to the ancient institution of the Church, the rudest should be catechized.

And since the reason for the Catechism consists of many questions, if the one who is instructed is of adult age, he answers by himself what is asked; But if it is a boy, the godfather answers for him according to the rite, and makes the solemn promise.

What is the use of Exorcism.

The Exorcism follows, which is done with sacred and religious words and prayers to expel the Devil and break and weaken his forces.

Why is salt brought to the mouth of one who is baptized?

Other ceremonies are added to the Exorcism, each of which, because they are mystical, has its own illustrious significance. For when salt is introduced into the mouth of the one who is to be taken to Baptism, it is evident that this means that he, through the doctrine of faith and the gift of grace, must be freed from the putrefaction of sins, perceive the taste of good works and delight in the food of divine wisdom.

67. What does the sign of the Cross mean when applied to many parts of the body?

The forehead, eyes, chest, shoulders and ears are also marked with the sign of the Cross: all of which declares that through the mystery of Baptism the senses of the baptized are opened and strengthened, so that he may receive God and understand and keep his precepts.

Why are the noses and ears of those who are to be baptized anointed with saliva?

Afterwards, his nose and ears are smeared with saliva, and he is immediately sent to the fountain of Baptism, so that, just as that blind man of the Gospel whom the Lord ordered to wash his mud-smeared eyes with the water of Siloam regained his light, so we also understand that the power of the sacred ablution is such that it gives the mind light to perceive the heavenly truth.

What does that renunciation of Satan made by the one who offers to be baptized teach?

Once these things are done, other ceremonies and rites are applied next to the fountain of Baptism, from which the sum of the Christian religion can be known. For the Priest asks three times, with formulaic words, to the one who is to be baptized: Do you renounce Satan, and all his works, and all his pomps? And he, or the Godfather in his name, answers each question: I resign. Therefore, he who is going to give his name to Christ must first of all promise holy and religiously that he will abandon the Devil and the world, and that there will never be a time when he will not detest both as an abominable enemy.

After this, the one to be baptized is anointed with the oil of the catechumens on the chest and between the backs. In the chest, so that by the gift of the Holy Spirit he may cast out error and ignorance, and receive right faith, because the righteous live by faith. Between the backs, so that by the grace of the Holy Spirit it shakes off negligence and torpor, and exercises good operation; because faith without works is dead.

In what way the one who is to be baptized makes the profession of his faith.

Later, being next to the same font of Baptism, he is questioned by the Priest in this way: Do you believe in God the almighty Father? To which he responds: I think. And so on, asked about the other articles of the symbol, he professes his faith with solemn religion. And it is manifest that in these two promises all the force and discipline of the Christian law is contained.

Why is the person who is about to be bathed with the salutary water asked if he wants to be baptized.

But when it is time to administer Baptism, the Priest asks the one who is to be baptized if he wants to be baptized: and when he answers for himself, or in his name the Godfather if he is a child, he immediately washes him with the salutary water in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Because just as man, obeying the serpent of his own will, was justly condemned, so the Lord did not want anyone to be enrolled in the number of his own except as a voluntary soldier, so that, spontaneously obeying divine commands, he might obtain eternal salvation.

Why is the head of the baptized immediately anointed with Chrism?

Now, after the Baptism has been completed, the Priest anoints the top of the head of the baptized with Chrism, so that he understands that from that day on he is united to Christ as a head like a member, and grafted into his body, and that for that reason he is called a Christian of Christ, and Christ of Chrism. And what the Chrism means, Saint Ambrose attests, which is sufficiently understood by the things that the Priest then prays.

What designates the white vestment, or the small white shroud, which is given to the baptized.

Then the Priest dresses the baptized with a white garment, saying: Receive the white garment, which you may keep immaculate before the tribunal of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that you may have eternal life: and the children, who do not wear a garment, are given with the same words a small white shroud. With this symbol the holy Fathers teach that it means both the glory of the resurrection, to which we are reborn through Baptism, and the radiance and beauty with which, washed away the stains of sins, the soul is adorned in Baptism; and also the innocence and integrity that the baptized must maintain throughout life.

What is the reason for the lit candle in your hand.

And then a lighted candle is given to the hand, which shows that the faith inflamed by charity, which he received in Baptism, must be nourished and increased by the study of good works.

Why and what kind of name should be imposed on the baptized.

Finally a name is imposed on the baptized; which should be taken from one who, because of his excellent piety and religion of mind, has been counted in the number of Saints. Thus, in fact, it will be easy for each one, by the similarity of the name, to be excited to imitate virtue and holiness; and furthermore, let him also invoke whom he strives to imitate in prayer, and hope that he will come to him as an advocate to defend the salvation of both soul and body. For this reason, those who so carefully seek and impose Gentile names on children, and especially those who were the most evil of all, must be rebuked; For from this we can understand how little the study of Christian piety is valued by those who so delight in the memory of impious men, that they want the ears of the faithful to resonate everywhere with such profane names.

Sum of the things that have been discussed about these mysteries.

If the Pastors had explained these things about the Sacrament of Baptism, it would seem that almost nothing had been omitted that should be considered to belong in the highest degree to this knowledge. It has been demonstrated, in fact, what the very name of Baptism means; what is its nature and substance; and what parts it consists of. It has been said by whom it was instituted, what ministers are necessary to prepare the Sacrament, and who should be used as pedagogues to support the weakness of the baptized. It has also been transmitted to whom and in what disposition Baptism should be administered; what is its virtue and effectiveness; and finally, the rites and ceremonies to be observed have been explained quite abundantly, as requested by the proposed reason. And let the Pastors remember that all these things should be taught primarily for this cause: so that the faithful may be perpetually occupied in this care and thought, so that they may keep faith in those things which they so holy and religiously promised when they were initiated with Baptism, and may institute that life which corresponds to the most holy profession of the Christian name.

OF THE SACRAMENT OF CONFIRMATION.

CHAPTER III

1. Why today more than ever the virtue of Confirmation must be explained.

If the diligence of Pastors was once required in explaining the Sacrament of Confirmation, now it is certainly necessary to illustrate it as much as possible, when in the holy Church of God this Sacrament is completely omitted by many, and there are very few who strive to reap the fruit of the divine grace that they should draw from it. Therefore, the faithful must be instructed about the nature, strength and dignity of this Sacrament, both on the day of Pentecost, on which it is mainly administered, and also on other days, when the Pastors judge that it can be conveniently done, so that they understand that not only should it not be neglected, but it must be received with utmost piety and religion, lest through their fault and with maximum damage it should happen that this divine benefit appears to have been showered on them in vain.

2. Why the Church calls this Sacrament Confirmation.

But to begin with the name, it must be taught that the Church calls this Sacrament Confirmation for this reason: because he who has been baptized, when he is anointed by the Bishop with the sacred Chrism, adds those solemn words: I sign you with the sign of the Cross, and I confirm you with the Chrism of salvation, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit: if nothing else prevents the effectiveness of the Sacrament, it begins to be more firm with the vigor of a new virtue, and therefore a perfect soldier of Christ.

Confirmation is a true Sacrament of the new law.

In Confirmation, for its part, the Catholic Church always recognized the true and proper reason for the Sacrament: which both the Pontiff Melquiades and many other most holy and ancient Pontiffs openly declare. And Saint Clement could not prove the doctrine of this truth with a more serious sentence. He says in effect: Everyone must hasten without delay to be reborn for God, and then to be sealed by the Bishop, that is, to perceive the septiform grace of the Holy Spirit, otherwise he cannot be a perfect Christian who, out of injury and will, and not forced by necessity, has omitted this Sacrament, as we received from the blessed Peter, and the other Apostles taught by command of the Lord. And this same faith was confirmed by their doctrine by those who, filled with the same Spirit, shed their blood for Christ, namely Urban, Fabian and Eusebius, Roman Pontiffs, as can be seen from their decrees.

The sacred Doctors who made mention of this Sacrament.

Furthermore, the concordant authority of the holy Fathers is added, among whom Dionysius the Areopagite, Bishop of Athens, when teaching how this sacred ointment should be made and used, says: Thus, he says, the Priests dress the baptized with clothing congruent with purity, to take it to the Pontiff: and the latter, pointing out the baptized with the sacred and completely divine ointment, makes him a partaker of the Most Holy Communion. Eusebius of Caesarea also attributed so much to this Sacrament that he did not hesitate to say that the heretic Novatus could not deserve the Holy Spirit because, although he had been baptized, in serious illness he was not marked with the seal of the Chrism. But we have very clear testimonies of this thing, both from Saint Ambrose in that book that he wrote about those who are initiated, and from Saint Augustine in the books that he published against the letters of Petilian the Donatist, of which both considered that in such a way the truth of this Sacrament cannot be doubted, that they also teach it and confirm it with places in Scripture. Therefore the one relates those words of the Apostle: Do not grieve the Spirit

…Holy One of God, in whom you were sealed: and the other, what is read in the Psalms: As the ointment on the head, which descends on the beard, the beard of Aaron: and also that of the Apostle himself: The charity of God has been poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit who has been given to us, testified that they refer to the Sacrament of Confirmation.

5. What is the difference between Baptism and Confirmation.

Although it has been said by Melquíades that Baptism is united to the highest degree with Confirmation, it should not be considered, however, that it is the same Sacrament, but very different from the other. It is clear, in fact, that the variety of the grace that each Sacrament confers, and of the thing subject to the senses that that same grace means, makes the Sacraments also various and diverse. Thus, since by the grace of Baptism men are begotten to a new life, and by the Sacrament of Confirmation those who have already been begotten become men, having evacuated the things that were of children, it is sufficiently understood that as much as in natural life the generation of growth is distant, so much do Baptism, which has the power to regenerate, and Confirmation, by virtue of which the faithful grow and assume perfect vigor of mind, differ from each other. Furthermore, since a new and different kind of Sacrament must be constituted when the spirit incurs some new difficulty, it is easily perceived that, just as we need the grace of Baptism to inform the mind with faith, so it is also in the greatest degree appropriate that the spirits of the faithful be confirmed with another grace, so that by no danger or fear of punishment, torture or death they allow themselves to be dissuaded from the confession of the true faith. Which, as is done with the sacred Chrism of Confirmation, it is openly deduced that the reason for this Sacrament is different from Baptism.

Therefore the Pontiff Melquíades continues with careful prayer the distinction between the two, writing thus: In Baptism man is received for the military, and in Confirmation he is armed for fighting; At the fountain of Baptism the Holy Spirit confers fullness for innocence, but in Confirmation he ministers perfection for grace; In Baptism we regenerate for life, after Baptism we are confirmed for the fight; in Baptism we are washed, after Baptism we are strengthened; Regeneration in itself saves in peace those who receive Baptism, Confirmation arms and instructs for combat. And these things have not only been transmitted by other Councils, but decreed mainly by the sacred Tridentine Synod, so that not only is it no longer licit to feel otherwise about them, but not even to doubt them in any way.

Who is the author of the Sacrament of Confirmation.

And as it has been demonstrated above how necessary it was to teach in common about all the Sacraments from whom they originated, the same should also be transmitted about Confirmation, so that the faithful are more affected by the sanctity of this Sacrament. Therefore, the Pastors must explain that Christ the Lord was not only its author, but that, as witnessed by the holy Roman Pontiff Fabian, he precepted the rite and the words of the Chrism that the Catholic Church uses in its administration. Which can easily be proven to those who confess that Confirmation is a Sacrament, since all the sacred mysteries surpass the forces of human nature, and cannot be instituted by anyone other than God. And we must now say what its parts are, and first of all about the matter.

What is the matter of this sacred mystery.

This is called Chrism; name taken from the Greeks, and although profane writers mean by it any kind of ointment, nevertheless those who deal with divine things, by common custom of speaking, accommodated it only to that ointment that is made of oil and balm with the solemn consecration of the Bishop. Wherefore two corporeal things mixed together supply the matter of Confirmation: and this composition of diverse things, just as it declares the manifold grace of the Holy Spirit which is conferred on those confirmed, so it also sufficiently shows the excellence of the same Sacrament. And that this is the matter of this Sacrament, both the holy Church and the Councils have perpetually taught it, as Saint Dionysius and many other very serious Fathers have transmitted it: and in the first place the Pontiff Fabian, who testified that the Apostles received the confection of the Chrism from the Lord and left it to us.

What does the oil mean in the matter of Confirmation.

And in truth no other matter could seem more suitable than that of Chrism to declare what is effected with this Sacrament. Because the oil, because it is greasy and because of its nature it flows and pours out, expresses the fullness of the grace that through the Holy Spirit redounds and is poured out from Christ's head to others, like the ointment that descends into Aaron's beard, to the hem of his garment. For God anointed him with the oil of joy more than his companions: and of his fullness we have all received.

What does the balm mixed with the oil warn about here?

The balm, in truth, whose smell is most juicy, what else does it mean but that the faithful, when they are perfected with the Sacrament of Confirmation, pour out that sweetness of all the virtues, so that they can say that of the Apostle: We are to God a good odor of Christ?

CHAPTER 2

Furthermore, the balm has the virtue of not allowing anything that has been smeared with it to rot; which seems very suitable to signify the virtue of this Sacrament, since it is clear that the minds of the faithful, prepared with the heavenly grace conferred in Confirmation, can easily be defended from the contagion of crimes.

Why is it necessary for the Chrism to be consecrated by the Bishop.

The Chrism is therefore consecrated with solemn ceremonies by the Bishop. Thus, in effect, the Pontiff Fabian transmitted, very clearly due to his holiness and the glory of martyrdom, that our Savior taught it at the Last Supper, when he entrusted the Apostles with the reason for making the Chrism. Although why it should have been done this way can also be shown by reason. For in most of the other Sacraments Christ instituted their matter in such a way as to grant them sanctity also. For he not only wanted water to be the element of Baptism, when he says: If anyone is not born of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God; but when he himself was baptized, he made it from then on to be endowed with the power to sanctify. Therefore Saint Chrysostom said: The water of Baptism could not purge the sins of believers if it had not been sanctified by the touch of the Body of the Lord. Therefore, since the Lord did not sanctify this matter of Confirmation with the very use and treatment, it is necessary that it be consecrated with holy and religious prayers, and that this confection cannot belong to anyone other than the Bishop, who has been established ordinary minister of the same Sacrament.

11. What is the form of this Sacrament.

But it will also be necessary to explain the other part of which the Sacrament is constituted, namely the form, and the words that are applied to the sacred anointing; and the faithful must be admonished so that, when receiving this Sacrament, then above all, when they notice that it is pronounced, they excite the spirits to piety, faith and religion, lest something could be an impediment to heavenly grace. With these words, then, the form of Confirmation is completed: I sign you with the sign of the Cross, and I confirm you with the Chrism of salvation, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. But if we also reduce truth to reason, the same can be easily proven. Because the form of the Sacrament must contain all those things that explain the nature and substance of the Sacrament itself.

How it is confirmed that this is the perfect form of this Sacrament.

And in Confirmation these three things must be observed above all: the divine power, which acts as the main cause in the Sacrament; the vigor of mind and spirit, which by the sacred anointing is conferred on the faithful for salvation; and finally the sign that marks the one who is to descend to the contest of the Christian militia. And first of all those words: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, which are put last; Secondly these: I confirm you with the Chrism of salvation, which are in the middle; Thirdly, those that are placed at the beginning of the form: I sign you with the sign of the cross, they sufficiently declare it. Although even if for some reason it could not be proven that this is the true and absolute form of this Sacrament, the authority of the Catholic Church, by whose teaching we have always been taught, would not allow us to doubt this thing in any way.

13. Who is the minister of the Sacrament of Confirmation.

Pastors must also teach to whom the administration of this Sacrament has primarily been entrusted. Because, as there are many, according to the Prophet, who run and yet are not sent, it is necessary to transmit who their true and legitimate ministers are, so that the faithful people can obtain the Sacrament and the grace of Confirmation. Thus, only the Bishop has the ordinary power to make this Sacrament, as the sacred letters show. For in the Acts of the Apostles we read that, when Samaria had received the word of God, Peter and John were sent to them, and they prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit: for it had not yet come upon any of them, but they had only been baptized. In which place it can be seen that the one who had baptized, because he was only a Deacon, had no power to confirm; but that office was reserved for more perfect ministers, that is, for the Apostles. Furthermore, wherever the sacred Scriptures mention this Sacrament, the same thing can be observed. The same is also shown by the decrees of the Supreme Pontiffs. And there is no lack of very clear testimonies from most holy Fathers and Pontiffs, from Urban, Eusebius, Damasus I, Innocent I, Leo I, to demonstrate this thing; as is manifest by his decrees. Saint Augustine also seriously complains about the corrupt custom of those of Idumea and Alexandria, whose Priests dared to administer the Sacrament of Confirmation. And with good reason this was done, so that

…office was deferred to the Bishops, Pastors can declare it with this similarity. Because just as in the construction of buildings, although the workers, who are inferior ministers, prepare and arrange the cement, lime, wood and other materials, nevertheless the completion of the work corresponds to the architect; so also this Sacrament, by which it is perfected as a spiritual building, was not to be administered by any other but by the high Priest.

Why godparents are assumed in Confirmation, and what affinity is contracted in Confirmation.

A Godfather is also added, as has been shown to be done in Baptism. Because if those who submit to a gladiatorial combat need someone by whose art and advice they are taught with what blows and attacks, saving themselves, they can finish off the adversary; How much more will the faithful, when with the Sacrament of Confirmation, covered and armed as with very strong weapons, descend into the spiritual contest in which eternal salvation is proposed, need a guide and monitors? Rightly, then, godparents should also be invoked for the administration of this Sacrament, with whom the same spiritual affinity is contracted that prevents legitimate nuptial pacts, as we previously taught when dealing with the godparents that should be used in Baptism.

16. The Sacrament of Confirmation is not necessary as a means, but it should not be omitted.

But as it often happens that the faithful, when receiving this Sacrament, use either too hasty haste, or a certain dissolute negligence and delay (since of those who have reached such a degree of impiety that they dare to despise and abhor it, there is nothing we can say), it is also necessary to open to the Pastors who, of what age, with what study of piety those to whom it is appropriate to give Confirmation should be endowed. And above all it must be taught that this Sacrament has no such need that without it no one can be saved. Although it is not necessary, it should not nevertheless be omitted by anyone, but rather the utmost care should be taken to ensure that no negligence is committed in a thing full of holiness, by which the divine gifts are so abundantly imparted to us. Because what God proposed in common to all for sanctification, must also be desired by all with great study.

It shows that the Sacrament of Confirmation must be received by everyone.

Describing the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, he says: And suddenly there was a noise from heaven, like a rushing wind, and it filled the whole house. Afterwards, few things were interposed: And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit. From whose words it can be understood that, since that house carried the figure and image of the holy Church, the Sacrament of Confirmation, whose beginning was taken from that day, belongs to all the faithful. And this is also easily deduced from the very reason for the Sacrament; because those for whom spiritual growth is necessary, and who are to be brought to the perfect habit of the Christian religion, must be confirmed with that sacred Chrism. And this is not in the best interest of anyone. Because just as nature sees that those who are given birth grow and reach the perfect age, even if sometimes they do not get what they want; Thus the common mother of all, the Catholic Church, vehemently desires that in those whom she regenerated through Baptism the form of the Christian man may be perfectly completed. And since this is effected by the Sacrament of the mystical anointing, it is evident that it belongs equally to all the faithful.

At what age should Christians be admitted to this Sacrament.

In which it must be observed that, in truth, the Sacrament of Confirmation can be administered to everyone after Baptism; but it is less convenient for this to be done before the children have the use of reason. Therefore, if it does not seem that the twelfth year is to be expected, it is most advisable to defer this Sacrament at least until the seventh. Because Confirmation was not instituted for the need of salvation, but so that by its virtue we would be optimally instructed and prepared when we had to fight for the faith of Christ, for which type of fight no one would judge children who still lack the use of reason suitable.

19. In what way those who are already older should prepare themselves piously for this Sacrament.

From these things it follows, therefore, that those who are to be confirmed as adults, if they wish to obtain the grace and gifts of this Sacrament, must not only contribute faith and piety, but also grieve from the heart for the most serious sins they have committed. In which we must work so that they also confess their sins first, and with the exhortation of the Pastors they are encouraged to undertake fasts and other works of piety, and they are admonished to renew that laudable custom of the ancient Church of not receiving this Sacrament except on fasting: which must be considered that the faithful could easily be persuaded, if they understood the gifts and admirable effects of this Sacrament.
