How many are the effects of Confirmation.

Thus, Pastors will teach that Confirmation has in common with the other Sacraments that it confers new grace, if no impediment intervenes. For it has been demonstrated that these sacred and mystical signs are of such a condition that they declare and effectuate grace. From which it follows that they also condone and forgive sins; For it is not even licit to pretend grace together with sin. But in addition to these things, which must be considered common with the others, in the first place it is properly attributed to Confirmation that which perfects the grace of Baptism. Because those who have been made Christians by Baptism, like newly begotten children, still have a certain tenderness and gentleness, and later with the Sacrament of Chrism they become more robust against all the attacks of the flesh, of the world and of the Devil; and his spirit is completely confirmed in faith to confess and glorify the name of our Lord Jesus Christ: from which no one will doubt that the same name was also invented.

Where does the name Confirmation come from?

Because no, as some no less imperita than impiously pretended, the word Confirmation is deduced from the fact that in ancient times those who had been baptized as children, when they were adults, were taken to the Bishop to confirm the Christian faith they had received in Baptism, so that Confirmation does not seem to differ in any way from Catechesis; of which custom no approved testimony can be adduced: but the name was imposed on the thing because by the virtue of this sacrament God confirms in us what he began to work with Baptism, and brings us to the perfection of Christian solidity. And it not only confirms, but also increases; of which Melquiades testifies thus: The Holy Spirit, who descends upon the waters of Baptism with salutary descent, at the fountain confers fullness for innocence, at Confirmation he lends the increase for grace. Afterwards it not only increases, but increases in a certain admirable way. And the Scripture meant and expressed this very beautifully with the metaphor of the dress. Because the Lord Savior says, when speaking of this Sacrament: Remain in the city until you are clothed with the virtue from above.

22. The virtue of Confirmation must be declared by the things that happened to the Apostles.

And if the Pastors want to show the divine effectiveness of this Sacrament (which undoubtedly must have maximum power to move the spirits of the faithful), it will be enough to explain what happened to the Apostles themselves. Because they, before the passion, or during the very hour of the passion, were so weak and reluctant, or when the Lord was captured they immediately took flight: and Peter, who had been designated as the Stone and foundation of the Church, and had shown utmost perseverance and greatness of exalted spirit, terrified by the voice of a single little woman, denied not once or twice, but three times that he was a disciple of Jesus Christ: and after the resurrection they all, for fear of the Jews, kept themselves shut up in house. But on the day of Pentecost everyone was filled with so much virtue of the Holy Spirit that, while they boldly and freely spread the Gospel that had been entrusted to them not only in the region of the Jews, but throughout the world, they considered that nothing happier could happen to them than to be considered worthy of suffering contumelia, chains, torments and crosses for the name of Christ.

Confirmation prints character, and cannot be reiterated.

Furthermore, Confirmation has that power of imprinting character; Therefore it happens that it can in no way ever be reiterated: which was also observed above in Baptism; and the Sacrament of Orders will also be explained more clearly in due time. Therefore, if these things were explained often and accurately by the Pastors, it will hardly be possible that the faithful, knowing the dignity and usefulness of this Sacrament, would not strive to receive it with utmost diligence, saintly and religiously. It now remains to briefly touch on some things about the rites and ceremonies that the Catholic Church uses when administering this Sacrament; whose explanation how useful it will be will be understood by the Pastors if, when this place is discussed, they want to repeat the things that were previously said.

Why the forehead of those who are confirmed is anointed like a cross.

Those who are confirmed, therefore, are anointed on their foreheads with the sacred chrism: because with this Sacrament the Holy Spirit is poured into the spirits of the faithful, and increases their vigor and strength, so that in the spiritual contest they fight manfully and can resist the very weakest enemies. Therefore it is declared that they should not be deterred by any fear or shame, the affections of which usually appear especially on the forehead, from the free confession of the Christian name. Furthermore, that note with which the Christian is distinguished from others, like the soldier from others by certain insignia, had to be printed on the most visible part of the body.
Ambrose, lib. 4 of the Sacraments, c. 6. Alexander Pope, ep. 1, and is found in Cons. dist. 2, c. Nihil.

At what time is this Sacrament primarily conferred.

But it has also been observed with solemn religion in the Church of God that this Sacrament is administered mainly at Pentecost; because on this day above all the Apostles were strengthened and confirmed with the virtue of the Holy Spirit, with the memory of whose divine act the faithful would be admonished of what and how great mysteries should be meditated in the sacred anointing.

Why the Bishop slaps the confirmed person and prays for peace.

Afterwards, the one who has been anointed and confirmed, so that he remembers that he must be prepared as a strong athlete to suffer with an undefeated spirit all adversities for the name of Christ, is lightly wounded on the cheek with the hand of the Bishop. Finally, peace is given to him, so that he understands that he has achieved the fullness of heavenly grace and the peace that surpasses all sense. And this is the sum of the things that about the sacrament of chrism must be explained by the Pastors, not so much with naked words and prayer, but with a certain inflamed study of piety, so that they seem to insert them into the spirits and most intimate thoughts of the faithful.

OF THE SACRAMENT OF THE EUCHARIST.

Why the mysteries of the Eucharist must be treated and received with utmost reverence.

Just as of all the sacred mysteries that the Lord our Savior entrusted to us as most certain instruments of divine grace, there is none that can be compared with the most holy Sacrament of the Eucharist: so also no graver animosity of any crime should be feared from God than if a thing filled with all holiness, or rather containing the same author and source of holiness, is not treated by the faithful either holy or religiously. And the Apostle saw this wisely, and he openly warned us about it: because after declaring what a great crime those who do not discern the Body of the Lord were obligated to commit, he immediately added: For this reason there are many sick and disabled among you, and many sleep. So that, therefore, the faithful people, when they have understood that divine honors must be paid to this heavenly Sacrament, may reap the rich fruits of grace and escape the most just wrath of God, all those things that seem to best illustrate his majesty must be explained by the Pastors with great care.

2. For what reason and when the Sacrament of the Eucharist was instituted.

In which it will be necessary that, following the reason of the Apostle Paul, who professed to have given to the Corinthians what he had received from the Lord, they explain first of all to the faithful the institution of this Sacrament. And that the thing was done in this way is clearly inferred from the Evangelist: Because as Jesus had loved his own, he loved them to the end: and to give this love a divine and admirable pignus, knowing that the time had come to pass from this world to the Father, never to be absent from his own at any time, he carried it out with inexplicable advice, which surpasses all the order and condition of nature. For, having celebrated with the disciples the Passover supper of the lamb, so that the figure might yield to the truth and the shadow to the body, he took the bread, and giving thanks to God, blessed it and broke it, and gave it to his disciples, and said: Take and eat, this is my Body, which will be given for you; Do this in memory of me. In the same way he also took the chalice, after supper, saying: This chalice is the new testament in my Blood: do this as many times as you drink, in memory of me.

Why is this Sacrament called the Eucharist?

As the sacred Writers understood that in no way could a single word demonstrate the dignity and excellence of this admirable Sacrament, they strove to express it with several names. Sometimes, in fact, they call it the Eucharist; word that we can translate into Latin either for good grace, or for thanksgiving. And rightly in truth it should be called good grace, both because it prefigures eternal life, of which it is written: The grace of God, eternal life, and because it contains within itself Christ the Lord, who is the true grace and the source of all charisms. No less aptly do we interpret it as thanksgiving: for when we immolate this most pure host, we give immense thanks to God every day for all the benefits he has given us,

CHAPTER 3.

…and first of all for such an excellent good of his grace, which he confers on us with this Sacrament. But this same name fits optimally with the things that we read that Christ the Lord accomplished in instituting this mystery. Because taking the bread, he broke it and gave thanks. David also, when he contemplated the magnitude of this mystery, before pronouncing that song: The merciful and compassionate Lord made a memorial of his wonders, he gave food to those who fear him, he considered that thanksgiving should come first, when he says: Confession and magnificence is his work.

Why is this Sacrament named Communion, sacrament of peace and charity.

It is also frequently declared under the name of sacrifice, the mystery of which will be spoken of more fully shortly afterwards. It is also called Communion, a word that is evidently taken from that place of the Apostle where he says: Is not the chalice of blessing that we bless the communication of the Blood of Christ? and the bread that we break, is it not a participation in the Body of the Lord? Because, as Damascene explained, this Sacrament unites us to Christ and makes us partakers of his flesh and deity, and reconciles us and unites us among ourselves in the same Christ, and as it were brings us together in a single body. As a result, it was also called the Sacrament of Peace and Charity, so that we would understand how unworthy those who exercise enmities are of the Christian name; and that hatred, dissidence and discord, as abominable pests of the faithful, must be completely exterminated, especially when with the daily sacrifice of our religion we profess that we should preserve nothing with more study than peace and charity.

In what way the same Sacrament is called Viaticum and Supper.

But it is also frequently called Viaticum by the sacred Writers, both because it is the spiritual food with which we sustain ourselves in the pilgrimage of this life, and because it paves the way for us to eternal glory and happiness. Therefore we see that it is observed by ancient institution of the Catholic Church that no one of the faithful leaves life without this Sacrament. And the very ancient Fathers, following the authority of the Apostle, sometimes also called the sacred Eucharist by the name of Supper, because it was instituted by Christ the Lord in that salutary mystery of the Last Supper.

The Eucharist cannot be made or consumed with ordinary food or drink.

Nor is it licit to prepare or consume the Eucharist in the manner of ordinary food or drink, because the custom introduced in greeting by the Apostles, as transmitted to memory by the ancient writers, has been retained and preserved perpetually, so that it is perceived only by those who are fasting.

The Eucharist is a true Sacrament in name.

But, once the reason for the name has been explained, it will be necessary to teach that this is a true Sacrament, and one of those seven that the holy Church has always cultivated and venerated religiously. Because, when the consecration of the chalice is done, it is called the mystery of faith. Furthermore, by omitting almost infinite testimonies from sacred writers who perpetually felt that this should be counted among the true sacraments, the same is convinced of the very reason and nature of the Sacrament. Because in it there are signs external and subject to the senses: it then has the significance and efficacy of grace: and apart from the institution of Christ, neither the Evangelists nor the Apostle leave room for doubt. All of which things, since they concur in one to confirm the truth of the Sacrament, it is seen that there is no need for other arguments.

That there are many things in this Sacrament to which the name Sacrament is appropriate.

But Pastors must diligently observe that there are many things in this mystery to which the sacred Writers sometimes attributed the name of Sacrament. Sometimes, in fact, it has been customary to call Sacrament both the consecration and the perception, and frequently also the Body and Blood of the Lord that is contained in the Eucharist. Because Saint Augustine says that this Sacrament consists of two things: of the visible species of the elements, and of the invisible Flesh and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ himself. And in the same way we affirm that this Sacrament must be adored, understanding of the Body and Blood of the Lord. But it is clear that all these things are called Sacraments in a less proper way. But the same species of bread and wine have the true and absolute reason for this name.

How the Eucharist differs from all other Sacraments.

But how much this Sacrament differs from the others is easily deduced. Because the other Sacraments are perfected with the use of matter, namely when it is necessary to administer them to someone. Baptism, in fact, acquires the nature of a Sacrament then, when in fact the man is washed with water. More for the

…the consecration of its own matter is sufficient for the perfection of the Eucharist; because it is still a true Sacrament, even if it is reserved in the tabernacle. Later, when making the other Sacraments, no mutation is made of the matter and the element into another nature: because the water of Baptism, or the oil of Chrism, when those Sacraments are administered, do not lose the previous nature of water and oil: but in the Eucharist, what before the Consecration was bread and wine, once the Consecration is made, is truly the substance of the Body and Blood of the Lord.

The double matter of the Eucharist does not constitute two Sacraments.

Although there are two elements, namely bread and wine, from which the entire Sacrament of the Eucharist is made, however, taught by the authority of the Church, we confess that they are not several Sacraments, but one. Otherwise the septenary number of the Sacraments could not be recorded, as has always been transmitted and decreed by the Lateran, Florentine and Tridentine Councils. Because as by the grace of this Sacrament a single mystical body is made, in order for the Sacrament itself to be appropriate to the thing it accomplishes, it must be one; and one, indeed, not because it is undivided, but because it has the significance of one thing. Because just as food and drink, which are two different things, are applied to one thing, namely to restore the strength of the body; Thus it was also convenient that two different species of the Sacrament corresponded to them, which meant the spiritual food with which the minds were sustained and recreated. Therefore the Lord Savior said: My Flesh truly is food, and my Blood truly is drink. But it is necessary to diligently explain what the Sacrament of the Eucharist means, so that the faithful, contemplating the sacred mysteries with their eyes, may at the same time satisfy their spirits with the contemplation of divine things.

Of what things the significance is given.

There are truly three that this Sacrament indicates to us. The first is the passion of Christ the Lord, which has already passed; for he himself taught: Do this in memory of me: and the Apostle testified: As often as you eat this bread and drink the Cup, you will announce the death of the Lord, until he comes. The second is the divine and heavenly grace, which is presently conferred with this Sacrament to nourish and preserve the soul. Because just as through Baptism we are born to a new life, through Confirmation we are strengthened to be able to resist Satan and openly profess the name of Christ; Thus with the Sacrament of the Eucharist we are fed and sustained. The third is the one that predicts the future, the fruits of eternal youth and glory that we will reap in the heavenly homeland as a promise from God. These three, then, which are manifestly distinguished by the variety of the present, past and future time, are signified in such a way by the sacred mysteries, that the whole Sacrament, although it consists of diverse species, refers to declaring each of them as to the significance of a single thing.

What is the matter of this Sacrament, and what kind of bread is to be consecrated.

But above all, the matter of this Sacrament must be known by the Pastors, both so that they themselves can prepare it correctly, and also so that the faithful are warned of what it is a symbol of, and become inflamed in the study and desire of the thing it signifies. Therefore, the matter of this Sacrament is twofold: one is the bread made of wheat, which will be discussed first; The other will have to be talked about later. Because, as the Evangelists Matthew, Mark and Luke teach, Christ the Lord took the bread in his hands, blessed it and broke it, saying: This is my Body. Also in John our Savior himself called himself bread, when he said: I am the living bread that came down from heaven. But since there are several kinds of bread, or because they differ in the material, as when one is made of wheat, another of barley, or of legumes and other fruits of the earth, or because they are endowed with different qualities (since leaven is added to one, and the other may lack leaven altogether): as to the first, the words of the Savior show that bread must be made of wheat. Because by common custom of speaking, when bread is said in an absolute way, it is sufficiently evident that wheat bread is meant. This is also declared by the figure of the Old Testament. Because it had been commanded by the Lord that the shewbread, which signified this Sacrament, was made of fine flour.

It is convenient that the bread from which the Eucharist is made be unleavened.

But just as no bread, except wheat, should be considered a suitable material for the Sacrament (this was taught to us by apostolic tradition, and confirmed by the authority of the Church),
Lev. 24, 5-6. Honorius III, ep. to the Brisians, as is famous. Missar. c. end. and St. Thomas in 3. Mt. 26, 27; Mc. 14, 12; Lk. 22, 7. Ex. 12, 15. Jn. 13, 1.

…so also from the things that Christ the Lord accomplished it is easy to understand that it must be unleavened. Because he himself, from the first day of Unleavened, on which it was not lawful for Jews to have anything fermented at home, made and instituted this Sacrament.

And if anyone opposes the authority of the Evangelist John, who commemorates that all these things were done before the day of the feast of the Passover, that reason can easily be dissolved. For the day which the other Evangelists called the first day of Unleavened, because on Thursday evening began the day of the feast of Unleavened, in which time our Savior celebrated the Passover, that same day John describes as the eve of the Passover; for considering that the space of the natural day, which begins with the rising sun, should be noted first. Therefore, Saint Chrysostom also interprets the first day of the Unleavened as that day when at sunset the unleavened fruits were to be eaten. But how much the consecration of unleavened bread is appropriate to the integrity and purity of mind that the faithful must bring to this Sacrament, we teach from the Apostle when he says: Purge out the old leaven, that you may be new dough, as you are unleavened: for our Passover, Christ, has been sacrificed: so let us celebrate not in old leaven, nor in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

Unleavened bread is not entirely necessary for the Eucharist.

Nor, however, should it be considered that this quality is so necessary that, if it is missing from the bread, the Sacrament cannot be made. Because both kinds of bread have the true and proper reason and name of bread. Although it is not permissible for anyone, by private authority, or rather recklessness, to change the laudable rite of his Church. And it is even less permitted to do so to the Latin priests, who were also ordered by the Supreme Pontiffs to make the sacred mysteries only from unleavened material. And it is enough to have explained these things about one of the materials of this Sacrament: in which, however, it must be noted that it has not been defined how much material must be used to make the Sacrament, since neither can a certain number of those who can or should perceive the sacred mysteries be defined.

What material should be used for the consecration of the Blood of the Lord.

It remains to be said about the other matter and element of this Sacrament. It is the wine squeezed from the fruit of the vine, to which a little water has been mixed. Because the Lord Savior used wine in the institution of this Sacrament, the Catholic Church always taught it, when he himself said: From now on I will not drink of this fruit of the vine until that day. In which place Chrysostom: Of the fruit, he says, of the vine, which certainly produced wine, not water; so that the heresy of those who felt that only water should be used in these mysteries seemed to have started so long ago.

16. Water must be mixed with the wine in the Sacrament.

And the Church of God always mixed water with wine: first of all, because it is proven by the authority of the Councils and by the testimony of Saint Cyprian that this was done by Christ the Lord. Afterwards, because with this mixture the memory of the blood and water that came from his side is renewed. And furthermore, the waters, as we read in the Apocalypse, designate the people: therefore the water mixed with the wine means the union of the faithful people with Christ the head. And this the holy Church has perpetually preserved by apostolic tradition.

It is not absolutely necessary to use water; and the amount of water must be less than that of wine.

But although the reasons for mixing the water are so serious that it is not licit to omit it without mortal sin, nevertheless if it is missing, the Sacrament can be recorded. But Priests must warn that, just as it is advisable to use water with wine in the sacred mysteries, so too little should be poured. Because by sentence and judgment of the Ecclesiastical Writers that water becomes wine. Therefore, the Pontiff Honorius writes about this: A pernicious abuse has grown in your parts, namely, that a greater quantity of water is used in sacrifice than wine; when according to the reasonable custom of the general Church it should be used with much more wine than water. These two, then, are only the elements of this Sacrament: and it has rightly been sanctioned by various decrees that it is not lawful to offer anything but bread and wine, which some were not afraid to do. But we must see how suitable these two symbols of bread and wine are to declare those things of which we believe and confess that they are Sacraments.

How many and how great things the bread and wine represent in the Sacrament.

In the first place, in fact, they signify Christ to us, insofar as it is the true life of men. For the Lord Himself says: My Flesh truly is food, and my Blood truly is drink.

CHAPTER 4 and 5.

…the Body of Christ the Lord provides the food of eternal life to those who receive His Sacrament purely and holyly, it is rightly made up above all with those things with which this life is contained, so that the faithful can easily understand that with the communion of the precious Body and Blood of Christ the mind and spirit are saturated.

These same elements are also of no small value for men to receive that knowledge that there is in the Sacrament the truth of the Body and Blood of the Lord. For, as we notice that the bread and wine are changed daily by the force of nature into human flesh and blood, we can more easily be induced by this similarity to believe that the substance of the bread and wine is converted by the heavenly blessing into the true Flesh of Christ and his true Blood.

This admirable mutation of the elements also provides some help to illuminate what is being done in the soul. For just as, although no mutation of the bread and wine appears outwardly, nevertheless their substance truly passes into the Flesh and Blood of Christ; So also, although nothing in us seems changed, interiorly we are nevertheless renewed to life, when we receive true life with the Sacrament of the Eucharist.

Added to this is that, since the one body of the Church is composed of many members, with nothing does that union shine more clearly than with the elements of bread and wine. For bread is made of many grains, and wine is made of many clusters; and thus they declare that we, being many, are very closely united by the bond of this divine mystery, and as if made one body.

What form should be used to consecrate the bread.

Now it is a question of the form that should be used to consecrate the bread: certainly not because these mysteries are transmitted to the faithful people, unless necessity forces it (because it is not necessary that those who have not been initiated into the sacred be instructed in these things); but so that due to ignorance of the form the Priests do not sin very clumsily when preparing the Sacrament. Thus, by the holy Evangelists Matthew and Luke, and also by the Apostle, we are taught that this is the way: THIS IS MY BODY. For it is written: And while they were supping, Jesus took bread, and blessed it, and broke it, and gave it to his disciples, and said, Take and eat: This is my Body. Which form of consecration, as observed by Christ the Lord, has been perpetually used by the Catholic Church. The testimonies of the holy Fathers, which would be infinite to enumerate, and the decree of the Florentine Council, which is patent and at hand to all, must be omitted in this place; especially when from those words of the Savior: Do this in memory of me, the same can be known. For what the Lord commanded to be done must refer not only to what he had done, but also to the things he had said: and it must be understood to belong above all to the words, which were spoken no less to effect than to signify. But also by reason he can be easily persuaded; because the form is that which signifies what is carried out in this Sacrament. And since these words signify and declare what is done, that is, the conversion of the bread into the true Body of our Lord, it follows that the form must be constituted in those same words, in whose sentence we can take what the Evangelist said: He blessed. Because it seems that it should be understood in the same way as if he had said: Taking the bread, he blessed it, saying: this is my Body.

Not all the words that by custom of the Church are used in consecration are necessary.

Although the Evangelist preceded those words: Take and eat; However, it is clear that they do not mean the consecration of the matter, but only the use. Therefore, they must truly be uttered entirely by the Priest, but they are not necessary to make the Sacrament: in the same way that that conjunction "enim" is also uttered in the consecration of the Body and Blood. Otherwise it would happen that, if this Sacrament were not to be administered to anyone, it would not be appropriate or could not be made: when, however, it is not licit to doubt that the Priest, pronouncing the words of the Lord according to the custom and institution of the holy Church, truly consecrates the suitable material of the bread; although later it happens that the Holy Eucharist is never administered to anyone.

What is the way to make the Blood.

And as for what concerns the consecration of wine, which is the other matter of this Sacrament, for the same reason that we commemorated above, it is necessary that the Priest have known and understood its form. It must, therefore, be believed with certainty that it is understood in these words: FOR THIS IS THE CHALICE OF MY BLOOD, OF THE NEW AND ETERNAL TESTAMENT, MYSTERY OF FAITH, WHICH WILL BE POURED FOR YOU AND FOR MANY IN REMISSION OF SINS. From whose words several of the sacred Scriptures are truly gathered: and some have been preserved in the Church by apostolic tradition. For what is said: This is the Chalice,

1 Cor. 11, 25; Lk. 22, 20; Mt. 26, 28. The word "Eternal" is found in Hebr. 13, 20; Apoc. 14, 6. ... is written by Saint Luke and by the Apostle: and what follows: of my Blood, or my Blood, of the New Testament, which for you and for many will be shed in remission of sins, was said in part by Saint Luke, in part by Saint Matthew: but those words "Eternal" and "Mystery of faith" were taught to us by holy tradition, interpreter and custodian of the Catholic truth.

This is shown to be the true form of consecration.

But in this way no one will be able to doubt, if we also pay attention in this place to what was said before about the form of consecration that is applied to the element of bread: for it is clear that in those words that mean that the substance of the wine is converted into the Blood of the Lord, the form of this element is contained. Therefore, as those words openly declare, it is manifest that no other form should be established. They also express certain admirable fruits of the Blood shed in the passion of the Lord, which belong in the highest degree to this Sacrament. One is access to the eternal inheritance, which comes to us by right of the new and eternal Testament. Another is access to justice through the mystery of faith. For God proposed Jesus as a propitiator through faith in his Blood, so that he might be just and justifier of him who has faith in Jesus Christ. The third is the remission of sins.

The form of the consecration of the Blood is exposed.

And since these same words of consecration are full of mysteries, and suit the matter very well, it is advisable to ponder them with more diligence. What is truly said: Because this is the chalice of my Blood, must be understood thus: THIS IS MY BLOOD, which is contained in this Chalice. And rightly and appropriately, while this Blood is consecrated as the drink of the faithful, mention must be made of the Chalice. For the Blood would not seem to signify such a drink sufficiently, if it had not been received in some vessel. Follows later: From the New Testament; which was added for this reason: that we might understand that the Blood of Christ the Lord is not given to men in figure, as was done in the old Testament (for we read of this in the Apostle to the Hebrews that without blood the Testament was not dedicated), but truly and in fact, which belongs to the new Testament. Therefore the Apostle says: Therefore he is the mediator of the new Testament (Christ), so that, by interceding death, those who are called may receive the promise of eternal inheritance. And the word "Eternal" must refer to the eternal inheritance, which through the death of Christ the Lord, eternal testator, comes to us by right.

What is subjoined, Mystery of faith, does not exclude the truth of the thing, but means that what is hidden and very remote from the sense of the eyes must be believed with certain faith. But with these words a different sentence is held in this place from that which they have when they are also attributed to Baptism: because, by discerning with faith the Blood of Christ latent under the species of wine, it is called the Mystery of faith: but Baptism, inasmuch as it embraces the entire profession of the Christian faith, is rightly called by us the Sacrament of faith, and by the Greeks a Mystery. Although we also call the Blood of the Lord the mystery of faith for another reason, namely because in it human reason experiences, above all, a great deal of difficulty and work, when faith proposes that we believe that Christ the Lord, true Son of God, and at the same time God and man, suffered death for us; which death is designated with the Sacrament of the Blood.

Why, above all, in the consecration of the Blood, mention is made of death.

Therefore in this place the passion of the Lord is commemorated more aptly than in the consecration of the Body with these words: That it will be poured out in remission of sins. Because the Blood consecrated separately has greater power and moment to place before the eyes of all the passion of the Lord, and death, and the kind of passion. But those words that are added: For you and for many, were taken one from Matthew and another from Luke, each one from each, which however the holy Church, instructed by the spirit of God, put together at the same time: and belong to declare the fruit and usefulness of the passion. Because, if we look at its virtue, we will have to confess that the Blood was shed by the Savior for the salvation of all: but if we think about the fruit that men perceived from it, we will easily understand that that usefulness does not reach everyone, but only many. Therefore, when he said "For you," he meant either those who were present, or the chosen ones of the people of the Jews, who were the disciples, except Judas, with whom he spoke. And when he added "By many," he meant to mean the other elect of the Jews or the Gentiles. It was right, then, that it was not said "For all," when in this place the discourse dealt only with the fruits of the passion, which only brought the fruit of salvation to the elect. And this is what those words of the Apostle look at: Christ was offered only once to exhaust the sins of many; and what the Lord says in John: I pray for them, I do not pray for the world, but for these that you gave me, because they are yours. Many other mysteries lie hidden in the words of this consecration; which the Pastors, with assiduous meditation and study of divine things, by themselves, with the Lord's help, will easily attain.

It is not appropriate in this Sacrament to apply the judgment of meaning.

But now the discourse returns to the explanation of those things that should in no way be allowed to be ignored by the faithful. And as the Apostle warns that a very serious crime is committed by those who do not discern the Body of the Lord, first of all let the Pastors teach that the spirit and reason must be separated from the senses with all study. Because if the faithful are persuaded that this Sacrament contains only what they perceive with their senses, they will necessarily be led to extreme impiety; Therefore, feeling with their eyes, touch, smell and taste nothing more than the species of bread and wine, they will have judged that in the Sacrament there is only bread and wine. Care must be taken, therefore, that the minds of the faithful are abstracted as much as possible from the judgment of the senses, and are excited to contemplate the immense virtue and power of God.

What is carried out mainly in this Sacrament by the virtue of mystical consecration.

Because above all there are three admirable things worthy of acceptance that the Catholic faith believes and confesses without a doubt that are carried out in this Sacrament with the words of consecration. The first is that the true body of Christ the Lord, the same one who was born of the Virgin and sits in heaven at the right hand of the Father, is contained in this Sacrament. The second is that no substance of the elements remains in it, although nothing can seem more alien and remote from the senses. The third is what is easily deduced from both, although the words of the consecration express it above all: that the accidents that are either discerned with the eyes or perceived with the other senses are without anything subject, in a certain admirable and inexplicable way. And all the accidents of bread and wine can be seen, which however do not inhere in any substance, but exist by themselves; for the substance of the bread and wine changes in such a way in the same Body and Blood of the Lord, that the substance of the bread and wine ceases to be altogether.

It is true that the same Body of Christ that was born of the Virgin Mary is contained in the Eucharist.

But, to deal with the first things first, let Pastors endeavor to explain how perspicuous and clear are the words of our Savior, which demonstrate the truth of his Body in the Sacrament: for, when he says: This is my Body: This is my Blood: no one who is of sound mind can be ignorant of what we must understand; especially when the discourse deals with human nature, which the Catholic faith does not allow anyone to doubt was true in Christ: so that the most holy and learned man Hilary wrote clearly that regarding the truth of the Flesh and Blood of Christ, when by the very profession of the Lord and by our faith his flesh is truly eaten, no room for ambiguity has been left.

How is it also convinced that the true Body of Christ is in the Eucharist.

But there is also another place that Pastors must clarify, from which it can be openly known that the true Body and Blood of the Lord are contained in the Eucharist. For the Apostle, after commemorating that the bread and wine were consecrated by the Lord and that the sacred mysteries were administered to his Apostles, subjoined: Let a man prove himself, and so eat of that bread and drink of the cup: for he who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment for himself, not discerning the Body of the Lord. And if, as the heretics claim, nothing else should be venerated in the Sacrament but the memory and sign of the passion of Christ, what need was there to exhort the faithful with such grave words to prove themselves? Because with that grave voice of judgment the Apostle declared that some nefarious crime is committed by which, impurely immersing the Body of the Lord that lies hidden in the Eucharist, it is not distinguished from any other type of food. Which also above in the same epistle the Apostle explained more abundantly with these words: Is not the chalice of blessing that we bless the communication of the Blood of Christ? and the bread that we break, is it not a participation in the Body of the Lord? Which words demonstrate the true substance of the Body and Blood of Christ the Lord. These places, then, of Scripture must be explained by the Pastors, and above all it must be taught that nothing doubtful or uncertain has been left in them; especially when this sacrosanct authority of the Church of God has interpreted them.

In what way the sentence of the Church of Christ regarding the meaning of the Scriptures and the truth of the Body of the Lord in the Eucharist should be investigated.

We can reach the knowledge of whose sentence by two means and reason. The first is when we consult the Fathers, who flourished from the beginning of the Church and in every successive age, and are excellent witnesses of ecclesiastical doctrine. And these, with the utmost consensus, all very openly transmitted the truth of this dogma: of which, since it is a laborious task to adduce each of the testimonies, it will be enough to note or rather indicate a few, from which a judgment can easily be made of the others. Therefore, let Saint Ambrose first offer his faith, who in the book about those who are initiated into the mysteries testified that in this Sacrament the true Body of Christ is added, just as the true Body was taken from the Virgin, and that this must be held with the most certain faith; and in another place he teaches that before the consecration there is bread there, but after the consecration the Flesh of Christ. Let another witness approach, Saint Chrysostom, of no less faith and gravity, who, although in many other places he professes and teaches this same truth, especially in the hom. 60 about those who impurely sum up the sacred mysteries; and likewise in the hom. 44 and 45 about Saint John; because it says: Let us obey God, and do not contradict, even if what is said seems contrary to our thoughts or our eyes; Because his word is infallible, our sense is easily seduced. And with these are everywhere consistent the things that Saint Augustine, a staunch advocate of the Catholic faith, always taught, and in the first place when expounding the title of Psalm 33.

because he writes: Carrying oneself in one's hands is impossible for man, and only Christ can do; because he was carried in his hands when, commending his own body, he said: This is my Body. And Cyril (I ignore Justin and Irenaeus) states so openly in lib. 4 about John that the true Flesh of the Lord is in this Sacrament, that his words cannot be obscured by any fallacious and captious interpretations. And if the Pastors also require other testimonies from the Fathers, it will be easy to add the saints Dionysius, Hilary, Jerome, Damascene, and innumerable others, whose very serious sentences regarding this matter, united in one by the industry and labor of learned and pious men, we read everywhere.

How many times has the contrary opinion been condemned in the Councils of the Church.

There remains the other way by which it is licit to investigate the judgment of the holy Church in things that belong to faith, namely the condemnation of contrary doctrine and opinion. And in truth it is clear that the truth of the Body of Christ in the holy Sacrament of the Eucharist has always been so diffused and disseminated throughout the Church, and received with a concordant will by all the faithful, that when, five hundred years ago, Berengar dared to deny it and to affirm that there was only a sign, to the point at the Council of Vercelli, which had been convened by the authority of Leo IX, condemned by the sentences of all, he himself condemned their heresy to anathema; who later, when he returned to the same madness of impiety, was condemned in three other Councils, that of Tours and two Romans, of which one was convened by Nicholas II and the other by Gregory VII, Supreme Pontiffs. Later Innocent III confirmed that sentence in the Great Lateran Council: and henceforth by the Florentine and Tridentine Synods the faith of the same truth has been declared and established more openly. If, then, the Pastors expound these things diligently (to say nothing of those who, blinded by errors, hate nothing more than the light of truth), they will be able to confirm the weak and attract the spirits of the pious with a certain utmost joy and delight.

31. How faith in the truth of the Body of Christ in this Sacrament is included in the same Symbol.

Especially when the faithful are not allowed to doubt that the other articles of faith also include the faith of this dogma. Because when they believe and confess the supreme power of God over all things, it is necessary that they also believe that he did not lack the power to carry out this maximum work that we admire and cultivate in the Sacrament of the Eucharist. Then, when they believe in the holy Catholic Church, it necessarily follows that they believe at the same time that it is what we have explained, the truth of this Sacrament.

How much the dignity of the Church militant is shown by the majesty of this mystery.

But there is nothing truly that can be added to the joy and fruit of the pious, when they contemplate the dignity of this most high Sacrament. In the first place, in fact, they understand how perfect the Evangelical law is, which has been given to have in reality itself what in the time of the Mosaic law had been illuminated only with signs and figures. Therefore it was divinely said by Dionysius that our Church is medium between the Synagogue and the supreme Jerusalem, and therefore a participant in both. And in truth the faithful will never be able to sufficiently admire the perfection of the holy Church and the height of its glory, when only one degree seems to mediate between it and heavenly beatitude. Because we have this in common with the heavenly ones: that we both have Christ God and man present; but, by the only degree in which we are distant from them, the former enjoy the blessed vision of what is present; We venerate with firm and constant faith the present, and yet remote from the sense of the eyes, which is hidden with the admirable veil of the sacred mysteries. Furthermore, the faithful experience in this Sacrament the most perfect charity of Christ our Savior; because it suited his goodness in the highest degree never to take from us the nature that he had taken from us, but to want, as much as possible, to be and dwell with us, so that at all times it would seem to be truly and properly said: His delights are to be with the children of men.

CHAPTER 7.

Of the concomitance of the parts of the Body of Christ in this Sacrament.

The bones, the nerves and everything that belongs to the perfection of man, together with the divinity, are truly present here.

And already in this place it must be explained by the Pastors that not only the true Body of Christ, and everything that belongs to the true reason of the body, such as the bones and the nerves, but also the entire Christ is contained in this Sacrament. It must be taught, for its part, that Christ is the name of God and of man, namely of a single person in whom the divine and human nature are united; wherefore it embraces both substance, and the things which are consequent upon both substance, the divinity, and the whole human nature, which consists of the soul, and of all the parts of the body, and also of the blood: all of which things must be believed to be in the Sacrament. Because in heaven all humanity is united to divinity in a single person and hypostasis, it is impious to suspect that the Body that is in the Sacrament is separated from the same divinity.

34. The Blood, the Soul and the Divinity are not in the Eucharist in the same way as the Body of Christ.

In which, however, it is necessary for Pastors to warn that not all things are contained in this Sacrament with the same reason or virtue. Because there are some that we say are in the Sacrament by the force and effectiveness of the consecration: since those words effect what they signify, the writers of divine things called being in the Sacrament by force of the Sacrament what is expressed with the form of the words. Thus, if it happened that something was completely separated from other things, they taught that only what the form signified would be in the Sacrament, and not the rest: but some things are contained in the Sacrament because they are united to those things that are expressed with the form. Because as the form applied to consecrating bread means the Body of the Lord, when it is said: This is my Body; The same Body of Christ the Lord will be in the Eucharist by force of the Sacrament: but because the Blood, the Soul and the Divinity are united to the Body, these too will all be in the Sacrament, not truly by virtue of the consecration, but as those that are united to the Body. And these are said to be in the Sacrament by concomitance: for which reason it is manifest that all of Christ is in the Sacrament. Because if any two things are joined together in fact, where one is, the other must also be. It follows, therefore, that all Christ is contained equally in both the species of bread and in that of wine, so that, just as in the species of bread there is not only the Body, but also the Blood and truly all Christ; So on the contrary, in the species of wine there is not only the Blood, but the Body and truly all of Christ.

35. Why in the Eucharist there is double consecration.

But although this must be true and very persuasive to all the faithful; However, with optimal rights, it was instituted that two consecrations be made separately. Firstly, that the passion of the Lord may be more represented, in which the Blood was divided from the Body; For whose sake at the consecration we remember that the Blood was shed.

Furthermore, it was in the highest degree convenient that, since we were to use the Sacrament to nourish the soul, it was instituted by way of food and drink, of which it is evident that the perfect nourishment of the body consists.

All Christ is present in any particle of either species.

Nor should it be omitted that not only in one species or another, but in any particle of either species, the whole of Christ is contained: thus in effect Augustine wrote: Each one receives Christ the Lord, and in each of the portions it is whole, and it is not diminished by each one, but is offered whole in each one: and this can also be easily gathered from the Evangelists. For it must not be believed that each piece of bread was consecrated by the Lord with its own form of words, but with the same at the same time all the bread that was to be sufficient to prepare the sacred mysteries and distribute them to the Apostles: which regarding the chalice appears to have been done when he himself said: Take and divide among yourselves. Up to this point the things that have been explained pertain to the Pastors showing that the true Body and Blood of Christ are contained in the Sacrament of the Eucharist.

After the consecration no substance of the matter of the Sacrament remains.

Now, which was the other purpose, they also taught that the substance of the bread and wine does not remain in the Sacrament after the consecration. And this, although it may rightly have maximum admiration, is nevertheless necessarily united with what has been previously demonstrated. Because if it is the true Body of Christ under the species of bread and wine

… after the consecration, it is absolutely necessary, since it was not there before, that this has been done either by mutation of place, or by creation, or by conversion of something else into it. But it is manifest that it cannot be done by mutation of place that the Body of Christ is in the Sacrament because it had come from one place to another; because in this way it would happen that it would be missing from the seats of heaven, since nothing moves if it does not leave the place of the one that moves. And that the Body of Christ is created is less credible, and cannot even fit into thought; It remains, therefore, that the Body of the Lord is in the Sacrament because the bread becomes it. Therefore it is necessary that no substance from the bread remain.

Transubstantiation, approved by the Councils, has a basis in the Scriptures.

Induced by this reason, the Fathers and our elders in the great Lateran and Florentine Councils confirmed with open decrees the truth of this article; and by the Tridentine Synod it was defined more explicitly as follows: If anyone says that in the sacred Sacrament of the Eucharist the substance of the bread and wine remains together with the Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema. And these things were easy to gather from the testimonies of the Scriptures: in the first place, because in the institution of this Sacrament the Lord Himself said: This is my Body. For the force of the voice "This" is such that it demonstrates the whole substance of the thing present: and if the substance of the bread remained, it would in no way seem to be truly said: This is my Body. After Christ the Lord in John: The bread, he says, that I will give, is my flesh for the life of the world; calling his flesh bread. And a little later he subjoined: Unless you eat the Flesh of the Son of Man and drink his Blood, you will have no life in you: and again: My Flesh truly is food, and my Blood truly is drink. Therefore, when with such clear and perspicuous words He named His Flesh bread and true food, and His Blood true drink, He seems to have sufficiently declared that in the Sacrament no substance of the bread and wine remains.

How the Fathers recognized Transubstantiation in this Sacrament.

And that this was perpetually the consistent doctrine of the holy Fathers, whoever has traveled through them will easily understand. Saint Ambrose writes like this: You perhaps say: my bread is usual bread, but this bread is bread before the words of the Sacraments; When the consecration has been accomplished, the bread is made the Flesh of Christ. And in order to prove it more easily, he then adds several examples and similarities. Elsewhere, when he interpreted those words: All things that the Lord willed he made in heaven and on earth, He says, he says, although the figure of the bread and wine is seen, nothing should be believed except the Flesh of Christ and the Blood after the consecration. And with almost the same words, expounding the same sentence, Saint Hilary taught that, although outwardly bread and wine may be seen, nevertheless it truly is the Body and Blood of the Lord.

For what reason the Eucharist after the consecration is also called bread.

But let the Pastors warn in this place that it should not be admired if after the consecration it is also called bread. Because the Eucharist has been called by this name, both because it has the species of bread, and because it still retains the natural power to feed and nourish the body, which is typical of bread. And that this is the custom of the sacred letters of calling things the way they appear to be, is sufficiently shown by what is said in Genesis: that three men appeared to Abraham, who were nevertheless three Angels. And those two who appeared to the Apostles when Christ the Lord ascended into heaven, being Angels, are called men.

In what way is such an admirable conversion of substances carried out.

It is extremely difficult to explain this mystery. But nevertheless the Pastors will make an effort, for those who have benefited most in the knowledge of divine things (because those who are even weaker would have to be feared that they would be oppressed by the magnitude of the thing), they will make an effort, I say, to transmit the way of this admirable conversion; which is done in such a way that the entire substance of the bread by divine virtue becomes the entire substance of the Body of Christ, and the entire substance of the wine becomes the entire substance of the Blood of Christ, without any mutation of our Lord. For Christ is neither begotten, nor changes, nor grows, but remains entirely in his substance. Mystery that when Saint Ambrose declares: You see, he says, how effective the sermon of Christ is: if, then, there is so much force in the sermon of the Lord Jesus, that they began to be those who were not, namely the world; How much more is it an operator for them to be what they were and change into something else? …body of the holy Virgin, not because the same assumed Body descends from heaven, but because the same bread and wine are transmuted into the Body and Blood of Christ.

The name Transubstantiation was conveniently imposed on this stupendous conversion.

This admirable conversion, then, was conveniently and properly called Transubstantiation by the holy Catholic Church, as the sacred Tridentine Synod taught. Because just as natural generation, because in it the form changes, can rightly and properly be called transformation: so also, because in the Sacrament of the Eucharist the whole substance of one thing passes into the whole substance of another thing, the word Transubstantiation was rightly and wisely invented by our elders.

The mode of Transubstantiation, and the place in which Christ is in this Sacrament, should not be inquired with curiosity.

But what has been repeated so many times by the holy Fathers, the faithful must be admonished not to inquire with too much curiosity in what way that mutation can be made. Because it cannot be perceived by us, nor in natural mutations, nor in the very creation of things do we have any example of this thing. But what this is must be known by faith: how it is done must not be inquired with curiosity. And Pastors must use no less caution when also explaining that mystery of how the Body of Christ the Lord is all contained even in the smallest particle of bread. Because disputes of this kind will hardly ever be instituted; But nevertheless, when Christian charity postulates it, remember above all to pre-empt the minds of the faithful with that voice: Not every word will be impossible for God.

The Body of Christ in the Eucharist is not as if in a place.

Then teach that Christ the Lord in this Sacrament is not as if in a place. For the place follows the things themselves insofar as they are endowed with some magnitude: but we do not say that Christ the Lord is in the Sacrament of that reason by which he is great or small, which belongs to quantity, but in so far as he is substance. Because the substance of the bread becomes the substance of Christ, not the magnitude or quantity. And no one doubts that substance is contained equally in small and large space. For also the substance of the air and all its nature is both in the small and in the large part of the air; and it is equally necessary that the whole nature of water be no less in the urn than in the river. Therefore, since the substance of the bread succeeds the Body of our Lord, it is necessary to confess that it is in the Sacrament in exactly the same way as the substance of the bread was before the consecration. And whether it was a large amount or a small amount, it didn't matter at all to the thing.

In this Sacrament there is no substance to which the accidents of bread and wine inhere.

The third thing remains, which in this Sacrament seems maximum and admirable; which, having already explained the other two things, it must be considered that it can be treated more easily by the Pastors: namely, that the species of bread and wine appear in this Sacrament without any subject matter. Because, as it has been shown before that the Body and Blood of the Lord are truly in the Sacrament, in such a way that no substance of the bread and wine subsists; and since those accidents cannot affect the Body and Blood of Christ; It remains that, above all the order of nature, they sustain themselves without relying on anything else. This was the perpetual and constant doctrine of the Catholic Church: which may also be easily confirmed by the authority of those testimonies by which it was formerly made manifest that no substance of bread or wine resides in the Eucharist.

46. ​​Why Christ wanted to give his Body and Blood under the form of bread and wine.

But nothing is more suitable for the piety of the faithful than, omitting the most subtle matters, to venerate and cultivate the majesty of this admirable Sacrament, and then to recognize in it the supreme providence of God, who instituted that the sacrosanct mysteries be administered under the species of bread and wine. Because, since the common nature of men abhors in the highest degree to feed on food of human flesh or drink of blood, he most wisely caused the Most Holy Body and Blood to be administered to us under the species of those things, bread, I say, and wine, from whose daily and common food we delight in the highest degree. And those two benefits are also added: of which the first is that we have been freed from the slander of the infidels, from which we could not easily escape if we seemed to eat the Lord under his own species. The other is that, while we submerge the Body and Blood of the Lord in such a way that, nevertheless, what is truly done cannot be perceived with the senses, this is very valuable to increase faith in our minds: which, as the sentence of Saint Gregory is divulged, has no merit where human reason offers experience. But these things that have been explained up to this point will only have to be explained with great caution, according to the capacity of the listeners and the needs of the times.

What goods are achieved by those who have worthily taken communion with the Body and Blood of the Lord.

But in truth, the things that can be said of the admirable virtue and the fruits of this Sacrament, it should not be considered that there is any class of faithful to whom the knowledge of these things does not belong, and to whom it should not seem in the highest degree necessary. Because for the faithful to understand the usefulness of the Eucharist, for this reason they must mainly know the things that are discussed in so many words about this Sacrament. But, as its immense benefits and fruits cannot be explained by any prayer, one place or another must be treated by the Shepherds, so that they may show how much copy and abundance of all goods is included in those sacrosanct mysteries. And they will achieve this somewhere like this: if, making clear the power and nature of all the Sacraments, they compare the Eucharist to the fountain and the others to the streams. Because it must truly and necessarily be said to be the source of all graces, since it contains within itself in an admirable way the very source of the heavenly charisms and gifts, and the author of all the Sacraments, Christ the Lord, from whom, as a source, all the good and perfection they have is derived to the other Sacraments. From this, then, we can easily gather the very extensive gifts of divine grace that are imparted to us with this Sacrament.

The comforts that bread and wine bring to the body, those that the Eucharist brings to the soul in a most excellent way.

It will also seem to be done conveniently if we consider the nature of the bread and wine, which are symbols of this Sacrament. Because the uses that bread and wine bring to the body, all of these the Sacrament of the Eucharist provides to the health and youth of the soul, with reason that is truly better and more perfect. Because this Sacrament does not change in our substance, like bread and wine; but we somehow become its nature; so that Saint Augustine's words can be rightly transferred to this place: I am a delicacy of the great; grow, and you will eat me; and you will not change me into you, like the delicacy of your flesh, but you will change into me.

In what way grace is conferred by this Sacrament.

And if grace and truth were made through Jesus Christ; It is necessary that it also influences the soul, when it is received purely and holyly, by the one who said of himself: He who eats my Flesh and drinks my Blood remains in me, and I in him. Because to those who join this Sacrament affected by the study of piety and religion, no one should doubt that they so admit into themselves the Son of God that they are inserted into his body as living members. For it is written: He who eats me, he also will live through me: likewise: The bread that I will give is my Flesh for the life of the world. Which place Cyril, interpreting it, says: The Word of God, uniting himself to his own flesh, made it life-giving. It was fitting for him, then, to unite in a certain admirable way to the bodies through his sacred Flesh and precious Blood, which we receive in the life-giving blessing in the bread and wine.

The man stained with sins and dead is not vivified by the submission of the Eucharist, although this Sacrament is said to confer grace.

But what is said, that grace is conferred through the Eucharist, it is appropriate for Pastors to warn that it should not be understood in this way, as if it were not necessary that the one who in fact is to usefully perceive this Sacrament should have first obtained grace. Because it is clear that, just as natural food is of no benefit to dead bodies, so also to the soul that does not live from the Spirit the sacred mysteries are of no benefit. And that is why they have the species of bread and wine, to signify that they were not instituted to revoke the soul to life, but to preserve it in life. But this has been said for this reason: because also the first grace (with which it is fitting that everyone be adorned before daring to touch the sacred Eucharist with their mouths, lest they eat and drink judgment on themselves) is conferred on no one if he does not perceive this same Sacrament with desire and vow. Because it is the end of all the Sacraments, and a symbol of ecclesiastical unity and conjunction, and outside the Church no one can obtain grace.

How the soul is remade and nourished with this spiritual delicacy.

Then, as the body is not only preserved with the natural delicacy, but also grows, and the taste perceives from it every day new voluptuousness and softness; so also the food of the sacred Eucharist not only sustains the soul, but adds strength to it, and makes the spirit move more and more with the delight of divine things;
