52. Through the Eucharist the lightest sins are forgiven.

That through the Eucharist the lighter sins, which are usually called venial, are remitted and condoned, there is no reason to doubt. Because whatever the soul lost through the ardor of greed, while it offended a little in some minor thing, the Eucharist, cleansing those same minor faults, restores all of this. As also (and it does not seem that it should deviate from the proposed similarity) that which, by the force of innate heat, decays and perishes every day, we feel that little by little it is added and remade with natural food. Therefore Saint Ambrose deservedly said of this heavenly Sacrament: This daily bread adds to the remedy of daily weakness. But these things must be understood of those sins with the sense and delight of which the soul is not moved.

53. By this same Sacrament the soul is preserved from future evils.

Furthermore, there is in the sacred mysteries that power to keep us pure and intact from crimes, and unharmed by the onslaught of temptations, and as with heavenly medicine they prepare the soul, so that it cannot be easily infected and corrupted by the poison of some deadly disturbance. And also for this reason, as Saint Cyprian attests, when in ancient times the faithful were vulgarly taken by tyrants to torment and death for the confession of the Christian name, so that they would not be overcome by the acerbity of the pains and faint in the salutary contest, it was an ancient custom in the Catholic Church for the Bishops to provide them with the Sacraments of the Body and Blood of the Lord. But it also inhibits and represses the libido of the flesh. Because while it kindles the spirits more with the fire of charity, it is necessary that it extinguishes the ardor of concupiscence.

How through this Sacrament access to eternal glory is opened.

Finally, so that with a single word all the uses and benefits of this Sacrament can be understood, it must be said that the sacred Eucharist has great power to achieve eternal glory. For it is written: He who eats my Flesh and drinks my Blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day. By the grace of this Sacrament, in fact, the faithful, while living this life, enjoy utmost peace and tranquility of conscience; Then, recreated by their virtue, in no other way than Elijah, who with the strength of bread baked under ashes walked to the mountain of God Horeb, when the time had come to emigrate from life, they ascend to eternal glory and beatitude. All these things will be abundantly explained by the Pastors, if they either take to deal with chapter 6 of Saint John, in which the multiple effects of this Sacrament are opened, or by reviewing the admirable acts of Christ the Lord, they show that, when with reason and merit we estimate that those in whose houses he was received as a mortal were most blessed, or those who recovered their health by the touch of his dress or fringe; Much more blessed and happy are we, into whose soul the one endowed with immortal glory does not gravitate to enter, to heal all its wounds, and unite it to himself adorned with the most ample gifts.

55. In how many ways we commune the Body and Blood of the Lord.

But it must be taught from whom those enormous fruits of the sacred Eucharist that have now been commemorated can be perceived; and that there is no single reason for taking communion, so that the faithful people learn to emulate the best charisms. Rightly and wisely, then, our elders, as we read in the Tridentine Synod, distinguished three reasons for subsuming this Sacrament. Because some receive only the Sacrament, like sinners who are not afraid to receive the sacred mysteries with impure mouths and hearts, of whom the Apostle says that they eat and drink the Body of the Lord unworthily. Saint Augustine writes of these thus: He who does not abide in Christ, and in whom Christ does not abide, certainly does not spiritually eat his Flesh, although carnally and visibly he oppresses with his teeth the Sacraments of the Body and Blood. Those who, therefore, thus affected receive the sacred mysteries, not only do not reap any fruit from them, but, as the Apostle himself attests, they eat and drink judgment for themselves. Others are said to join the Eucharist only in spirit: they are those who with desire and vow eat that proposed heavenly bread, inflamed with living faith that works by dilection; from which, if not all, they certainly reap maximum fruits of usefulness.

Finally others are those who perceive the sacred Eucharist with sacrament and spirit; which, when according to the doctrine of the Apostle they have first tried themselves, and adorned with the nuptial garment they have accessed this divine table, they collect from the Eucharist those rich fruits that we mentioned before. Therefore it is manifest that they deprive themselves of maximum and heavenly goods who, while also being able to be prepared to receive the Sacrament of the Body of the Lord, are content to receive Holy Communion only in spirit.

It is shown that before someone accesses the Eucharist their spirit must be prepared.

But it must already be taught why it is appropriate for the minds of the faithful to be prepared before coming to the sacramental perception of the Eucharist. And in the first place, in order to show that this preparation is in the greatest degree necessary, the example of our Savior must be proposed. Because before giving the Apostles the Sacraments of his precious Body and Blood, even though they were already clean, he washed their feet; to declare that all diligence must be used, lest we lack something in the utmost integrity and innocence of mind when we go to perceive the sacred mysteries. Then let the faithful understand that, just as if someone joins the Eucharist with an optimally affected and prepared spirit, he or she adorns himself with the most ample gifts of heavenly grace; On the contrary, if you receive it unprepared, you not only receive no comfort, but also maximum inconvenience and damage. Because it is characteristic of optimal and maximally salutary things that, if we use them in time, they take great advantage; but if they are applied in another's time, they bring perdition and ruin. Therefore it should not be surprised that the enormous and most illustrious gifts of God, when received with a well-established spirit, are of maximum help for us to achieve heavenly glory: but when we present ourselves unworthy of them, they bring eternal death. And this is proven with the example of the ark of the Lord: because the Ark of the Covenant, which the Israelite people had nothing more illustrious, to which the Lord had also given maximum and innumerable benefits, taken away by the Philistines, brought upon them great pestilence and calamity combined with eternal disgrace. Likewise, foods that, received through the mouth, descend into a truly well-affected stomach, nourish and sustain the bodies: but those that tend to be poured into a stomach full of vicious humors produce serious illnesses.

57. How should the spirit be prepared for the Eucharist.

Let the faithful therefore use that first preparation: let them discern table from table, this sacred one from the other profane ones, this heavenly bread from the common one. And this is done when we believe with certainty that the true Body and Blood of the Lord is present, whom the Angels worship in heaven, at whose presence the pillars of heaven tremble and fear, with whose glory heaven and earth are filled. This truly is discerning the Body of the Lord, which the Apostle admonished: whose magnitude of mystery, however, it is better to venerate than to inquire too curiously into its truth in disputes. And that other preparation is in the highest degree necessary: ​​that each one ask himself if he has peace with others and if he truly and heartily loves his neighbors: If, then, you offer your gift at the altar, and there you have remembered that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled with your brother, and then when you come you will offer your gift.

Then we must diligently scrutinize our conscience, lest perhaps we be contaminated by some mortal sin, of which it is necessary to repent, so that it is first washed with the medicine of contrition and confession: because it is defined by the holy Tridentine Synod that it is lawful for no one who is stimulated by the consciousness of mortal sin, if he has been given the faculty of the Priest, to receive the sacred Eucharist before purging himself with confession. sacramental, no matter how contrite he may seem.

Furthermore, let us quietly think with our minds how unworthy we are of the Lord granting us this divine benefit, which is why we must say from the heart that of the Centurion, of whom the Savior himself testified that he had not found so much faith in Israel: Lord, I am not worthy that you come under my roof. Let us also inquire of ourselves if it is licit for us to usurp that of Peter: Lord, you know that I love you. Because it is worth remembering that the one who had sat in the fellowship of the Lord without the wedding garment was thrown into the dark prison and addicted to eternal punishments.

He who wants to take communion must also take some reason from the body.

In truth, there is no need only for the preparation of the spirit, but also of the body: because we must access the sacred table on an empty stomach: in such a way that at least from midnight of the preceding day until that point of time in which we receive the Eucharist, we have not eaten or drunk anything at all.

Ch. 7. Fourth: humble self-esteem must come first. Mt. 8, 8. Fifth: it must be seen if we are endowed with true charity. Jn. 21, 17. Mt. 22, 11. It is necessary that those who receive communion be fasting, from Cons. dist. 2, c. Liquidis.

…also asks for the dignity of such a great Sacrament that those who are united in marriage abstain for a few days from the concubinage of wives, admonished by the example of David, who, when he was going to receive the bread of the Showbread from the Priest, confessed that he and his boys were pure from the custom of wives for three whole days. These are almost the things that the faithful should observe to the maximum degree, in order to prepare themselves before usefully receiving the sacred mysteries. Because the rest that seem to have to be provided for in this matter can easily be reduced to these same chapters.

All Christians are obliged to consume the Eucharist at least once a year.

But so that perhaps they do not become more reluctant to receive this Sacrament because they consider it very serious and difficult to use so much preparation, the faithful must often be warned that that law of receiving the sacred Eucharist has been proposed to all. Furthermore, it is established by the Church that anyone who has not taken communion at least once each year at Easter is excluded from the Church.

How many times and at what times should the Eucharist be perceived.

Nor, however, should the faithful be content with, obeying the authority of this decree, receiving the Body of the Lord only once a year; but they consider that the Communion of the Eucharist should be reiterated more often. But if this is more appropriate each month, or each week, or each day, a certain rule cannot be prescribed for everyone: however that is the most certain norm of Saint Augustine: Live in such a way that you can submerge each day. Therefore, it will be the office of the Parish Priests to often exhort the faithful that, just as they consider it necessary to supply the body with food every day, so they do not abandon the care of feeding and nourishing the soul every day with this Sacrament. Because it is manifest that the soul needs no less spiritual delicacy than the body does of the natural. And he will vehemently take advantage in this place to repeat those maximum and divine benefits that, as has been demonstrated before, we obtain from the sacramental communion of the Eucharist. That figure should also be added, when every day it was necessary to replenish the body's strength with manna; and likewise the authorities of the holy Fathers, who greatly recommend the frequent perception of this Sacrament. Because it was not only from a single holy Father Augustine that sentence: Every day you sin, every day adds up: but if someone carefully observes, he will easily find that the meaning of all the Fathers who wrote about this thing was the same.

61. It is shown that in ancient times the custom of taking communion was common in the Church.

And that in truth there was a time when the faithful received the Eucharist every day, we will understand from the Acts of the Apostles. Because all those who then professed the Christian faith were so burning with true and sincere charity that, as they devoted themselves without intermission to prayers and other offices of piety, each day they were prepared to immerse themselves in the sacred mysteries of the Body of the Lord. Later Anacletus, most holy Martyr and Pontiff, renewed somewhere that custom that seemed to be interrupted. Because he mandated that the ministers who attended the sacrifice of the Mass take communion; which he claimed to have been established by the Apostles. For a long time there was also that custom in the Church that the Priest, having concluded the sacrifice, when he had summed up the Eucharist, returned to the people who were present, invited the faithful to the sacred table with these words: Come, brothers, to Communion: then those who were prepared summed up the sacrosanct mysteries with great religion. But when later charity and the study of piety had cooled down so much that the faithful barely acceded to it, it was sanctioned under the Pontiff Fabian that three times a year, on the Nativity of the Lord, and on the Resurrection, and on Pentecost, everyone should imbibe the Eucharist: which was later confirmed by many Councils, and mainly by the first of Agde.

Finally, when things had been brought to such a point that not only was that holy and salutary precept not kept, but the Communion of the sacred Eucharist was even deferred for many years, it was decreed in the Lateran Council that at least once every year, at Easter, all the faithful should receive the sacred Body of the Lord; and those who had neglected to do so would be prohibited from entering the Church.

It is not advisable to administer the Eucharist to children who do not yet use reason.

But although this law, sanctioned by the authority of God and the Church, belongs to all the faithful; It must be taught, however, that those who do not yet have the use of reason due to weakness of age are excepted: because these neither know how to discern the sacred Eucharist from profane and common bread, nor can they contribute to receiving it piety of mind and religion. And this also seems very foreign to the institution of Christ the Lord: because he says: Take and eat: and it is quite evident that infants are not suitable for taking and eating. The custom of also providing infants with the sacred Eucharist was truly ancient in some places, but nevertheless both for those reasons that have been mentioned before, and for others that are most convenient to Christian piety,

At what age should children be given the sacred mysteries.

And at what age the sacred mysteries should be given to children, no one can better establish it than the father and the Priest to whom they confess their sins: because it belongs to them to explore and ask the children if they have received any knowledge of this admirable Sacrament and if they like it.

64. It is sometimes licit to admit the insane to Communion.

Furthermore, to the insane, who are then alien to the sense of piety, it is in no way appropriate to give the Sacraments; although, if before falling into madness they showed pious and religious will of mind, it will be lawful to administer the Eucharist to them at the end of their lives according to the decree of the Council of Carthage; provided that there is no danger of vomiting or other indignity or inconvenience to be feared.

Lay people should not receive communion under either species.

And as for the rite of communion, let the Parish Priests teach that by law of the Holy Church it is prohibited that anyone, without the authority of the Church itself, outside the Priests who make up the Body of the Lord in the sacrifice, add the sacred Eucharist under one species or another: because, as has been explained by the Tridentine Synod, although Christ the Lord at the Last Supper instituted this most high Sacrament in the species of bread and wine and gave it to the Apostles: it does not follow, however, that the Lord Savior has established this law that the sacred mysteries must be administered to all the faithful under one kind or another. For our Lord Himself, when speaking of this Sacrament, often made mention of only one species, as when He says: If anyone eats this bread, he will live forever: and: The bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world: and: He who eats this bread will live forever.

Reasons why the Church granted the laity the use of only one species.

And it is manifest that the Church was induced by many and indeed very serious reasons to not only approve this custom of communing mainly under one species, but also to sign it with the authority of the decree.

In the first place, the utmost care had to be taken to ensure that the Blood of the Lord was not shed on the ground: which indeed did not seem to be easily avoided if it had been necessary to minister it to a great multitude of people.

Furthermore, since the sacred Eucharist must be prepared for the sick, there was great fear that, if the species of wine were preserved longer, it would become sour.

Furthermore, there are many who cannot stand the taste of wine in any way, or even the smell. Therefore, so that what must be given for the sake of spiritual health would not harm the health of the body, it was very prudently sanctioned by the Church that the faithful receive only the species of bread.

Added to the other reasons is that in many provinces there is an extreme shortage of wine: and it cannot be brought from elsewhere without maximum expense, and only by very long and very difficult routes.

Then, what belongs most to the matter, the heresy of those who denied that under both species is the whole of Christ, and affirmed that under that of bread is contained only the lifeless Body, and under that of wine the Blood, was contained. So that the truth of the Catholic faith might be placed more before the eyes of all, with most wise counsel, Communion of a single kind was introduced, that is, of bread. There are also other reasons given by those who argue with this argument; which, if it seems necessary, may be adduced by the Parish Priests. Now about the Minister, although almost no one can ignore it, it must be dealt with, lest something that belongs to the doctrine of this Sacrament be omitted.

67. The Minister of this Sacrament himself is the Priest.

Thus, it must be transmitted that only Priests have been given the power to prepare the sacred Eucharist and distribute it to the faithful. And that custom has always been kept in the Church that the faithful people received the Sacraments from the Priests, and the Priests, when doing what was sacred, communed themselves, was explained by the holy Tridentine Synod; and showed that this custom, as coming from the apostolic tradition, must be religiously retained; especially when Christ the Lord left us an illustrious example of this, who both consecrated his most holy Body and offered it with his hands to his Apostles. But so that the dignity of such a great Sacrament could be consulted for any reason, not only was the power to administer it only to the Priests, but also by law the Church prohibited anyone, unless they were consecrated, from daring to handle or touch the sacred vessels, the linens and the other instruments necessary for their preparation, unless some serious need occurred.

68. The Eucharist can be consecrated or administered by bad Priests.

From which both the Priests themselves and the other faithful can understand how much religion and holiness those who agree to consecrate, or administer, or submerge the Eucharist should be endowed with. Although what was said before about the other Sacraments, that they are no less administered by the wicked if the things that belong to their perfect reason are rightly kept, the same applies to the Sacrament of the Eucharist. For it should not be believed that all these things rest on the merit of the ministers, but that they are accomplished by the virtue and power of Christ the Lord. These are the things that must be explained about the Eucharist, inasmuch as it is a Sacrament. Now, what remains to be said, as far as it is Sacrifice, should be explained; so that the Parish Priests understand what primarily of this mystery, as the holy Synod decreed, they must transmit to the faithful people on Sundays and holidays.

The Eucharist is the peculiar Sacrifice of the New Testament, most acceptable to God.

Because this Sacrament is not only a treasure of heavenly riches, with which, if we use it well, we reconcile the grace and love of God; but in him there is a certain main reason why we can return some grace for the immense benefits heaped upon us. And how pleasing and acceptable this victim is to God, if it is sacrificed rightly and legitimately, can be gathered from this. For if you did not want the sacrifices of the old law, of which it is written: Sacrifice and oblation; and again: If you had wanted sacrifice, I would have given it truly; You will not delight in burnt offerings; In such a way they pleased the Lord, that the Scripture testifies that God smelled the odor of sweetness, that is, that they were pleasing and accepted to Him: what should we expect from that Sacrifice in which the same one from whom the heavenly voice was twice heard is immolated and offered: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased? This mystery, then, the Parish Priests will diligently expound, so that when the faithful gather to the divine thing, they learn to meditate attentively and religiously on those sacred things in which they assist.

What are the causes for which the Eucharist was instituted by Christ the Lord.

In the first place, then, they will teach that the Eucharist was instituted by Christ the Lord for two reasons: one is, so that it would be the heavenly food of our soul, with which we could protect and preserve the spiritual life: the other, so that the Church would have a perpetual Sacrifice with which our sins would be atoned for, and the heavenly Father, often seriously offended by our crimes, would be translated from wrath to mercy, from the severity of justice. animosity towards clemency. The figure and likeness of this thing can be seen in the Passover lamb, which used to be offered and eaten by the children of Israel as a Sacrifice and Sacrament. Nor in truth, when our Savior was going to offer himself to God the Father on the altar of the cross, could he give any more illustrious significance of his immense charity towards us than when he left us a visible Sacrifice, with which that bloody sacrifice that shortly after was to be immolated once on the cross was renewed; and his memory until the end of the century will be cultivated every day with great utility by the Church spread throughout the world.

How the Sacrament is distinguished from the Sacrifice.

For their part, these two reasons differ greatly from each other. Because the Sacrament is perfected with consecration: but all the power of the Sacrifice lies in its being offered. Therefore the sacred Eucharist, while it is contained in the tabernacle or carried to the sick, is considered a Sacrament, not a Sacrifice. Then also, insofar as it is a Sacrament, it provides those who add the divine Host with cause of merit and all those benefits that have been commemorated above: but insofar as it is a Sacrifice, it contains not only the efficiency of deserving, but also of satisfying. Because just as Christ the Lord in his passion deserved and satisfied for us; Thus those who offer this Sacrifice, with which they communicate with us, deserve and satisfy the fruits of the Lord's passion.

At what time was this New Testament Sacrifice instituted.

From the institution of this Sacrifice the holy Tridentine Synod left no room for ambiguity: because it declared that it was instituted by Christ the Lord at the Last Supper; and at the same time he condemned with anathema those who affirm that the true and proper Sacrifice is not offered to God, or that offering is nothing other than giving to Christ to be eaten.

It is not lawful to offer Sacrifice to Saints, or to any creature.

Nor did he omit to diligently explain that the Sacrifice is made to God alone. For although the Church sometimes celebrates Masses in memory and honor of the Saints, it nevertheless taught that the Sacrifice is not offered to them, but to God alone, who crowned the Saints with immortal glory. Therefore, not even the Priest usually ever says: I offer you the Sacrifice, Peter or Paul; but while he sacrifices to God alone, he thanks him for the distinguished victory of the most blessed martyrs; and implores their patronage in such a way that they deign to intercede for us in heaven, whose memory we make on earth.

Where is that doctrine of Sacrifice and Priesthood of the new law to come from?

But these things that the Catholic Church has transmitted regarding the truth of this Sacrifice, it received from the words of the Lord, when on that last night, entrusting these same sacred mysteries to the Apostles: Do this, he says, in memory of me. For them, as defined by the holy Synod, he then instituted Priests, and commanded that they, and those who succeeded them in the priestly office, should immolate and offer their Body; and this is also sufficiently demonstrated by the words of the Apostle written to the Corinthians, when he says: You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons: you cannot be partakers of the table of the Lord and of the table of demons. Because just as the table of demons must be understood as the altar on which they were immolated: so also (so that what the Apostle proposes may be concluded with probable argument) the table of the Lord cannot mean anything other than the altar on which the Sacrifice to the Lord was made.

With what figures and prophecies this Sacrifice was primarily signified in ancient times.

And if we look for the figures and oracles of this Sacrifice from the Old Testament; First of all, Malachi openly prophesied about him with these words: From the rising of the sun to the great setting is my name among the nations; and in every place a pure oblation is sacrificed and offered to my name, because my name is great among the nations, says the Lord of hosts. Furthermore, this host, both before and after the law was given, was announced with various types of Sacrifices. Because all the goods that were meant in those Sacrifices, this single victim, as perfection and absolution of all, embraced them. However, in nothing can its image be seen more expressed than in the sacrifice of Melchizedek: because the Savior himself, declaring that he had constituted himself a Priest eternally according to the order of Melchizedek, offered his Body and Blood at the last supper under the species of bread and wine to God the Father.

The same sacrifice that was offered on the cross is performed in the Mass.

We confess one, then, and the same Sacrifice and there must be the one that is performed in the Mass and the one that was offered on the cross; as the Host is one and the same, namely Christ our Lord, who bloodily sacrificed himself on the altar of the cross. Because the bloody Host and the bloodless Host are not two Hosts, but one; whose Sacrifice, after the Lord commanded: Do this in memory of me, is renewed every day in the Eucharist.

77. He is also only one Priest.

But also one and the same Priest is Christ the Lord. Because the Ministers who make the Sacrifice do not assume their person, but that of Christ, when they make his body and blood. Which is also shown with the same words of the consecration. Because the Priest does not say: This is the Body of Christ; but: This is my Body, bringing to know the person of Christ the Lord, converts the substance of the bread and wine into the true substance of his body and blood.

The Mass is a Sacrifice of both praise and propitiation.

This being so, without a doubt it must be taught, as the holy Synod also explained, that the sacrosanct Sacrifice of the Mass is not only praise and thanksgiving, or a bare commemoration of the Sacrifice that was made on the cross, but also truly a propitiatory Sacrifice, with which God makes himself blessed and propitious to us. Therefore, if with a pure heart, burning faith, and intimate pain for our crimes, we immolate and offer this most holy Host, there should be no doubt that we will obtain mercy from the Lord, and grace in timely help. Because the Lord is so delighted with the smell of this victim, that he imparts to us the gift of grace and penance, condoning sins. For this reason, that prayer of the Church is also solemn: As many times as the commemoration of this Host is celebrated, so many times is the work of our redemption carried out: namely, those magnificent fruits of the bloody Host flow to us through this bloodless Sacrifice.

79. The fruit of the Sacrifice of the Mass also reaches the deceased.

Later the Parish Priests will teach that the power of this Sacrifice is such that it not only benefits the one who immolates and the one who adds, but also all the faithful, whether they live with us on earth, whether they are dead, whether they are dead in the Lord, or whether they are not yet completely atoned. Because no less by the most certain tradition of the Apostles is it usefully offered for them than for the sins, sorrows, satisfactions and any calamities and anguish of the living.

No Mass should be said privately from the common one.

From which it is easily perceived that all Masses must be considered common, as those that belong to the common usefulness and salvation of all the faithful.

What do the ceremonies of this Sacrifice belong to?

For its part, this Sacrifice has many and to the highest degree

… distinguished and solemn rites, none of which should be considered superfluous or vain; But everyone seeks to ensure that the majesty of such a great Sacrifice shines more clearly, and that the faithful are excited to contemplate the divine things that are hidden in this Sacrament, by intuiting the salutary mysteries. But it is not necessary for us to say more about these things; both because this argument seems to postulate a longer explanation than is appropriate for the proposed institution; as because the Priests will have at hand almost innumerable libels and comments that pious and very learned men have written about this matter. Up to this point, then, it will be enough to have explained, with the Lord's help, the main chapters of those things that belong to the Eucharist, both insofar as it is a Sacrament and insofar as it is a Sacrifice.

OF THE SACRAMENT OF PENITENCE.

CHAPTER V

The doctrine of Penance must be carefully and frequently inserted into the ears of Christians.

Just as the fragility and weakness of human nature is known to everyone, and each one easily experiences it in himself; Thus, no one can ignore how much need there is for the Sacrament of Penance. And if the diligence that must be used by Parish Priests in each argument must be measured by the magnitude and weight of the thing they deal with; We will fully confess that never in the explanation of this place will they be so diligent that it may seem sufficient. Furthermore, this Sacrament must be treated more carefully than Baptism, because Baptism is administered only once and cannot be reiterated: but Penance is given place as many times, and the need to reiterate it as many times is imposed, as many times after Baptism it happens to sin. Because thus it has been said by the Tridentine Synod, that the Sacrament of Penance is as necessary to salvation for those already regenerated as Baptism is for those not yet regenerated: and that vulgar sentence of Saint Jerome is greatly proven by all those who later transmitted sacred things: that Penance is the second table. Because just as, when the ship is broken, there is only one refuge left to save life, if perhaps it is lawful to snatch a plank from the shipwreck; Thus, after losing the innocence of Baptism, if someone does not take refuge in the table of Penance, he must undoubtedly despair of his salvation. But these things are said not only to excite the Pastors, but also the other faithful, lest perhaps they be reprimanded for neglecting something that is most necessary. Because in the first place, remembering the common fragility, they must desire with all study that, aided by divine help, they can progress in the path of the Lord without falling or any slip. And if at times they have offended, then looking at the supreme kindness of God, who like a good shepherd tends to bind up the wounds of his sheep and heal them, they will think that this most salubrious medicine of Penance should never be deferred to another time.

How varied the meaning of the word Penance is.

But to undertake the thing itself, the various power and notion of this name must first be explained, lest anyone be misled by the ambiguity of the voice. Because some take Penance as satisfaction: others, very remote from the doctrine of the Catholic Faith, when they consider that Penance

CHAPTER 9.

Multiple meaning of the word Penance.

…it has no reason for the past tense, and it is nothing other than a new life, they define it. It must be taught, therefore, that the meaning of this name is multiple. In the first place, in fact, Penance is said of those who dislike something that they previously liked, without having any reason as to whether this thought was good or bad. Thus it weighs on everyone, whose sadness is according to the century, not according to God; whose Penance of this kind does not bring salvation, but death. Another is Penance, when someone of the admitted crime, which in truth he previously pleased, conceives pain not for the sake of God, but for himself. The third is, when not only because of the admitted crime do we grieve with an intimate sense of spirit, or also give some external sign of that pain, but we are in that mourning for the sake of God alone. And to each of the genres of Penance that have been commemorated, the voice of Penance properly fits. Because, when in the sacred letters we read that God repents, it is evident that it is said by translation. Because sacred letters use that type of speech adapted to the customs of men, when they declare that God has ordered to change something, which in no other way seems to make men, who, if something bothers them, strive with all study to change it. So it is written that He was sorry for having made man; and in another place, of having made Saúl King.

What is the distinction between the meanings of Penance.

But between these meanings of Penance it is worth observing a great distinction. Because the first must be put into vice, the second is a certain affection of a moved and disturbed mind: the third we say belongs to virtue as much as it is a Sacrament; whose significance is typical of this place. And in the first place it must be treated as part of virtue, not only because the faithful people must be instituted by the Pastors to every type of virtue; but also because the actions of this virtue provide the material in which the Sacrament of Penance is concerned; and if first one does not correctly understand what the virtue of Penance is, it is necessary that one also ignores the force of the Sacrament.

Let it be inner Penance.

Therefore, above all, the faithful must be admonished and exhorted to work with all restraint and study on the intimate Penance of the spirit, which we call virtue; without which what is applied with external things will be of very little benefit. The intimate Penance is that, when from the heart we convert to God, and we detest and hate the crimes committed by us; and at the same time we consider it certain and deliberate to amend the bad habits of life and corrupt customs, not without hope of obtaining forgiveness from the mercy of God. And this is followed by pain and sadness, which is disturbance and affection, and by many is called passion, as a companion attached to the detestation of sins. For this reason, among several of the holy Fathers, the definition of Penance is declared with such torment of the spirit.

5. Faith is not part of Penance.

But in him who repents, it is necessary that faith precede Penance. For no one can be converted to God who lacks faith, from which it follows that in no way can one rightly say part of Penance.

6. The intimate Penance of the spirit must be considered a virtue.

And that this intimate Penance, as we said before, belongs to virtue, is openly shown by many precepts that have been transmitted about Penance. Because the Law prescribes only those actions that are undertaken with virtue. Furthermore, no one can deny that pain, when, in what way and to what extent it is appropriate, is of virtue. And for this to be done rightly, lend the virtue of Penance. Because sometimes it happens that from admitted crimes men perceive less pain than is just; In fact, as it is written by Solomon, there are some who rejoice when they have done wrong. And again others give themselves so much to grief of mind and anguish that they also completely despair of salvation: what Cain may seem like, who says: Greater is my iniquity than I deserve forgiveness: and what certainly was Judas, who, driven by penitence, lost his life and soul by hanging. So that we can remain calm in pain, we are helped by the virtue of Penance.

7. In what way one who truly repents must be affected.

But the same can also be inferred from those things that the one who truly repents of sin proposes as an end. First of all, this is its purpose: to abolish sin, and cleanse all guilt and stain from the soul. The second thing is to satisfy God for the admitted crimes: which is evident that it refers to justice. Because, although the reason of justice itself cannot mediate between God and men, because they are so far apart; However, it is clear that there is some justice, of the kind that exists between the father and the children, between the lord and the servants. The third thing is for man to return to the grace of God, whose offense and hatred he incurred due to the ugliness of sin. And all these things sufficiently declare that Penance looks to virtue.

By what degrees one ascends to that divine virtue of Penance.

But it must also be taught by what degrees it is lawful to ascend to this divine virtue. First of all, then, the mercy of God warns us, and converts our hearts to Himself. Which when the Prophet prayed: Convert us, he says, Lord, to you, and we will convert.

Then, illuminated by this light, we reach out with our spirit to God by faith: For he who draws near to God must believe, as the Apostle testifies, that he exists, and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him.

Furthermore, the movement of fear continues, and given the acerbity of the tortures, the spirit is revoked from the sins. And those words of Isaiah seem to refer to this: As one who conceives, when she has approached childbirth, cries out, grieving in her pains; This is how we have been made. Here then comes the hope of imploring God's mercy, with which, standing upright, we can amend life and customs. Finally our hearts are kindled with charity, from which is born that liberal fear worthy of upright and naive children: and thus, fearing only one thing, lest in something we read the majesty of God, we completely abandon the habit of sinning. By these degrees, then, as by steps, one arrives at this most excellent virtue of Penance.

What is the main fruit of the virtue of Penance.

Which altogether must be esteemed divine and celestial virtue, to which, namely, the sacred letters promise the Kingdom of heaven. For in Saint Matthew it is written: Do penance: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand; and in Ezekiel: If the wicked do penance for all his sins that he has committed, and keep all my precepts, and do justice and righteousness, he will live life: and in another place: I do not want the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live. Which is quite evident that it must be understood of the eternal and blessed life.

10. What should be felt about external Penance: and why Christ wanted to refer it to the number of the Sacraments.

Of external Penance, for its part, it must be taught that it is that in which the reason for the Sacrament consists, and that it has certain external things subject to the senses, with which those that are done internally in the soul are declared. In the first place, however, it seems that it should be explained to the faithful why Christ the Lord wanted Penance to refer to the number of the Sacraments. And of this thing that was entirely the cause: so that it would be less licit for us to doubt the remission of sins that God promised when he says: If the wicked do penance, etc.: because it would be vehemently necessary to be in suspense of mind about the intimate Penance, when each one must fear his own judgment in the things he rightly does. So that the Lord might grant this request of ours, he instituted the Sacrament of Penance, with which through the absolution of the Priest we would trust that our sins had been remitted to us, and our consciences would become more peaceful through the faith that rightly should be had in the virtue of the Sacraments. Because in no other way should the voice of the Priest who legitimately forgives our sins be received than that of Christ the Lord, who says to the Paralytic: Trust, son, your sins are remitted to you. Later, since no one can obtain salvation except through Christ and through the benefit of his passion, it was convenient and most useful for us to institute a Sacrament of such a kind, by whose power and efficiency the Blood of Christ, flowing to us, would wash away the sins admitted after Baptism, and thus we would confess to refer the benefit of reconciliation to our Savior alone.

11. In what way Penance is a true Sacrament of the new Law.

And that Penance is a Sacrament, the Pastors will easily show it that way. Because just as Baptism is a Sacrament, because it erases all sins, and especially that which was contracted by origin: for the same reason Penance, which removes all sins sustained after Baptism by will or by action, must be truly and properly said Sacrament. Then, what is main, such as those things that externally,

Both by the penitent and by the Priest, those that are carried out internally in the soul are made and declared; Who will deny that Penance is endowed with the true and proper reason of Sacrament? For the Sacrament is a sign of a sacred thing; and the sinner who repents, with notes of things and words clearly expresses that he has separated his mind from the stupidity of sin: and likewise from the things that are done and said through the Priest, we easily know the mercy of God that remits the same sins. Although this openly indicates those words of the Savior: I will give you the keys of the Kingdom of heaven... and whatever you loose on earth, it will also be loosed in heaven. Because the absolution of the Priest stated in words, means that remission of sins that he effects in the soul.

The Sacrament of Penance can be repeated.

Not only should the faithful be taught that Penance must be included in the number of Sacraments, but also in those that can be repeated. For when Peter asked if forgiveness of sin should be given up to seven times, the Lord answered: I am not telling you up to seven times: but up to seventy times seven. Therefore, if you have to deal with men of such a class that they seem to distrust the supreme goodness and clemency of God, your spirit must be confirmed and you should rise up in the hope of divine grace. Which they will easily achieve so much with the treatment of this place and others that will occur in many sacred letters; as also with those reasons and arguments that it will be licit to take from the book of Saint Chrysostom of the Fallen, and from the books of Saint Ambrose of Penance.

What and what kind is the matter of Penance.

Now, since nothing should be more noticeable to the faithful people than the matter of this Sacrament; It must be taught that in this this Sacrament differs in the greatest degree from the others, because the matter of the other Sacraments is something natural, or made by art: but of the Sacrament of Penance the acts of the penitent are as matter, namely Contrition, Confession and Satisfaction, as has been declared by the Tridentine Synod; which, insofar as they are required in the penitent by the institution of God for the integrity of the Sacrament and the full and perfect remission of sins, for this reason they are called parts of Penance. Nor in truth are these acts called by the Holy Synod as matter because they do not have a true reason for matter, but because they are not of that kind of matter that is applied externally, like water in Baptism and chrism in Confirmation. And what has been said by others, that the same sins are the matter of this Sacrament, will not seem to be said completely differently if we carefully observe: because just as we say that the matter of fire is the wood, which is consumed by the force of the fire; Thus the sins that are erased by Penance can rightly be called the matter of this Sacrament.

What is the form of the Sacrament of Penance.

But neither should the Pastors omit the explanation of the form, because the knowledge of this thing excites the spirits of the faithful to perceive with great religion the grace of this Sacrament. And the form is: I absolve you: which is not only lawful to infer from those words: Whatever you loose on earth, it will also be loosed in heaven; but we receive it from the same doctrine of Christ the Lord transmitted by the Apostles. And since the Sacraments mean what they effect; and those words: I absolve you, show that the remission of sins is effected by the administration of this Sacrament, it is manifest that this is the perfect form of Penance. Because sins are like bonds with which souls are constrained, and from which they are loosened by the Sacrament of Penance. Which is no less truly pronounced by the Priest also of that man who first by the force of the most ardent Contrition, nevertheless acceding to the vow of Confession, has obtained forgiveness of sins from God.

15. With what fruit other prayers are added to the form of the Sacrament.

Many prayers are also added, not really necessary to the form, but to remove those that, due to the fault of the person to whom it is administered, could impede the strength and efficiency of the Sacrament.

How much the power of the Priests of Christ in judging the leprosy of sin differs from the power of the Priests of the old Law.

For which sinners give immense thanks to God, who has given such ample power in the Church to the Priests. Because no, as in the old Law the Priests with their testimony only renounced that someone had been freed from leprosy; Thus now in the Church that power has been given to Priests to declare that someone has been absolved of sins; but truly as ministers of God they absolve, which God himself, the author and father of grace and justice, does.

With what habit and with what rites should penitents recommend their action.

Diligently, for their part, the faithful will also observe the rites that are applied to this Sacrament: because in this way it will happen that the things that they have achieved with this Sacrament will adhere more to their minds, namely that they have been reconciled as servants to the most merciful Lord, or rather as children to the best father; and at the same time they will understand more easily what should be done by those who want (and everyone should want) to prove themselves grateful and fond of such a great benefit. Because he who is burdened by his sins, throws himself with a humble and dejected spirit at the feet of the Priest, so that when he behaves so humbly, he can easily recognize that the roots of pride must be uprooted, from which all the crimes he cries for had their origin and were born; and in the Priest, who sits in him as a legitimate judge, he venerates the person and power of Christ the Lord: because the Priest, as in other things, so in the administration of the Sacrament of Penance, executes the office of Christ. Afterwards the penitent enumerates his sins in such a way that he confesses to be worthy of the greatest and most bitter animosity, and suppliantly asks for forgiveness of the crimes. Which things, in truth, all have very certain testimonies of their antiquity from Saint Dionysius.

What main fruits do men capture from the Sacrament of Penance?

But nothing will truly benefit the faithful so much, and nothing will give them greater joy in undertaking Penance, than if it had often been explained by the Parish Priests how much usefulness we derive from it. Because truly about Penance you will understand that this can be said: that its roots are truly bitter, but the fruits are very sweet. The whole force of Penance, then, is that it restores us to the grace of God, and unites us to him with utmost friendship. And this reconciliation sometimes
1 Reg. 15. How is it understood that some sins are not remitted. Mt. 12, 31. 32. Of which it is said in Ps.

…in pious men who holy and religiously perceive this Sacrament, maximum peace and tranquility of conscience is usually followed with utmost youthfulness of spirit. Because there is no crime so serious and nefarious that by the Sacrament of Penance it is not erased not only once, but again and often. Of which thing the Lord through the Prophet says thus: If the wicked will do penance for all his sins that he has committed, and will keep my precepts, and will do justice and justice, he will live life and will not die: I will not remember all his iniquities that he has committed. And Saint John: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to remit our sins to us; and shortly after: If anyone sins, he says (without excepting any kind of sin), we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is a propitiation for our sins; and not only for ours, but also for those of the whole world.

For what reason is it said that some sins cannot be remitted.

But what we read in the Scriptures is that some did not obtain mercy from God, although they had implored it vehemently; We truly understand this to have been done for this reason: because they did not truly and heartily repent of the crimes. Therefore, when sentences of this kind occur in the sacred letters or among the most holy Fathers, with which they seem to affirm that some sins cannot be remitted; It is convenient to interpret them in such a way that we understand that the request for forgiveness is extremely difficult. Because just as some disease is said to be unhealable for that reason, because the sick person is so affected that he hates the force of salutary medicine: so there is a certain type of sin that is not remitted or condoned, because it rejects the very remedy of salvation, the grace of God. In this sentence it has been said by Saint Augustine: So great is the stain of that sin, when after the knowledge of God, by the grace of Christ, someone impugns brotherhood, and against grace itself is agitated with brands of envy, that he cannot submit to the humility of deprecating, even if due to a bad conscience he is forced to recognize and announce the sin.

No one can obtain the remission of sins without Penance.

But to return to Penance, this power to erase sins is so characteristic of it that without Penance it is in no way licit to ask for the remission of sins, or even to expect it. For it is written: If you do not do penance, you will all likewise perish: which has truly been said by the Lord of the most serious and deadly sins: although also the lighter sins, which are called venial, need some kind of Penance. Because Saint Augustine says: As there is a certain Penance that is done every day in the Church for venial sins, it would truly be in vain if venial sins could be remitted without Penance.

How many are the integral parts of Penance.

But since it is not enough to speak universally about those things that somehow fall into action, the Pastors will take care to transmit one by one those of which the faithful can perceive the reason for true and salutary Penance. And it is proper to this Sacrament that, in addition to the matter and the form, which are common to all Sacraments, it also has those parts, as we said before, which constitute the entire Penance, namely Contrition, Confession and Satisfaction, of which Saint Chrysostom speaks in these words: Penance obliges the sinner to suffer all things willingly; in his heart Contrition, in his mouth Confession, in work all humility, or fruitful Satisfaction. And these parts are said to be of that kind of parts which are necessary to constitute some whole: for, just as the body of man consists of many members, hands, feet, eyes, and other parts of this kind, of which if any are lacking, it rightly appears imperfect; but perfect, if no one is missed; In the same way Penance is also constituted of these three parts in such a way that, although, as far as its nature is concerned, Contrition and Confession are sufficient, with which man becomes just; However, if the third part, that is Satisfaction, does not also agree, it is necessary that something is completely lacking in perfection. Therefore, these parts are connected to each other in such a way that Contrition includes the advice and purpose of confessing and satisfying, Confession includes Contrition and the will to satisfy, and Satisfaction is preceded by the remaining two.

22. In what way these three parts of Penance are linked.

And from these three parts we can adduce that reason: that with the spirit, with the words and with the thing itself, sins are committed against God. Therefore it was convenient that we

CHAPTER 6 and 14.

... submitting ourselves to the will of God, against whom the sin has been committed, and to the keys of the Church itself, with the same things with which the Most Holy Numen of God had been violated for us, let us also appease his wrath and... Because Penance is like a certain compensation for crimes, coming from the will of the one who repents, and... Therefore, the will to compensate is also required, which is mainly about Contrition; and it is necessary that the penitent submit to the judgment of the Priest, who bears the person of God, so that the punishment can be established for him according to the magnitude of the crimes: from which both the reason and need for Confession and Satisfaction can be perceived.

Let Contrition be properly in this matter.

And since it is appropriate to transmit to the faithful the strength and nature of these parts, one must first begin with Contrition, and diligently explain it. Because at no point in time, when past sins return to memory, or when we offend something, should the spirit of Contrition be empty. This is defined by the Fathers at the Tridentine Council: Contrition is pain of mind and detestation of the sin committed, with the purpose of not sinning from now on. And shortly after the movement of Contrition it is subjoined: Thus it finally prepares for the remission of sins, if it is united with the trust of divine mercy and with the vow to provide the other things that are required to rightly sustain this Sacrament. From this definition, then, the faithful will understand that the force of Contrition is not only placed on someone stopping sinning; or has the purpose of instituting a new kind of life, or is already instituting it; but above all, hatred of the bad past life and atonement must be awakened. And this is confirmed to the greatest degree by those cries of the Holy Fathers, which we read to have been frequently poured out in the sacred letters; I have grown weary, says David, in my groaning, I will wash my bed every night; and: The Lord heard the voice of my cry: and again another: I will acknowledge before you all my years in the bitterness of my soul. Which voices indeed, and others of this kind, expressed a certain vehement hatred of the anteact life and detestation of sins.

Why Contrition was called pain by the Fathers of the Council.

And because Contrition is defined by pain, the faithful must be warned not to consider that pain is perceived with the sense of the body. Because Contrition is an action of the will. And Saint Augustine attests that pain is a companion of Penance, not Penance. But the detestation and hatred of sin was meant by the Fathers with the word pain; so much so because the sacred letters use it that way; for David says: How long shall I put counsels in my soul, sorrow in my heart for the day?; as because the pain in the lower part of the soul, which has the force to covet, is born from contrition itself: so that contrition was not inconveniently defined with pain, because it produces pain, and to declare it, penitents usually also change their clothing. Of which the Lord in Saint Matthew says: Woe to you, Chorazin, woe to you, Bethsaida, because if the virtues that have been done in you had been done in Tire and Sidon, long ago they would have done penance in sackcloth and ashes!

25. Why the detestation of sin is called contrition by the Theologians.

Rightly, for its part, the name contrition was imposed on the detestation of the sin of which we speak, to signify the force of pain, taking the likeness of corporeal things, which are often broken by stone or other harder matter; so that with that word it would be declared that our hearts, which were hardened by pride, are crushed and crushed by the force of Penance. Therefore no other pain, whether due to the death of parents or children, or arising from any other calamity, is called by this name; but it is typical of only that pain with which we are affected by the lost grace of God and by stained innocence.

With what other words is the same detestation of sin usually declared?

But also with other words the same thing is usually declared: because it is also said contrition of the heart, because the name of heart is frequently usurped by the sacred letters by the will. For just as the principle of the movements of the body is taken from the heart, so the will moderates and governs all the other forces of the soul. It is also called compunction of the heart by the holy Fathers, who preferred to inscribe the written books of contrition: Of the compunction of the heart. Because just as with iron, swollen ulcers are cut, so that the included virus can come out; Thus the hearts, as if applied with the scalpel of contrition, are incised, so that they can eject the deadly virus of sin. Therefore it was also called splitting of the heart by the Prophet Joel: Turn, he says, to me with all your heart, in fasting, and in weeping, and in planctu, and rend your hearts.

Why the pain of sins in contrition must be maximum and most vehement.
