…can be invented, it will be easy to demonstrate it with these reasons. Because as perfect contrition is an action of charity, which proceeds from that fear that belongs to children; It is clear that the same mode of charity and contrition must be established. But since the charity with which we pray to God is the most perfect love, it follows from this that contrition has united the most vehement pain of the soul. Because just as we must worship God in the highest degree, so we must detest what alienates us from God in the highest degree: in which it must also be observed that with the same genre of speaking the magnitude of charity and contrition is signified in sacred letters. Of charity it has been said: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart: again, what belongs to contrition, the Lord cries through the Prophet: Turn to me with all your heart. Furthermore, if just as God is the supreme good among all things that must be contemplated, so also sin is the supreme evil among all things that men must hate; It follows that for the same reason for which we confess that God must be diligent in the highest degree, for the same reason it is necessary that the supreme hatred of sin capture us again. And that the love of God must come before all things, in such a way that not even for the sake of preserving life it is lawful to sin, those words of the Lord openly teach us: He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and: He who wants to save his soul will lose it. But it must also be noted that, just as, as Saint Bernard attests, no end or mode is prescribed for charity (Because the way, he says, of worshiping God is to worship Him without mode), so no manner is defined for the detestation of sin. Furthermore, it must be not only maximum, but also vehement and completely perfect, so that it excludes all ignavia and discord. For in Deuteronomy it is written: When you seek the Lord your God there, you will find him; If, however, you will seek him with all your heart and with all the tribulation of your soul. And in Jeremiah: You will seek me and find me, when you search for me with all your heart, and I will be found by you, says the Lord.

True contrition does not cease to be true even if the sensible pain of sins has not been absolute.

Although, if it is less permissible for us to make it perfect, contrition can nevertheless be true and effective: because it often happens that things subject to the senses affect us more than spiritual things. For this reason, some sometimes feel a greater sense of pain for the death of their children than for the clumsiness of sin. The same judgment must be made if tears do not follow the acerbity of pain: which however in penitence must be desired and recommended in the highest degree. Indeed, that sentence of Saint Augustine about this thing is illustrious. There is not, he says, the bowels of Christian charity in you, if you mourn the body from which the soul has withdrawn; but the soul from which God has withdrawn, you do not mourn. And this is what those words of our Savior adduced above refer to: Woe to you, Chorazin, woe to you, Bethsaida! And the examples of the Ninevites, of David, of the sinner, of the Prince of the Apostles are very clear, who all, imploring God's mercy with many tears, implored forgiveness of sins.

The deadly sins must be detested one by one in contrition.

To the highest degree, for their part, the faithful must be exhorted and admonished to strive to apply the pain of contrition to each of the mortal crimes. This is indeed how Hezekiah describes contrition when he says: I will acknowledge before you all my years in the bitterness of my soul. Because to recognize all the years is to shake off the sins one by one, to hurt them from the heart. But also in Ezekiel we read written: If the wicked will repent for all his sins, he will live life. And in this sentence Saint Augustine says: Let the sinner consider the quality of the crime in the place, in the time, in the truth, in the people.

Sometimes it is enough to universally detest their sins.

Nor, however, in this matter should the faithful despair of the supreme goodness and clemency of God: because he, as he is most desirous of our salvation, does not interpose any delay in granting us forgiveness, but embraces the sinner with paternal charity, as soon as he has collected himself, and universally detested his sins (which later in another time, if he had the power, he had the mind to recall to memory and detest one by one) he had converted to the Lord: thus in effect he commands us to wait for the Prophet, when he says: The impiety of the wicked will not harm him, on any day in which he has turned from his impiety.

What things are first necessary to true contrition.

From these things, then, it will be possible to deduce those that are in the highest degree necessary for true contrition, of which it is advisable to accurately teach the faithful people, so that each one understands by what reason he can compare it, and has the rule with which to judge how far it is from the perfection of this virtue. In the first place, it is necessary to hate and grieve all the sins that we have admitted, lest, if we only grieve for some, a fictitious and simulated, and not salutary, penance arises for us. For, as it was said by the holy Apostle James: Whoever kept the whole law, but offended in one, has become guilty of all. The second thing is that contrition itself has united the will to confess and satisfy, which will be dealt with later in due time. The third thing is that the penitent entertains a certain and stable desire to amend his life. This indeed the Prophet openly taught us in these words: If the wicked do penance for all his sins that he has committed, and keep all my precepts, and do justice and justice, he will live life and will not die; of all his iniquities that he did I will not remember: and soon afterwards: When the wicked shall turn from his wickedness that he did, and do justice and righteousness, he himself shall quicken his soul: and few things interposed: Repent, he says, and do repentance for all your iniquities, and iniquity shall not be a ruin for you: put away from you all your transgressions in which you have transgressed, and make yourselves a new heart and a new Spirit. Christ the Lord also commanded the same thing to the woman who was caught in adultery: Go, he says, and sin no more. Likewise to that paralytic whom he had healed next to the probatic pool: Behold, he says, you have been made whole, sin no more.

It is shown that the pain of past guilt and the purpose of caution in the future are necessary to contrition.

But also nature itself and reason clearly show that those two things are first of all necessary to contrition, namely the pain of admitted sin and the purpose and caution that nothing of this kind be committed in the future. Because whoever wants to be reconciled with a friend whom he has injured with some injury, it is necessary that he be sorry for having been insulting and contumelious towards him, and that he diligently promise in the rest of the time not to appear to have injured the friendship in any way. Which two things must have obedience attached: because it is appropriate for man to obey the law, whether natural and divine, or human, to which he is subject. Therefore, if the penitent has taken something from another by force or fraud, it is necessary that he restore it: and he must also satisfy the penitent with the compensation of some comfort or office, whose dignity or life he has violated by word or deed. Because what we read in Saint Augustine is trite in everyone's sermon: Sin will not be remitted if what was taken is not restored.

Others must be forgiven if we want to be forgiven.

Nor, in truth, among the other things that belong to the highest degree to contrition, should care be taken with less diligence and necessity that whatever injuries you have received from another be remitted and condoned. Thus in effect our Lord and Savior admonishes and denounces: If you renounce to men their sins, your heavenly Father will also renounce your crimes to you: but if you do not renounce to men, neither will your Father renounce your sins to you. These are the things that the faithful must observe in contrition: the others that can easily be linked to this by Pastors, will truly make contrition in its kind more perfect and absolute; but they should not be considered so necessary that without them the reason for true and salutary Penance cannot be established.

What is the own strength and usefulness of Contrition.

But since it should not be enough for Pastors if they teach the things that seem to belong to salvation, if they do not also work with all care and industry so that the faithful direct their lives and their actions to that same reason that has been prescribed for them; He will vehemently take advantage of often proposing the strength and usefulness of contrition. Because, like most other studies of piety, such as beneficence towards the poor, fasting, prayers and other holy and honest works of this kind, due to the fault of the men from whom they come, they are sometimes repudiated by God; the same contrition certainly can never not be pleasant and acceptable to him. Because the Prophet says: You will not despise a contrite and humiliated heart, God. Furthermore, as soon as we conceive it in our minds, the remission of sins is attributed to us by God, as those words of the same Prophet declare elsewhere: I said: I will confess my injustice against me to the Lord, and you remitted the impiety of my sin. And we notice this thing in the figure of the ten lepers, who, sent by our Savior to the Priests, were freed from leprosy before they reached them. From which it is lawful to know that the force of true contrition (of which it has been said above) is such that for its benefit we immediately ask the Lord for forgiveness of all human crimes.

From what reason we reach the perfection of Contrition.

It will also be of much value to excite the minds of the faithful if the Pastors transmit some reason with which each one can exercise himself in Contrition. For their part, it is advisable to admonish everyone, frequently shaking their conscience, to see if they have kept the things that have been prescribed by God or by Ecclesiastical sanctions. And if someone recognizes that he is guilty of some crime, immediately accuses himself, and suppliantly presents forgiveness to the Lord, he requests that he be given space both to confess and to satisfy, and first of all ask to be helped with the prison of divine grace, lest from now on he admit those same sins of which he vehemently repents. Because Pastors must also take care that the utmost hatred of sins is aroused in the faithful; so much so because its ugliness and clumsiness is extreme; as because they bring us very serious damages and calamities. Because it alienates us from the benevolence of God, from whom we have received maximum benefits and it was lawful for us to expect and obtain much greater ones, and it adds us to eternal death to be perpetually affected with the torments of the greatest pains. So much for Contrition; Now let's come to Confession, which is the other part of Penance.

What is the prestige of the Confession, and how necessary its institution has been to Christian salvation.

And how much care and diligence the Pastors must put into explaining it, they will easily understand from this: that almost all the pious are persuaded that whatever holiness, piety and religion there is at this time in the Church by the supreme gift of God, largely to Confession... the enemy of the human race, when he thinks of uprooting the Catholic faith, through the ministers of his impiety and satellites has endeavored to oppose it with all his forces as a citadel of virtue. Christian. In the first place, then, it must be taught that the institution of Confession has been to us in the highest degree useful, and even necessary. Because even if we grant this, that through Contrition sins are erased, who ignores that it must be so vehement, acrid and incense, that the acerbity of the pain can be equaled and compared with the magnitude of the crimes? But since very few would reach this degree, it also happened that very few could hope for forgiveness of sins in this way. Therefore it was necessary for the most merciful Lord to consult more easily the common salvation of men. Which in truth he carried out with admirable counsel when he gave the Church the keys of the heavenly kingdom.

Confession perfects Contrition.

Because by the doctrine of the Catholic faith everyone must be believed and affirmed with constancy: if someone is so affected in spirit that he grieves for the admitted sins, and at the same time considers not sinning from now on; although he is not affected by such pain that it can suffice to ask for forgiveness; To him, however, when he has rightly confessed his sins to the Priest, by the force of the keys all crimes are remitted and condoned; so that it has been deservedly celebrated by the most holy men our Fathers that by the keys of the Church access to heaven is opened, which no one is allowed to doubt, when we read decreed by the Florentine Council that the effect of penance is the absolution of sins. But in addition to this, it is licit to know how much usefulness Confession brings, because for those whose customs of life are corrupted, we experience that nothing is so useful in amending customs as if they sometimes reveal to a prudent and faithful friend the hidden cogitations of their spirit, all the deeds and sayings, that can help them with work and advice. For the same reason, those who are agitated by the conscience of crimes should be esteemed in the highest salutary degree, who open to the Priest, as Vicar of Christ the Lord, to whom the most severe law of perpetual silence has been proposed, the illnesses and wounds of their soul. Because they will immediately find medicines prepared for them, which not only have a certain heavenly force to heal the present illness, but also to prepare the soul in such a way that from then on it will not be easy to relapse into the same type of morbidity and vice. Nor should that usefulness of Confession be omitted, which to a great extent belongs to the society and conjunction of life: because it is clear that, if you exempt the Sacramental Confession from Christian discipline, all things will be full of hidden and heinous crimes, which later also other much more serious ones, men depraved by the habit of sin will not fear to commit openly: because the shame of confessing imposes as brakes on cupidity and license to commit crimes, and inhibits improbability. But now that the usefulness of Confession has been explained, it will be necessary to convey to the Pastors what its nature and strength are.

Definition and nature of Sacramental Confession.

They define it, therefore, to be the accusation of sins, which belongs to the genus of the Sacrament, raised in order to seek forgiveness through the virtue of the keys.

Sins must be enumerated in Confession with an accusatory spirit. Prov. 2, 14. St. Chrysostom, Hom. 20 in Gen. Augustine, serm. 8 of the Words of the Lord, and in lib. of true and false Penance, cap. 10. Gregory, Hom. 40 in the Evangels. and lib. 10 Morality. chap. 15. Trid Conc. sess. 14 of Penit. chap. 5 and Can. 6 . Alexander of Ales 4. p. q. 70, mem. 3, art. 2. Mt. 9; Mt. 18, 18; Jn. 20, 22-23.

…which belongs to the genre of the Sacrament, raised in order to request forgiveness through the virtue of the keys. And it is rightly called accusation, because sins should not be commemorated in such a way as if we flaunted our crimes, as those do who rejoice when they have done wrong; or at all be narrated as if we expose something conceived to idle listeners for the sake of delight: but they must be enumerated with an accusatory spirit in such a way that we also desire to avenge them on ourselves. And for the sake of asking for forgiveness we confess sins, because this judgment is very different from the forensic questions of capital things, in which confession has been constituted by punishment and torture, not the liberation of guilt and the forgiveness of error: in almost the same sentence, although with other words, the most holy Fathers seem to have defined confession; as when Saint Augustine says: Confession is that by which the latent illness is opened with hope of forgiveness; and Saint Gregory: Confession is the detestation of sins: one and another of which, from what is contained in the definition above, can easily be referred to.

For what reason and when was confession instituted by Christ.

But now, what should be considered maximum of all, the Parish Priests will teach, and without a doubt will transmit to the faithful, that this Sacrament was instituted by Christ the Lord, who made all things good and for the sole cause of our salvation, for his supreme goodness and mercy. For he breathed on the Apostles, gathered together after the resurrection in one place, saying: Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you remit, they are remitted, and whose sins you retain, they are retained. Therefore, since the Lord gave to the Priests the power to retain and remit sins, it is evident that they also were constituted judges of this thing.

From what other places in Scripture do we conclude that confession was instituted by Christ.

And the Lord seemed to mean the same thing when he gave the Apostles the task of untying Lazarus, raised from the dead, from the bonds with which he was constrained. Because Saint Augustine explains that place like this: The Priests themselves, he says, can now benefit more, forgive more the confites, to whom they refer the crime: the Lord, namely through the Apostles themselves, offered the Disciples to untie Lazarus whom he had raised up, showing that the power to untie has been granted to the Priests. To which also belongs what he commanded those who were cured of leprosy on the way to show themselves to the Priests and submit to their judgment.

How from the words of the Lord it is necessarily deduced that the confession must be made to the Priest, and that the successors of the Apostles are judges.

Therefore, since the Lord gave to the Priests the power to remit and retain sins, it is evident that they also were constituted judges of this thing. But since, as the holy Tridentine Synod wisely admonished, no true judgment can be made of anything, nor can the mode of justice be found in repeating the punishments of crimes, if the cause has not been clearly known and understood; From this it follows that through the confession of the penitents all sins must be made known to the Priests one by one. These things, then, the Pastors will teach, which have been decreed by the holy Tridentine Synod and perpetually transmitted by the Catholic Church. Because if we read the most holy Fathers carefully, nowhere will there fail to occur very open testimonies with which it is confirmed that this Sacrament was instituted by Christ the Lord, and that the law of Sacramental confession (which they call with the Greek word Exomologesis and Exagoreusis) must be received as Evangelical. And if we also scrutinize the figures of the Old Testament, those various kinds of Sacrifices that were made by Priests to atone for sins of various kinds certainly seem to belong to the confession of sins.

With what fruit the Church added certain ceremonies to Sacramental Confession.

But just as the faithful should be taught that confession was instituted by the Lord Savior; Thus it is also advisable to warn them that certain rites and solemn ceremonies have been added by authority of the Church; which, although they are not required for the reason of the Sacrament, nevertheless bring its dignity more before the eyes, and prepare the minds of the confidants, inflamed with piety, to more easily obtain the grace of God.

…have been added by authority of the Church; which, although they are not required for the reason of the Sacrament, nevertheless bring its dignity more before the eyes, and prepare the minds of the confidants, inflamed with piety, to more easily obtain the grace of God. For when, with our heads uncovered, bowed at the feet of the Priest, with our faces bowed to the ground, stretching out our hands in supplication, and giving other signs of this kind of Christian humility, we confess our sins, from these things we clearly understand both that in the Sacrament the heavenly power must be recognized, and that divine mercy must be required and demanded by us with the utmost study.

Those who are subject to capital sins cannot recover salvation without Confession.

And no one now considers that the Confession was truly instituted by the Lord, but in such a way that he did not make its use necessary. For this is what the faithful establish: that it is appropriate that he who is oppressed by a mortal crime be revoked to spiritual life by the Sacrament of Confession: which in truth with a most beautiful metaphor we see openly meant by the Lord, when he called the power to administer this Sacrament keys of the kingdom of heaven. Because just as no one can enter any place without the work of the one to whom the keys have been entrusted; Thus we understand that no one is admitted to heaven if the doors are not opened by the Priests to whose faith the Lord gave the keys. Otherwise there would seem to be no use of keys at all in the Church; and in vain will he who has been given the power of the keys prohibit someone from accessing heaven, if he can nevertheless open another way of entry. And Saint Augustine truly knew this clearly when he says: Let no one say to himself: I do Penance secretly before the Lord; God, who will forgive me, knows what I do in my heart. Has it been said without cause: Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven? Have the keys been given to the Church of God without cause? And in the same sentence, Saint Ambrose wrote in the books of Penance, when he started the heresy of the Novatians, who affirmed that only the Lord should reserve the power to remit sins. Who, he says, venerates God more, he who obeys his commands, or he who resists? God commanded us to temper his ministers, whom when we obey, we defer honor to God alone.

44. At what time of age and year should you confess.

But since it can in no way be doubted that the law of Confession has been given and established by the Lord himself; It follows that it must be seen who, at what time of age and year, must obey it. In the first place, then, from the canon of the Lateran Council, whose beginning is Omnis utriusque sexus, it is perceived that no one is ascribed to the law of Confession before that age in which he can have the use of reason. Nor, however, has that age been defined with a certain number of years; but it seems universally that it must be established that since that time Confession has been indicated to the child, when he has the strength to discern between good and evil, and fraud can fit into his mind. Because when each one has reached that time of life in which he must deliberate about eternal salvation, then for the first time he must confess his sins to the Priest, since otherwise it is licit for no one to hope for salvation who is oppressed by the conscience of crimes. And at what time it is best to confess, with that canon of which we have mentioned before, it was decreed by the holy Church. Because he commands that at least once every year all the faithful confess their sins.

How many times should Christians use this benefit.

But if we consider what the reason for our salvation postulates, in truth how many times we either prevent the danger of death, or we undertake to deal with something whose handling is not suitable for a man contaminated by sins (as when we administer or receive the Sacraments), so many times Confession should not be omitted. And it is equally advisable to keep the same when we fear that we will be caught forgetting some guilt that we have admitted. Because we cannot confess sins that we do not remember; nor do we ask the Lord for forgiveness of sins, if the Sacrament of Penance does not erase them through Confession.

All sins must be opened one by one in Confession.

But as many things must be observed in Confession, some of which belong to the nature of the Sacrament, others are not so necessary; These will have to be treated exactly. Because there is no shortage of libels and comments from which it is easy to undermine the explanation of all these things. That, for their part, above all, let the Parish Priests teach that in Confession care must be taken to ensure that it is complete and absolute. Because all mortal sins should be revealed to the Priest. Because the venials, who do not divert us from the grace of God,

... and in which we work more frequently, although we confess them rightly and usefully (which is demonstrated by the use of the pious), they can nevertheless be omitted without guilt, and expiated for many other reasons: but the deadly sins, as we have already said, must be enumerated one by one, although they lie very hidden, and are of that kind that are interdicted in the two extreme chapters of the Decalogue. For it often happens that those wound the soul more seriously than those in which men openly and publicly tend to sin: thus it has truly been defined by the Holy Tridentine Synod, and has always been transmitted by the Catholic Church, as the testimonies of the holy Fathers declare. Because it is in Saint Ambrose in this way: No one can be justified from sin if he has not confessed the sin. Saint Jerome also confirms the same thing in Ecclesiastes; because it says: If the serpent has bitten someone secretly, and without any conscious awareness has infected him with the poison of sin, if he remains silent and does not do Penance, nor does he want to confess his wound to his brother or teacher, the teacher who has a tongue to heal will not be able to take advantage of him. Furthermore, Saint Cyprian in the Book of the Lapses teaches this very openly with these words: Although you are not constrained by any fanatory of sacrifice or libel, nevertheless because you thought about it, painfully confess that same thing before the Priests of God. Finally this is the common voice and sentence of all the Doctors of the Church.

47. The circumstances of the sins must be patted down.

But in Confession the utmost care and diligence that we usually put into the most serious things must be used, and the entire study must be conferred in such a way that we heal the wounds of the soul and uproot the roots of sin. In truth, it is not only appropriate to explain by narrating serious sins, but also those things that surround each sin and greatly increase or decrease pravity.

Because certain circumstances are so serious that the reason for the deadly sin consists only of them: therefore all these must always be confessed. Because if someone has killed a man, it must be explained whether he was initiated into the sacred or was profane; and equally if he cohabited with a woman, it is necessary that he open up whether she was free by the law of marriage, or the wife of another, or propinqua, or consecrated to God with the promise of some vow. Because these constitute different kinds of sins; so that the first is truly called simple fornication, the second adultery, the third incest, the fourth sacrilege by the Doctors of divine things. Theft must also be numbered among the sins: but if someone steals a gold, he sins altogether more lightly than the one who steals one hundred or two hundred, or some enormous force of gold, and especially the one who took sacred money. Which reason also belongs to the place and time, whose examples are more notable in the books of many than for us to commemorate them. These, then, as we said, must be enumerated: but those that do not greatly increase the pravity of the thing can be omitted without crime.

The Confession in which something serious is spontaneously kept silent must be reiterated.

But it is so necessary for confession (as we said before) to be complete and absolute, that if someone purposely omits some of those that must be explained, and confesses only the rest, not only does he not get any comfort from that confession, but he also binds himself with a new crime: nor should such an enumeration of sins be called by the name of confession in which the reason for the Sacrament is found; Furthermore, it is necessary for the penitent to repeat the confession, and make himself guilty of that sin of having violated the sanctity of the Sacrament with the simulation of the confession.

The Confession in which something has been omitted due to forgetfulness or slight carelessness should not be reiterated.

But in truth, if for another reason it seems that the confession has lacked something, or because the penitent has forgotten some crimes, or because he has not so accurately persecuted the latebras of his conscience, when nevertheless he had in mind to confess all the sins in their entirety, there will be no need for him to reiterate the confession: it will be enough, for his part, if when the sins that he had forgotten have returned to memory, he confesses them to the Priest in another time.

...it must be warned, lest perhaps we have scrutinized our conscience with too much dissolution and remission, and have so carelessly studied to repeat by memory the admitted sins, that we may deservedly seem to have not even wanted to remember them: because if this has been done, it will be necessary to reiterate the confession altogether.

The confession must be bare, simple and open.

Furthermore, care must be taken that the confession is bare, simple and open, not artificially composed, as some do who seem to rather explain the reason for their life than confess their sins. Because that confession must be the one that opens us to the Priest as we know ourselves, and demonstrates certain things as true and doubtful things as doubtful. And whether or not sins are reviewed, or sermons unrelated to the thing we are dealing with are ingested, it is clear that confession lacks this virtue.

51. Confession must be prudent and shameful.

Those who use prudence and shame in explaining things should also be strongly recommended. Because it should not be dealt with in too many words, but those that pertain to the nature and reason of each sin should be opened with a brief prayer that has modesty attached to it.

52. Confession cannot be made by internuncio or by letters.

But how religiously the right of the ordinary Priest was formerly preserved in the most ancient Church, is easily understood from the ancient decrees of the Fathers; with which care was taken that no Bishop or Priest would dare to do anything in another's Parish without the authority of the one who presided over him, or unless great necessity seemed to force him. This was truly sanctioned by the Apostle when he commanded Titus to establish Priests in each of the cities, who would feed and educate the faithful with the heavenly delicacy of doctrine and the Sacraments.

55. Any Priest can absolve the sinner in need.

Although, if the danger of death is prevented and the Priest's own power is not given, so that no one perishes on this occasion, the Tridentine Council that has been preserved in the Church of God teaches that it is lawful for each Priest not only to condone all kinds of sins, of whatever power, but also to absolve from excommunication.

Where is the power of jurisdiction proven? Council of Antioch, Chalcedon and others. Titus 1, 5. How much power of each Priest in the danger of death regarding absolution. Tridentine Synod of Penit.
