CHAPTER 21
Of the things that regarding the use of Confession must be observed by the Priest around the penitent.

…the Minister of the sacrament is endowed with both science and erudition and prudence; because at the same time he carries the person of the judge and the doctor. And as far as the first thing is concerned, it is sufficiently established that a non-vulgar science is necessary, with which it can both investigate sins, and judge from the various types of sins which are serious and which are light, according to the order and type of each man. But since he is a doctor, he also needs extreme caution. Because it must be diligently provided that those remedies are applied to the sick person that seem most likely to heal his soul and immunize it from now on against the force of morbidity. From which the faithful will be able to understand that each one must take care with the utmost study to choose that Priest to whom he recommends integrity of life, doctrine and prudent judgment.

Therefore, as the salvation of those must be helped with all study; This first thing the Priests will diligently observe in the penitent: whether he has true contrition for his sins, and whether it is true and deliberate for him to abstain from sins from now on. And if you notice that he is affected in this way, admonish him and vehemently exhort him to give maximum thanks to God for such a great and singular benefit, and never fail to ask for the prison of heavenly grace, equipped and covered with which he can easily resist and repel the pious cupidities.

He must also be taught not to let any day pass without meditating something on the mysteries of the passion of our Lord, and to be excited and inflamed to imitate him and love him with utmost charity. Because with this meditation you will be able to feel more protected every day from all the temptations of the devil. Because there is no other reason why we so quickly or lightly, challenged by the enemy, succumb in spirit and strength, but that we forget those heavenly things.

How the confessor should behave towards those who excuse his sins.

First of all, for their part, the arrogance of some who strive either to defend or to make light of their crimes with some excuse must be repressed. For, for example, when someone confesses to having been moved too vehemently by anger, he immediately assigns the cause of this disturbance to another, of whom he complains that he was first injured. He must be warned, therefore, that this is a sign of a weak mind and of a man who either despises or is completely ignorant of the magnitude of his sin, and therefore that this type of excuse belongs more to increasing than to diminishing sin. For he who thus strives to prove his fact seems to profess that he will then use patience when he is injured by no one with injury: of which in truth nothing can be more unworthy of the Christian man.

How will the confessor consult those who are ashamed to confess their sins, or approach it unprepared.

More pernicious, on the other hand, must be estimated the guilt of those who, prevented by a certain foolish shame, do not dare to confess their sins. To these, then, it is advisable to add encouragement by exhorting, and they must admonish themselves that there is nothing for which they should fear to open their vices; and no one should appear admirable if he understands that men sin; which in truth is common morbidity of all, and falls properly into human imbecility. There are others who, either because they rarely confess their sins, or because they have not put any care and cogitation into investigating their crimes, do not know either how to issue a confession of what has been committed, or where the beginning of this office should be taken. Which in truth it is necessary to object more sharply, and above all to teach that, before someone accesses the Priest, with all study he must take care of being moved by contrition for his sins; which in truth cannot be provided in any way if they are not remembered one by one.

How the modesty of some should be consulted.

But as it sometimes happens that women, having forgotten some crime in the previous confession, do not dare to return again to the Priest, because they fear either falling into suspicion of great impropriety before the people, or being deemed to seek the praise of a singular religion; Often both publicly and privately it must be taught that no one is of such memory that he can remember all his deeds, sayings and cogitations: therefore the faithful should not be dissuaded by anything from returning to the Priest, if they have returned to the memory of some crime that had previously been omitted. These things, then, and many others of this kind must be observed in confession by Priests. Now we must come to the third part of Penance, which is called Satisfaction.

What does Satisfaction mean in general, and what in the matter of confession.

First of all, then, the name and force of satisfaction must be stated. Because from here the enemies of the Catholic Church have taken away ample opportunity for dissidence and discord with maximum perdition for the Christian people. And Satisfaction is the complete solution of the thing due. Because what is enough, nothing seems to be missing. Therefore, when we speak of the reconciliation of grace, it means the same thing to satisfy as to give to another as much as may suffice to the angry spirit to avenge the injury: and thus satisfaction is nothing other than the compensation of the ill-intentioned injury to another. And what belongs to this place, the Doctors of divine things usurped the name of Satisfaction to declare that compensation when man pays something to God for the sins committed.

63. How many are the degrees of that Satisfaction that includes some compensation for sin.

In which genus, as there may be many degrees, it follows that...

For this reason it has been received by ancient custom of the Church that, when penitents are absolved of sins, some penalty is inflicted on them; whose solution to punishment has often been called satisfaction. And the same name also means any kind of punishment that we endure for sins, not really constituted by the Priest, but spontaneously sustained by us or repeated by ourselves.

Let this satisfaction be that belongs to the Sacrament of Penance.

But this in no way belongs to Penance as it is a Sacrament; but only that part of the Sacrament should be considered that which we said is paid to God for sins by precept of the Priest: with this adjunct, that we have it established and deliberate in our minds to avoid sins with all study. This is how some defined it: To satisfy is to deny God the honor due. And since no one can pay God due honor if he does not completely avoid sins, it appears quite a bit. And to satisfy is to excise the causes of sins, and not to indulge access to their suggestion. In whose sentence others felt that satisfaction is the purgation with which all that is sordid that has remained in the soul due to the stain of sin is washed away, and we are absolved from the penalties defined by time to which we were subject. This being so, it will be easy to persuade the faithful how necessary it is for penitents...

Not always with the remission of eternal punishment, which follows the condonation of guilt, is temporal punishment remitted.

They must be taught, in fact, that there are two things that follow sin: the stain and the penalty. And although always, guilt is waived, at the same time the torture of eternal death constituted in hell is also condoned; However, it does not always happen, as has been declared by the Tridentine Synod, that the Lord remits the relics of sins and the punishment defined for a certain time that is due to sins. Of which there are perspicuous examples in the sacred letters, in the third chapter of Genesis, in Numbers 12 and 20 and in many other places: but let us contemplate that most clear and most illustrious of David, to whom although Nathan had said: The Lord has also taken away your sin; You will not die: however, he announced to her that the son who had been born to him from her adultery would die, and then he suffered very serious calamities from his house.

Why does God not indulge man as much through the Sacrament of Penance as through Baptism.

But why it has been done that all punishment is not condoned for the Sacrament of Penance equally as for Baptism, has been clearly explained by the holy Tridentine Synod in these words: The reason of divine justice demands that in a different way those who committed crimes out of ignorance before Baptism be received in grace by God, and in a different way in truth those who, once freed from the bondage of sin and the devil, and received the gift of the Holy Spirit, They were not afraid to knowingly violate the temple of God and grieve the Holy Spirit. And it is appropriate to divine clemency that sins should not be waived to us in such a way without any Satisfaction, that, given the opportunity, considering the sins lighter, as insulting and contumelious to the Holy Spirit, we do not fall into more serious ones...

In what way others are helped from the pains that are inflicted on us.

Furthermore, the examples of our Penance teach others how they themselves should establish life and follow piety. Because when other men sense the penalties that have been inflicted on us for sins, they understand both that they must use extreme caution throughout life, and that they must correct pristine customs. For this reason it has been most wisely observed by the Church that, when a public flagicione has been committed by someone, public penance was also given to him, so that the rest, terrified by fear, would from then on avoid the sins more diligently; which was also sometimes done in more serious occult crimes. But, as we said, in the public this was perpetual: that those who had committed them, before they had undergone public penance, did not absolve themselves. Meanwhile, for their part, the Pastors prayed to God for their salvation, and did not stop exhorting the penitents themselves to do the same. In which genre the care and concern of Saint Ambrose was supreme.

How after God's mercy in sin there is also room for justice.

The divine Bernard also affirms that two things are found in sin: the stain of the soul and the wound: and the same stupidity is removed by the mercy of God; But to heal the wounds of sins, that cure that is applied in the remedy of Penance is greatly necessary. Because just as, once the wound is healed, certain scars remain that must also be healed: so in the soul, once the guilt is forgiven, there remain relics of the sins that must be purged. The same completely confirms the sentence of Saint Chrysostom, when he says: It is not enough to remove the arrow from the body, but also the wound inflicted by the arrow must be healed: so also in the soul, after receiving forgiveness of sin, the wound left must be healed by Penance. Very frequently, in fact, we are taught by Saint Augustine that these two things must be noticed in Penance: the mercy and justice of God; mercy, with which he condones sins and the eternal punishments due to them; justice, with which man is punished with penalties defined by time.

70. Through Penance we escape the penalties prepared by God for us.

Finally, the penalty of Penance suffered by us anticipates the animosity of God and the tortures committed against us. Thus indeed the Apostle teaches when he says: If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged: but when we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord, so as not to be condemned with this world. These things, when they have been explained to the faithful, will hardly be able to prevent them from being excited to the greatest degree to the works of Penance.

From where our works are both meritorious and satisfactory.

And how much its strength is can be gathered from this: that it all depends on the merit of the passion of Christ the Lord. From which also with honest actions we obtain those two greatest goods: one is that we deserve the rewards of immortal glory: in such a way that also the chalice of cold water that we will give in his name does not lack mercy: the other, that we satisfy for our sins.

Two things must be noted in Penance. By the merit of Christ's passion, our works are meritorious and satisfactory. Trid. Sinod. sess. 14 of Penit. c. 8, Can. 13 y 14 , and sess. 6 of the Justification, c. 16. Mt. 10, 42; Mc. 9, 40. In what way the merits of the saints also benefit others. Conc. Trid. sess. 14, c. 8.

72. Our satisfaction does not obscure the satisfaction and merit of Christ.

Nor in truth does this obscure the most abundant and cumulative satisfaction of Christ the Lord, but rather on the contrary it happens that it makes it much clearer and more illustrious. For the grace of Christ seems to be all the more abundant, as not only those things are communicated to us that he alone, but also those that, as head in the members, he merited and paid to his holy and just men: for which reason it is manifest that it happens that the just and honest actions of the pious have so much weight and dignity. For Christ the Lord, as head in the members and vine in the branches, continually pours out his grace on those who are united to him through charity. Which grace indeed always precedes, accompanies and follows our good works, and without which we can in no way merit and satisfy God. And so it happens that the just seem to lack nothing, when with the works they carry out by the virtue of God they can both satisfy the divine law according to the human and mortal condition, and deserve eternal life, which they would obtain if, adorned with the grace of God, they had died of life. For that voice of the Savior is well-known: But whoever drinks this water that I will give him will never thirst forever; but the water that I will give him will become in him a fountain of flowing water for eternal life.

For any work to have true power to satisfy, which ones are mainly necessary.

But two things are mainly required in satisfaction: the first is that the one who satisfies be just and a friend of God: because works that are done without faith and charity can in no way be pleasing to God: the second, that works of such a kind are encouraged that by their nature they bring discomfort and pain. Because as they are compensations for past crimes, and as the Holy Martyr Cyprian says, redeemers of sins, it is absolutely necessary that they have some bitterness: although it does not always follow that those who engage in those annoying actions have the sense of pain. Because often either the habit of suffering or the charity kindled in God makes things that are very serious to endure not even felt. Nor does it happen, however, that those same works do not have the power to satisfy: for this is characteristic of the children of God, to be inflamed in such a way with their love and piety that, tormented with extremely arduous tasks, they either feel almost nothing inconvenient, or they endure everything with the most lethargic spirit.

74. How many are the works of satisfaction.

But all kinds of satisfaction will be taught by the Pastors that should be conferred mainly to these three: prayer, fasting, almsgiving: which in truth correspond to the three goods of the soul, of the body and of those that are called external comforts, all of which we have received from God. And there can be nothing more suitable and convenient for removing the roots of all sins. For as everything in the world is the lust of the flesh, or the lust of the eyes, or the pride of life; No one fails to see that these three causes of morbidity are directly opposed by so many other medications, namely fasting to the first, almsgiving to the second, and prayer to the third. Furthermore, if we also look at those who are offended by our sins, it will be easy to understand why all satisfaction refers mainly to these three: and these are God, our neighbor and ourselves. Therefore we smite God with prayer, we satisfy our neighbors with alms, and we truly punish ourselves with fasting.

75. The afflictions that are extrinsically sent to men are also satisfactory.

But as many and various fatigues and calamities oppress us while we are in this life; First of all, the faithful must be taught that those who with a patient spirit endure whatever laborious and inconvenient things God has sent, have achieved ample material to satisfy and deserve: but those who, invitingly and repugnantly, sustain such punishment, deprive themselves of all fruit of satisfaction, but only endure the animosity and torture of God who avenges sins with just judgment.

One can satisfy for another, but not confess or contrite.

And in this the supreme goodness and clemency of God must be preached with maximum praise and thanksgiving, who condoned this to human imbecility: that one could satisfy for another: which indeed is in the highest degree proper to this part of Penance. Because just as, as far as contrition and confession are concerned, no one can grieve or confess for another; thus those who are endowed with divine grace can, in the name of another, pay what is due to God: wherefore it happens that in some way the one seems to bear the burdens of the other. Nor indeed has any of the faithful been left room to doubt this, who in the Apostles' Creed confess the communion of saints. Because as we are all reborn to Christ washed with the same Baptism, we are partakers of the same Sacraments, and mainly we recreate ourselves with the food and drink of the same Body and Blood of Christ the Lord; This clearly demonstrates that we are all members of the same body. Therefore, as the foot does not perform its function only for its usefulness, but also for that of the eyes; nor again, because the eyes see, should it refer to their own usefulness, but to the common usefulness of all the members; Thus the offices of satisfaction must be considered common among us.

Not all the virtue of contentment can be communicated to others.

Nor, however, is this true without any exception, if we look at all the comforts that are captured from it: because the works of Satisfaction are also certain medicines and cures, which are prescribed to the penitent to heal the poor affections of the spirit: of whose fruit of usefulness it is manifest that those who do not satisfy by themselves completely lack. These things, then, about the three parts of Penance, contrition, confession and satisfaction, must be copiously and elucidatedly explained.

Absolution should not be prevented from those who do not promise to restore what was taken.

But above all, it is appropriate for Priests to observe that, having heard the confession of sins, before absolving the penitent of sins, they diligently take care that, if he should have taken anything from the thing or existence of his neighbor, whose sin deservedly appears to be worthy of condemnation, he compensates it with cumulat a Satisfaction: because no one should be absolved if he does not first promise to restore the things he were each one's. But since there are many who, although they prolixly promise that they will do enough for the job, it is nevertheless true and deliberate never to fulfill the promises; they must at all be forced to make restitution; and often that of the Apostle must be instilled in them: He who stole, let him steal no more; rather work, doing with your hands what is good, so that you have something to give to those who are in need.

Of what kind of satisfaction should be imposed on the penitent.

By imposing, for their part, the penalty of satisfaction, the Priests will consider that nothing should be established at their discretion, but that all things should be directed with justice, prudence and piety. And so that with this rule sins appear to be measured, and penitents recognize more the seriousness of their crimes, it will sometimes be worth telling them what penalties have been established for certain crimes by the prescription of the ancient Canons, which are called penitentials. Thus, universally the mode of satisfaction will be tempered by the reason for guilt. But of all kinds of satisfactions it is most appropriate to prescribe to penitents that on certain and defined days they take time off to prayer, and make prayers to God for all, and especially for those who have died in the Lord from this life. It is also advisable to exhort them to often encourage and willingly repeat the same works of satisfaction prescribed by the Priest; and in such a way that they compose their customs, that, diligently absolute all those that belong to the Sacrament of Penance, yet they never interrupt the studies of the virtue of Penance. And if at times also due to a public offense public penance must be prescribed, even if the penitent avoids it and deprecates it, it will not be easily heard: but it is better to persuade him to receive with a free and calm spirit those that will be salutary for both him and others. These things about the Sacrament of Penance and each of its parts must be taught in such a way that not only the faithful understand them perfectly, but also, with the Lord's help, they induce the spirit to actually pay them piously and religiously.

OF THE SACRAMENT OF EXTREME ANOINTING.

CHAPTER VI

1. Why the Shepherds of souls must often discuss the Sacrament of Extreme Unction before the people.

As the holy oracles of the Scriptures teach thus: In all your works remember your last days, and eternally you will not sin, Parish Priests are tacitly admonished that no time should be omitted from exhorting the faithful people to engage in assiduous meditation on death. And since the Sacrament of Extreme Unction cannot but have united the memory of that supreme day; It is easily understood that it should be discussed often, not only for the reason that it is most convenient to open and explain the mysteries of those things that belong to salvation; but also because the faithful, repeating in their minds that the need to die has been proposed to everyone, will inhibit the pious cupidities. Therefore it will happen that in the very expectation of death they will feel less disturbed; but give immortal thanks to God, who, just as the Sacrament of Baptism opened our access to true life, so also, so that upon passing away from this mortal life we ​​would have a more expeditious path to heaven, he instituted the Sacrament of Extreme Unction.

Why is this Sacrament called Extreme Unction?

So that, therefore, the things that are most necessary to this explanation may be explained, with almost the same order that has been kept in the other Sacraments; First of all, it must be conveyed that this Sacrament has been called Extreme Unction for this reason: because this, of all the sacred anointings that the Lord our Savior entrusted to his Church, is the last one that must be administered. Therefore this same Anointing for our elders has also been called the Sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick, and the Sacrament of those who come out: with whose words the faithful can easily return to the memory of that very new time.

In what way the very reason of Sacrament is suitable for Extreme Unction.

And that the very reason of Sacrament is appropriate for Extreme Unction, first of all it must be explained. And this will become evident if we pay attention to the words with which the holy Apostle James promulgated the law of this Sacrament: Is anyone among you sick? says; call the Priests of the Church, and pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord, and the prayer of faith will save the sick, and the Lord will relieve him; and if he is in sins, they will be remitted to him. Because when the Apostle affirms that sins are condoned, he thereby declares the strength and nature of the Sacrament. And that this was the perpetual doctrine of the Catholic Church regarding Extreme Unction, is both attested by many other councils, and by the Tridentine Synod it has been declared in such a way that it constituted the penalty of anathema against all those who dared to teach or feel otherwise. And also Innocent first recommends this Sacrament to the faithful to the highest degree.

As several Anointings are done here, several Sacraments must also be said.

Constantly, therefore, it must be taught by Pastors that it is true Sacrament; and not several, but one, although it is administered by several anointings, to each of which its own prayers and peculiar form must be applied. And it is one not by the continuation of the parts that cannot be divided, but by perfection: of the kind that are all the others that consist of many things. For just as the house, which is composed of many and diverse things, is perfected in one form; Thus this Sacrament, although it is constituted of many things and words, is nevertheless a single sign, and has the efficiency of a single thing that it signifies. The Parish Priests will also teach what the parts of this Sacrament are, the element, I say, and the word. Because these have not been omitted by Saint James, in which it is lawful to notice their mysteries in each one.

What is the matter of the Extreme Unction.

Its element, then, or matter, as the Councils and mainly the Tridentine Council decreed, is the oil consecrated by the Bishop, namely a liquid not squeezed from any rich and fatty nature, but only from the berries of the olive trees. And most aptly this matter means what is effected internally in the soul by the force of the Sacrament. Because just as oil greatly benefits the pain of the body; Thus the virtue of the Sacrament reduces sadness and pain of the spirit. Furthermore, oil restores health, brings hilarity and lends light to the light; and then it is to the greatest extent possible to recreate the forces of the fatigued body. All of which things declare what is effected in the sick person by divine virtue through the administration of this Sacrament. Enough of these things about the matter.

In what way this Sacrament is perfected.

The form, for its part, of the Sacrament is the word and that solemn precation that the Priest applies to each of the anointings, when he says: By this holy anointing I forgive you to God whatever you committed crimes through vice of the eyes, or the nose, or the touch. And that this is the true and proper form of this Sacrament, the holy Apostle James means when he says: And pray over it... And the prayer of faith will save the sick. From which it is legal to know that the form must be uttered as a precaution; although the Apostle did not express in what words it should primarily be conceived. But this has remained until us by faithful tradition of the Fathers, in such a way that all the Churches retain that reason of form that is used by the holy Roman Church, mother and teacher of all. Because although some change the words somewhat, when instead of "I forgive you to God" they put "Remita" or "Pardon", sometimes also "Heal what you committed": nevertheless, since no mutation is made of the sentence, it is clear that the same form is religiously kept by all.

Why is the form of this Sacrament contained as a precaution?

Nor in truth does anyone wonder why the form of the other Sacraments has been made to mean in an absolute way what it effects, as when we say: I baptize you, or: I sign you with the sign of the Cross; or it is pronounced as by those who reign, as when in the administration of the Sacrament of Orders it is said: Receive the power; but this single form of the Extreme Unction is absolved with certain caution. Because this has been established with optimal right: since this Sacrament is applied so that, in addition to the spiritual grace it provides, it also restores healing to the sick; However, since it does not always follow that the sick recover from illnesses, for this reason the form is prepared with caution, so that from the benignity of God we may achieve what the force of the Sacrament does not usually accomplish with constant and perpetual order. For their part, their own rites are also applied in the administration of this Sacrament: but the majority of them contain prayers which the Priest uses to pray for the salvation of the sick. Because no other Sacrament is made with more prayers; and rightly indeed, because at that time the faithful should mainly be helped with pious obsertions. Therefore, all the others who then happen to be present, and mainly the Parish Priests, must pray to God from the heart and entrust with all study to his mercy the life and salvation of those who work.

Who is the author of this Sacrament.

But as it has been demonstrated that the Extreme Unction must be truly and properly included in the number of the Sacraments; It also follows that its institution has proceeded from Christ the Lord: which was later proposed and promulgated to the faithful by the holy Apostle James. Although the Savior himself seems to have given some kind of this Anointing when he sent his disciples two by two before his face. For of those in the Evangelist it is written thus: They went out and preached that they should do Penance, and they cast out many demons, and they anointed many sick with oil and healed them; which Anointing must be believed to have been not invented by the Apostles, but precepted by the Lord, not endowed with any natural virtue, but rather mystically instituted to heal the spirits rather than to heal the bodies. Which is what Saint Dionysius, Ambrose, Chrysostom and Gregory the Great affirm: so that in no way should there be any doubt that this one of the seven Sacraments of the Catholic Church should be received with utmost religion.

9. To whom Extreme Unction should be administered.

But the faithful must be taught that, although this Sacrament belongs to all, there are nevertheless certain types of men excepted to whom it should not be administered. And in the first place, those who are healthy and firm in body are excepted. Because the Extreme Unction should not be paid to these, the Apostle teaches as much when he says: Is anyone among you sick?, as reason shows: since it was instituted for this reason, not only to provide medicine to the soul, but also to the body. Thus, as only those who work morbidly need healing; For this reason, this Sacrament should also be offered to those who seem to become so dangerously ill that it is to be feared that the supreme day of life will not come to them. In which, however, those who usually observe that time of anointing the sick when, having lost all hope of salvation, they begin to lack life and senses, sin very seriously. Because it is clear that in order to perceive the grace of the Sacrament more magnificently, it is very valuable if the sick person, when his integrity and reason are still in force, and when he can provide faith and religious will of mind, is anointed with the sacred oil. For this reason, the Parish Priests must warn to apply heavenly medicine mainly at that time, in truth always due to its extremely salutary power, when also due to the piety and religion of those who must be cured they understand that it will be more beneficial. To no one, therefore, who is not affected by serious morbidity, it is licit to give the Sacrament of Anointing, even if it poses the danger of life; because it prepares a dangerous navigation; because he is going to enter a battle from which certain death prevents him; or also if, condemned to death, he is taken to torture. Furthermore, all those who lack the use of reason are not suitable to sustain this Sacrament; and children, who do not admit any sins whose relics need to be healed with the remedy of this Sacrament: likewise the insane and furious, unless at times they had the use of reason, and at that time they mainly gave meaning of pious spirit, and suffered to be anointed with the sacred oil.

Because he who from the very beginning was never the owner of the mind and reason, should not anoint himself; On the contrary, in truth, if the sick person, even with an intact mind, wanted to participate in this Sacrament, later fell into madness and fury.

Which parts of the body should be anointed are here.

Not all parts of the body should be anointed, but only those that nature has attributed to man as instruments of the senses; the eyes for the sake of vision, the ears for the sake of hearing, the noses for the sake of smell, the mouth for the sake of taste or sermon, the hands for the sake of touch; which, although it is equally diffused throughout the body, yet in that part it is chiefly vigorous. And this rite of anointing is retained by the universal Church, and also optimally suits the nature of this Sacrament; because it is like medicine. And as in morbidities of the body, although the whole body is badly affected, the cure is applied only to that part from which, as a source and origin, the morbidity arises; That is why the entire body is not anointed, but rather those members in which the power of feeling mainly emanates, also the kidneys, as the seat of voluptuousness and libido; and then the feet, which are for us the beginning of entering and moving from place to place.

The Extreme Unction can be reiterated.

In which it is worth observing that in the same illness, when the sick person is placed in the same danger of life, he should only be anointed once. And if after this Anointing has been given, the sick person convalesces, as many times afterwards he falls into that discrimination of life, as many times the subsidy of the same Sacrament can be applied to him. From which it is seen that it must be replaced in the number of those Sacraments that are usually reiterated.

With what religion and preparation this Sacrament should be sustained.

And as with any study, it is important to take care that nothing impedes the grace of the Sacrament; and nothing is more opposed to it than the consciousness of some deadly sin; The perpetual custom of the Catholic Church must be kept that before Extreme Unction the Sacrament of Penance and the Eucharist be administered.

And then the Parish Priests should strive to persuade the sick person to offer himself to the Priest to be anointed with that faith with which those who were to be healed by the Apostles used to offer themselves in ancient times. First of all, for its part, the salvation of the soul must be desired, then the health of the body, with that adjunction: if this were to benefit eternal glory. Nor should the faithful doubt that those holy and solemn prayers are heard by God, of which the Priest uses, carrying not his person, but that of the Church and our Lord Jesus Christ. With which the only thing above all should be exhorted to take care that the Sacrament of this most salubrious oil is administered to them holy and religiously, when it seems to both incite the fight more bitterly and to deplete the strength of both the mind and the body.

By what minister this Sacrament should be perceived.

And we have learned who the Minister of Extreme Unction is from the same Apostle who promulgated the law of the Lord; because he says: Call the Priests; with whose name it does not mean those who are of older age, as the Tridentine Synod wisely explained, or those who obtain the first place in the people; but to the Priests who, by the laying on of the hands of the Bishops themselves, have been rightly ordained. The Priest, therefore, has been entrusted with the administration of this Sacrament. Nor, however, by decree of the Holy Church to any Priest, but to the Pastor himself who has jurisdiction, or to another to whom he has given the power to perform that office, is it lawful to administer this Sacrament. And above all it must be noted that the Priest in that administration, as is also done in the other Sacraments, supports the person of Christ our Lord and of the holy Church, his bride.

What fruits return to men through the use of this Sacrament.

The utilities that we grasp from this Sacrament must also be explained more exactly, so that if nothing else can attract the faithful to receive it, they may at least be induced by the same utility: since it is thus arranged that we measure almost all things by our comforts. The Pastors will teach, therefore, that with this Sacrament the grace that remits sins is given, and mainly the lighter ones, and as they are called by common name, venial: because the actual sins are removed with the Sacrament of Penance. Because this Sacrament was not instituted in the first place for the remission of the most serious crimes, but only Baptism and Penance effect this by their force. Another is the usefulness of the sacred Anointing: that it frees the soul from the languor and the weakness that it contracted from sins, and from all the other relics of sin. And the most opportune time for this cure must be estimated when we are afflicted by serious morbidity and the danger of life is prevented. Because it is inherent to man by nature that he fears nothing in human things in the same way as death: and this fear is greatly increased by the memory of past crimes; especially when we are urged by the very serious accusation of our conscience; because as it is written: The timid come to the cogitation of their sins, and they translate their iniquities in front of them.

Afterwards that cure and cogitation anguish vehemently: that shortly afterwards it is necessary to be before the tribunal of God, by which the most just sentence must be given to us according to what we have deserved. And it often happens that the faithful, wounded by this terror, feel agitated in admirable ways. And nothing leads more to the tranquility of death than if we abject sadness and with slow spirit await the advent of the Lord; and let us be prepared to willingly return our deposit, whenever he wants to repeat it from us. So that, therefore, the minds of the faithful may be freed from this request, and the spirit may be filled with pious and holy joy, the Sacrament of Extreme Unction accomplishes this.

In what way, when demons leave the soul, the Demons attack us.

Furthermore, we also get something else (which may deservedly seem the maxim of all) from him; because although the enemy of the human race, while we live, never stops dreaming of our death and ruin; However, at no time does every nerve strive more vehemently to lose us completely, and if possible, to tear from us the hope of divine mercy, than when it warns that the supreme day of life is approaching. Therefore, with this Sacrament, the faithful are provided with weapons and forces with which they can break the strength and attack of the adversary and strongly repel him. Because the spirit of the sick person is relieved and uplifted with the hope of divine goodness; and confirmed by it, it bears more lightly all the inconveniences of morbidity, and more easily evades the artifice and callousness of the same Demon that stalks the heel.

In what way can the healing of the body be accessed from this Sacrament.

Finally, if necessary, the health of the body is also added. And if the sick at that time also achieve less, it must be believed that this does not happen due to a vice in the Sacrament, but rather for that reason: because the majority of them, either of those who anoint themselves with the sacred oil, or of those who administer it, have weaker faith: because the Evangelist testifies that the Lord did not create many virtues among his people due to their unbelief. Although it can also be rightly said that the Christian Religion, since it took deeper roots in the minds of men, no longer needs such gadgets of miracles than they once seemed necessary at the beginning of the nascent Church. But nevertheless in this place faith must be greatly excited. Because in whatever way, as far as the health of the body is concerned, it falls by the counsel and will of God, the faithful must rely on a certain hope that by the virtue of this sacred oil they will achieve spiritual healing, and that, if it happens that they die from life, they will perceive the fruit of that illustrious voice with which it is written: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. These things of the Sacrament of Extreme Unction have indeed been said briefly; But if these same chapters of things were explained by the Pastors more fully and with the diligence that is appropriate, there should be no doubt that the faithful will perceive from this doctrine the maximum fruit of piety.

OF THE SACRAMENT OF ORDER.

CHAPTER VII

Why Parish Priests must expound to the people with great diligence the doctrine of the Sacrament of Holy Orders.

If anyone has diligently considered the nature and reason of the other Sacraments, he will easily perceive that all of them depend on the Sacrament of Orders in such a way that without it in part they cannot be made and administered; In part they seem to lack a solemn Ceremony and a certain religious rite and worship. Therefore it is necessary that Pastors, continuing the established doctrine of the Sacraments, consider that they must deal with even more diligence also with the Sacrament of Orders. For their part, they will take full advantage of this explanation, first of all to themselves, then to the others who have entered into the reason for Ecclesiastical life, finally also to the faithful people; to themselves, because while they are versed in the treatment of this argument, they are more moved to resuscitate that grace that they have achieved with this Sacrament; to the others who have been called to the lot of the Lord, partly so that they may be affected by the same study of piety, partly in truth so that they may perceive the knowledge of those things with which, once instructed, they can more easily equip themselves on the path to the subsequent degrees; to the remaining faithful, first of all so that they understand what honor the ministers of the Church are worthy of; Secondly, because it often happens that there are many, who either with hope have destined their children, still infants, to the ministry of the Church, or who by their spontaneous will want to follow that kind of life; to whom it is certainly by no means equitable to ignore the things that primarily belong to this reason.

Mal. 2, 7. Ex. 22, 28. Jn. 5, 23. Jn. 20, 21; Mt. 28, 19. Eph. 4, 12. Of what class they should be elected to the Priesthood, is more fully treated in sect. 33 of this chapter. Trid. Sinod. sess. 23 of the Order, c. 4 and c. 7. Hebrew 5, 4; 2 Pair. 26, 16. Those who say they are called by God. Jer. 23, 21. With how much circumspection one must access sacred Orders.

No dignity is more excellent on earth than the Order of the Priesthood.

First of all, then, the nobility and excellence of this institution must be transmitted to the faithful, if we look at its highest degree, that is, the Priesthood. Because as the Bishops and Priests are like interpreters and certain internuncios of God, who in his name teach men the divine law and the precepts of life, and carry on earth the person of God himself, it is manifest that their function is such that no greater one can be invented: for which reason they are deservedly not only called Angels, but also Gods, because they have among us the strength and the numen of the immortal God. For although at all times they have obtained the highest dignity, yet the Priests of the New Testament far surpass in honor all others. Because the power both to make and offer the Body and Blood of our Lord, and to remit the sins that have crept into them, also surpasses human reason and intelligence: how much less can something equal and similar to it be found on earth.

Who consider themselves divinely called to the Priesthood and Ecclesiastical ministries.

Then, for his part, just as our Savior was sent by the Father, and the Apostles and Disciples throughout the world by Christ the Lord; Thus every day the Priests, endowed with the same power as those, are sent to the consummation of the Saints, to the work of the ministry, to the edification of the Body of Christ. The onus, then, of such a great office should be imposed recklessly on no one, but only on those who can sustain it with holiness of life, doctrine, faith and prudence. Nor let anyone take the honor to himself, except he who is called by God like Aaron. And those who are called by the legitimate ministers of the Church are said to be called by God. Because those who arrogantly introduce themselves and intrude themselves into this ministry, it must be taught that the Lord understood them when He said: He did not send the Prophets, and they ran: of whose kind of men nothing can be more unhappy and miserable, nothing more calamitous to the Church of God.

Who must be judged of perversely accessing sacred Orders, and of entering the Church from another side.

But as in every action that is undertaken and it matters greatly what end each one establishes (because given the optimal end, all things follow rightly), from this above all those who want to be initiated into the sacred must be warned not to propose anything unworthy of such a great office; which place should be treated with all the more diligence, the more seriously at this time the faithful tend to sin in this matter. Because some are converted to this reason for living with the advice of stopping the things necessary for sustenance and clothing; in such a way that apart from the quest or nothing else they seem to look at the Priesthood, like other men vulgarly do at any kind of sordid artifice. Because although by the Apostle's sentence nature and the divine Law command that he who serves the altar live from the altar; However, accessing the altar for the sake of quest and profit is the ultimate sacrilege. For others, the cupidity of honors and ambition leads them to the Priestly order. Others really want to get started to abound in wealth; from which matter it is argued that if some opulent Ecclesiastical benefit is not deferred to them, they have no cogitation of the sacred Order: and these are those whom our Savior calls mercenaries; and of whom Ezekiel said that they fed themselves and not the sheep; whose clumsiness and improbability not only spreads great darkness over the Priestly Order, in such a way that almost nothing can now be held by the most despised and abject faithful people; but it also ensures that they themselves get nothing more from the Priesthood than Judas did from the office of the Apostolate, which brought him eternal ruin. But those who deservedly claim to enter the Church through the door, who are legitimately called by God to hold Ecclesiastical offices for the sole reason of serving the honor of God.

Those who through sacred Orders have dedicated themselves to the Church, in what part must they surpass and excel the rest of the people.

Nor, however, should this be taken as such, as if the same Law had not been imposed equally on all. Because men have been conditioned for this reason: to worship God, which mainly the faithful who have obtained the grace of Baptism must give with all their heart, all their soul and all their strength. But those who want to begin with the Sacrament of Orders must propose this: not only to seek the glory of God in all things (which in truth appears to be common both to all and mainly to the faithful), but also, addicted to some certain ministry of the Church, to serve Him in holiness and justice. Because just as in the army all the soldiers truly obey the laws of the Emperor, but among them however one is Centurion, another Prefect, and others perform other offices; Thus, although all the faithful must with all study follow piety and innocence (with which God is mainly worshiped), it is nevertheless appropriate that those who have been initiated with the Sacrament of Orders execute certain main offices and functions in the Church. Because they do what is sacred for themselves and for the entire people, as they transmit the force of the divine Law, and they exhort and instigate the faithful to keep it with a quick and prudent spirit, and they administer the Sacraments of Christ the Lord, with which all grace is imparted and increased, and, to embrace it with a single word, segregated from the rest of the people, they exercise themselves in the ministry of much the greatest and most willing of all. Once these things have been explained, then, the Parish Priests will agree to transmit those that are proper to this Sacrament; so that the faithful who want to be co-opted into the Ecclesiastical Order understand what kind of office they are called to, and how much power has been divinely given to the Church itself and its Ministers.

Of how many kinds is the Ecclesiastical power.

This, for its part, is double: Order and Jurisdiction. The power of Order refers to the true Body of Christ the Lord in the sacred Eucharist: but the power of Jurisdiction is all about the mystical body of Christ. Because it belongs to her to govern and moderate the Christian people, and to direct them to eternal and heavenly beatitude.

What does the power of the Order extend to?

But the power of the Order not only contains the power and power to consecrate the Eucharist, but also prepares and makes the minds of men suitable to receive it, and embraces all other things that in any way can refer to the Eucharist. And several testimonies from sacred Letters can be adduced from it; but those are lucid and very serious that are read in Saint John and Matthew. For the Lord says: As the Father has sent me, so I send you... receive the Holy Spirit, whose sins you remit, they are remitted, and whose sins you retain, they are retained: and: Truly I say to you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven. Which places, laid out by the Pastors according to the doctrine and authority of the holy Fathers, will be able to provide maximum light to the truth.

The Priesthood of Christ is more sublime than that of the Law of nature, or even that of Moses.

This power, for its part, greatly surpasses that which in the Law of Nature was granted to certain men who took care of sacred things. Because it is also necessary for that age that preceded the written Law to have had its Priesthood and its spiritual power, since it is sufficiently proven that it had the Law. Because these two things are so united, the Apostle testifies, that once one of them is transferred, it is necessary that the other be transferred at the same time. Thus, as by natural instinct men recognized that God must be worshiped; It was consequently that in any republic some were prefixed to the procurement of sacred things and divine worship, whose power was in some way said to be spiritual.

The Israeli people did not lack the same power either; which, although it was superior in dignity to that with which the Priests were endowed in the Law of nature, should nevertheless be esteemed much inferior to the spiritual power of the Evangelical Law. Because this is heavenly, and also surpasses all the virtue of the Angels: and it does not originate from the Mosaic Priesthood, but from Christ the Lord, who was not a Priest according to Aaron, but according to the order of Melchizedek: because he, who was endowed with supreme power to give grace and to remit sins, left this power to his Church, although defined by virtue and ascribed to the Sacraments. Therefore, to exercise it, certain ministers were established, and they consecrated themselves with solemn religion; whose Consecration is called the Sacrament of Orders, or sacred Ordination.

What is Order, and why the Ecclesiastical function is called Order.

For their part, it pleased the holy Fathers to use this word, which has the greatest significance, to indicate the dignity and excellence of the ministers of God. Because Order, if we take its own force and notion, is the arrangement of superior and inferior things, which are in such a way compatible with each other that one refers to the other. Therefore, as in this ministry there are many degrees and various functions, and all of them are distributed and placed with a certain reason; rightly and conveniently it seems that the name of Order was imposed on it.

Order is Sacrament in its true name.

And that among the other Sacraments of the Church, the sacred Ordination, the holy Tridentine Synod, must be numbered
of the City of God, chap. 13. Trid Conc. sess. 23 of the Order, c. 2 and 3, Can. 3 .

and 5 of Reform.

…he confirmed it with that reason that has often been repeated. Because as the Sacrament is a sign of a sacred thing; and what is done externally with this consecration means the grace and power that is attributed to the one who consecrates himself; It is quite clear that it follows that Order must truly and properly be said to be a Sacrament. Therefore the Bishop, offering to the one who is ordained a Priest the chalice with wine and water and the paten with bread, says: Receive the power to offer the Sacrifice, etc.: with which words the Church has always taught that, while the matter is exhibited, the power to consecrate the Eucharist is transmitted, impressing the character in the mind, to which is attached the grace to perform that office rightly and legitimately. Which the Apostle declares in these words: I warn you to resurrect the grace of God that is in you through the laying on of my hands; because God did not give us a spirit of fear, but of virtue, and of diligence, and of sobriety.

Why several Orders of ministers were instituted in the Church.

And now, to use the words of the sacred Synod, since the administration of such a great Priesthood is a divine thing, it was appropriate, so that it could be exercised more worthily and with greater veneration, that in the Church, with a very orderly disposition, there were several and diverse Orders of ministers, who by office served the Priesthood; and these were distributed in such a way that those who were already insigned with the clerical Tonsure, were promoted by the minors to the majors.

How many there are Orders of ministers of the Church, and for what reason they are distributed in common.

It should be taught, therefore, that all these Orders are contained in the septenary number, and that this has always been transmitted by the Catholic Church, whose names are these: Ostiario, Lector, Exorcist, Acolyte, Subdeacon, Deacon, Priest. And that this number of ministers has been correctly defined in this way can be proven by those ministries that seem necessary to the sacrosanct Sacrifice of the Mass and the Eucharist, either to prepare it or to administer it (for which reason they were mainly instituted). Of these, some are major, which are also called sacred, others minor. Major, or sacred, are the Priestly Order, the Diaconate and the Subdiaconate: the minor ones refer to the Acolytes, Exorcists, Readers, Ostiaries: about each of whom few things should be said, so that the Parish Priests have from where to primarily institute those whom they know are to be initiated into some Order.

What do the clerical Tonsure and the name of Clergy mean?

One must begin, for its part, with the first Tonsure, which it is truly advisable to teach that it is a certain preparation to receive the Orders. Because just as men usually prepare for Baptism with exorcisms, for Marriage with betrothal; Thus, when they dedicate themselves to God with their hair tonsured, it is opened to them as an access to the Sacrament of Orders: because it is declared of what kind he who wishes to imbue himself with the sacred must be. Because the name of Cleric, which was then imposed on him for the first time, has been deduced from the fact that he begins to have the Lord as his lot and inheritance, as among the people of the Hebrews those who were mancipated to divine worship; to whom the Lord prohibited any part of the fields in the land of the Promise from being distributed, when he said: I am your part and your inheritance. Although this is common to all the faithful, it is necessary that it is primarily appropriate for those who have consecrated themselves to the ministry of God.

14. Why do Clerics wear a round crown on their heads?

For their part, the hair is dyed in the form and likeness of a crown, which should be preserved perpetually; and as each one is later placed in a higher degree of Order, so the shape of his orb must be more circumscribed. Which in truth teaches the Church that has been received from the tradition of the Apostles, since Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, Augustine, Jerome, very ancient and very serious Fathers, made mention of this way of tonder.

And first of all it is said that the Prince of the Apostles induced that custom in memory of the crown that, woven of thorns, was imposed on the head of our Savior, so that what the wicked invented for the ignominy and torment of Christ, the Apostles could use for decorum and glory; and at the same time they will mean that the ministers of the Church must take care that in all things they bear the species and figure of Christ our Lord.

Although there is no shortage of those who affirm that with this note the royal dignity is declared, which seems to be most suitable for those who have been called to the lot of the Lord. Because what the Apostle Peter attributes to the faithful people: You chosen race, royal Priesthood, holy people, with a certain peculiar and more proper reason we understand that it belongs to the Ecclesiastical ministers.

Although there is no shortage of those who believe that the most perfect profession of life suggested by the Clerics is signified by the figure of the circle, which is the most perfect of all; or that the contempt for external things and the emptiness of the spirit of all human cares are declared, because the hair is dyed, something superfluous in the body.

What is the function of the Ostiaries.

After the first Tonsure, the first degree to the Order of Ostiario is usually made. Their job is to guard the keys and the door of the temple, and to remove from access to the temple those who were prohibited from entering. He also attended the holy sacrifice of the Mass, taking care that no one came closer than appropriate to the sacred altar and questioned the Priest who was doing the divine thing. Other ministries were also entrusted to him; as can be perceived from the rites applied to its consecration. Because the Bishop, giving the keys received from the altar to the one whom he wants to establish Ostiario: This is how he acts, he says, as one who has to give an account to God of these things that are opened with these keys. And how great the dignity of this Order was in the ancient Church is understood from what we notice that is kept in these times in the Church. Because the office of Treasurer, who was the same custodian of the Sacrarium, which belonged to the Ostiaries, is considered even now among the most honest functions of the Church.

16. What is the office of the Reader in the Church.

The second degree of the Order is the office of the Reader. It belongs to him to recite in the Church with a clear voice and distinctly the books of the Old and New Testaments, and mainly those that are usually read in the nightly psalmody. Its parts were also to transmit to the faithful the first rudiments of the Christian religion. The Bishop, therefore, present the people, at their ordination, giving them the book in which the things that belong to this function are written, says: Receive, and be a narrator of the word of God, having, if you have faithfully and usefully fulfilled the office, part with those who from the beginning ministered the word of God well.

What is the responsibility of the Exorcists by trade.

The third is the Order of Exorcists, who have been given the power to invoke the name of the Lord over those who are possessed by unclean spirits. For this reason the Bishop, when he institutes them, offers them the book in which the Exorcisms are contained, using that formula of words: Receive, and commend to memory, and have the power to lay hands on the energumen, whether baptized or catechumenous.

18. What are the parts of the Acolytes.

The fourth degree is that of the Acolytes, and the last of all those who are called minor and not sacred. Their job is to accompany the senior ministers, Subdeacons and Deacons, in the ministry of the altar, and to lend them their work. Furthermore, they carry and preserve the lights when the Sacrifice of the Mass is celebrated, and mainly when the Gospel is read, which is why they were called by another name Ceroferarios: when they are ordained, then, this rite is usually kept by the Bishop: first of all, after diligently admonishing them of their office, he gives each of them the lights in this way: Receive the Ceroferario with the candle, and know that you are obliged to light the lights of the Church in the name of the Lord: then also the empty urceolas with which water and wine are ministered in the Sacrifice: Receive the urceolas to suggest the wine and water in the Eucharist of the Blood of Christ, in the name of the Lord.

What is the ministry of the Subdeacon, and what kind of rites are used in his consecration.

From the minor and non-sacred Orders, of which up to now has been said, legitimate access and promotion to the major and sacred ones is opened. In the first degree of them is placed the Subdeacon; whose office is, as the name itself declares, to serve the Deacon at the altar. Because he must prepare the sacred linens, the vessels, the bread and the wine necessary for the use of the Sacrifice. Now offer the water to the Bishop and Priest when they wash their hands at the Sacrifice of the Mass. He also reads the Epistle, which was formerly recited by the Deacon at Mass, and attends the sacred as a witness, and prohibits the Priest who does the sacred from being disturbed by anyone. And these things that belong to the ministry of the Subdeacon, it is lawful to know them from the solemn ceremonies that are used in their consecration. Because in the first place the Bishop admonishes that the law of perpetual continence has been imposed on this Order; and says that no one should be co-opted into the Order of Subdeacons who does not intend to receive this law willingly; Then, after the solemn precation of the Litany, he enumerates and explains what the offices and functions of the Subdeacon are. These things done, each of those who are ordained receives from the Bishop the chalice and the sacred paten: and from the Archdeacon (so that it may be understood that the Subdeacon serves the office of the Deacon) the urceolas filled with wine and water, together with the basin and the linen with which they wipe their hands, the Bishop saying: See what kind of ministry is transmitted to you; That is why I admonish you to display yourselves in such a way that you can attack God. Other prayers are also added: finally, when the Bishop has adorned the Subdeacon with the sacred vestments, to each of which own words and ceremonies are applied, he gives him the book of the Epistles, and says: Receive the book of the Epistles, and have the power to read them in the holy Church of God both for the living and for the dead.

Clement, ep. 1 to James brother of the Lord. Conc. Trid. sess. 23 in the Reform Decree, c. 14. That the Deacons were able to preach is shown in the first place by the example of Stephen. Fact. 6 and Felipe Hech. 8 and of St. Vincent, witnessed by St. Augustine.

What is the office of the Deacon.

The second degree of sacred Orders is obtained by the Deacon: whose ministry extends more widely, and has always been held more holily. Because it belongs to him to perpetually follow the Bishop, guard him who preaches, and be ready for him and the Priest who does the sacred or administers other Sacraments, and read the Gospel in the Sacrifice of the Mass. In ancient times it often excited the spirits of the faithful to attend to the sacred; He also ministered the Blood of the Lord, in those Churches in which it was customary for the faithful to submerge the Eucharist under one type or another. Furthermore, the Deacon was entrusted with the dispensation of Ecclesiastical goods, so that each one could provide what was necessary for sustenance.

It also belongs to the Deacon, as the eye of the Bishop, to investigate who in the city spends their life piously and religiously, and who otherwise; who are suitable at fixed times for the Sacrifice and preaching, and who in turn are not suitable; so that, when he has made the Bishop more certain of all, he can either privately exhort and admonish each one, or publicly correct and rebuke, as he has understood will be most beneficial. He must also recite the names of the catechumens, and place before the Bishop those who are to be initiated with the Sacrament of Orders.

Furthermore, it is lawful for him, if the Bishop and the Priest are absent, to explain the Gospel, however not from the highest place, so that it may be understood that this is not his own office.

From what class Deacons should be chosen.

And how much diligence must be used so that no one unworthy of that office ascends to this degree of Order, the Apostle shows when he explained to Timothy the customs, virtue and integrity of the Deacon. The rites and solemn ceremonies with which it is consecrated by the Bishop also sufficiently declare this. Because the Bishop uses more and more holy prayers for the ordination of the Deacon than for that of the Subdeacon, and adds other ornaments of sacred vestments. Furthermore, he lays his hands on him, which we actually read was done by the Apostles when they instituted the first Deacons. Finally he gives him the book of the Gospels with these words: Receive the power to read the Gospel in the Church of God both for the living and for the deceased in the name of the Lord.

What is the dignity and breadth of the Priesthood.

The third, and the highest of all the sacred Orders, is the Priesthood: and those who are endowed with it, the ancient Fathers usually call by two names. Sometimes they are called Presbyters, which in Greek means elders, not only because of the maturity of age, which is in the highest degree necessary for this Order, but much more because of the gravity of customs, doctrine and prudence. For as it is written: Venerable old age is not that of many days, nor is it counted by the number of years: gray hair is the senses of man, and the age of old age is the immaculate life. Sometimes they are called Priests, both because they are consecrated to God, and because it is their responsibility to administer the Sacraments and treat sacred and divine things.

Of how many kinds is the Priesthood of both the new and the old Law.

But as in the sacred letters a double Priesthood is described, one interior, the other exterior; One must be distinguished from the other, so that it can be explained by the Pastors of which one is understood in this place. So far as the interior Priesthood is concerned, all the faithful, after they have washed themselves with the salutary water, are called Priests, and especially the righteous, who have the spirit of God and by the benefit of divine grace have become living members of Jesus Christ the High Priest. Because these, with faith inflamed by charity, immolate spiritual hosts to God on the altar of their mind: in which genre all good and honest actions that refer to the glory of God must be numbered. Therefore in the Apocalypse we read thus: Christ washed us from our sins in his Blood, and made us kingdom and Priests to God and his Father. In which sentence it has been said by the Prince of the Apostles: Build yourselves like living stones, a spiritual house, a holy Priesthood, offering spiritual hosts acceptable to God through Jesus Christ: And the Apostle exhorts us to present our bodies as a living host, holy, pleasing to God, our rational gift. David had also said long before: The sacrifice to God is the troubled spirit; the contrite and humiliated heart, God, you will not despise: all of which is easily understood as looking to the inner Priesthood.

CHAPTER 1.

The external Priesthood does not fall on all Christians. Trid. Sinod. of Order, sess. 23, Ch. 1 and Can. 1 . Also in the old law is the double Priesthood.

In addition to the internal Priesthood, it is shown that there is another external one.

The external Priesthood, for its part, is not suitable for the multitude of all the faithful, but for certain men, who, instituted with the legitimate laying on of hands and with solemn ceremonies of the holy Church, and consecrated to God, are assigned to some own sacred ministry. This distinction of the Priesthood can also be observed in the old law: because of the interior it was demonstrated shortly before that David spoke. From the outside, for its part, no one can ignore how many precepts the Lord gave to Moses and Aaron. Furthermore, he assigned the entire Leviticus Tribe to the ministry of the Temple, and he ensured by law that no one from another Tribe dared to enter into that function. For which King Ozias was struck with leprosy by the Lord, because he had usurped the Priestly office, and he paid very serious penalties for his arrogance and sacrilege. Since, therefore, it is licit to notice the same distinction of the Priesthood in the Evangelical law, the faithful must be taught that it is now a question of the external Priesthood, which has been attributed to certain men. Because only this belongs to the Sacrament of Orders.

What are the functions of the Priests.

The office of the Priest, then, is to make sacrifice to God and administer the Ecclesiastical Sacraments, as is perceived from the rites of consecration. Because the Bishop, when he institutes someone a Priest, first places his hands on him together with all the Priests who are present; then, adapting the stole to the shoulders, he forms it in front of the chest in the shape of a cross; With which it is declared that the Priest is clothed with the virtue from above, with which he can endure the cross of Christ the Lord and the gentle yoke of the divine law, and transmit it not only with words, but with the example of the most holy life acted. Then he anoints the hands with sacred oil; then he gives him the chalice with wine and the paten with the host, saying: He receives the power to offer the Sacrifice to God, and to celebrate Masses, both for the living and for the dead: with whose ceremonies and words he is constituted interpreter and mediator of God and men; which must be considered the main function of the Priest. Finally, hands were again placed on his head: Receive, he says, the Holy Spirit: to whomever you remit the sins, they are remitted, and to whomever you retain, they are retained: and he attributes to him that heavenly power of retaining and remitting sins that the Lord gave to his disciples. And these are the proper and main offices of the Priestly Order.

Although there is one Order of the Priesthood, there is not only one degree of Priests.

Which, although it is one, nevertheless has several degrees of dignity and power. The first is that of those who are simply called Priests; whose functions have so far been declared.

The second is that of the Bishops, who are prefixed to each of the Episcopates; so that they not only govern the other ministers of the Church, but also the faithful people, and provide for their salvation with utmost vigilance and care. Therefore in sacred letters they are often called Shepherds of the sheep: whose office and position Paul described, as we read in the acts of the Apostles, in that concion that he had to the Ephesians. And likewise through Peter, Prince of the Apostles, a certain divine rule of the Episcopal ministry has been transmitted: to which, if the Bishops strive to direct their actions, there should be no doubt that they are and consider themselves good Pastors. But the same Bishops are also called Pontiffs, taking the name of the Ethnics, who used to call the Princes of the Priests Pontiffs.

The third degree is that of the Archbishops, who preside over several Bishops, who are also called Metropolitans; because they are antistites of those cities that are considered mothers of that province. For this reason they have a higher place than that of the Bishops, and have greater power, although in terms of Ordination they do not differ anything from the Bishops.

In the fourth degree are the Patriarchs, that is, the first and supreme Fathers.

From the ancient seats of the Patriarchs.

Formerly in the entire Church, apart from the supreme Roman Pontiff, there were only four Patriarchs, and not all of them, however, equal in dignity. For that of Constantinople, although this honor was deferred to him after all the others, nevertheless by the majesty of the empire he obtained a higher place. The next is that of Alexandria, whose Church Mark the Evangelist founded by order of the Prince of the Apostles. The third was Antioch, where Peter first placed his headquarters. The extreme degree is that of Jerusalem, whose Church James, brother of the Lord, built.

The Roman Pontiff is the greatest of all Bishops, and this by divine right.

In addition to all these, the Catholic Church has always venerated the Roman Pontiff Maximus, whom in the Synod of Ephesus Cyril of Alexandria calls Archbishop, Father and Patriarch of the entire world. Because as he sits in the chair of Peter, Prince of the Apostles, in which it is clear that he sat until the end of his life, he recognizes in him the highest degree of dignity and the breadth of jurisdiction, not truly given by any Synodal or other human constitutions, but divinely. For which reason he presides as father and moderator of all the faithful and of the Bishops and the other Antistites, of any office and power with which they are endowed, the universal Church, as successor of Peter and true and legitimate Vicar of Christ the Lord. From these things, then, the Pastors will teach what the main offices and functions of the Ecclesiastical Orders and degrees are, and who is the minister of this Sacrament.

Who is the legitimate minister of the Sacrament of Orders.

Because it is clear that that administration belongs to the Bishop: which will also be easy to verify with the authority of the holy letters, with the most certain tradition, with the testimony of all the Fathers, with the decrees of the Councils, with the use and custom of the Holy Church. Although some Abbots have sometimes been allowed to administer minor and non-sacred Orders; However, no one doubts that this is the Bishop's own office; which only of all, besides no one, it is licit to initiate in the remaining Orders, which are called greater and sacred. Because only a Bishop ordains Subdeacons, Deacons and Priests. The Bishops, by tradition of the Apostles that has been perpetually preserved in the Church, are consecrated by three Bishops.

Why is it that those who are promoted to the Orders require singular probity.

It now follows that it be explained who is suitable for this Sacrament, and mainly for the Priestly Order, and what is mainly required of them. From this, in fact, it will not be difficult to establish what should be observed in the other Orders that are given, according to the office and dignity of each one. And that in this Sacrament maximum caution must be used is deduced as follows: because others give grace for the sanctification and use of those by whom it is received; But those who are initiated into the sacred become partakers of heavenly grace for this reason: so that through their ministry the salvation of the Church and even of all men may be consulted. From which we understand that it has been done that only on fixed days, on which solemn fasts are also indicated due to the ancient custom of the Catholic Church, are ordinations carried out; namely, so that the faithful people may implore God with pious and holy prayers as ministers of such sacred things, who may seem more capable of carrying out the power of such a great ministry correctly and with the benefit of the Church.

How much integrity of life and customs is required in those who are ordained.

In the first place, therefore, in whom a Priest is to be created, it is highly appropriate that integrity of life and customs be recommended; Not only because, if, conscious of some deadly sin, he tries to initiate it, or even suffers it, he forces himself with a new and maximum crime; but also because he must put the light of virtue and innocence before others. Of this thing, what the Apostle precepts to Titus and Timothy must be declared by the Pastors; and at the same time it must be taught that those vices of the body that in the old law by the Lord's prescription excluded someone from the ministry of the altar, in the evangelical law must be transferred mainly to the vices of the soul. Therefore we note that that holy custom is kept in the Church that those who are to be initiated into the sacred strive first to diligently purge their conscience with the Sacrament of Penance.

What and how much doctrine is required in the Priest.

Furthermore, not only should the Priest be required to have that knowledge that pertains to the use and treatment of the Sacraments, but it is also appropriate that he be so instructed in the science of sacred letters that he can transmit to the people the mysteries of the Christian faith and the precepts of the divine law, incite them to virtue and piety, and revoke the faithful from vices. Because of the Priest there are two offices; of which one is to prepare and administer the Sacraments correctly: the other, to educate the people entrusted to their faith in those things and institutions that are necessary for salvation. For Malachi testifies thus: The lips of the Priest will guard knowledge, and from his mouth they will require the Law, because he is the Angel of the Lord of hosts. So that, therefore, in one of these, if he is adorned with mediocre knowledge, he can lend what he owes; The other certainly does not desire vulgar, but rather exquisite doctrine: although the highest science of recondite things is not equally required of all Priests, but rather that which is sufficient for each one for the function of the office and ministry undertaken.

Trid. Sinod. sess. 23, c. 12 of Reform. The first effect is the sanctification of the one who is ordained. See the Florentine Council.
