Who should not be admitted to the dignity of the Priesthood.

To children, for their part, and to women and the insane, because they lack the use of reason, this Sacrament should not be given, although, if it were also administered to them, it should be believed with certainty that the character of the Sacrament is imprinted on their soul. And what year of age should be expected in each of the Orders, it will be easy to know from the decrees of the sacred Tridentine Council. Servants are also excepted. For he who is not in his own right, but is in the power of another, should not dedicate himself to divine worship. In addition, men of blood or murderers; because by Ecclesiastical law they repel each other, and are irregular. Also the spurious ones, and all those who have not been procreated from legitimate marriages. The Church teaches that those who ascribe to the sacred have nothing in themselves for which they can rightly be despised and looked upon with contempt by others. Finally, those who are deformed or handicapped due to some notable bodily defect should not be admitted. Because that ugliness and weakness is both offensive and necessary to prevent the administration of the Sacraments.

34. What are the main effects of this Sacrament.

But now that these things have been explained, it remains for the Pastors to teach what the effects of this Sacrament are. And it is clear that, although the Sacrament of Orders, as has been said before, looks in the highest degree to the usefulness and beauty of the Church, nevertheless also in the soul of him who is initiated into the sacred it effects the grace of sanctification, with which he becomes suitable and skilled to rightly carry out his office and administer the Sacraments: just as by the grace of Baptism anyone becomes fit to perceive the other Sacraments. It is also manifest that with this Sacrament another grace is attributed, namely the principal power, which refers to the most holy Sacrament of the Eucharist: in the Priest in full and perfect truth, as the one who alone can make up the Body and Blood of our Lord: but in the other ministers of the lower Orders, greater or lesser, according as each one approaches more or less with his ministry to the Sacraments of the Altar. And this is also called spiritual character, because those who have been imbued with the sacred are distinguished from the other faithful by a certain interior note impressed on the soul, and are mancipated to divine worship. Which the Apostle seems to have looked at when he said to Timothy: Do not neglect the grace that is in you, which was given to you by prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. And elsewhere: I admonish you to resurrect the grace of God that is in you through the laying on of my hands. These things said about the Sacrament of Orders are enough. Because we have professed to transmit to the Pastors only the main chapters of things, so that the arguments of teaching the faithful people and educating them in Christian piety would be subordinated to them.

OF THE SACRAMENT OF MARRIAGE.

CHAPTER VIII

Why Parish Priests must carefully monitor so that the Christian people are aware of the nature and sanctity of Marriage.

As the blessed and perfect life of the Christian people must be proposed to the Pastors, in truth it would be to them in the highest degree what the Apostle wrote to the Corinthians that he desired in these words: I desire, in fact, that all of you should be like me; namely, that everyone followed the virtue of continence. For nothing more blessed can happen to the faithful in this life, than that the spirit, not distracted by any care of the world, and all libido of the flesh calmed and extinguished, rests in the sole study of piety and in the cogitation of heavenly things. But as, according to the same Apostle testifies: Each one has his own gift from God: one truly like this, another like that; and Marriage is adorned with great and divine goods, in such a way that among the other Sacraments of the Catholic Church it is truly and properly numbered, and the Lord honored with his presence the celebrity of the nuptials: it quite appears that his doctrine must be transmitted; especially when it is permissible to note that both Saint Paul and the Prince of the Apostles left written exactly in various places the things that not only belonged to the dignity, but also to the offices of Marriage. Because inspired by the divine spirit they optimally understood how many and how great

…comforts can come to Christian society if the faithful knew and kept inviolate the sanctity of Marriage; and on the contrary, if they are ignored or neglected, they bring many and maximum calamities and damages to the Church. First of all, then, the nature and strength of Marriage must be explained: because as vices often bear the likeness of what is honest, it is advisable to take care that the faithful, deceived by the false species of Marriage, do not stain the soul with clumsiness and nefarious libido: for the sake of which declaration, one must begin with the significance of the name.

Why that holy copulation is expressed with the names of Marriage, conjugal or nuptials.

It is called Marriage because a woman must primarily marry to become a mother; or because conceiving, giving birth and educating offspring is the mother's job. It is also called union conjugation, because the legitimate woman binds herself with the man as with a single yoke. Furthermore, nuptials, because, as St. Ambrose says, by grace of modesty the maidens veiled themselves: which also seemed to declare that they must be obedient and subject to men.

3. What is Marriage.

This is truly defined by the common sentence of the Theologians: Marriage is the marital conjunction of a man and a woman between legitimate persons, which retains the undivided commonality of life. In order that the parts of this definition may be understood more clearly, it must be taught that, although all these things are in the perfect Marriage, namely the internal consensus, the external agreement expressed in words, the obligation and the bond that is effected from that agreement, and the copulation of the spouses with which the Marriage is consummated; However, none of these properly have the force and reason of Marriage, but rather that obligation and connection that has been meant with the word conjunction. It is added, for its part, marital, because other types of pacts with which men and women are obliged to provide each other with work, whether for reasons of price or something else, are completely unrelated to the reason for Marriage. It follows later: between legitimate persons, because those who by law are completely excluded from the conjunction of nuptials cannot enter into Marriage; nor, if they enter, is it time. For, for example, those who within the fourth degree are united by kinship, and the boy before the fourteenth year, or the maiden before the twelfth, whose age is constituted by the laws, cannot be qualified to enter into the just covenants of Marriage. And what has been placed in the extreme place, which retains the undivided commonality of life, declares the nature of the indissoluble bond with which man and woman are united.

4. Where the main force of Marriage consists.

From these things, then, it is clear that the nature and reason of Marriage consists of that bond. Because what other definitions of very clear males seem to attribute to this is consensus, as when they say that conjugation is the consensus of the male and the female; This must be taken as follows: that the same consensus is the effective cause of Marriage: which the Fathers taught in the Florentine Council. Because the obligation and the nexus can only arise from consensus and agreement.

5. Of what kind is consensus required in Marriage, and for what reason it should be declared.

But it is most necessary that the consensus be expressed in words that signify the present tense. Because marriage is not a simple donation, but a mutual pact: and so it happens that the consensus of one alone cannot be enough to unite Marriage, but it must be mutual between two: and it is clear that to declare the mutual consensus of the mind, words are necessary.

Because if Marriage could consist of internal consensus alone, without any external significance, it would also seem to follow that, when two who were in very different places and to a maximum degree diverse consented to the nuptials, before one had declared to the other his will or by letters or by messengers, they were united with the law of true and stable Marriage: which, however, is foreign to reason and custom and the decrees of the holy Church.

Mutual consensus expressed in words of future tense does not effectuate Marriage.

Rightly, for its part, it is said that it is convenient for the consensus to be expressed in words that have present tense significance. Because those that indicate the future time do not unite the Marriage, but rather promise it: then, those that are future, it is clear that they are not yet; and those that are not, must be considered to have little or nothing firm or stable. Therefore, no one still has the right of marriage over that woman whom he promises to marry; nor has he immediately fulfilled what he promised he would do, although he must lend faith; and if he does not do so, he is convinced that he is guilty of violated faith. But he who unites himself to another with the pact of Marriage, although he may later regret it, he cannot change what has been done, nor do it irritated and infected. Therefore, since the obligation of conjugation is not a bare promise, but rather abolition of such a kind, with which in fact the man gives to the woman, and in turn the woman to the man, the power of her body; That is why it is necessary that Marriage be contracted with words that designate the present time; whose force of the words, after they have also been enunciated, remains, and has constrained the man and the woman with an indissoluble bond.

If, due to modesty or another impediment, consensus is not expressed in words, gestures and signals take the place of words.

But instead of words, both gestures and signs that openly indicate the intimate consensus can suffice for Marriage, as well as taciturnity itself, when the maiden does not respond out of shame, but the parents speak for her.

For true Marriage, concubinage is not required.

From these things, then, the Parish Priests will transmit to the faithful that the nature and strength of Marriage is placed in the bond and obligation; and that in addition to the consensus, expressed in the way that has been said, for true marriage to exist, concubinage is not necessarily required. For it is also quite manifest that the first parents, before sin, in whose time no copulation of the flesh had mediated between them, as the Fathers testify, were united in true marriage. Therefore it has been said by the holy Fathers that Marriage does not exist by concubinage, but by consensus; which we also read repeated by Saint Ambrose in the book of the Virgins.

Of how many kinds is the consideration of Marriage.

And now, having explained these things, it will be necessary to teach that Marriage has a double reason. Because either it must be considered as a natural conjunction (because conjugation was not invented by men, but by nature), or as a Sacrament, whose force exceeds the condition of natural things. And since grace perfects nature (and not first what is spiritual, but what is animal; then what is spiritual), the order of the thing postulates that it is first about Marriage as it consists of nature and belongs to the office of nature; and then the things that are convenient for it will be explained insofar as it is a Sacrament.

10. Who is the author of Marriage, as it means the office of nature.

First of all, then, the faithful must be taught that Marriage was instituted by God. For it is written in Genesis: Male and female created them, and God blessed them, and said: Be fruitful and multiply. And: It is not good for man to be alone; let us make him a helper like him: and shortly after: And for Adam no helper was found like him:

…so the Lord God caused a drowsiness to fall on Adam, and when he had fallen asleep, he took one of his ribs and filled flesh in its place, and the Lord God built the rib that he had taken from Adam into a woman, and brought it to Adam; And Adam said, This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh: she shall be called woman, because she was taken from man: therefore a man shall leave his father and mother, and cleave unto his wife, and they shall be two in one flesh. Which, by the same Lord author in Saint Matthew, show that Marriage was divinely instituted.

Marriage, as long as it is considered an office of nature, cannot be dissolved.

Nor in truth did God only institute Marriage; but, as the holy Tridentine Synod declares, he also added to it a perpetual and indissoluble knot: for the Savior says: What God has joined together, let no man put asunder. Because although it is appropriate for Marriage, as it is an office of nature, that it cannot be dissolved; However, this is done to the maximum extent as it is Sacramento. Of which also in all those that by the law of nature are proper to it, it achieves the highest perfection: however, also in the study of educating offspring and the other goods of Marriage it is repugnant that their bond be dissolvable.

The law of contracting has not been imposed on all men.

And what has been said by the Lord: Grow and multiply, seeks to declare for what cause Marriage had been instituted; not to impose necessity on each of the men. Because now, with the human race having increased, not only does no law oblige anyone to take a wife, but rather virginity is recommended in the highest degree, and each person is persuaded in the sacred letters that, since it is more prescient than the state of Marriage, it contains in itself greater perfection and holiness. For the Lord our Savior taught thus: He who is able to capitulate, capitulate; and the Apostle says: Of the Virgins I have no precept from the Lord, but I give advice, as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord to be faithful.

Why men and women should unite.

But the reasons why the man and the woman should be united must be explained. The first, then, is this same society desired by instinct of nature of different sexes, reconciled with the hope of mutual aid, so that one, helped by the work of the other, can more easily bear the inconveniences of life and sustain the weakness of old age. The second is the appetite for procreation, not so much in truth for the sake of leaving heirs of goods and wealth, but rather so that they may educate themselves as cultists of the true faith and religion.

…which in truth appears sufficiently from the sacred letters that those holy Patriarchs mainly proposed when they took wives. For this reason the Angel, when admonishing Tobias how he could repel the force of the evil Demon: I will show you, he says, who are those over whom the Demon can prevail: because these, who so stir up the conjugation that they exclude God from themselves and from their mind, and in such a way deplete their libido, like the horse and the mule that have no intellect, the Demon has power over them. Then he subjoined: You will take the virgin with fear of the Lord, induced more by the love of children than by libido, so that in the seed of Abraham you will obtain the blessing in the children. And this was also a reason why God instituted Marriage from the beginning. Therefore it happens that the crime of those who, united in Marriage, either prevent conception with medications, or abort childbirth is very serious: because these things must be considered an impious murder conspiracy.

Why Marriage was instituted after sin.

The third is the one that after the lapse of the first father acceded to the other causes, when due to the loss of justice in which man had been conditioned, appetite began to be repugnant to right reason, namely so that he who is aware of his weakness and does not want to endure the fight of the flesh, can use the remedy of Marriage to avoid the sins of libido. Of which the Apostle thus writes: For the sake of fornication let each man have his wife, and each her man: and a little later, when he taught that sometimes for the sake of prayer one must abstain from the debt of Marriage, he subjoined: And again return to the same thing, lest Satan tempt you because of your incontinence. These, then, are the causes, some of which must be proposed to each one who piously and religiously, as befits the children of saints, wants to marry. And if these causes are also accompanied by others by which men, induced, enter into marriage, and in the choice of the woman they prefer the latter to the former, such as the desire to leave an heir, wealth, form, the splendor of the lineage, the similarity of customs; Such reasons should not truly be condemned, when they are not repugnant to the sanctity of Marriage: because neither in the sacred letters is Patriarch Jacob rebuked for having preferred Rachel, attracted by her beauty, to Leah. These things should be taught about Marriage as it is a natural conjunction.

Why Marriage was increased by Christ with the dignity of Sacrament.

But since it is a Sacrament, it will be necessary to explain that its nature is much more important, and that it entirely refers to a higher end. Because just as Marriage, as a natural conjunction, was instituted from the beginning to propagate the human race; Thus later, so that a people could be procreated and educated to the worship and religion of the true God and our Savior Christ, the dignity of Sacrament was given to them. Because when Christ the Lord wanted to give some certain sign of that very close need that He had with the Church, and of His immense charity towards us, He declared the divinity of such a great mystery mainly with this holy conjunction of the male and the female. Which in truth is understood to have been done most aptly, because of all human needs none constrains men to each other more than the bond of Marriage, and man and woman are united to each other with maximum charity and benevolence. And that is why it happens that sacred letters frequently propose before our eyes this divine copulation of Christ and the Church with the resemblance of nuptials.

In what way Marriage is a true Sacrament of the Evangelical Law.

And since Marriage is a Sacrament, the Church, confirmed by the authority of the Apostle, has always taken it for granted and explored it. For thus he writes to the Ephesians: Men must take care of their wives as they do their bodies. He who pays attention to his wife, pays attention to himself. Because no one ever hates his flesh, but nourishes and shelters it, just as Christ also the Church: because we are members of his body, his flesh and his bones. For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, and they will become two in one flesh. This Sacrament is great: but I say it in Christ and in the Church. Because what it says: This Sacrament is great; No one should doubt that it must refer to Marriage, namely that the conjunction of the man and the woman, of which God is the author, is a Sacrament, that is, a sacred sign, of that most holy bond with which Christ the Lord is united to the Church.

How are you convinced from Paul's words that Marriage is a Sacrament.

And that this is the proper and true sentence of those words is shown by the ancient holy Fathers who interpreted that place: and the holy Tridentine Synod also explained it. It is clear, then, that the man is compared to Christ, the woman to the Church through the Apostle; that the man is the head of the woman, like Christ of the Church, and for that reason it happens that the man must worship the woman, and in turn the woman must love and cultivate the man. For Christ gave up the Church, and through it gave himself up: and again, as the Apostle himself teaches, the Church is subject to Christ. But that grace is also signified and given with this Sacrament, in which the reason for the Sacrament mainly lies, is declared by those words of the Synod: The grace, for its part, that would perfect that natural love, and confirm the indissoluble unity, and sanctify the spouses, Christ himself, instituter and perfecter of the venerable Sacraments, deserved it for us with his passion. Therefore it must be taught that by the grace of this Sacrament it is brought about that the man and the woman, united with the bond of mutual charity, rest one in the benevolence of the other, and do not seek foreign and illicit loves and concubines, but that in all things the marriage and the immaculate bed be honorable.

CATEC. FOR PASTORS · PART II. How it should be venerated. Because Christ loved the Church and gave himself for her; and at the same time, as the Apostle himself teaches, the Church is subject to Christ. That grace is also signified and conferred in this sacrament, in which the reason for sacrament especially consists, is declared by these words of the Synod: The grace, however, that perfected that natural love, confirmed the indissoluble unity and sanctified the spouses, Christ himself, the instituter and perfecter of the venerable sacraments, deserved it for us with his passion. Therefore it must be taught that by the grace of this sacrament it is made that the man and the woman, united with the bond of mutual charity, each rest in the benevolence of the other, and do not seek foreign and illicit loves and concubits, but that marriage and the immaculate bed be honorable in everything.

How much the Marriage of the Gospel of Marriage differs from the Law of nature or of Moses.

But how much the Sacrament of Marriage surpasses those Marriages that used to be entered into before or after the Law, it is licit to know from this: that although the Gentiles considered that there was something divine in Marriage, and for that reason they judged that vague concubits were alien to the Law of nature, and equally that rape, adultery and other types of libido should be vindicated; However, their marriages did not have any force from Sacramento at all. Among the Jews the laws of nuptials were usually kept more religiously: and it must not be doubted that their Marriages were endowed with greater sanctity. Because as they had received the promise that one day all people would be blessed in the seed of Abraham; It deservedly seemed to be an office of great piety among them to procreate children and propagate the offspring of the chosen people, from which Christ our Lord Savior, as far as human nature was concerned, had to originate. But those conjunctions also lacked the true reason for Sacrament.

Marriage in the Law of nature after sin, or in the Law of Moses, did not retain the decorum of its origin that it had from God.

Added to this is that, whether we look at the law of nature after sin, or at that of Moses, we easily notice that Marriage had decayed from the decorum and honesty of its first origin. For while the law of nature was in force, we find that many of the ancient Fathers took several wives at the same time. Later in the law of Moses it was permitted, given the libel of repudiation, if there was cause, to divorce the woman: both of which things have been suppressed by the Evangelical Law, and Marriage has been restored to its pristine state. Because polygamy was foreign to the nature of Marriage (although some of the ancient Fathers should not be accused, because not without God's indulgence they took several wives), Christ the Lord showed it with those words: For this reason a man will leave his father and mother, and will cleave to his wife, and they will become two in one flesh; and then subjoint: Thus, they are no longer two, but one flesh. With whose words he made it clear that Marriage was instituted by God in such a way that it was defined by the conjunction of only two, not several. Which also in another place he taught very openly: for he says: Whoever sends away his wife and takes another, commits adultery on her; And if a woman sends away her man and marries another, she commits adultery. Because if it were lawful for a man to take several wives, there would seem to be no reason at all why he should be guilty of adultery for taking another wife in addition to the wife he had at home, than for joining the first wife with another. And for that reason we understand that it happens that if any infidel, according to the custom and custom of his people, has taken several wives, when he has converted to the true religion, the Church orders him to leave all the others, and to have only the first instead of a just and legitimate wife.

The bond of Marriage cannot be broken by divorce.

But with the same testimony of Christ the Lord it is easily proven that with no divorce the bond of Marriage can be dissolved; because if after the libel of repudiation the woman were absolved from the law of the man, it would be lawful for her to marry another man without any crime of adultery. But the Lord openly denounced: Everyone who sends away his wife and takes another commits adultery. Therefore it is manifest that the bond of marriage with nothing but death is broken: which the Apostle also confirms when he says: A woman is bound to the law as long as her man lives; and if her man has fallen asleep, she is freed from the law: let her marry whoever she wants, only in the Lord: and again: To those who are united in Marriage, not I, but the Lord, precept that the woman should not be separated from the man; and if she separates, let her remain untouched, or be reconciled with her man. The Apostle gave that option to the woman who for just cause had left the man: that she either remain unmarried, or be reconciled with her man. Because not even the holy Church allows men and women to separate from each other without more serious reasons.

Why there is no reason why marriage should be dissolved.

And, lest perhaps the law of Marriage may seem harsher to anyone, because it can never be dissolved for any reason; It must be taught what the utilities are linked to it. In the first place, in fact, men in uniting Marriages must look more to virtue and similarity of customs than to wealth and beauty: with which in truth the common society is consulted to the greatest degree, no one can doubt. Furthermore, if marriage were dissolved with divorce, men would hardly ever lack causes for dissent, which would be challenged every day by the ancient enemy of peace and modesty. But now, when the faithful think with themselves that, although they also lack the conviviality and custom of marriage, they are nevertheless constrained by the bond of Marriage, and all hope of taking another wife has been cut off; Because of this, it happens that they tend to be quicker to anger and disagreements. And if sometimes they also divorce, and can no longer bear the spouse's desire, easily reconciled by friends, they return to their cohabitation.
sent. dist. 31. Scotus 4. sent. dist. 31, q. 1. 1 Cor. 7, 28. The first good of Marriage is children. 1 Tim. 2, 15.

Those separated by the libel of repudiation can unite again.

But in this place the salutary admonition of Saint Augustine should not be omitted by the Pastors. For he, to show the faithful that it should not be done reluctantly that with the wives whom they have dismissed for adultery, if they are sorry for the crime, they should be reduced to grace: Why, he says, will not the faithful man receive the woman that the Church receives? or why will the woman not forgive the adulterous but penitent man, whom Christ also forgave? For what the Scripture calls a fool who retains an adulteress; He feels it from the one who, when she has committed a crime, refuses to repent and desist from the clumsiness that she has begun. From these things, then, it is evident that the marriages of the faithful greatly surpass in perfection and nobility both the Marriages of the Gentiles and those of the Jews.

What are the goods that from this Sacrament return to the conjugates.

The faithful must also be taught that there are three goods of Marriage: offspring, faith and the Sacrament, with whose compensation those inconveniences that the Apostle indicates with these words are alleviated: Those of this class will have tribulation of the flesh; and it is effected that the conjunctions of bodies, which outside of Marriage should deservedly be condemned, are united with honesty.

The first good, then, is the offspring, that is, the children who arise from a just and legitimate wife. For the Apostle valued this so much that he said: A woman will be saved through the generation of children. Nor in truth should this be understood only of procreation, but also of the education and discipline with which children are educated to piety. Thus to the subjunctive point the Apostle: If they continue in the faith. For the Scripture admonishes: Have you children? erudite them, and curve them from their childishness. The Apostle also teaches the same, and Tobias, Job and other most holy Fathers offer very beautiful examples of his institution in the sacred letters. And what the offices of parents and children are will be explained more fully in the fourth precept.

What faith in Marriage is, and how it should be kept.

Faith follows, which is the other good of Marriage, not that habit of virtue with which we imbued ourselves when we perceived Baptism, but a certain fidelity with which the man to the woman and the woman to the man mutually bind themselves in such a way that the one gives to the other the power of his body; and promises that he will never violate that holy covenant of marriage. This is easily gleaned from those words that were uttered by the first father when he received Eve as his wife; which Christ the Lord later confirmed in the Gospel: Therefore a man will leave his father and mother, and will cleave to his wife, and they will be two in one flesh: likewise from that place of the Apostle: The woman has no power over her body, but the man: and in the same way the man has no power over his body, but the woman. Therefore, in the ancient law, very serious animosities were established by the Lord against adulterers, because they break this marital faith.

Furthermore, the faith of Marriage postulates that man and woman are united with a certain singular, holy and pure love: and not as adulterers love each other, but as Christ dilexit the Church. For this rule the Apostle prescribed when he says: Men, dilligate your wives, just as Christ also dilligates the Church; whom he certainly embraced with that immense charity, not for the sake of her comfort, but intending only the usefulness of his wife.

What is the Sacrament, when it is numbered among the assets of Marriage.

The third good is called Sacrament, namely the bond of Marriage, which can never be dissolved: because, as it is in the Apostle: The Lord precepts: Let the woman not be separated from the man; and if she separates, let her remain unmarried, or be reconciled to her man, and the man does not send the woman away. Because if Marriage, as it is a Sacrament, means the conjunction of Christ with the Church; It is necessary that, just as Christ is never separated from the Church, so the woman cannot be separated from the man, as far as the bond of Marriage is concerned. But, in order that this holy society may be preserved more easily without quarrel, the offices of man and woman, which have been described by Saint Paul and by the Prince of the Apostles Peter, must be transmitted.

26. What are the husband's main jobs.

Thus, the man's job is to treat the woman liberally and honorably, in which it is worth remembering that Eve was called a companion by Adam, when he says: The woman you gave me as a companion. For which reason some Fathers taught that she was not formed of the feet, but of the side of the man: just as she was not formed of the head, so that she might understand that she was not mistress of the man, but rather subject to the man. It also teaches that the man should always be occupied in the study of some honest thing, so as to provide the things necessary to support the family; so as not to languish with inert leisure, from which almost all vices have flowed; then, for his part, establish the family correctly, correct everyone's customs, support each one in the job.

What does the job of a wife require?

And again the parts of the woman are those enumerated by the Prince of the Apostles when he says: Women be subject to their men, so that even if some do not believe the word, through the conversation of women they may be won without a word, considering your chaste conversation in fear; of which the styling of the hair, or the circumference of gold, or the worship of the vestments of the vestments is not external; but the man who is hidden from the heart, in the incorruptibility of the quiet and modest spirit, which is rich in the sight of God; because in this way also the holy women who hoped in God adorned themselves, subject to their own men, as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him Lord. Let your main study also be to educate your children in the worship of religion, and to take diligent care of domestic things. At home, for your part, contain yourself willingly, unless necessity forces you to go out; and never dare to do that without the man's permission. Afterwards, in which the marital conjunction is primarily involved, always remember that, after God, no one should be loved more than a man, nor should anyone be esteemed more; which also in all things that are not adverse to Christian piety it is necessary to please and temper with utmost alacrity of spirit.

What should you feel about the rites of Marriage.

Consequent to the explanation of these things it will be that the Pastors also teach the rites that must be kept when contracting Marriage: from which it should not be expected that precepts will be transmitted in this place, because by the holy Tridentine Synod the things that in this matter must mainly be observed have been copiously and exactly established; Nor can that decree be ignored by the Pastors. It is enough, then, to admonish them to make every effort to learn from the doctrine of the sacred Council the things that belong to this part, and to expound them diligently to the faithful.

Clandestine marriages are not moments.

In the first place, for their part, so that adolescents and maidens, at whose age lies the greatest weakness of the council, deceived by the false name of nuptials, do not unwittingly enter into pacts of clumsy love, they will often teach that those Marriages that are not contracted present by the Parish Priest, or another Priest licensed by the same Parish Priest or the Ordinary, and with a certain number of witnesses, should not be considered true even for a moment.

It is also advisable to transmit the impediments of Marriage.

But the things that prevent Marriage must also be explained; In which argument many serious and very learned men who have written about vices and virtues have versed themselves so diligently that it will be easy for everyone to transfer to this place the things that they transmitted with their writings; especially when Pastors have the need to almost never leave those same books out of their hands. Thus, both those precepts, as well as those that have been sanctioned by the holy Synod of the impediment that arises or from the spiritual cognate, or of the justice of public honesty, or of fornication, they will read carefully, and they will take care to transmit them to the faithful.

What spirit must be affected by those who agree to Marriage.

From which it can be perceived what spirit the faithful should be affected by when they contract Marriage. Because they should not consider that they undertake something human, but divine, in which singular integrity of mind and piety must be used, as the examples of the Fathers of the old law sufficiently show; whose Marriages, although they were not endowed with the dignity of Sacrament, nevertheless they considered that they should always be cultivated with maximum religion and sanctity.

The consent of the parents must be required for the solidity of the Marriage.

Among other things, for their part, the children of families should be exhorted to the highest degree to pay to their parents, and to those in whose faith and power they are, that honor of not entering into marriages without their knowledge, and much less against their will and repugnance. Because in the Old Testament it is legal to note that children were always placed in Marriage by their parents. In which matter it seems that the Apostle also indicates that one must greatly defer to their will with these words: He who unites his virgin in marriage does well, and he who does not unite her does better.

What should be prescribed in the marital act.

There remains that extreme part of the things that belong to the use of Marriage, which must be treated by the Pastors in such a way that no word falls from their mouths that seems unworthy of the ears of the faithful, or that could hurt pious minds, or cause laughter. Because just as the Elocutions of the Lord are chaste elocutions, so it is also in the greatest degree appropriate for the doctor of the Christian people to use such a type of prayer that prefers a certain singular gravity and integrity of mind. Therefore, the faithful should mainly be taught those two things: firstly, that marriage should not be dedicated because of voluptuousness or libido; but must be used within those limits which, as we above showed, have been prescribed by the Lord. Because it is worth remembering what the Apostle exhorts: Those who have wives should act as if they did not have them; and then what has been said by Saint Jerome: The wise man must love his wife with judgment, not with affection: he will govern the impulses of voluptuousness, and will not rush into intercourse. Nothing is uglier than loving your wife like an adulteress.

34. Spouses must sometimes abstain from the office of Marriage.

But since all good things must be sought from God with holy prayers, the other thing is what should be taught to the faithful: that they sometimes abstain from the office of Marriage for the sake of praying and obserting God: and in the first place they should know that they must observe this at least three days before receiving the sacred Eucharist, and more often when the solemn fasts of Lent are celebrated, as rightly and holyly prescribed by our Fathers. Because in this way it will happen that the very goods of marriage feel increased every day with a greater accumulation of divine grace: and by following the studies of piety, they will not only spend this life calmly and placidly, but will also rely on the true and stable hope of obtaining the eternal goodness of God, which does not confuse.

CHAPTER I.

It is shown that the Decalogue is the sum of all the Precepts.

That the Decalogue is the sum and epitome of all laws, Saint Augustine entrusted it to letters. For although the Lord spoke many things, yet only two stone Tables are given to Moses, which are called Tables of the future Testimony in the ark. Namely, all the rest that God precepted are understood to depend on those ten Precepts that are written in the two Tables, if they are diligently sought and rightly understood: how these same ten Precepts in turn depend on those two, namely on the dilection of God and of the neighbor, on which all the law and the Prophets depend.
super Exodus, Q. 130. See St. Gregory of Nazianzus, orat. 40 in holy Baptism. Ex. 31, 18 and 33, 15. The Ten Precepts depend on the two precepts of charity. Mt. 22, 40.

Why it is most convenient for Pastors to retain and eloquently explain the Decalogue.

Therefore, as it is the sum of the entire Law, it is appropriate for Pastors to contemplate it day and night, not only to compose their lives to this standard, but also to educate the people entrusted to them in the law of the Lord. For the lips of the Priest will guard knowledge, and from his mouth they will require the law; for he is the Angel of the Lord of hosts: which belongs in the highest degree to the Shepherds of the new law, who, being closer to God, must be transformed from clarity to clarity, as by the spirit of the Lord. And since Christ the Lord named them with the name of light, they are properly shepherds of those, so that they may be light to those who are in darkness, scholars of the incipient, teachers of the infants: and if anyone has been warned in any crime, they who are spiritual should instruct such. Also in confessions they support the person of the judge, and according to the type and mode of the sins they give a sentence. Therefore, if they do not want their ignorance to be a fraud for themselves and also for others, it is necessary that they be extremely vigilant in this regard, and very exercised in the interpretation of the divine precepts, so that they can judge any action and the pretermination of the office by this divine rule; and as it is in the Apostle, transmit sound doctrine, that is, that which does not contain any error, and mediates the diseases of the spirit, which are sins; so that the people may be acceptable to God, a follower of good works. And already in such tractations the Pastor proposes to himself and to others those things with which he persuades that the law must be obeyed.

Who is the author of the Decalogue and the law of nature.

Among the other things, for their part, that can impel the minds of men to keep the commands of this law, that has the greatest force: that God is the author of this law. For although it is said that it was given by Angels, yet no one can doubt that God himself is the author of the law. To which point not only the words of the legislator himself, which will be explained shortly afterwards, but also almost infinite places in the Scriptures, which will easily occur to Pastors, provide quite ample testimony. For there is no one who does not feel that a law has been instilled in his soul by God, with which he can discern the good from the evil, the honest from the clumsy, the just from the unjust: whose force and reason of the law is not different from that which is written; Who is the one who dares to deny that, just as of the intimate, God is also the author of the written? It must, therefore, be taught that this divine light, already almost obscured by pious customs and daytime perversity, when God gave the law to Moses, rather made it more illustrious than brought a new one; lest perhaps when the people hear that the law of Moses has been repealed, they may consider that it is not considered these laws. Because it is most certain that these precepts should not be obeyed for this reason, because they were given by Moses: but because they are innate in the minds of all, and through Christ the Lord they have been explained and confirmed.

In what way the people can be excited to keep the law by the author of the law himself.

He will, however, profit greatly, and will have a great moment to persuade that cogitation: that it is God who brought the law: whose wisdom and equity we cannot doubt, nor escape from its infinite strength and power. Therefore, when through the Prophets God commanded that the law be kept, he said that he was the Lord God, and in the same exordium of the Decalogue: I am the Lord your God: and elsewhere: If I am Lord, where is my fear?

How great a benefit it is to have received the law of God.

For its part, it will not only excite the spirits of the faithful to keep the precepts of God, but also to give thanks, because God has explained his will, which contains our salvation. Therefore, not in a single place does the Scripture, declaring this maximum benefit, admonish the people to know their dignity and the beneficence of the Lord, as in Deuteronomy: This, it says, is your wisdom and intellect before the people, so that hearing all these Precepts they may say: Behold a wise and intelligent people, a great people. And again in the Psalm: He did not do so to every nation: and he did not make known his judgments to them.

Why did God anciently want to deliver his law to the Hebrews with such majesty?

But if the Parish Priest has also demonstrated by the authority of Scripture the reason for giving the law, the faithful will easily understand how piously and supplicatingly it is appropriate to cultivate the law of God received. Because three days before the law was brought, by God's command everyone was told to wash their clothes and not touch their wives, so that they would be more holy and prepared to receive the law, so that on the third day they would be present. Later, when they had been led to the mountain from which the Lord through Moses was to bring them the laws, Moses alone was told to ascend the mountain; where God came with maximum majesty, and surrounded the place with thunder, lightning, fire and dense fogs, and began to speak with Moses, and gave him the laws. Which divine Wisdom did not want to be done for any other reason, but to warn us that the law of the Lord must be received with chaste and humble spirit; and that if we neglect the precepts, we are prevented from the penalties prepared by divine justice.

Bernard in the serm. of Palm Sunday, and in the serm. of the Magdalene. …has been cast out of this world, there is no reason for anyone to stop because of the difficulty of the thing, because nothing is difficult for the one who loves.

How the law, promulgated with so much terror, can be fulfilled by men, and that nothing is easier than love.

Furthermore, let the Parish Priest show that the mandates of the law have no difficulty; which he will be able to teach even with this single reason of Saint Augustine, when he says: Who, I ask, is it said that it is impossible for man to love? love, I say, the beneficent Creator, the most loving Father, and then also his flesh in his brothers? but he who obeys has fulfilled the law. Therefore the Apostle John openly testifies that the precepts of God are not serious. Because nothing more just, nothing with greater dignity, nothing with greater fruit could be demanded of man, as witnessed by the blessed Bernard. Therefore Augustine admired the supreme dignity of God, thus speaking to God himself: What is man, that you want to be loved by him? And if he doesn't, do you threaten immense penalties? Isn't this one big enough, if I don't tell you?

And if someone makes that excuse, that he is prevented from loving God because of the weakness of nature; It must be taught that God, who required love, inserts the force of love into hearts by his Holy Spirit. And this good Spirit is given to those who ask for it from the heavenly Father; so Saint Augustine deservedly prayed: Give what you command, and command what you want. Because, then, God's help is ready for us, especially after the death of Christ the Lord; by which the Prince of this world has been cast out, there is no reason for anyone to stop because of the difficulty of the thing, because nothing is difficult for him who loves.

8. Are all men necessarily obliged to observe the law?

Furthermore, to persuade the same thing, it will be very valuable if it is explained that the law must necessarily be obeyed: especially when in our times there have been those who, whether the Law is easy or difficult, have nevertheless not feared to say impiously and to great harm to themselves that it is in no way necessary for salvation. Whose nefarious and impious sentence the Parish Priest will refute with the testimonies of the sacred Scriptures, and mainly of the Apostle himself, with whose authority those strive to protect their impiety. What, then, does the Apostle say? That it is not the foreskin, nor circumcision, something, but the observation of the commandments of God. And what in another place repeats the same sentence, and says that only the new creature in Christ is valid, we clearly understand that he calls the one who observes the commands of God a new creature in Christ. For he who has the commandments of God and keeps them obeys God, as the Lord Himself testifies in John: If anyone obeys me, he will keep my sermon. Because although man can justify himself, and become pious from impious, before he fulfills each of the Precepts of the Law with external actions; However, he who, due to age, can use his reason, cannot be made to become a righteous impious man, if he does not have the spirit prepared to keep all the Precepts of God.

What fruits do those who observe the divine Law achieve?

Finally, lest the Parish Priest omit something by which the faithful people are induced to keep the Law, he will demonstrate how rich and sweet its fruits are. Which you will easily be able to prove from the things that are written in the eighteenth Psalm: for in it the praises of the Law of God are celebrated; of which this is the maxim, which explains much more fully the glory and majesty of God than the heavenly bodies themselves do with their decorum and order; which, as they ravish all nations, though barbarous, to their admiration, so they cause them to recognize the glory, wisdom and power of the Artificer and Conditor of all things. And the Law of the Lord truly converts souls to God: because knowing his ways and the most holy will of God through the Law, we convert our feet to the ways of the Lord. And since only those who fear God are truly wise, this is later attributed to him: that he lends wisdom to the little ones. From here those who observe the Law of God are filled with true joys and knowledge of the divine mysteries, and also with enormous pleasures and rewards, both in this life and in the future century.

Since all things do the will of God, it is shown that it is very right for man to follow the same will.

Nor indeed only by grace of our usefulness, but for the sake of God, should the law be kept for us, who in the Law opened his will to the race of men: which, since other creatures follow it, it is much more equitable for man himself to follow it. Nor should it be ignored with silence that in this God has shown to the greatest degree his clemency towards us and the riches of his supreme goodness; because although without any reward he could have forced us to serve his glory, he nevertheless wanted to unite his glory with our usefulness; so that what is useful to man may also be glorious to God. Since, then, this is maximum and most clear, the Parish Priest will teach, as has been said by the Prophet in the last place, that in guarding those there is much reward. Because not only have we been promised those blessings that seemed to look more toward earthly happiness, so that we may be blessed in the city, blessed in the countryside, but copious mercy has been proposed in heaven, and a good measure, blessed, coagitated and superfluous, that we deserve with pious and just actions, with the adjutory of divine mercy.

OF THE FIRST PRECEPT.

CHAPTER II
I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage, etc.

In what way the Law of Moses binds men of all ages, and on what occasion it was promulgated to the Israelites.

Although the Law was given to the Jews on the mountain by the Lord; However, since it had long before been impressed and consigned by nature in the minds of all, and for that reason God wanted all men to obey Him perpetually, it will be of great benefit to diligently explain those words with which, as Moses was minister and interpreter, they were promulgated to the Hebrews, and the history of the Israelite people, which is full of mysteries.

Firstly, it will narrate that, of all the nations under heaven, God chose only one, which originated from Abraham, whom he wanted to be a pilgrim in the land of Canaan; the possession of which, although it had been promised to him, yet both he and his successors were lazy for more than four hundred years, before they inhabited the promised land; in which pilgrimage he never abandoned his care. They truly passed from people to people, and from kingdom to people; but he never suffered any injury done to them, in fact, he invested in the Kings. And before they went down to Egypt, he sent before them a man, by whose prudence both they and the Egyptians were freed from famine. And in Egypt he embraced them with such kindness that, Pharaoh being disgusted and condemned to his perdition, they increased in an admirable way: and when they were extremely afflicted, and treated as servants very harshly, he raised the leader Moses to take them out with a powerful hand. The Lord primarily remembers this liberation at the beginning of the Law with these words: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage.

Why the Jews were chosen by God as a people.

Of these things, for his part, the Parish Priest must warn in the highest degree that only one of all the nations was chosen by God, to whom he called his people, and to which he offered himself to be known and cultivated; not because it defeated the others in justice or in numbers, as God admonishes the Hebrews, but because it pleased God himself, rather to increase and enrich a small and inept people, so that its power and goodness would be more noticeable and illustrious among all. Therefore, since that was the condition of those men, he united with them and loved them, in such a way that, being Lord of heaven and earth, he did not confuse himself with being called their God, thereby provoking the other people to emulate him, so that, perceiving the happiness of the Israelites, all men would devote themselves to the worship of the true God; Just as Paul also testifies that he, proposing the happiness of the Gentiles and the true knowledge of God with which he had instructed them, provoked their flesh to emulation.

3. Why the Hebrews were harassed long and long before receiving the Law.

Then he will teach the faithful that God allowed the Hebrew fathers to go on pilgrimage for a long time, and that the later ones were also oppressed and harassed with very harsh servitude, for this reason: so that we may learn that not only the enemies of the world and pilgrims in the lands become friends of God; and so they are more easily received into the familiarity of God, if we have nothing at all in common with the world: and then, for its part, so that, transferred to the worship of God, we may understand how much happier ultimately those who serve God are than those who serve the world: of which thing the Scripture admonishes us; because he says: Nevertheless they will serve him, so that they may know the distance of my bondage and of the bondage of the kingdom of the lands.

It will also explain that after more than four hundred years, God lent the promises, so that those people could be nourished with faith and hope. Because God wants his students to depend on him perpetually, and place all their hope in his goodness, as will be said in the explanation of the first Precept.

Why was the Law given in such a place and time. Finally, you will note the place and time in which the people of Israel received this Law from God: namely, after having been taken out of Egypt and arrived in the desert, so that, attracted by the memory of the recent benefit and detained by the harshness of the place in which they found themselves, they would become more suitable to receive the Law. In fact, men feel above all linked to those who have experienced its benefit, and they take refuge in the protection of God when they are deprived of all human hope. From which it can be understood that the faithful are all the more inclined to embrace the heavenly doctrine the more they have separated themselves from the seductions of the world and the pleasures of the flesh; as it is written by the Prophet: “Whom will science teach? Who will he make understand what he hears? "To those weaned from milk, to those torn from the breasts."

What does this exordium mean and what mysteries are contained in it. Therefore, let the parish priest strive and do everything he can so that the faithful people always have these words in their minds: "I am the Lord your God"; of which they will understand that they have their Creator as Lawgiver, from whom they were made and are preserved, and they will rightly usurp that: "He is the Lord our God, and we are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand." The vehement and frequent admonition of these words will have such force that it will make the faithful more ready to observe the law and to abstain from sins. And what follows: "That I brought you out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage," although it seems to be appropriate only to the Jews freed from the dominion of the Egyptians, yet, if we consider the internal reason for universal salvation, it belongs much more to Christian men, who, not from Egyptian bondage, but from the region of sin and the power of darkness were taken away by God and transferred to the kingdom of the Son of his delight. Contemplating the magnitude of this benefit, Jeremiah predicted: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and it will be said no more: As the Lord lives, who brought the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt; but, As the Lord lives, who brought the children of Israel out of the land of the North and from all the lands to which he had driven them, I will bring them back to their land, which I gave to their fathers. Behold, I will send many fishermen, says the Lord, and they will catch them," and what follows. For the forgiving Father, through his Son, gathered into one the children who were dispersed, so that no longer as servants of sin, but of righteousness, we might serve him in holiness and righteousness before him all the days of our lives.

How the faithful should be affected by the principle of this Decalogue. Therefore the faithful, to all temptations, as with a shield, will oppose that of the Apostle: «We who have died to sin, how can we still live in it? We are no longer our own, but those of him who died and rose again for us. He is the Lord our God, who purchased us with his blood: how can we sin against the Lord our God and crucify him again? So that, therefore, truly free, and with that freedom with which Christ freed us, just as we present our members to serve injustice, so we present them to serve justice in sanctification.

You will have no other gods before me. What does this first precept cover in terms of what should be observed and what should be avoided? The parish priest will teach that the first place in the Decalogue is occupied by things that belong to God, and the next by those that belong to our neighbor; because of what we lend to our neighbor the cause is God: then we love our neighbor by God's precept, when we love him for God's sake; and these things are written on the first table. Secondly, it will show that these proposed words contain a double precept: one that has the power to command, and another to prohibit. For what is said: "You shall have no other gods before me," has this sentence united: "You shall worship me, the true God; "You shall not worship other gods."

How faith, hope and charity are contained in this precept. The first part contains the precept of faith, hope and charity: for when we say God, we confess that he is immutable, incommunicable, that he remains perpetually the same, faithful, upright, without any iniquity; from which it follows that, assenting to his oracles, it is necessary that we pay him all faith and authority. And whoever considers his omnipotence, clemency and ease and propensity to do good, can he not place all his hopes in him? And if you contemplate the riches of his kindness and kindness poured out on us, can you not love him? From here comes that proem, from here that conclusion that God uses when commanding and ordering in Scripture: "I, the Lord."

This precept is exposed as it is negative. The other part of the precept is that: "You shall have no other gods before me"; which formula of speech the Legislator used, not because this sentence was not sufficiently explained with the affirmation of the precept in this way: "You will only worship me as God": for if it is God, it is one; but because of the blindness of many, who once professed to worship the true God, and yet worshiped the multitude of gods. There were many of this type among the Hebrews themselves, who, as Elijah objected to them, limped on both sides, which also did the Samaritans, who worshiped the God of Israel and the gods of the Gentiles.

How is it to be estimated that this precept is the greatest of all. Having explained these things, it will be added that this is the first and greatest precept of all, not only for the order itself, but for reason, dignity and excellence. For God must have among us, in infinite parts, greater charity and authority than that of a lord or a king. He created us, he himself governs us; from him we were nourished in the mother's womb and from there brought out into this light; he supplies us with the things necessary for life and sustenance.

Who especially sin against this precept. Therefore, those who do not have faith, hope and charity sin against this precept, whose sin spreads widely. Among this number are those who fall into heresy, those who do not believe what Holy Mother Church proposes as faith; those who believe in dreams, omens and other vain things; those who abandon the hope of their salvation and do not trust in divine goodness; those who rely only on wealth, health and physical strength: things that have been explained more fully by those who wrote about vices and sins.

The cult that, according to the received usage of the Church, is paid to the Saints is not opposed to this precept. But also in the explanation of this precept it must be diligently taught that the veneration and invocation of the holy Angels and the blessed souls who enjoy heavenly glory, or also the worship of their own bodies and the ashes of the Saints, which the Catholic Church has always used, is not repugnant to this Law. For who is so insane that, when the King commands that no one presents himself as King or tolerates being honored with royal worship and honor, he immediately thinks that the King Don't you want honor to be given to your magistrates? Because although it is said that Christians worship the Angels after the example of the Saints of the Old Testament, they do not, however, pay them that veneration that they give to God. And if we sometimes read that the Angels refused to be venerated by men, it must be understood that they did so because they did not want to be given that honor that is due only to God.

How it is lawful to venerate the holy Angels is shown by the Scriptures. For the Holy Spirit, who says: "To God alone honor and glory," Himself commanded that we honor parents and elders. Furthermore, the holy men who worshiped one God, however, as it is in the divine Scriptures, worshiped kings, that is, they venerated them as supplicants. And if so much honor is paid to the kings, through whom God governs the world, to the angelic spirits, whom God wanted to be his ministers and whose work he uses not only for the government of his Church, but also of other things, and with whose help we are daily delivered from great dangers of soul and body, although they do not show themselves to us, will we not pay them so much greater honor as those blessed minds surpass them? in dignity to the kings themselves? Add to this the charity with which they love us, by which, moved by the provinces they govern, as is easily understood from the Scripture, they pour out prayers; which there is no doubt that they also lend to those of whom they are custodians; because they offer our prayers and tears to God. Therefore in the Gospel the Lord taught that little ones should not be scandalized, because his Angels in heaven always see the face of the Father who is in heaven.

That the holy Angels are to be invoked is proven by the Scriptures. They must be invoked, therefore, because they perpetually contemplate God and receive with great pleasure the sponsorship of our salvation that has been entrusted to them. There are testimonies of divine Scripture of this invocation. For Jacob, from whom he had fought, asks him to bless him, and even urges him; for he professes that he will not let him go if he does not receive the blessing: and he did not want it to be attributed to him only for the one whom he saw, but also for the one whom he did not see; when he said: "The Angel who frees me from all evils, bless these children." By the invocation of the Saints and the veneration of the relics the honor of God is in no way diminished. From which we can also deduce how far it is from honoring and invoking the Saints who sleep in the Lord and venerating their sacred relics and ashes, to diminish the glory of God; On the contrary, it increases to the highest degree, the more it excites and confirms the hope of men and exhorts them to the imitation of the Saints: an office approved by the second Council of Nicaea, that of Gangra and that of Trent, and the authority of the holy Fathers.

With what main arguments should the invocation of the Saints be stabilized? And so that the parish priest may be more instructed to refute those who oppose this truth, he should read above all Saint Jerome against Vigilantius and Damascene. To the reason of these, which is the main one, is added the custom received from the Apostles and retained and preserved perpetually in the Church of God. Who will seek a stronger or clearer argument for this than the testimony of divine Scripture, which admirably celebrates the praises of the Saints? Well, there are divine proclamations of some Saints; And if their praises are celebrated with sacred letters, what is there for men not to pay them singular honor? And they should be venerated and invoked all the more because they make assiduous prayers for the salvation of men, and through their merit and grace God confers many benefits on us. For if there is joy in heaven over a sinner who does penance, will not the heavenly citizens also help the penitents? Will they not, prayed, ask for the forgiveness of sins and reconcile us with the grace of God?

It is shown that the invocation of the Saints does not come from a certain distrust of divine help or from a weakness of faith. And if it is said, as some say, that the patronage of the Saints is superfluous because God comes to our prayers without an interpreter, these voices of the wicked are easily convinced by what Saint Augustine said: that many things are not granted by God except through the work and office of a mediator and preacher. This is confirmed by the illustrious examples of Abimelech and Job's friends, whose sins he did not forgive except through the prayers of Abraham and Job. And if it is also alleged that it is due to poverty and imbecility of faith that we use the Saints as internuncios and patrons, what will they respond to the example of the centurion, who even in that singular proclamation of faith that the Lord God gave him, nevertheless sent the elders of the Jews to the Savior so that they would pray for health to the sick boy?

The doctrine of a single mediator, Christ, does not take away the invocation of the Saints. Therefore, although it must be confessed that we have only one mediator, Christ the Lord, who only reconciled us with the heavenly Father by his blood, and who, having found eternal redemption, once entered the Sanctuary and does not cease to intercede for us; From this, however, it in no way follows that it is not lawful to resort to the grace of the Saints. Well, if for that reason it were not licit to use the help of the Saints because we have only one patron, Jesus Christ, the Apostle would never have done it if he wanted to be helped with so much study by the prayers of his living brothers. For no less would the prayers of the living than the deprecation of the Saints who are in heaven diminish the glory and dignity of the mediator Christ.

The following words do not constitute another precept, but one with the preceding ones. And what follows: «You shall not make for yourself any sculpture or likeness of anything that is in heaven above, nor of anything that is on the earth beneath, nor of anything that is in the water under the earth; you shall not worship them nor serve them": some, considering this to be another precept, wanted the last two to be contained in the force of a single precept. But Saint Augustine wanted those extremes to be united with these: a sentence that, because it is famous in the Church, we willingly follow. And although that very true reason is at hand that it was convenient that each person's reward and penalty should be united with the first precept. 21. The use of images received in the Church does not fight against this precept. Nor should anyone think that this precept completely prohibits the art of painting, modeling or sculpting. For in the Scriptures we read that by God's command simulacra and images were made, the Cherubim and the bronze serpent. It remains, then, for us to interpret that the images were prohibited for that reason, so that nothing of the true worship of God would be subtracted from the simulacra as gods to be worshiped.

In what main ways can the divine Majesty be violated by images. In two main ways, as far as this precept is concerned, it is manifest that the majesty of God is seriously offended: one, if idols and images are worshiped as God, or it is believed that there is some divinity or virtue in them for which they are to be worshiped; or that something must be asked of them, or that trust must be placed in images, as anciently the Gentiles did, who placed their hope in idols, which sacred letters everywhere rebuke. Another, if someone makes an effort to represent the form of divinity with some artifice, as if it could be seen with bodily eyes or expressed with colors or figures. For who could express God, as Damascene says, who does not fall under sight, who lacks a body, who cannot be circumscribed by any term or described by any figure? Something that is explained more fully in the second Council of Nicaea. Clearly, then, the Apostle said that they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of corruptible man, of birds, of four-footed animals, and of serpents: for they venerated all these things as God when they set up the images of these things; Therefore the Israelites, who before the image of the calf cried: "These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt," are called idolaters, because they changed their glory into the likeness of a calf eating hay. 23. And this sentence is contained in this precept.

If in the same way the punishment threatened here is to be instilled in the prevaricators of the carnal and the perfect. The second thing is that this appendage must be taught in a very different way to the perfect and in another way to carnal men. To the perfect, in fact, who are moved by the Spirit of God and obey Him with a prompt and joyful spirit, it is a very joyful announcement and great argument of the divine will toward them. They recognize, therefore, the care of their most loving God, who prays with rewards, now with sorrows, drives men almost to his worship and veneration; They recognize his immense benevolence towards them, that he wants to command them and that their works be used in the glory of the divine Name; and they not only recognize it, but they have great hope that, by commanding what he wants, he will also give the strength with which they can obey his law. But to the carnal, who have not yet been freed from the spirit of bondage and abstain from sins more out of fear of punishment than out of love of virtue, the meaning of this appendix is ​​grave and bitter. Therefore they must be relieved with pious exhortations and, where the law points, they must be led almost by the hand. The parish priest, however, whenever the opportunity is offered to explain a precept, keep these same things in mind. With two stings God excites men to observe the law. First, when one hears that the Lawgiver is a strong God, carnal presumption is broken.

What do those words propose to meditation: I am a strong God. Both to the carnal and to the spiritual, above all, two stings must be applied that, placed in the same appendage, incite men to the highest degree to observe the law. Well, the fact that God is called strong must be explained with more diligence, because the flesh, which is less moved by the terrors of the command, invents for itself various reasons with which it can escape the wrath of God and avoid the proposed punishment; but to him who is firmly persuaded that God is strong, he appropriates that of the great David: "Where shall I go from your spirit, and where shall I flee from your face?" The same flesh, sometimes distrusting the divine promises, believes that the forces of the enemies are so great that it is considered not equal to supporting them; but firm and stable faith, which does not waver, relying on divine strength and virtue, recreates and confirms men. For he says: "The Lord is my illumination and my salvation, whom shall I fear?"

What does it mean that God also calls himself jealous? The other sting is divine zeal itself. For sometimes men think that God does not care about human things, not even about whether we keep or neglect his law; from which follows great confusion of life: but when we believe that God is jealous, meditation on this thing easily keeps us in duty.

What kind of zeal is to be attributed to God. The zeal that is attributed to God does not mean any disturbance of the spirit, but rather that divine love and charity with which God does not suffer any soul to fortify with impunity away from him; and as many as he committed fornication, he loses. It is, then, the zeal of God his most calm and sincere Justice, with which the soul corrupted by false opinions and crooked cupidities is repudiated and separated from the connubial of God as an adulteress. But we experience this most gentle and sweetest zeal of God when His supreme and incredible will towards us is demonstrated to us with the same zeal. For there is no more ardent love nor greater and closer union among men than that of those who are united by marriage. Therefore, how much God loves us shows us when he frequently, comparing himself to a husband or husband, calls himself jealous. Therefore let the parish priest teach in this place that men must be so desirous of divine worship and honor that they can with more reason be called zealous than lovers, after the example of him who says of himself: "I have been jealous for the Lord God of hosts"; and imitate Christ himself, of whom it is that: "Zeal for your house has consumed me."
