How God visits the sins of the parents in the children until the third and fourth generation. The people must be taught that the penalty of the injunction reaches the third and fourth generation of the impious and criminals; Not because those who are later always pay the penalties for the crimes of those who are older, but that, even if they and their children have carried them with impunity, not all of their posterity will, however, avoid the wrath and punishment of God. Which happened to King Josiah; For this man, because of his singular piety, when God forgave him and granted him to be taken in peace to the sepulcher of his elders, so that he would not see the evils of the following times that due to the impiety of his grandfather Manasseh were to befall Judah and Jerusalem, after his death, the vengeance of God reached his posterity in such a way that not even the sons of Josiah were spared.

How these words agree with those of Ezekiel. And in what way these words of the Law are not opposed to that sentence that is in the Prophet: "The soul that sins, it will die," is openly shown by the authority of Saint Gregory, who agrees with all the other ancient Fathers. For it says: "Whoever imitates the iniquity of the wicked father is also constrained by his crime; but whoever does not imitate the father's iniquity is in no way burdened by his crime. From which it follows that the wicked son of a wicked father not only pays for his own sins that he added, but also for those of the father; when to the father's vices, of which he knows that the Lord is angry, he is not afraid to add his own malice; and it is just that he who under the severe judge is not afraid to imitate the ways of the wicked father, should be forced in the present life to also pay for the sins of the wicked father. The priest will later remember how much the goodness and mercy of God surpasses his own justice: he is angry even to the third and fourth generation, but he shows mercy to thousands. 37. How they are considered to hate divine laws. In what was said: "of those who hate me", the magnitude of the sin is shown. For what is more disgraceful and detestable than hating the same supreme goodness, the same supreme truth? And this belongs only to all sinners, because just as he who has the commandments of God and keeps them loves God, so he who despises the law of the Lord and does not keep his commandments must rightly be said to hate God. Whatever that is: Showing mercy to those who love me. And the last thing: "to those who love me", teaches the way and reason to keep the law. For it is necessary that those who keep the Law of God be brought to its obedience with the same charity and love with which they are towards God. OF THE SECOND PRECEPT. CHAPTER III. You shall not take the Name of the Lord your God in vain.

Why did he want to give law to honor his own name. In the first precept of the divine Law, by which we are commanded to worship God piously and holyly, this one that follows in second place is necessarily contained (for whoever wants honor to be paid to him, also asks that we accompany him with the highest honor of words, and prohibits the opposite; which is openly indicated by those words of the Lord in Malachi: "The son honors the father, and the servant his master; if, then, I am a Father, where is my honor?"). God, however, due to the magnitude of the thing, wanted to give separately this Law to honor his own divine and most holy name, and prescribe it to us in clear words. Hatred of God is the greatest of all sins. St. Thomas in 1. 2. q.
art. 4 and in 2. 2. q. 34, art. 1. Jn. 14, 21. With love and charity the law is to be perfected. See Synod of Trent on Justification, sess. 6.

CHAPTER 16. On this precept see St. Thomas 2. 2. q. 122, art. 3; see also the Master in 3. sent. dist. 39. Mal. 1, 6. Ps. 88, 8. Is. 6. Under the negative precept the stated affirmation is included, because the denial presupposes the affirmation. Aristotle, book. 2 from Heaven. CATEC. FOR PASTORS. PART III. 2. How much effort parish priests should make in explaining this precept. Which, in truth, must be an argument to the parish priest in the first place that it will by no means be sufficient if he speaks of this thing in general: but that this is a place of such a nature that it is necessary for him to spend more time and explain to the faithful clearly, clearly and diligently what belongs to this treatise. Nor should this diligence be considered excessive, since there are not lacking those who are so blinded by the darkness of errors that they are not afraid to curse him whom the Angels glorify: not even because the law has been given once do they stop from undermining the majesty of God every day, and even almost every hour and moment they dare impudently. Well, who does not see that everything is affirmed with an oath? That everything is full of imprecations and execrations? To such a point that almost no one sells something, or buys, or does any business, without interposing the religion of the oath and usurping a thousand times, even in the slightest and most vain thing, the most holy name of God. Therefore, greater care and diligence must be taken in the parish priest so that he often warns the faithful how serious and detestable this crime is. What does this second precept command or prohibit? In the explanation of this precept, it is first noted that, along with what the Law prohibits from being done, it is also linked to the prescription of those things that men must provide. And one thing and another must be taught separately: first, so that the things that are to be translated are more easily explained, what the Law commands; then also what a closed season. Well, what it commands is: that the name of God must be honored and that one must swear holy oaths by him; and at the same time what it prohibits: that no one despise the divine name, that no one take it in vain, nor swear by it falsely, frustratingly or recklessly.

What is meant here by the name of God. In that part, then, in which we are ordered to pay honor to the divine name, the parish priest commands the faithful that they must not pay attention only to the letters and syllables of the name of God, or at all to the naked word alone; but we must come to that consideration of what is the value of that word that signifies the omnipotent and everlasting majesty of the one and triune Numen. From this it is easy to see how vain is the superstition of some Jews who, in order to write the name of God, did not dare to pronounce it, as if divine force were in those four letters and not in the thing. But even if it is said in a singular number: "Thou shalt not take the name of God," it is not to be understood of a single name, but of all those that are usually attributed to God: for many names have been imposed on God, such as Lord, Almighty, Lord of hosts, King of kings, Mighty One and others of this kind that are read in the Scriptures, all of which have equal and the same veneration. Then it must be taught how the due honor is paid to the divine name: for the Christian people, in whose mouths the praises of God are to be assiduously celebrated, it is not licit to ignore anything that is most useful and perishable for salvation.

In what way we are deemed to venerate or honor the divine name. Although there are many reasons to praise the divine name, those that will be mainly discussed here seem to have the strength and weight of all. First of all, God is praised when, in the presence of everyone, we confidently confess God and our Lord, and preach Christ, the author of our salvation, as we recognize him. Likewise when we do holy and diligent work on the word of God, with which his will is enunciated; We assiduously occupy ourselves with its meditation, we learn it with study, now by reading, now by listening, as is suitable and convenient for the person and profession of each one. Then we venerate and cultivate the divine name when, for the sake of office and religion, we celebrate divine praises and give him singular thanks for all things, both prosperous and adverse; for the Prophet says: "Bless the Lord, my soul, and do not forget all his rewards"; and there are many Psalms of David with which, with a certain egregious piety towards God, he very softly sings his divine praises. There is also that admirable example of patience of Job, who, fallen into those maximum and horrible calamities, nevertheless never stopped praising God with an exalted and undefeated spirit. We, then, when we are tormented with pains of soul and body, when we are tortured with miseries and labors, let us immediately convert all the study and the strength of our spirit to praising God, saying that of Job: "Blessed be the name of the Lord." 6. How we also obey this precept in another way. Nor is God's name less honored if we confidently implore his help, so that he either delivers us from those evils or gives us perseverance and strength to endure them with fortitude. This is what the Lord wants: “Call on me, he says, in the day of tribulation; I will deliver you and you will glorify me.

CATEC. FOR PASTORS. PART III. you will glorify me; Of whose imploration there are illustrious examples both in many other places and mainly in Psalms 16, 43 and 128. Furthermore, we honor the name of God when we take Him as a witness to make faith: a way that differs greatly from the superior ones. For the things we remember above are in themselves so good and desirable that nothing can be happier or more desirable to man than if in the diligent execution of them he exercises himself day and night: "I will bless, says David, the Lord at all times, his praise always in my mouth"; but the oath, although it is good, its frequent use is in no way praiseworthy.

Why the more frequent use of the oath should not be approved. The reason for this difference is that the oath was instituted only for that reason: so that it would be a certain remedy for human imbecility and a necessary instrument to prove what we say. For just as it is not convenient to apply medicines to the body except when necessary, and their frequent use is completely harmful: so also, if there is no serious and just cause, it is not healthy to use the oath; and if it is used more frequently, it is so far from being beneficial that it causes great harm. For this reason Saint Chrysostom clearly teaches that not at birth, but when the world was already grown, when the evils spread far and wide occupied the entire globe of the earth, and nothing remained in its place and order, but all disturbed and confused things were carried up and down with great confusion of things; and what is most serious of all evils: almost all mortals had thrown themselves into the ugly servitude of idols, so finally, after a long interval, the oath was introduced into the custom of men; For when no one was easily led to believe in so much perfidy and iniquity of men, they invoked God as a witness. 8. What is the reason for the oath, and what it is properly. But since in this part of the precept the main reason for teaching the faithful is how they should use the oath piously and holyly, it must first be said that swearing is nothing other than taking God as a witness, whatever the form and conception of the words: for "God is my witness" and "by God" are the same. It is also an oath when to make faith we swear by created things, such as by the sacred Gospels of God, by the Cross, by the relics of the Saints and their names and others of this kind: since these same things do not in themselves contribute any authority or strength to the oath, but this is provided by God himself, whose splendor of divine majesty shines in those things. From which it follows that those who swear by the Gospel swear by God himself, whose truth is contained and declared in the Gospel: and in the same way by the Saints, who are temples of God and who believed the evangelical truth and cultivated it with all observance and spread it widely throughout people and nations.

Of that form of oath that is made by execration. The same reason is for that oath that is pronounced by execration, which is that of St. Paul: "I call upon God as a witness over my soul": for in this way someone subjects himself to the judgment of God as the avenger of lies. Nor do we deny that some of these formulas can be taken in such a way that they do not have the force of an oath: but it is useful to observe in these also what has been said about an oath, and to adhere completely to the same norm and rule. 10. How many kinds is the oath? There are, then, two types of swearing. The first is called assertion, namely, when we religiously affirm something of a present or past thing, like the Apostle in the letter to the Galatians: "Behold before God I do not lie." The other is called promissory, to which the injunctions also refer, looking to the future time; when we promise and confirm with certainty that something will be: of this kind is that of David, who swore to Beersheba his wife, by the Lord his God, that Solomon his son would be heir of the kingdom and would succeed him in his place. 11. How many things are required for the legitimate oath. But although it is truly enough for the oath to take God as a witness; However, for it to be right and holy, many more things are required, which must be diligently explained. Which briefly, according to divine witness Jerome, Jeremiah enumerates when he says: "You shall swear: As the Lord lives in truth, in judgment and in justice": with whose words he briefly and summarily understood those in which the entire perfection of the oath is contained: truth, judgment and justice.

and 3, 5. "I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles, etc." When you swear by a created thing, you do not exclude God, who gave strength to things. How the oath is truly taken. The first place in the oath is, therefore, the truth: namely, that what is affirmed is true in itself, and that the one who swears believes that it is so, not carried out rashly or by slight conjecture, but by very certain arguments. The other type of oath, with which we promise something, requires the truth in the same way. For he who promises something must be in such a spirit that, when the time comes, he will actually provide it and fulfill what he promised: for the honest man will never receive a commitment to do what he considers contrary to the most holy precepts and the will of God; But whatever is lawful to promise and swear, once promised, he will never change it; unless, by chance, the condition of things has changed, it has begun to be such that if he wanted to keep the faith and live up to what was promised, he would incur the hatred and offense of God. And that truth is necessary to an oath is also indicated by David with those words: "He who swears to his neighbor and does not deceive." 13. Who is said to swear in court, and for what reason the oath should not be deferred to children. The trial follows second. For the oath is not to be used rashly and inconsiderately, but with consultation and thought. Therefore, he who is going to swear first considers whether he is forced by necessity or not, and carefully considers the whole thing, whether it is of such a nature that it seems to require the oath. Also pay attention to the time, look at the place and circumscribe many other things that are linked to things; be not driven by hate, nor by love, nor by any disturbance of the spirit, but by the force and necessity of the thing itself. For if this consideration and diligent warning have not preceded, the oath will be hasty and reckless: of this kind is the irreligious affirmation of those who swear on something very light and vain without reason or advice, but out of a certain perverse custom. Which we see sellers and buyers doing everywhere every day: for those, to sell as much as possible, these in turn to buy as little as possible, do not hesitate to praise or revile venal things with oaths. And since judgment or prudence is needed, and children, due to their age, cannot yet perceive and distinguish with such acuity, that is why it was established by Saint Cornelius the Pontiff that no oath be required of children before puberty, that is, before the fourteenth year.

How one swears in justice. Justice remains, which is required above all in promises. Therefore, if someone promises something unjust and dishonest, he sins by swearing and, by fulfilling his promise, he accumulates crime upon crime. There is an example of this in the Gospel of King Herod, who, forced by a reckless oath, gave the dancing girl the head of John the Baptist as a prize for the dance. Such was also the oath of the Jews, who devoted themselves (as it is in the Acts of the Apostles) with that condition of not tasting anything until they had killed Paul.

With what main reasons is it understood that it is sometimes lawful to swear. Having explained these things in this way, there is no doubt that anyone who has kept all these things and has fortified the oath with these conditions can swear safely, as with certain convicts. But it is easy to prove it also with many arguments: for the Law of the Lord, which is immaculate and holy, commanded it: "You will fear the Lord your God, and him only you will serve, and you will swear by his name"; and for David it is said: "All who swear by him will be praised." Furthermore, the sacred letters indicate that the very luminaries of the Church, the most holy Apostles, sometimes used the oath: and this appears from the epistles of the Apostle. Add that the Angels themselves also sometimes swear: for by Saint John the Evangelist in the Apocalypse it is written that the Angel swore by him who lives forever. Furthermore, God himself also swears, the Lord of the Angels: and in the Old Testament in many places God confirms his promises with an oath; like Abraham and David, who left that of God's oath: "The Lord has sworn, says he, and will not repent: You are a Priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek."

It is proven that the oath sworn ritually must be praised. Nor is the reason obscure to understand why the oath is praiseworthy, if the whole thing is considered more carefully and its origin and purpose are looked at. For the oath comes from faith, by which men believe that God is the author of all truth, that he can never be deceived nor deceive others; to whose eyes all things are naked and open, and who finally with admirable providence cares for all human things and administers the world. Imbued, then, with this faith, men take God as a witness of the truth, for whom not having faith will be impious and nefarious.

This is how Aug. interprets it in lib. 1 of the Lord's sermon on the mount, c. 30, and cause 22 is found, q. 1, chap. Ita ergo. Mt. 5, 37. How many evils the habit of swearing brings with it. CATEC. FOR PASTORS. PART III. Imbued, then, with this faith, men take God as a witness of the truth, for whom not having faith will be impious and nefarious.

The end of the oath is the end of controversies and litigation. And as far as the end is concerned, this is what the oath aims at and aims at entirely: to prove the justice and innocence of man and to put an end to litigation and controversies: which the Apostle also teaches in the Epistle to the Hebrews.

How Christ forbade the oath. Nor are those words of our Savior in Saint Matthew repugnant to this sentence: "You have heard that it was said to the ancients, 'You shall not perswear, but you shall fulfill your oaths to the Lord.' But I tell you: Do not swear at all, not even by heaven, because it is the throne of God; nor by the earth, because it is his footstool; nor for Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King; nor will you swear by your head, because you cannot make a hair white or black. Let your word be: yes, yes; no no; and what is more of this is evil. With these words it should not be said that the oath is condemned in general and universally; For we have already seen above that the Lord himself and the Apostles swore frequently: but the Lord wanted to argue the perverse judgment of the Jews, with which they had persuaded themselves that in the oath nothing was to be taken care of except for lies: and thus they themselves swore very frequently with regard to the very light things and at no time did they themselves swear very frequently and required oaths from others. This custom rebukes and reproaches the Savior, and teaches that the oath must be abstained from altogether, unless necessity requires it.

How Christ said that what is added to the simple assertion of truth is evil. For by human imbecility the oath was instituted, and in truth it comes from evil: since it either indicates the inconstancy of the one who swears, or the contumacy of him on whose account we swear, who cannot otherwise be induced to believe. But the need to swear has an excuse. And truly, when the Savior says: “Let your word be: yes, yes; no, no,” by this formula of speaking he sufficiently declares that he prohibits the custom of swearing in conversations of familiar and light things: for which reason we are principally admonished by the Lord not to be too easy and prone to swear; and this must be taught with diligence and instilled in the ears of the faithful: since almost infinite evils arise from the excessive habit of swearing, and it is verified with the authority of the sacred letters and with the testimonies of the most holy Fathers. In Ecclesiasticus it is written: «Do not accustom your mouth to swearing; for in it there are many stumbling blocks"; likewise: "The man who swears much will be filled with iniquity, and the plague will not depart from his house." You can read more about this thing in Saint Basil and Saint Augustine in the books against lying. And up to this point of what was ordered; now it is said about what is forbidden.

Why false and reckless swearing is such a great sin. We are forbidden to take the divine Name in vain. Well, it appears that someone who is forced to swear an oath not by advice, but by recklessness, is obligated with a grave sin. And that this is a very serious crime is also declared by those words: "You shall not take the Name of the Lord your God in vain"; as if they provided the reason why this fact is so outrageous and nefarious: namely, because it undermines His majesty, whom we profess to be our God and Lord. By this precept, then, men are prohibited from swearing falsely: for he who does not avoid such a great crime as taking God as a false witness, does a signal injury to God; since either it imprints the stain of ignorance, when it considers that the truth of something is hidden from it, or certainly of improbability and twisted affection, when wanting to confirm the lie with its testimony.

How those who swear to be true what is true perjure. However, not only he who swears to be true what he knows to be false swears falsely; but also he who affirms with an oath what, being true, he nevertheless considers false. Well, since a lie is a lie because it is uttered against the mind and the feeling of the soul, it is evident that the latter lies outright and is perjured.

He who swears falsely what he considers to be true, how he sins. In the same way, he also perjures what he believes to be true and yet is actually false; unless, as much as he could, he had used care and diligence to have the whole thing ascertained and explored. For although his speech is agreed with the mind, he is nevertheless guilty of this precept. 23. He who does not keep what he swore or promised to do, sins in what way. The same sin must be considered guilty of the one who promises with an oath to do something, when, however, he either did not have the mind to fulfill what he promised, or if he did, in fact he does not perform it. Which also concerns those who, having bound themselves to God with a vow, do not fulfill it.

A deadly sin is he who swears, or against the evangelical counsel, so that he sins. Furthermore, this precept is sinned if justice is lacking, which is one of the three companions of the oath. Thus, if someone swears that he will commit some mortal sin, for example the death of a man, he is guilty of this precept, even if he says it seriously and from the heart, and the oath has truth, which we declare is required in the first place. To these must be added those types of swearing that come from a certain contempt, when someone swears that he will not obey the evangelical counsels: of this type are those who exhort celibacy and poverty. Well, although no one should necessarily follow them; If someone, however, swears that he does not want to obey those counsels, with that oath he despises and violates the divine counsels.

He who swears on slight conjectures sins. Furthermore, he who swears what is true, and believes that it is true, based on certain slight conjectures and requests from afar, violates this law and sins in judgment. For although truth accompanies such an oath, falsehood nevertheless somehow underlies it. For he who swears so carelessly is in great danger of perjuring himself.

He who swears by false gods sins gravely. Furthermore, he who swears by false gods swears falsely. For what is more alien to the truth than taking lying and fictitious gods as witnesses as the true God? 27. He who dishonors the word of God, or misinterpreting it, or converting it to vain things, sins. But, since the Scripture, when it prohibited perjury, says: "Neither shall you stain the name of your God," the negligence that must be avoided in the other things to which honor is due by the authority of this precept is prohibited; which is the word of God, whose majesty is reverenced not only by the pious, but sometimes also by the impious; as in the history of the Judges there is a memory of the king of the Moabites Eglon. But he offends with utmost insult the word of God who twists the sacred Scripture from its right and genuine sentence to dogmas and heresies of the impious: of which crime the Prince of the Apostles admonishes us with those words: "There are in them some things difficult to understand, which the unlearned and unstable twist, as well as the other Scriptures, to their own perdition." Furthermore, the sacred Scripture is contaminated with ugly and dishonest stains when nefarious men twist to profane things any of their oracles and sentences, which must be cultivated with all veneration, namely, jokes, fabulous things, vain things, flattery, detractions, fortunes, famous libels and if there are others of this kind, in which the sacred Synod commands that the sin be warned.

How those who do not call upon God in their calamities sin. Furthermore, just as those who implore his help and assistance in their calamities honor God, so do those who do not invoke his help deny the honor due to God: whom David rebukes when he says: “They did not call upon God; There they trembled with fear where there was no fear. 29. The most serious of all these sins is blasphemy against God and his Saints. But those who dare to blaspheme and execrate with impure and contaminated mouths the sacrosanct Name of God, which must be blessed by all creatures and exalted with supreme praise, commit themselves with a much more detestable crime; or also the name of the Saints who reign with God. Which sin is so atrocious and inhuman that sometimes sacred letters, if it is blasphemy, use the name blessing. 30. Why certain threats are subject to this precept. It usually vehemently inhibits the license; That is why the parish priest, to move the minds of men more and encourage them more easily to keep this precept, will diligently explain the other part of it and as an appendix: "For the Lord will not hold him innocent who takes the Name of the Lord his God in vain." And first teach that with great reason it was made that threats were added to this precept: with which both the gravity of sin and the benignity of God towards us is recognized; who, since he does not delight in the perdition of men, with these salutary threats stops us so that we do not incur his wrath and offense, namely so that we experience him as rather benevolent than angry. The Pastor urges this place and insists with great study so that he recognizes the seriousness of the crime and detests it more vehemently, and puts greater diligence and caution in avoiding it. Also show how much the proclivity of men is to commit this sin, so that it would not be enough to just give the law if threats were not also added. Well, it's incredible how useful this thought is. For just as nothing is as damaging as a certain unsuspecting security of mind, so the knowledge of one's own imbecility is of great benefit. Also declare that God has not established any certain punishment, but rather threatens whoever commits this crime universally, that he will not carry it out unpunished. Therefore the various tortures with which we are afflicted every day should warn us of this sin.

From this it can be easily conjectured that men fall into maximum calamities for not obeying this precept: and when these are proposed to them, it is probable that from now on they will be more cautious. The faithful, therefore, terrified with holy fear, flee from this sin with all study. For if every idle word must be accounted for in the extreme judgment, what must be said of the very serious crimes that present great injury to the divine Name? OF THE THIRD PRECEPT. CHAPTER IV. Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day: Six days you will work and do all your works. But the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, nor your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your donkey, nor the foreigner who is within your gates. For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day; That is why the Lord blessed the Sabbath day and sanctified it.

What is commanded to the faithful with this third precept. With this precept of the law, that external worship that is due to God of us is rightly and orderly prescribed. For this is like a certain fruit of the previous precept; because whom we worship piously with our intimate senses, guided by the faith and hope that we have placed in him, we cannot help but venerate him with external worship and give him thanks. And as these things cannot easily be provided by those who are engaged in the business of human things, a certain time has been established in which they can be carried out comfortably.

Why care must be taken primarily in the parish priest so that what is prescribed here is retained in the perpetual memory of the faithful. Therefore, since this precept is of such a nature that it brings admirable fruit and usefulness, it is extremely important that the parish priest takes great care in explaining it. And to inflame your study, that first word of the precept has great force: Remember. For just as the faithful must remember such a precept, so it is up to the Pastor to often reduce it to his memory by admonishing and teaching. And how important it is for the faithful to observe this precept is evident from the fact that, by diligently observing it, they will more easily be induced to keep the other commands of the law. Well, among other things that they must provide on holidays, they need to congregate in the Church to hear the word of God; and when they have been taught the divine justifications, they will also succeed in keeping the law of the Lord with all their heart. For this reason, the celebration and worship of the Sabbath is very frequently commanded in the sacred letters, as can be seen in the Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy, in Isaiah, also in Jeremiah and in Ezekiel the prophets; in all of which places this precept of Saturday worship has been transmitted. 3. How Princes are to be exhorted to help the Prelates of the Church. Princes and Magistrates must be admonished and exhorted to help the Prelates of the Church with their authority in those things that mainly concern retaining and increasing this worship of God; and command the people to obey the precepts of the Priests. And as regards the explanation of this precept, care must be taken to teach the faithful in what ways this precept agrees with the others, and in what it differs from them. In this way you will know the cause and the reason why we do not sanctify the Sabbath, but the Lord's Day.

All the precepts of the Decalogue are natural, except the precept of observing the Sabbath. S. Aug. ep. 119 to Januario, c. 12. St. Thomas in 2. 2. q. 122, art. 4. Also before the law given by Moses there was a precept to sanctify the Sabbath. CATEC. FOR PASTORS. PART III. It has that first word of the precept: Remember. For just as the faithful must remember such a precept, so it is up to the Pastor to often reduce it to his memory by admonishing and teaching. And how important it is for the faithful to observe this precept is evident from the fact that, by diligently observing it, they will more easily be induced to keep the other commands of the law. Well, among other things that they must provide on holidays, they need to congregate in the Church to hear the word of God; and when they have been taught the divine justifications, they will also succeed in keeping the law of the Lord with all their heart. For this reason, the celebrity and worship of Saturday is very frequently commanded in sacred letters.

How does this precept differ from the other laws of the Decalogue. A certain difference seems, therefore, that the other Precepts of the Decalogue are natural and perpetual, and in no way can they change. From which it resulted that, although the law of Moses has been abrogated, nevertheless the Christian people keep all the Precepts contained in the two tables. Which is done not because Moses had ordered it so, but because it suits nature; by whose force men are driven to keep them. But this precept of the Sabbath cult, if we look at the established time, is not fixed and constant, but changeable; nor does it belong to customs, but to ceremonies; nor is it natural, because we were not taught or instituted by nature to pay the external worship of God preferably on that day than on another: but from the time in which the Israelite people were freed from the servitude of Pharaoh, they sanctified the Sabbath day. 5. At the time of Christ's death, the ceremonies of the law being suppressed, the Sabbath also, insofar as it was ceremonial, was suppressed. The time, however, in which the Sabbath was to be taken away is the same in which the other Hebrew cults and ceremonies were to become obsolete, namely, with the death of Christ. Since those ceremonies were like shadowed images of light and truth, it was necessary that upon the advent of light and truth, which is Jesus Christ, they should be removed. Of which St. Paul wrote to the Galatians, when he rebuked the cultivators of the Mosaic rite: «You keep the days, and the months, and the times, and the years; I fear for you that perhaps he has labored among you in vain": and in the same sentence he wrote to the Colossians. And this is the difference.

How the third precept agrees with the other nine. However, this precept is appropriate with the others not because of the rite and ceremonies, but because it has something that concerns customs and the law of nature. For the worship and religion of God, which is expressed with this precept, exists by right of nature, since by nature it is ordained that we occupy ourselves for a few hours with things that pertain to the worship of God; from which it is argued that in all nations we see that there have been certain established and public fairs, which were dedicated to the performance of sacred and divine things. For it is natural for man to give a certain time to the necessary functions of things, such as rest of the body, sleep, and others of this kind; and as with the body, in the same way it has been done by reason of nature that the mind is also granted some time to refresh itself in the contemplation of God. And so, since there must be some part of time in which divine things are cultivated and the worship due to God is paid, this truly belongs to the precepts of customs.

The Apostles ordained the Lord's Day instead of the Sabbath. For which reason the Apostles of those seven days determined to consecrate the first one to divine worship, which they also called the Lord's Day. PART III. one on Saturday, which is the Lord's day, as St. Chrysostom interprets, commands that collections be made, so that we understand that even then in the Church the Lord's day was considered holy. Now, however, so that the faithful know what they should do on that day and what actions to abstain from, it is not unusual for the parish priest to diligently interpret the entire precept to the letter, which can rightly be distributed into four parts.

What is generally prescribed with this word Remember. Propose, then, first in general what is prescribed by these words: "Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day." For that reason the word Remember was added to the beginning of the precept, because the worship of this day belongs to the ceremonies. From which it seemed that the people should be warned, since the law of nature, although it teaches that at some time God must be worshiped with a religious rite, did not, however, prescribe on what day it should primarily be done. Furthermore, the faithful must be taught that from these words we can deduce the way and the reason with which it is appropriate to do work throughout the week, namely in such a way that we always look to the holy day, in which, since God must be given an account of our actions and works, it is necessary that we do such works that they are neither repudiated by the judgment of God nor are they, as it is written, in sobbing and scruple of the heart. Finally, we are taught what we must certainly warn: that there will be no shortage of occasions in which we are caught by forgetting this precept, either from the example of others who neglect it, or from the study of spectacles and games, with which we are generally separated from the holy and religious worship of this day. But let's come to what is demonstrated by the significance of the Sabbath.

What is Saturday and Sabbath in the sacred letters. Saturday is a Hebrew name that, if interpreted in Latin, is called cessation; That is why Sabbath is called in Latin to cease and rest. For whose significance it was made that the name of Saturday was called the seventh day; because, the universality of the world being absolute and perfect, God rested from every work he had done: and this is what the Lord calls this day in the Exodus. Later, however, not only this seventh day, but because of its dignity also the week itself was called by that name; in which sense the Pharisee said in St. Luke: "I fast twice on the Sabbath." And this about the significance of Saturday.

How it is said that the faithful sanctify the Sabbath. The sanctification of the Sabbath in the sacred letters is the cessation that is made of the work of the body and of business, as these words of the precept that follow openly show: "Thou shalt not work"; and not only does this mean (otherwise it would be enough to say in Deuteronomy: "Observe the Sabbath day"), but when in the same place it is added: "That you may sanctify it," with this word it is shown that the Sabbath day is religious and consecrated to divine actions and to the holy offices of things. Thus, then, we celebrate the Sabbath day fully and perfectly when we lend to God the offices of piety and religion; and this is plainly the Sabbath that Isaiah calls delicate; because the holidays are like delights to the Lord and to pious men. Therefore, if works of mercy are added to this religious and holy worship of Saturday, the rewards proposed to us in the same chapter are certainly greatest and many.

What is the genuine meaning of the previous words. Thus, then, the true and proper meaning of this precept is that man dedicate himself in spirit and body to that care that, at some established time, free from business and work of the body, he piously adore and venerate God.

What is demonstrated in the other part of the precept. In the other part of the precept it is shown that the seventh day has been divinely dedicated to the worship of God. For thus it is written: “Six days you will work and do all your works; but the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God. Which words refer to that sentence that we interpret the Saturday as consecrated to the Lord, and that we pay him tribute on that day to the services of religion, and we understand that the seventh day is a sign of the Lord's rest.

Why was it convenient for the Jews to prescribe a certain day, and this the seventh, for religious services. This day, however, was dedicated to divine worship because it was less convenient for the rude people to have the power to choose the time at their discretion, lest by chance they should imitate the rites of the Egyptians. Thus, among the seven days, the last one was chosen to worship God: something that is truly full of mystery. For this reason the Lord in the Exodus and in Ezekiel calls it a sign: «Take heed, he says, that you keep my Sabbath; for it is a sign between me and you throughout your generations, so that you may know that I am the Lord, who sanctifies you. 14. Of what things was Saturday's celebrity a sign. It was, therefore, a sign indicating that men should dedicate themselves to God and present themselves as saints before him, since we see that that day is also dedicated to him; since that day is holy because mainly on it men must cultivate holiness and religion.

CHAPTER 51. CATEC. FOR PASTORS. PART III. It was also a sign and monument of the creation of this admirable universality. It was also a sign given to the memory of the Israelites, with which, admonished, they remembered that with the help of God they had been released and freed from the very hard yoke of Egyptian servitude: which the Lord shows with those words: "Remember that you also served in Egypt, and the Lord your God brought you out of there with a strong hand and an outstretched arm; "That is why he commanded you to observe the Sabbath." It is also a sign of both the spiritual and celestial Sabbath.

May it be the spiritual Sabbath of the Christian people. The spiritual Sabbath consists of a certain holy and mystical rest: namely, when the old man, buried with Christ, is renewed for life and diligently exercises himself in those actions that befit Christian piety. For they who were once darkness and are now light in the Lord must walk as children of light in all goodness, righteousness and truth, and not participate in the fruitless works of darkness.

May it also be the Saturday of the Blessed. The heavenly Sabbath is, as St. Cyril of Alexandria says, treating that place of the Apostle: "There remains, then, a Sabbath for the people of God," that life in which, living with Christ, we will enjoy all good things, sin rooted out, according to that: "There will be no lion there, nor evil beast will ascend there, but there will be a path and a way, and it will be called a holy way": for all good things reach the minds of the Saints in the vision of God. Therefore the faithful must be exhorted with these words and the Pastor incite them: "Let us hasten, then, to enter into that rest."

The Jews had other holidays besides the seventh. In addition to the seventh day, the Jewish people had other festive and sacred days established by the divine Law, in which the memory of the maximum benefits was renewed.

Why the Apostles consecrated to divine worship not the seventh day of the week, but the first. It pleased, however, the Church of God that the worship and celebrity of the Sabbath day should be transferred to the Lord's day. For just as on that day the light first illuminated the globe of the earth, so by the resurrection of our Redeemer, who opened for us access to eternal life, which was on that day, our life was called from darkness to light; from which the Apostles also wanted it to be called the Lord's Day. Furthermore, we note that this day is solemn in sacred letters, because on that day the creation of the world began, and because on it the Holy Spirit was given to the Apostles.

Why were other holidays added to the Lord's Day for Christians. Other holidays, however, from the beginning of the Church and in the following times were instituted by the Apostles and our holy Fathers, so that we could piously and holyly cultivate the memory of the benefits of God. Among them, those days that, due to the mysteries of our redemption, are consecrated to religion are considered very celebrated; then, those who dedicate themselves to the holy Virgin Mother, and also to the Apostles and Martyrs and the other saints who reign with Christ; In whose victory the goodness and power of God is praised, due honors are paid to them, and the faithful people are encouraged to imitate them.

How with this precept the faithful are encouraged to flee from idleness. And as for keeping this precept, that part of it that is expressed in these words has great force: «Six days you will work; but the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God", the priest must diligently explain that part. For from these words we can deduce that the faithful must be exhorted not to spend their lives in idleness and laziness; but rather, remembering the apostolic voice, let each one do his business and work with his hands, as he had been commanded. Furthermore, with this precept the Lord commands that we carry out our works on those same six days, lest something of what must be done or accomplished on the other days of the week be left for the holiday, and thus the spirit is distracted from the care and study of divine things.

What is mainly prohibited to do on holidays. Then the third part of the precept must be explained, which in some way describes how we must sanctify the Sabbath day; and mainly explains what we are prohibited from doing on that day. Therefore the Lord says: "You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, nor your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your donkey, nor the foreigner who is within your gates." With which words we are first instructed to completely avoid everything that can impede divine worship: for it is easily perceived that every kind of servile work is prohibited, not because of its nature it is clumsy or bad, but because it diverts our mind from divine worship, which is the end of the precept. Therefore sins must be avoided all the more by the faithful, since they not only distract the mind from the study of divine things, but also separate us completely from the love of God.

External actions that refer to the worship of God are not prohibited on the Sabbath. However, those actions or works that concern divine worship, even if they are servile, are not prohibited; how to arrange the altar, decorate the temples for some holiday, and so on; and that is why the Lord said that the Priests in the temple violate the Sabbath and are without crime.

Certain menial works are also granted on holidays out of necessity. But it should not be considered that by this law the works of those things are prohibited, the loss of which would be caused if they were omitted on the festive day, just as sacred ceremonies have also been permitted. The Lord declared many other things in the Gospel that can be done on feast days, which the parish priest will easily observe in Saint Matthew and Saint John.

Why did the Lord want the donkeys to rest? But so that nothing would be omitted whose action would prevent this worship of the Sabbath, mention was made of the donkey, with whose type of animals men are prevented from sanctifying the Sabbath day. For if on the Sabbath the use of the donkey is intended for the action of some work, the work of the man who handles the donkey is also necessary for this purpose; and thus he cannot do the work by himself, but he helps the man who undertakes it: and on that day it is not lawful for anyone to do work: therefore not for the donkeys, whose work men use for this purpose. Therefore, the law of this precept also aims to ensure that, if God wants men to be spared the work of donkeys, they must be even more careful not to be inhuman to those whose work and industry they use. The male and female servants must not deviate from the worship of God on the holiday.

In what works Christians should mainly exercise themselves on holidays. Nor should the parish priest omit to diligently teach in what works and actions Christian men should exercise themselves on holy days. These are of such a nature that we approach the temple of God and in that place, with sincere and pious attention of mind, we attend the sacrifice of the sacrosanct Mass; and let us frequently apply to the healing of the wounds of the soul the divine Sacraments of the Church, which were instituted for our salvation. There is nothing, however, that can be done more opportunely or better to Christian men than to frequently confess their sins to Priests: to perfect which the parish priest can exhort the people, taking the reason and copy of this thing from what regarding the Sacrament of Penance has been transmitted and commanded in its place. And he will not only excite the people to this Sacrament, but he will assiduously and repeatedly exhort them to frequently perceive the sacred Sacrament of the Eucharist. Furthermore, the sacred preaching must be listened to attentively and diligently by the faithful: for there is nothing less tolerable or so flatly unworthy as despising the words of Christ or hearing them negligently. The exercise and study of the faithful in divine prayers and praises should be frequent, and their main care should be to learn diligently what concerns the institution of the Christian life and to exercise themselves assiduously in those offices that contain piety, giving alms to the poor and needy, visiting the sick, piously consoling those who lie afflicted with pain: for, as it is in Saint James: "Religion pure and immaculate before God and Father is this: to visit the orphans and the widows in their tribulation. From what has been said it will be easy to deduce what is committed against the rule of this precept.

Why was it necessary to allocate certain days to divine worship. The office of the parish priest must also consist of having at hand certain places from which he takes reasons and arguments with which the people are persuaded to the highest degree to keep the law of this precept with great study and exact diligence. The Mass must be heard in its entirety on the feast day. The Sacrament of Penance and the Eucharist must be frequented on holidays.

PART III. have at hand certain places from which you can take reasons and arguments with which the people are persuaded to the highest degree to keep the law of this precept with great study and exact diligence. For this it is very important that the people understand and see clearly how just and in accordance with reason it is that we have certain days that we dedicate entire days to divine worship, and that we recognize, adore and venerate our Lord, from whom we have received supreme and innumerable benefits. Well, if he had ordered that we pay him the cult of religion every day, wouldn't every effort have been made, for his benefits to us, which are maximum and infinite, to be obedient to him with a prompt and joyful spirit? Now, however, with only a few days established for its worship, there is no reason for us to be negligent or difficult in the exercise of this office, which we cannot omit without serious guilt.

How useful it is to those who have assiduously obeyed this precept. Let the parish priest then show how much the virtue of this precept is, when those who have rightly kept it seem to be in the sight of God and converse with him: for by praying we contemplate the majesty of God and converse with him, and by listening to the preachers we receive the voice of God, which reaches our ears through the work of those who preach piously and holy things divine; and in the sacrifice of the altar we worship the present Lord Christ: and these goods are enjoyed mainly by those who diligently keep this precept.

What must be felt, on the contrary, of those who have completely neglected this law. But those who completely neglect this law, since they do not obey God and the Church or hear their precept, are enemies of God and the holy laws: which can be seen from the fact that this precept is of such a nature that it can be kept without any work. For since God does not impose tasks on us that, even the most difficult ones, we should undertake for his sake, but commands that on those festive days we be quiet and free from earthly cares, it is a sign of great temerity to refuse the law of this precept. The punishments that God took from those who violated him should be an example to us, as can be understood from the book of Numbers. In order not to fall into this offense against God, it will be worth repeating often in thought that word Remember, and putting before your eyes those great benefits and comforts that are perceived from the worship of the holidays, as has been stated above, and many others of this kind that the good and diligent Pastor, as the reason for the occasion demands, will be able to pursue abundantly and widely. OF THE FOURTH PRECEPT. CHAPTER V. Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live long on the land that the Lord your God will give you. 1. What is the dignity of this precept, and how it agrees with superiors. As in the superior precepts there is utmost strength and dignity, it is right that those that we now pursue, because they are maximally necessary, occupy the next place: since those continually look to the end, which is God; These instruct us in the charity of our neighbor: and if we progress further, they lead us to God, that is, to that extreme by whose grace we love our neighbor himself. Therefore Christ the Lord said that those two precepts of loving God and neighbor are similar to each other. This place, however, can hardly say how many uses it has, since it produces its fruits, truly magnificent and excellent; and it is as a sign from which obedience and worship of the first precept shines: "For he who does not love, says Saint John, his brother, whom he sees, God, whom he does not see, how can he love him?" In the same way, if we do not venerate or cultivate our parents, whom we must love after God, when they are almost always within our sight; To God, supreme and optimal father, who does not fall under any aspect, what honor, what worship will we pay him? From which it is evident that both precepts agree with each other. In the precepts of the first table there is great dignity, but in those of the second table there is great necessity.

How widely the force of this precept extends, and how much parents are helped by this precept. The use of this precept extends very widely: for in addition to those who begat us, there are many others whom we must venerate instead of parents, either by the name of power, or by dignity, or by usefulness, or by some eminent office and position. It also relieves the work of parents and all the elderly; For since they take care in the first place that those under their power live rightly and in accordance with the divine law, this care will be very easy if everyone understands that, as the author and warner of God, the highest honor must be paid to the parents. And so that we can provide it, it is necessary to know a certain difference between the precepts of the first and the second table.

For what purpose was the distinction made between the precepts of the law in two tables. These things, then, must first be explained by the parish priest; and in the first place let it be noted that the divine precepts of the Decalogue were engraved on two tables: in one of which, as we have received from the holy Fathers, were contained those three that have already been expounded.

the rest were included in the other table. And this description was very appropriate for us so that the order itself could distinguish the reason from the precepts: since everything in the sacred letters is commanded or prohibited by divine law, arises from one of two kinds; or charity towards God, or towards men, is seen in every office.

And in truth charity towards God is taught by the three highest precepts: but what concerns the union and society of men is contained in the remaining seven precepts. Therefore, not without cause, such a distinction was made, so that some precepts refer to one table and others to the other.

How is charity towards God contained in the first three precepts, and charity towards one's neighbor in the others, and what is the difference between the two. For the three superior precepts, of which it has been said, the subject matter they treat is God, that is, the Supreme Good; to others, the good of their neighbor: to those the supreme love is proposed, to these the next: those look to the end, these to the things that refer to the end. Furthermore, God's charity depends on himself; because God must be loved extremely for himself, not because of anything else. But the charity of one's neighbor has its origin in the charity of God, and must be directed to it as to a certain rule. For we hold our parents dear, if we obey our lords, if we revere those who precede us in dignity; This has to be done mainly because their procreator is God, and he wanted them to be in front of others, with whose work he governs and protects other men: who, being the author for us to venerate such people, therefore we must lend it, because they are dignified by God with this same honor. It follows that the honor we pay to parents must be considered paid more to God than to men. This is how it is in Saint Matthew, when it comes to observance towards superiors: "He who receives you, receives me"; and the Apostle in the Epistle to the Ephesians, instructing the servants: "Servants, he says, obey carnal lords with fear and trembling in the simplicity of your heart, as Christ, not serving in sight, as pleasing men, but as servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart."

How the charity of God is not limited to any purpose, but the charity of one's neighbor is limited to its purposes. It is added that no honor, no pity, no worship is worthily paid to God, in whom love can be infinitely increased; and that is why it is necessary that our charity towards him becomes more ardent day by day; whom by his command we must love with all our heart, with all our soul, with all our strength. But the charity with which we embrace our neighbors is limited to its purposes. For the Lord commands to love our neighbors as ourselves: and if anyone has gone beyond those goals in such a way as to pay equal love to God and to our neighbors, he commits the ultimate crime: "If anyone comes to me, says the Lord, and does not hate his father and his mother, and his wife, and his children, and his brothers, and his sisters, and even his own soul, he cannot be my disciple": in which sentence it was also said: "Let the dead bury their dead", when someone wanted to first bury the father and then follow Christ. Whose most lucid explanation is in Saint Matthew: "He who loves his father or mother more than me is not worthy of me."

How parents should be loved, and why sometimes they should not be obeyed. Nor, however, is there any doubt that parents are to love and observe each other vehemently; But for piety it is first of all necessary that God, who is the father and maker of all, be given the main honor and worship; and that is why mortal parents must be loved in such a way that all the force of love is referred to the heavenly and everlasting Father. And if sometimes the commands of the parents are repugnant to the Precepts of God, there is no doubt that the children must put the will of God before the desire of the parents, remembering that divine sentence: "It is necessary to obey God more than men."

6. CATEC. FOR PASTORS. PART III. 7. What does the word Honor properly denote in the sentence of this precept. Having explained these things, the priest will interpret the words of the precept, and first what is Honor. It is, in effect, feeling honorably about someone and esteeming in the highest degree all the things that are theirs. All these things are linked to this honor: love, observance, obedience and worship. And wisely the voice of Honor was put into the law, not of love or fear, although parents must love and fear each other very much. For he who loves does not always observe and venerate; he who fears does not always love; But whomever someone honors from the heart, he also loves and reveres him. When the priest has explained these things, he will then deal with the parents, and who are those who are called by this name.

Who are understood here by the name of Father. For although the law speaks mainly of those parents of whom we have been begotten; However, this name also concerns others, to whom the law also seems to embrace, as we easily gather from many places in divine Scripture. In addition, then, to those who procreated us, there are also other types of fathers in sacred letters (as we touched on above), to each of whom their honor is due. And first the Prelates of the Church, and the Pastors, and the Priests are called fathers, as stated by the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians: “No, he says, I am writing this to confuse you, but to admonish you as my dearest children; For although you have ten thousand teachers in Christ, you do not have many fathers, because in Christ Jesus through the Gospel I begot you"; and in Ecclesiasticus it is written: "Let us praise the glorious men and our fathers in their generation." Afterwards, those to whom the Empire, or the Magistrate, or the power, who govern the Republic, have been entrusted, are called Fathers. Thus Naaman was called father by the servants. Furthermore, we call parents those to whose care, faith, probity and wisdom others entrust themselves: of this type are tutors and curators, pedagogues and teachers. Therefore the sons of the Prophets called Elijah and Elisha father. Finally, we call parents the elderly and those consumed by age, whom we must also revere. And this is the maximum in the precepts of the parish priest: let him teach that parents, of whatever gender they may be, and especially those from whom we were born, must be honored for us; of which the divine law speaks mainly. 9. Why the children of Christians should pay the main honor to parents according to the flesh. For they are like certain images of the immortal God, and in them we contemplate the image of our origin; from them life was given to us; God used them to give us spirit and mind; By them we were led to the Sacraments, instructed in religion, in human and civil cultivation, and educated in the integrity and sanctity of customs. Let the parish priest teach, however, that the name of Mother was rightly expressed in this precept, so that we may consider her benefits and merits towards us, with how much care and concern she carried us in her womb, with how much work and pain she gave birth to us and educated us.

With what reasons carnal parents are honored. Furthermore, parents must be observed in such a way that the honor we pay them seems to come from love and the intimate feeling of the soul, to whom this office is owed in the highest degree, since they are so attached to us that no work, no strife, no danger they avoid for our sake, and nothing can happen to them more pleasant than to feel that they are dear to their children, whom they love to the highest degree. Joseph, when in Egypt he was close to the King in honor and greatness, honorably received the father who had come to Egypt; and Solomon rose up to the mother who came, and, venerating her, placed her on the royal throne at the right. There are also other offices of honor that must be conferred on parents. Well, we also honor them when we supplicatingly ask God that everything happen well and happily to them, that they be in maximum grace and honor among men, that they be highly recommended to God himself and to the Saints who are in heaven. We also honor parents when we refer our reasons to their discretion and will. Of which Solomon is a supporter: "Hear, he says, my son, the discipline of your father, and do not forsake the law of your mother, so that grace may be added to your head and a collar to your neck."

Likewise we honor parents when we imitate their righteous deeds and customs: for it seems that we pay a lot of tribute to those to whom we want to be as similar as possible. We also honor the parents whose advice we not only seek, but also follow.

How to help parents in need, and especially in danger of death. Likewise, to those we help, imparting to them what sustenance and cultivation desire. This is proven by the testimony of Christ, who condemns the impiety of the Pharisees: "Why do you also, he says, transgress the commandment of God through your tradition? For God said: Honor your father and mother; and whoever curses father or mother, let him die. But you say: Anyone who says to father or mother: Every gift from me benefits you; and he will not honor his father or his mother: and you have made void the commandment of God by your tradition. And in truth we must always pay parents the offices of honor, especially when they become dangerously ill. Well, care must be taken that they do not omit anything that concerns the confession of sins or the other Sacraments that Christian men must perceive when death approaches; and let it be our care that pious and religious men visit them often, that they either confirm the weak and help them with advice, or raise the well-animated to the hope of immortality; so that, having excited the mind from human things, they turn it all towards God. In this way, armed with the most blessed retinue of faith, hope and charity and the prison of religion, they will believe that death is not only not to be feared, since it is necessary, but that, since it facilitates access to eternity, it is also to be desired.

How we display honor to dead parents. Finally, honor is also paid to dead parents if we give them a funeral, if we ennoble the obsequies; if we impart the honor of burial; if we take care of the fairs and the anniversary sacrifices; if we diligently fulfill what was bequeathed to them.

In what way Bishops and Priests are to be honoured. We must honor, however, not only those from whom we have been born, but also others who are called Fathers, such as Bishops and Priests, Kings, Princes, Magistrates, Tutors, Curators, Teachers, Pedagogues, Elders, and others of this kind. They are worthy, in fact, of receiving the fruits of our charity, our obedience, our help, but some more than others. Of the Bishops and the other Pastors it is thus written: "The Priests who preside well, be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who work in the word and in the doctrine." Now, however, how great documents of love for the Apostle did the Galatians give? to whom he gave that illustrious testimony of benevolence: "Well, I bear witness to you that, if it were possible, you would have gouged out your eyes and given them to me."

How the things necessary for sustenance are to be supplied to the Priests. Furthermore, the Priests are also to be supplied with the things required for the necessary uses of life. Therefore the Apostle: "Who, he says, ever fights at his own expense?"; and in Ecclesiasticus it is written: «Honor the Priests, and purify yourself with your arms; Give them part, as you have been commanded, of the firstfruits and of the purification. They must also be obeyed, the Apostle teaches: "Obey, he says, your Prelates and submit to them: for they watch as those who must give an account of your souls." Furthermore, by Christ the Lord it was commanded that we obey even evil Shepherds, when He says: “On the chair of Moses the Scribes and Pharisees sat: all things therefore, whatever they tell you, observe them and do them; but do not according to their works: for they say and do not do. 15. It is shown that honor must be given to political Magistrates. The same must be said of Kings, Princes, Magistrates and others to whose power we are subject. What kind of honor, worship and observance should be paid to them, the Apostle explains at length to the Romans, and admonishes that they should also be prayed for; and Saint Peter: "Be subject," he says, "to every human creature for God's sake, now to the King as preeminent, now to the dukes as sent by him." For if we pay them any worship, it refers to God: for the excellent degree of dignity of men has veneration because it is in the form of divine power: in which we also venerate the Providence of God, who attributed to them the procurement of public office and uses them as ministers of his power.

Why bad political Magistrates should also be obeyed, and when not. For not the improbability or wickedness of men, if such are the Magistrates, but the divine authority that is in them, we revere: so that, what by chance will seem very admirable, although they are towards us with an enemy and defenseless spirit, although they are implacable; However, there is no cause worthy enough for us not to observe them very informally. Well, there were also great offices from David towards Saul, although it was more offensive to him, which he implies with those words: "With those who hated peace, he was peaceful." But if they command something improperly or iniquitously, as they do not do this by power, but by injustice and perversity of mind, they are in no way to be heard. When the parish priest has explained these things one by one, then consider what reward and how convenient he has proposed to those who obey this divine precept.
