St. Thomas in 2. 2. q. 122, art. 5 ad 4. The happy use of one life and another is promised. 1 Tim. 4, 8. Job 3, 3 and 10. Ps. 119, 5. Phil. 1, 23. Deut. 5, 16. Eph. 6, 3. The reward promised here is not so much deposited in daylight as in the safety of life. Sat. 4, 11. CATEC. FOR PASTORS. PART III.

What a reward has been divinely proposed for obedience to parents. For in this there is maximum fruit: that they live long, because they are worthy of enjoying the benefit the more daytime, the memory of which they preserve perpetually. As, then, those who cultivate parents restore grace to those from whom they have the use of light and life, with right and merit they prolong life to the utmost old age. The illustrious explanation of the divine promise must also be added: for not only is the use of the everlasting and blessed life promised, but also of this one that we live on earth. Whose sentence Saint Paul interprets when he says: "Piety is useful for everything: having promise of the life that is now and the life to come."

How much the promise of daytime life is to be valued here. Nor is this favor meager or despicable, although for the most holy men, like Job, like David, like Paul, death would have been optional, and for hard-working and miserable men the spread of life is unpleasant. Well, the addition of those words: "That the Lord your God will give you," not only promises plenty of time to live, but also leisure, quiet, safety to live well. For in Deuteronomy it not only says: "That you may live a long time", but also adds: "that it may be well with you"; which the Apostle later repeated.

How those who honor their parents, even if they die soon, perceive the reward of this precept. We say, however, that these goods assist those to whose piety God restores grace. Otherwise there will be no faith and constancy of the divine promise; when sometimes those who showed greater mercy to their parents have shorter lives. To whom this truly happens, or because those who leave life earlier are optimally consulted, before departing from the religion of virtue and office; for they are taken away so that malice does not change their intellect, or so that fiction does not deceive their soul; or because, when it prevents the perdition and disturbance of all things, they are called by the bodies to escape the acrimony of common times: "For from the face of malice, says the Prophet, the just is gathered." This is done so that their virtue or salvation is not endangered when God demands the punishments of crimes from mortals; or so that in very sad times they do not feel bitter grief for the calamities of relatives and friends. Therefore it is to be feared more when premature death befalls good men.

With what penalties are afflicted those who violate this precept. And just as those who are pleasing to their parents have been offered by God the favor and the fruit of the office; Thus, very serious penalties are reserved for ungrateful and impious children. For it is written: "Whoever curses his father or mother, let him die the death"; and: "He who afflicts the father and flees from the mother will be ignominious and unhappy"; and: "He who curses his father or his mother, his lamp will go out in the midst of darkness"; and: "The eye that mocks the father and despises the birth of its mother, may the ravens of the torrents pluck it and the children of the eagle eat it." Of those who insulted the parents we read that there were many; in whose vengeance the wrath of God was kindled. Well, he did not leave David unpunished, but rather paid the due penalties for Absalom's crime, whom he punished for his crime by being pierced with three spears. Of those who do not obey the Priests it is written: "Whoever becomes arrogant, not wanting to obey the rule of the Priest who at that time ministers to the Lord his God, by decree of the judge that man will die."

By what principal reasons can parents become worthy of that divinely prescribed honor. And just as by divine law it has been sanctioned that children pay honor to their parents, that they obey, that they show obsequiousness; Thus, it is the duties and responsibilities of parents to imbue their children with the most holy disciplines and customs, and to give them optimal precepts of living, so that, educated and prepared for religion, they venerate God holy and inviolate: which we read that Susanna's parents did. Therefore, the Priest admonishes parents to present themselves to their children as teachers of virtue, equity, continence, modesty and holiness; and especially three things in which they often tend to offend: first, that they should not speak or determine anything more harshly against their children, which the Apostle thus commands in the Epistle to the Colossians: "Fathers, do not provoke your children to indignation, so that they may not become faint-hearted." For there is a danger that they will be in a broken and dejected spirit, while they fear everything. Therefore command that they avoid excessive severity, and prefer to correct their children rather than take revenge. 22. How parents should not be reticent towards their children, nor leave them too large assets, working too much. Then, if any fault has been committed, as punishment and reprobation are necessary, do not send anything dissolute to the children out of indulgence: for children are often depraved by the excessive leniency and ease of the parents. Therefore I dissuaded them from dissolute indulgence with the example of Eli, the high priest, who, because he had been more lenient with his children, was afflicted with the greatest punishment. Finally, do not, which is very ugly, take preposterous advice in the education and doctrine of your children. Well, many are occupied with this single thought and care: leaving their children riches, money, splendid and extensive assets.

whom they do not exhort to religion, nor to piety, nor to the discipline of the good arts, but rather to avarice and to increase the family wealth; nor do they strive for the esteem and salvation of their children, as long as they are pecuniary and very rich; What could be said or thought more clumsily? Thus it turns out that they do not so much transfer copies of things as their crimes and evils, with which they finally present themselves as guides not to heaven, but to the eternal tortures of hell. Let the Priest, then, instruct the parents with optimal precepts and excite them to the example of Tobias and to such virtue; so that, when they have educated their children well in the worship of God and in holiness, they may also receive from them the rich fruits of love, observance and gift. OF THE FIFTH PRECEPT. CHAPTER VI. Thou shalt not kill. 1. What is the fruit and usefulness of that doctrine that is included in this precept. That beatitude that has been proposed to peaceful men: "For they will be called children of God," must move Pastors to the utmost degree to transmit to the faithful diligently and accurately the discipline of this precept. For to reconcile the wills of men no better reason can be initiated than if the law of such precept, correctly explained, is kept holy and as it should be by all; because then it is licit to expect that men, united with utmost consonance of spirit, will cultivate concord and peace to the highest degree. But how necessary it is to explain this precept is evident from the fact that it is one of the main ones that God interposed to men: "The blood, he says, of your souls I will require at the hand of all beasts and at the hand of man." In the Gospel also, in which the ancient laws were first explained by the Lord, among them this is the first, of which in Saint Matthew it is thus written: "For it was said: Thou shalt not kill"; and the rest about this thing is later commemorated in the same place. Furthermore, the faithful must listen attentively and willingly to this precept. Well, if you look at its strength, it is worth protecting the life of each one; because with these words "Thou shalt not kill" homicide is completely interdicted. Thus, each of the men must receive it with as much voluptuousness of spirit as if, given the wrath of God and other very serious penalties, it had been nominally prohibited that any of them be harmed.

It is not of iniquity, and many other things there. See also St. Thomas in 2. 2. q. 64, art. 2. Ps. 100, 8. That in just war it is lawful to kill men is gathered from Gen. 14, 5. Exod. 17, 9. 10. 1 Reg. 14, 15 and 17. Exod. 32, 26. CATEC. FOR PASTORS. PART III. Therefore, as this precept is pleasant to hear, so caution against that sin which is prohibited by the precept must be pleasant.

What is prohibited and what is ordered with this precept. When the Lord explained the force of this law, he showed that it contains two things: one, that we do not kill, which we have been forbidden to do; another, what we are commanded to do: that we embrace our enemies with concord, friendship and charity, have peace with everyone, and patiently endure all inconveniences.

It is lawful to feed on beasts and kill animals. In that matter, however, that killing is prohibited, it must first be taught what killings are of such a nature that are not prohibited by this law of precept. For it has not been forbidden to kill beasts, because if the Lord has granted it to men to feed on them, it is also lawful to kill them. Of which Saint Augustine says: «When we hear, it says, Thou shalt not kill, we do not understand that this has been said of plants, because they have no meaning; nor of the irrational, because they associate with us for no reason.

It is lawful in judgment to condemn men to death or to kill them. Another type of permitted slaughter is that which concerns those Magistrates to whom the power of death has been given, with which, according to the prescription of laws and judgment, they punish criminal men and defend the innocent. In which position, when properly occupied, not only are they not guilty of slaughter, but they obey in the highest degree this divine law by which slaughter is prohibited. Well, as this law has proposed that purpose of consulting the life and salvation of men; Also the animosities of the Magistrates, who are legitimate avengers of crimes, aim at the same thing: that, audacity and injury being repressed with torture, the lives of men are safe. Therefore David: "In the morning, he says, he killed all the sinners of the earth, to destroy from the city of the Lord all those who work iniquity."

How those who kill in just war are not guilty of massacre either. For which reason neither do those who in just war, not motivated by greed or cruelty, but only by the study of public utility, take the lives of their enemies. There are also massacres of this kind that are nominally carried out by God's command. The sons of Levi did not sin, for in a single day they killed so many thousands of men: after which slaughter, thus spoke Moses to them: "You have consecrated your hands today to the Lord."

He who kills a man by chance is not guilty of this precept. Nor is he guilty of this precept who, not spontaneously or thoughtfully, but accidentally kills a man. Of which in the book of Deuteronomy it is like this: "Whoever hurts his neighbor without knowing it, and of whom it is proven that yesterday and the day before yesterday he had no hatred against him, but had simply gone with him to the forest to cut wood, and while cutting the wood the ax escaped from his hand, and the iron, falling from the handle, wounded his friend and killed him, etc." These massacres are of such a nature that, since they are not inferred by will or industry, they are therefore not fully enumerated among the sins. Which is proven by the sentence of Saint Augustine: "Far, he says, from what we do for good or for a lawful thing, if by chance something bad happens against our will, it will be imputed to us."

How is the person who did it per case guilty of murder? In which, however, one can sin for two reasons: one, if someone engaged in an unjust thing kills a man (for example, if someone hit a pregnant woman with his fist or foot, which resulted in abortion, that would truly have been outside the will of the attacker, but not outside of his guilt, since it was not lawful for him to hit the pregnant woman in any way); another, if, not having looked at all things, he would kill someone negligently and unintentionally.

It is also legal to kill another for the sake of defending one's own salvation. For which reason also, if someone, in order to defend his salvation, using all caution, kills another, it sufficiently appears that he is not subject to this law. And these, in truth, that we have just commemorated, are the massacres that are not contained in this precept of the law; Except for which, all others are prohibited, whether looking at the murderer, at the one who is killed, or at the ways in which the killing is carried out. 9. It is not lawful for anyone to carry out slaughter by private authority. Well, as far as those who do the killing are concerned, no one is excepted; Not the rich, not the powerful men, not the lords, not the fathers, but, once all pleasure and discrimination has been removed, everyone has been prohibited from killing.

There is absolutely no one who cannot be safe by this law. If you look, however, at those who are killed, this law applies to all of them: nor is there a man so humble and of such abject condition that he is not defended by the force of this law. Nor is it lawful for anyone to kill himself; For no one has such power over his life that it is lawful for him to procure death at his discretion; and that is why with the words of this law it has not been prescribed like this: Do not kill another, but simply: Do not kill.

In how many ways can this precept be violated? If, however, we look at the multiple ways of carrying out the slaughter, no one is excepted. For not only is it not lawful for anyone to take a man's life with his own hands, or with iron, or with stone, or with a staff, or with a noose, or with poison; but it has been completely prohibited from being done for advice, help, assistance or for any other reason. In which the delay and stupor of the Jews was added, who believed they were keeping this precept if they only abstained from killing with their hands. But to the Christian man, who through Christ's interpreter has learned that this law is spiritual, namely the one that commands us to have not only pure hands, but also a chaste and sincere spirit, that is not entirely sufficient, which they estimated themselves to provide more than. For not even being angry with anyone is lawful, it has been transmitted in the Gospel, when the Lord says: «But I say to you: everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment; and whoever says to his brother raca, will be guilty of the council; and whoever says he is foolish will be guilty of the Gehenna of fire. 13. How someone can sin or not sin by being angry. From whose words it is evident that he who is angry with his brother is not without guilt, even if he contains the anger locked up in his soul; and whoever has given any meaning to that anger, sins gravely; and much more seriously the one who is not afraid to receive his brother harshly and insult him. And indeed this is true if there is no underlying cause for anger; For the cause of the wrath that is granted by God and by the laws is that when we punish those who obey our empire and power, if there is guilt in them. For the anger of the Christian man should not come from the senses of the flesh, but from the Holy Spirit; since it is fitting that we be temples of the Holy Spirit, in which Jesus Christ dwells.

How perfectly men observe this law, and how many sin against it. There are also many things transmitted by the Lord that concern the perfect reason for this law, which are those: «Do not resist the evil one, but if someone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also; And whoever wants to contend with you in judgment and take away your tunic, let him also have your cloak; and whoever I force you to take a thousand steps, go with him another two. From what has already been commemorated it can be seen how prone men are to those sins that are prohibited by this precept; How many are found that, if less with the hand, at least with the spirit, they commit the crime of massacre.

How much God hates murder in sacred letters. And since remedies have been applied to this very dangerous disease in sacred literature, it is the priest's job to diligently transmit them to the faithful. The main one, however, is that they understand how nefarious the sin of the slaughter of man is; and this can be perceived from many and maximum testimonies of the holy letters: because God detests murder to such an extent in the holy letters, that he says that he will demand from the beasts the penalty of the slaughter of men, and orders the killing of the wild beast that has injured the man. Nor did he want man to hate blood for any other reason, but so that in every way the mind and hands would abstain from the nefarious slaughter of man.

How great a crime the killing of man is is shown by reason. For murderers are bitter enemies of the human race and even of nature: who, whatever is in them, reverse all the work of God when they take away man, for whose sake he testifies that he made all things and all things were procreated. Furthermore, in Genesis, when it is prohibited to kill man because God created him in his image and likeness, it is a great insult to God, and it seems like imposing violent hands on him, who removes his image from the way. David having meditated on this with divine consideration of mind, became extremely indignant at the bloodthirsty men with those words: "His feet are swift in shedding blood"; and he did not simply say: They kill, but: They shed blood: which words he uttered for the amplification of that detestable crime and to show their inhuman cruelty; and to declare in the first place how hasty they carry themselves to that crime with a certain diabolical impulse, he said: "Swift are their feet."

CHAPTER 48. 1 Jn. 3, 15. 1 Cor. 13, 4. How charity is all these things, see St. Thomas in 2. 2. q. 23, art. 4 ad 2. Lc. 21, 19. Office of charity. See St. Thomas in 2. 2. q. 31, art. 1. 1 Cor. 13, 4. St. Thomas in 2. 2. q. 23, art. 8 and 9. Mt. 5, 44. CATEC. FOR PASTORS. PART III.

What does God command to do in this precept. Now, however, what Christ the Lord commands to be kept in this precept is to ensure that we have peace with all: for he says, when he was interpreting this place: "If you offer your gift at the altar, and there you remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled with your brother, and then when you come, offer your gift"; and what follows. Which things will be explained in this way by the parish priest, who teaches that without exception everyone must be embraced with charity: to which, in the explanation of this precept, he will incite the faithful as much as he can, because in him the virtue of loving one's neighbor primarily shines. Well, since with this precept hatred is openly prohibited, because he who hates his brother is a murderer; It certainly follows that the precept of love and charity is given.

What offices of charity are contained in this precept. And as with this law, charity and love of neighbor have been prescribed, the precepts of all those offices and actions that usually follow from the same charity are also transmitted. "Charity is patient, says Saint Paul"; We are therefore commanded to be patient, in which the Savior teaches that we will possess our souls. Beneficence is then companion and partner of charity, because "charity is benign." The virtue, however, of kindness and beneficence extends widely, and its office is mainly concerned with those things: that we supply the poor with the necessary things, give food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked; and the more someone needs our help, the more liberality we confer upon him. 18. How of all the offices of charity the most perfect is the dilection of enemies. These offices of beneficence and kindness, which are illustrious in themselves, become more illustrious if they are lent to enemies. For the Savior says: "Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you"; which the Apostle also admonishes with those words: «If your enemy is hungry, feed him; If he is thirsty, give him a drink; for by doing this, you will heap coals of fire on his head; "Do not allow yourself to be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good." Finally, if we look at the law of charity, which is benign, we will understand that all the offices that concern meekness, leniency and the other virtues of this kind are prescribed by this law.

In what primarily does the charity of neighbor that is commanded here shine? But by far the most excellent of all offices, the most full of charity, in which it is primarily appropriate that we exercise ourselves, is that: that we remit and condone the injuries we have received with an equitable spirit. In order for us to do this outright, the divine letters often, as has been said above, admonish and exhort us; when they not only call blessed those who do it outright in this way; but they also affirm that forgiveness of errors has been given to them by God: but those who neglect to do this same thing, or refuse it altogether, do not achieve it. But since the desire to take revenge is almost ingrained in the minds of men, it is necessary for the parish priest to put maximum diligence in not only teaching that the Christian man must forget injuries and remit them, but also deeply persuading the faithful. And since much mention is made of this same thing in the sacred writers, consult them to refute the pertinacity of those who are with an obstinate and affirmed spirit in the desire to take revenge, and keep at hand the arguments that those very serious Fathers and maximally adapted to this thing piously used.

With what main reasons should hatred be repressed, and the faithful should be induced to forget injuries? But these three things must mainly be explained. The first is that the person who is considered to have received injury is persuaded to the highest degree that the person whom he wishes to avenge was not the main cause of the detriment or injury. This is what that admirable Job did, who, seriously injured by the Sabeans, by the Chaldeans and by the Devil, however, without taking any account of them, as an upright man and a very pious man, used rightly and piously those words: "The Lord gave, the Lord took away." Thus, then, with the prayer and example of that most patient man, Christian men may be persuaded of what is most true: that all the things that we suffer in this life come from the Lord, who is the father and author of all justice and mercy.

The men who persecute us are ministers and satellites of God, even if they do so out of ill will. Nor does he truly punish us (whose kindness is immense) as enemies, but rather he corrects and punishes us as children. Nor, if we rightly note, in these things are men anything other than ministers and as satellites of God: and although man can hate someone badly and desire him badly; However, it cannot harm him in any way except with God's permission. For this reason, Joseph was induced to endure the impious advice of the brothers with an equitable spirit; Thus David the insults that Shimei did to him. The same type of argument that Saint Chrysostom dealt with seriously and eruditely is very relevant to this same thing: namely, that no one is injured except by himself. For those who believe that they have been treated insultingly, if they repeat the thing with themselves in the right way, will find outright that they have not received any insult or harm from others. Well, although the things with which they are injured happen extrinsically; However, they offend themselves most when they nefariously contaminate the spirit with hatred, cupidity and anger.

What comforts accrue to those who willingly condone injuries. The second is what embraces two main comforts, which concern those who, led by pious study towards God, willingly remit insults. Of which the first is that which God promised to those who remit the debts of others: that they also will ask for the forgiveness of sins: from which promise it easily appears how pleasant this office of piety is to Him. The other comfort is that we achieve a certain nobility and perfection; because by condoning injuries we become in some way similar to God, "who makes his sun rise on the good and the evil, and rains on the just and the unjust."

What and how many inconveniences come from the hatred of enemies. Finally, we must explain those inconveniences that we fall into when we do not want to condone the injuries that have been done to us. Thus, let the parish priest put before the eyes of those who cannot induce the mind to forgive their enemies, that hatred is not only a serious sin, but also that due to the diuturnity of sinning it is seriously adhered to. For when the one in whose mind this affection has settled, thirsts for the blood of his enemy, filled with the hope of avenging him, he will so occupy himself days and nights in a certain perennial bad agitation of the mind, that he never seems to cease from the thought of the slaughter or of some nefarious thing. From which it follows that either never, or with maximum business, he is urged to either forgive completely, or at least somewhere remit the insults. Therefore it is rightly compared to a wound to which a driven dart adheres. 24. It is shown that many sins are born from hatred. There are also many inconveniences and sins that are linked to this single sin of hatred as with a certain bond. And that is why Saint John said this way in this sentence: "He who hates his brother is in darkness, and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going: because the darkness has blinded his eyes." Therefore, it is necessary that it falls more often. Well, how can someone approve of the sayings or actions of someone they hate? From here arise rash and wicked judgments, anger, envy, detractions and others of this kind; in which those who are united by kinship or friendship usually also get involved. Thus it often turns out that from one sin there are many. Nor is it said without reason that this sin is of the devil; since he was a murderer from the beginning. Therefore the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, when the Pharisees were endeavoring to bring death upon him, said that they were begotten of the father Devil. 25. Remedies against the sin of hatred. But in addition to what has been said, from which the reasons for detesting this crime can be derived, other remedies have also been transmitted, and these are extremely appropriate, in the monuments of holy letters. Of the Angel by whom the divine Peter was freed from prison. With what reason do faithful men recognize God's paternal care of men? It is proven that no crimes of men, no matter how great they may be, can exhaust the kindness of God. This is exactly how it is: when we consider ourselves most lost and deprived of God's prison, then mainly because of his immense goodness God seeks us out and heals us. Not only of second things, but also of calamities sent, the goodness of the heavenly Father must be measured.

What is the third reason with which God cumulatively shows the benefit of paternal charity towards the human race. They have great strength, therefore, to declare the main reason of God in loving and protecting the race of men, creation and governance. But nevertheless that work of redeeming man stands out in such a way between the two superior ones, that the most beneficent God and our Father illustrated with this third benefit cumulatively the utmost kindness towards us. Therefore the parish priest will transmit to the spiritual children and assiduously instill in their ears this most generous charity of God towards us, so that they understand that, because they were redeemed, in an admirable way they became children of God: "For He gave, says John, the power to become children of God: and of God they were born." For which reason Baptism, which we have as the first pignus and monument of redemption, is called the Sacrament of regeneration; because from there we are born children of God: for the Lord Himself says: “That which was born of the Spirit is spirit. And you must be born again. Likewise the Apostle Peter: "Born again not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible seed, through the word of the living God."

By the singular benefit of God through redemption we were made children of God. Through the weight of this redemption we also received the Holy Spirit and were worthy of the grace of God. With whose marriage we are adopted children of God, as the Apostle Paul wrote to the Romans: «You did not receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the spirit of adoption as sons; in which we cry: Abba (Father)! Whose strength and effectiveness of adoption Saint John explains in this way: "See what charity the Father gave us, so that we might be called and become children of God."

What Christians, already made children of God, after so many offices of paternal charity received, should render to the Father. Having explained these things, the faithful people must be admonished what they in turn owe to the most loving Father God, so that they understand what love and piety, what obedience and veneration it is appropriate to pay to the Creator, Governor and Redeemer, and with what hope and confidence it is appropriate to invoke him. Because he punishes those who sin to make them better with that discipline, and with the present animosity redeem them from everlasting perdition. The faithful must be instilled that God never forgot us. What's more: console yourselves with that solace of the divine oracle, which was said in the Apocalypse: "I argue and punish those I love." Rest in the Apostle's exhortation to the Hebrews: "My son, do not despise the discipline of the Lord, nor be weary while you are admonished by Him. Our. 14. Why are we commanded to call God with the plurality word Our Father. When we each invoke the father, and call him our own, we are taught that from the gift and right of divine adoption it necessarily follows that all the faithful are brothers, and must love each other fraternally. «For all of you, he says, are brothers; for one is your Father, who is in heaven. Therefore also in the epistles the Apostle calls all the faithful brothers. From which is also made that necessary consequence: that by the same adoption of God not only are all the faithful united to each other with fraternal necessity, but, because the only begotten Son of God is man, they are also named and are brothers of Him. For in the Epistle to the Hebrews, when speaking of the Son of God, the Apostle wrote: "He is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying: I will announce your name to my brothers," which was so much before predicted by David of Christ the Lord. Christ himself also speaks in this way in the Evangelist to the women: "Go, tell my brothers that they are going to Galilee, there they will see me." Which is recorded to have been said by Him then, when already raised from the dead He had achieved immortality: lest anyone consider that this fraternal cognation was dissolved with His resurrection and ascension to heaven. In fact, it is so far from the resurrection of Christ to settle this conjunction and charity, that from that seat of majesty and glory, then, when He will judge all men of all memory, we will receive that the least of the faithful must be called by Him with the name of brothers.

With what reason are the faithful counted among the brothers of Christ. How, however, can it happen that we are not brothers of Christ, of whom we are called joint heirs? Because He is the firstborn constituted heir of all; but we, secondly begotten, joint heirs of Him according to the manner of the heavenly gifts, according to the reason of charity, with which we would have lent ourselves ministers and coadjutors of the Holy Spirit, with whose author we are impelled and inflamed to virtue and salutary actions, so that, supported by His grace, we may descend manfully into the contest of salvation, which, wisely and constantly prepared, and traveled through the space of this life, we receive the just reward of the crown of the heavenly Father, established for all those who have maintained the same course: "For God is not, as the Apostle says, unjust, to forget our work and diligence."

How we should pray for one another, and esteem each other brothers. That, however, We must utter this voice of Ours from the heart is declared by the sentence of Saint Chrysostom, who says that God willingly hears the Christian who deprecates not only for himself, but for another, because to pray for himself is from nature, for another from grace; On one hand it forces necessity, on the other it exhorts fraternal charity. To which he subjoined those: "She who recommends fraternal charity is more helpful to God than she who pronounces necessity." In such a great matter of salutary prayer, the parish priest must admonish and exhort everyone of any age, gender and order, to remember this common fraternal need, to behave courteously and fraternally, and not to prefer one another with insolence. Because although in the Church of God there are different degrees of offices; However, that variety of degrees and positions in no way removes the conjunction of fraternal necessity, in the same way that in the body of man the various use and the diverse function of the members does nothing by which this or that part of the body loses the position and the name of member.

For what reasons are Christians copulated with such a great conjunction of necessity. Propose yourself to him who has royal power: then, if he is faithful, is he not the brother of all those who are contained in the communion of the Christian faith? Maximum: why so? For there is no other God, from whom the rich and kings were born, from whom the poor and those in the power of kings existed; but one God, and father, and Lord of all. Thus, then, there is one nobility of the spiritual birth of all, one dignity, one splendor of the genus: when we are all born from the same Spirit, from the same Sacrament of faith, children of God, and joint heirs of the same inheritance.
The spiritual nobility of all Christians is one.

Nor do copious and powerful men have another Christ God; another the most tenuous and minute; They are not initiated with other Sacraments, nor do they expect another inheritance from the heavenly kingdom. We are all brothers, and, as the Apostle says to the Ephesians, we are members of the body of Christ, of his flesh and bones. Which the Apostle himself means in the Epistle to the Galatians: «You are all children of God through faith that is in Christ Jesus; for all of you who were baptized into Christ put on Christ; There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female. For you are all one in Christ Jesus. This thing, however, must be explained exactly by the Shepherds of souls, and this sentence must be wisely delayed. Because it is a place suited no less to confirm and excite inept and abject men, than to inhibit and depress the arrogance of the talkative and powerful. To remedy the problem of men, the Apostle urged this fraternal charity, and instilled it in the ears of the faithful.

What should the Christian meditate when he pronounces that exordium of precaution: Our Father. When, then, you go to make these prayers to God, Christian, remember that you are approaching the Father God as a son. So, then, when you begin the precation and say that: Our Father, think to what place the supreme kindness of God raised you, who did not command you to approach the Lord as a servant, inviting and timid, but to confuse the father as a voluntary and safe son. In whose memory and cogitation, consider with what study and piety in your turn it is convenient for you to pray. Because you must work to present yourself as it is appropriate for the son of God to be; that is, that your prayer and your actions are not unworthy of the divine kind with which the most beneficent God wanted to deign you. The Apostle exhorts us to this reason for the office when he says: "Be imitators of God, therefore, as dearly loved children"; so that it can truly be said of us what the Apostle himself wrote to the Thessalonians: "For you are all children of light and children of God." That you are in heaven.

God being omnipresent: in what way is it said that he has his domicile peculiarly in heaven. It is known among all those who rightly feel about God that God is in every place and people: which is not to be understood as if He Himself, distributed in parts, with one part occupies and guards one place, with another another; because it is spirit, expert of all division. For who will dare to circumscribe God, as if placed in a vestige, for the purposes of some place, when He Himself says of Himself: "Do I not fill heaven and earth?" Which again must be taken as follows: that God embraces with his strength and virtue the heaven and the earth, and everything that is understood in the heaven and the earth, not however that He Himself is contained by any place. Because God assists all things, either creating them or preserving those created, without being circumscribed or defined by any region or by any ends, so that his nature and power do not constitute present everywhere. Which the blessed David expressed in those words: "If I ascend to heaven, there you are." But although God is present in all things, without being, as we said, defined by any terms; However, in the divine Scriptures it is often said that he resides in heaven. Which we see done because the heavens that we look at are the noblest part of the world, and remain uncorrupted, lending themselves in strength, magnitude and beauty to other bodies, and endowed with other stable movements. Thus, then, to excite the minds of men to contemplate his infinite power and majesty, which primarily shines in the work of heaven, God testifies in the divine Scriptures that he dwells in heaven: often also, which is, he declares that there is no part of the world that is not encompassed by his present power.

What meditation does that particle present to the faithful: That you are in heaven. Although in this cogitation the faithful will not only propose the image of the common father of all, but also that of God who reigns in heaven; then, and the spirit refers to hope and confidence, it brings them the nature of the Father God and, as that name is, both the Christian humility and piety attached to that illustrious nature and divine majesty of our Father, who is in heaven.

From the heavenly Father only heavenly goods, or those that are linked to them, must be chosen. The order of the requests must follow the order of the things to be desired. That the words also prefix to those who pray what is to be asked: because every postulation of ours that concerns the use and necessity of this life, if it is not united to the heavenly goods and is directed to that end, is inane and unworthy of the Christian. Therefore the parish priests will admonish the pious listeners of this reason for precaution; and they will verify the admonition with that authority of the Apostle: “If you have been raised with Christ, seek the things above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God; “Taste the things above, not those that are on the earth.” OF THE FIRST PETITION. CHAPTER X. Hallowed be your Name.

Why from the sanctification of the divine name we begin our desires. What must be asked of God, and in what order it must be done, was taught and reigned by the same Master and Lord of all. Because being the nuncio and interpreter of our study and desire for prayer, then we ask rightly, when the order of the postulations follows the order of the things to be desired. True charity admonishes us to give all our courage and study to God, who, since He alone is the supreme good, is rightly to be loved with a certain principal and singular love. Nor can one love God from the heart and only, if his honor and glory are not put before things of all natures. Because the goods, both ours and those of others, and all those that are named with the word good, coming from Him, yield to the same supreme good. Therefore, so that the prayer could proceed in order, the Savior constituted this request for the highest good as the prince and head of the remaining requests, teaching us that, before postulating the things that are necessary for us or for any neighbor, we must ask for those that are proper to the glory of God, and expose to God Himself our study and desire for that thing. Once this is done, we will remain in the office of charity, with which we are taught both to love God more than ourselves, and to ask first for what we desire for God, then for what we choose for ourselves.

Since the divine nature is such that it cannot be increased or lack anything, why was it necessary to postulate here the sanctification of the name of God. And since desire and petition are those things that we lack (not even God, that is, his nature, can be accessed, nor can the divine substance, which inexplicably is filled with all perfection, be increased with anything), it must be understood that the things that we ask of God for God himself, and that concern his external glory, are outside of this. Because we desire and ask that the name of God be better known among the people; may his kingdom be expanded; May they obey the divine Numen more every day; whose three things, Name, Kingdom, Obedience, are not in that same intimate good of God, but are assumed extrinsically.

Those words: As in heaven as on earth, may refer to the first three petitions, and how they are understood here. But so that it may be more clearly understood what force these petitions have and what they are worth, it will be the part of the Pastor to warn the faithful people that those words: In heaven as it is on earth, can refer to each of the first three postulations: so that: Hallowed be your name, in heaven as it is on earth; Likewise: Your kingdom come, both in heaven and on earth; Likewise: Your will be done, both in heaven and on earth. When, however, we ask that the name of God be sanctified, we feel that the holiness and glory of the divine name is increased. In which place the parish priest will warn and teach the pious listeners that the Savior does not say that he should be sanctified on earth in the same way as in heaven; that is, that terrestrial sanctification equals in breadth that of heaven (which in no way can be done), but rather that it be done out of charity and by intimate study of the soul.

How the name of God, holy in itself, can be sanctified by us. When, therefore, we preach that: Thy will be done, we ask first that the heavenly Father grant us the power to obey the divine commands, and to serve Him in holiness and justice all our days, so that we do all things according to His nutum and will: that we cultivate those offices of which we are admonished in the sacred letters, that, with Him as guide and author, we lend all the other things that befit those who were not born of the will of the flesh, but of God, following the example of Christ the Lord, who became obedient unto death, even death on a cross: that we be prepared to suffer all things rather than depart even in the least from his will.

Who mainly have been given to burn with the most ardent study and love of the things that are asked here. Nor is there anyone who burns with more ardent study and love of this petition than he who has been granted to look at the supreme dignity of those who obey God. Because he understands that the same thing is said very truly: that to serve God and obey him is to reign: "Whoever, says the Lord, who does the will of my Father who is in heaven, this is my brother, sister and mother": that is, I am with him most united with all the bonds of love and benevolence. There is almost no one of the holy men who has not vehemently postulated from God the main munera of this request, and all used it as a clear, although often varied, prayer. Among which we see the miraculous and gentle David postulate it variously: he already says: "I hope my paths are directed to keep your justifications!"; sometimes: "Lead me in the path of your commandments"; sometimes: "Direct my steps according to your eloquence, and let no injustice dominate me." To this belong those: "Give me intellect, and I will learn your commandments"; "Teach me your judgments"; "Give me intellect, so that I may know your testimonies." Often the same sentence is used in other words. Whose places must be diligently noted and explained to the faithful, so that everyone may understand how much force and copy of salutary things there is in the first part of this petition.

What do we also mean with this request. Secondly, when we preach that: Thy will be done, we detest the works of the flesh; of which the Apostle writes: "Nevertheless, the works of the flesh are manifest, which are fornication, uncleanness, impudence, lust, etc."; and "If you live according to the flesh, you will die": and we ask that God not allow us to perfect those that sense, greed, our imbecility have persuaded, but that he moderate our will with his will. Voluptuary men, who are fixed on the care and cogitation of earthly things, are alien to this will. Because they rush through their lust to possess what they coveted, and in that fruit of pure covetousness they put happiness, so that they say that he is also blessed who gets everything he chooses. We, on the contrary, ask God, as the Apostle says, that we do not care for the flesh in desires, but that His will be done.

Psalm 118, 5. 38. 133. 73. 108. 125. Galatians 5, 19-21. Romans 8, 13. Those involved in voluptuary and earthly affections, if they do not put away that covetousness, will not truly precarious this. Difficult is precarious against one's own greed, but nevertheless salutary and full of glory.

It is better to choose to do what God wants than what we covet. Although we are not easily induced to precarious God who does not satisfy our desires: this induction of the spirit is, in fact, difficult, because we ourselves somehow seem to hate ourselves by asking for that. Which is also attributed to stupidity by those who completely adhere to the body. But let us willingly submit to the reputation of stupidity for the sake of Christ, whose saying is: "If anyone wants to come after me, let him deny himself." Especially when we know that it is much clearer to choose what is right and just than to achieve that which is alien to reason, virtue, and the laws of God. And certainly anyone who achieves what they recklessly and driven by libidine coveted is in a worse place than the one who does not achieve what they optimally opted for.

Nor should those who have no kind of mercy ask God. Although we not only ask this: that God not grant us what we spontaneously covet, when it is clear that our study is depraved; but also that what, with the dreamer and promoter of the Devil, a pretended angel of light, we sometimes postulate as good, does not occur. That study of the Prince of the Apostles seemed very correct, and full of piety, when he strove to invoke the Lord's advice to go to death; and yet, because he was guided by human senses, not by divine reason, the Lord bitterly objected. What more lover of the Lord seems to have been able to postulate than the holy men James and John, angry with those Samaritans who had not wanted to receive the master in hospice, asked him to send fire down from heaven, to consume those harsh and inhuman? But by Christ the Lord they were rebuked with those words: "You do not know what spirit you are of: the Son of man did not come to lose souls, but to save them."

When what we covet refers to the conservation of nature, we must ask to the maximum degree that it be done, if God wills. Not only when what we covet is evil, or has a kind of evil, should we ask God for his will to be done, but also when it is truly not evil; as when the will follows that first inclination of nature, to desire those that preserve nature, and reject those that seem contrary to it. Therefore, when we have reached that point of wanting to ask for something of this kind, then let us say from the heart: YOUR WILL BE DONE: let us imitate the same one from whom we received the discipline of salvation: who, when moved by the natural fear of torments and the most bitter death; However, in that horror of extreme pain he referred his will to the will of God the Father: "Not my will, he says, but yours be done."

Since without God's help we cannot avoid sin, we also postulate this with this petition. But the race of men is admirably depraved; who, although they had also given force to their greed and had subjected it to the divine will, nevertheless without the help of God, with which we are both protected from evil and directed to good, they cannot avoid sins. Thus, then, we must confuse this precaution, and we must ask God that He Himself perfects in us what has been instituted, that He restrains the exultant movements of greed, that He makes the appetites obedient to reason, that at last he conforms us completely to His will. We also preach that the entire globe of the earth receives the knowledge of the will of God: so that the divine mystery hidden for centuries and generations may be known and divulged among all. So in heaven as on earth.

What does this clause want? We also postulate the form and prescription of this obedience, so that it is directed to that rule that in heaven both the blessed Angels keep and the remaining chorus of heavenly souls worship; so that, just as those spontaneously and willingly obey the divine Numen, so we obey the will of God, in the way that He Himself maximally desires, most liberally.

God is not to be served for the sake of price, but for love. And truly in the work and study that we dedicate to God, God requires of us the utmost love and the highest charity; so that, although with the hope of heavenly rewards we would have dedicated ourselves completely to Him, nevertheless let us hope for those things because it pleased the divine majesty that we enter into that hope. Therefore all our hope rests on that love towards God, who proposed eternal blessedness to our love by mercy. There are, in fact, those who lovingly serve someone, but nevertheless because of the price, to which they refer love. There are, furthermore, those who, moved only by charity and piety, see nothing in him to whom they give work but his goodness and virtue, by whose cogitation and admiration they consider themselves blessed because they can lend him their office.

Other expositions also of this clause. And this sentence has that apposition: AS IN HEAVEN AS ON EARTH. Mainly, in fact, we must strive to be obedient to God, in the way that we said blessed minds are; whose praises in that position of utmost obedience David continues in that Psalm: "Bless the Lord in all his virtues, his ministers, who do his will." And if someone, following Saint Cyprian, interprets those things in this way, so as to say: In heaven, in the good and pious; On earth, in the evil and impious, we also approve his sentence; so that by heaven the Spirit is understood, by earth the flesh; so that everyone and everything in everyone obeys the will of God. 22. In what way does this petition also contain thanksgiving. This petition also contains thanksgiving: because we venerate the most holy will of God, and, perfused with utmost joy, we celebrate all his works with utmost praise and congratulations, knowing with certainty that He did all things well. Because when it is clear that God is omnipotent, it necessarily follows that we understand that all things were made according to his nutum. When, however, we also affirm that He Himself, as He is, is the supreme good, we confess that none of His works is not good, when He imparted His goodness to all. And if in all of them we do not achieve divine reason, in all of them, however, despising the ambiguous cause and rejecting all hesitation, we confess that of the Apostle: "That his ways are unsearchable." But for this reason we also mainly worship the will of God: because through Him we were sealed with heavenly light. Because, snatched from the power of darkness, he transferred us to the kingdom of the Son of his delight.

What should this request refer to contemplation? But, in order to explain in the last place what concerns the meditation of this petition, we must return to what we touched on at the beginning: that the faithful people in the pronunciation of this petition must be of a submissive and humble spirit, believing with themselves that force of greed implanted in nature, which is repugnant to the divine will, thinking that in that office they are defeated by all the natures, of which it is thus written: "They all serve you": and that he is maximally imbecile, the that not only can it not perfect any work pleasing to God, but not even institute it, if it is not revolted with the help of God. And since nothing is more magnificent, nothing more eminent, as we said, than serving God and living according to his law and precepts; What could be more optionable for the Christian man than to walk in the ways of the Lord, to agitate nothing with the spirit, to stir up nothing with action, that would abhor the divine will? But so that he may take up that exercise and maintain that institute more diligently, he should ask from the divine books examples of those to whom, when they had not referred the reason for their advice to the will of God, all things went wrong.

How much comfort can we get to live peacefully from the meditation of this request. Finally, the faithful be admonished to rest in the simple and absolute will of God, let him who sees himself in a place inferior to that in which his dignity postulates carry his condition with an equitable spirit: do not desert his order, but remain in that vocation to which he was called; and subject your own judgment to the will of God, who consults us better than we ourselves can choose. If we are oppressed by the anguish of the family thing, by the health of the body, by persecutions, by other annoyances and hardships, it must be established with certainty that none of this can happen to us without the will of God, which is the supreme reason for all things; and for this reason we should not be moved more seriously, but rather carry it with an unconquered spirit, always having in our mouths that: "The will of the Lord be done"; and that of blessed Job: "As it pleased the Lord, so it was done: blessed be the name of the Lord." CATEC. FOR PASTORS. PART IV.

What is the reason of order observed in this Sunday prayer. The fourth petition, and the remaining petitions afterward, with which we properly and nominally postulate the subsidies of the soul and body, refer to the superior petitions. In fact, Sunday precaution has this order and reason: that the postulation of divine things is followed by the request of those that concern the protection of the body and this life. Because as to God, as to the ultimate end, men refer; Thus the goods of human life are directed to the divine with the same reason.

Why is it legal to choose and ask God for the goods of human life. Which in truth must be chosen and requested, either because the divine order postulates it, or because we lack those gadgets for the adeption of the divine goods, so that with those gadgets we can achieve the proposed end, which is contained in the kingdom and glory of the heavenly Father, and in cultivating and keeping those precepts that we are not unaware of being the will of God. Therefore, we must refer all the force and reason of this request to God and his glory.

For what purpose and manner temporal goods must be postulated. The parish priests will, therefore, lend their office to the faithful listeners, so that they understand that in asking for things that concern the use and fruit of earthly things, our spirit and our study must be directed to the prescription of God, and we must not decline from there anywhere. Because in what the Apostle writes: "We do not know whether we pray as we should," we sin mainly with these postulations of earthly and obsolete things. Therefore, these goods must be requested as appropriate; lest, postulating something perversely, we receive from God that answer: "You do not know what you ask." It will be, however, a certain note to judge which is the pragmatic request and which is right, the advice and the purpose of the one who postulates. Because if someone asks for earthly things with the intention of estimating them as completely good, and resting in them as in the chosen end, he requires nothing further, without a doubt he does not pray as he should. "For we do not ask, says Saint Augustine, for these temporalities as our goods, but as our necessities." Also the Apostle in the Epistle to the Corinthians teaches that all things that refer to the necessary uses of life must refer to the glory of God. "Eat, then, he says, whether you drink, whether you do something else, do all things for the glory of God."

How many and how great comforts man enjoyed in the state of innocence. But so that the faithful can see how much need this request has, the parish priests will commemorate how much need for external things there is for sustenance and for cultivating life, which they will understand better if a comparison is made of those that were necessary for the first father of our kind, and for the rest of men afterward, to live. Because even if he, in the most ample state of innocence, from which, and through his fault, all posterity fell, had the need to adsorb the delicacy to renew his strength: nevertheless between the needs of that and our life there is much difference. Because there would have been no need for clothing for the integument of the body, nor for a roof for shelter, nor for weapons for defense, nor for remedies for health, nor for many other things, whose subsidy we lack to protect this imbecility and fragility of nature: the fruit that the most happy tree of life would have lent without any work of its own or of the posters would have been sufficient for immortal life. Nor would man have been idle in the delights of such a great paradise, to which God had placed him in that domicile of the will to work: however, no work would have been bothersome to him, no charge of the non-jucundous office: he would have perpetually borne the sweetest fruits of the cultivation of the happy gardens; nor would his work or hope have ever failed him.

How many evils followed Adam's prevarication. But the offspring of the posteros not only deprived of the fruit of the vital tree, but also condemned with that horrible sentence: «Cursed is the earth in your work: with labor you will eat of it all the days of your life: thorns and thistles will sprout for you, and you will eat the grass of the earth; with the sweat of your face you will feed on bread, until you return to the land from which you were taken; for dust you are, and to dust you will return. To us, therefore, all things happened contrary to what would have happened to him and to the posters if Adam had been a hearer of the word of God; and so they returned and moved all the things to the lower part. In which it is very serious that the maximum expenses, the greatest work and sweat often do not follow any fruit: when the fruits given are oppressed in worse harvest, either by the harshness of the wild grasses that rise, or percussed and prostrate by clouds, wind, hail, urédine, rubigo perish; so that all the work of the year in a short time with some calamity from heaven or earth is reduced to nothing. This happens due to the immanity of our crimes, of which God, being averse, in no way blesses our works: but the horrible sentence that he pronounced on us at the beginning remains.

Men, to meet their needs, are obliged to work; who, however, if God does not favor, work in vain. Thus, then, the Pastor will bow in the treatise of this place, so that the faithful people know that because of them men fall into these anguish and miseries: and so that they understand that they must sweat and labor to prepare the things necessary to live; However, if God has not blessed our works, hope will be fallacious and all contention will be inane. Because "neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but he who gives the increase is God"; and: "Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain."

God must be asked to supply the things we lack, which he does lavishly. The parish priests will teach, then, that there are almost innumerable things that, if we lack them, we either lose our lives or have an uneventful life. Because, knowing this necessity of things and the imbecility of nature, the Christian people will be forced to approach the heavenly Father, and ask him supplicatingly for earthly and heavenly goods. He will imitate that Prodigal Son, who when in a distant region he began to lack, and there was no one, when he was hungry, to give him the siliques, once returning to himself, he understood that the remedy for the evils with which he was oppressed was to be desired nowhere but from the father. In which place the faithful people will also approach with more confidence to pray, if in the cogitation of divine benignity they remember that the father's ears are perpetually open to the voices of the children. Because while he exhorts us to ask for bread, he promises that he will give it abundantly to those who ask rightly. Because by teaching how we ask, he exhorts: exhorting, impels: impelling, promises: promising, he induces us to the hope of the most certain impetration.

What is meant by the name bread, and what is the ruling of this petition. With the spirits of the faithful people excited and inflamed, it follows that it must be declared what is postulated with this request: first, what is that bread that we ask for. It must be known, therefore, that in the divine letters with this name of bread many things are certainly meant, but mainly those two: first, everything that in sustenance and in other things we add to protect the body and life; then, everything that by God's blessing was given to us for the life and salvation of the spirit and soul. We ask, however, in this place for the subsidies of this life that we lead on earth, by the authority of the holy Fathers who feel this way.

It is shown that you can ask God for temporal benefits. Therefore those who say that it is not lawful for Christian men to ask God for the earthly goods of this life are in no way to be heard. Because this error is opposed, in addition to the consenting sentence of the Fathers, by many examples from both the Old and New Testaments. Jacob, in fact, making a vow, prayed thus: "If the Lord be with me, and keep me in the way in which I walk, and give me bread to eat and raiment to wear, and I return prosperously to my father's house, then the Lord will be my God to me, and this stone which I set up as a title will be called the house of God, and of all the things that you give me I will offer you tithes." Solomon also asked for a certain subsidy from this life when he warned that: "Do not give me begging or riches: give me only what is necessary for my sustenance." What, that the Savior of the human race orders to ask for those things that no one will dare to deny that pertain to the use of the body? "Pray," he says, "that it may not be your escape in the winter or on the Sabbath." What will we say about Saint James? Whose are those: «Is any of you sad? pray: he is of equal spirit, chant. What about the Apostle? that this is how he dealt with the Romans: "I pray, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the charity of the Holy Spirit, that you help me in your prayers for me to God, so that I may be delivered from the unbelievers who are in Judea." Therefore, when it has been divinely granted to the faithful to ask for these subsidies from human things, and as this perfect formula of praying has been transmitted by Christ the Lord, not even that remains in doubt: that this request is one of the seven. 10. What is meant here by the name of bread as it relates to the need of the body. We also ask for daily bread, that is, what is necessary for sustenance; so that by the name of bread we understand what is sufficient both for clothing to cover oneself and for food to eat, whether it be bread, or meat, or fish, or anything else. We see, in fact, that Elisha used this way of speaking, when he admonished the king to lend bread to the Assyrian soldiers, to whom a large supply of delicacies was given. We also know it is written about Christ the Lord: "He entered the house of a certain Prince of the Pharisees on the Sabbath to eat bread"; with whose voice we see the meanings that concern food and drink. For the absolute significance of this request, it must be noted, furthermore, that with this word bread we must not understand the abundant and exquisite copy of delicacies and clothing, but rather the necessary and simple one, in the way that the Apostle wrote: "Having food and what we cover with, with this let us be content"; and Solomon, as we said: "Give me only what is necessary for my sustenance."

Why let's not simply ask for bread here, but our own bread. We are also admonished from this frugality and parsimony with that voice that soon follows. Because when we say ours, we ask that bread for our need, not for lust: because we do not say ours because we can prepare it with our work without God: it is, in fact, in David: "They all look to you, so that you give them the food in its season: you giving them, they will take: you opening your hand, they will all be filled with goodness"; and in another place: "The eyes of all wait on you, Lord, and you give their food in due season": but because it is necessary, and by the father of all God, who with his providence feeds all animators, it has been attributed to us.

With our work we must prepare the bread that we want it to be, if we postulate our bread. Also for that reason our bread is appealed: because by right it must be acquired by us, not prepared with injury, fraud or theft: because those that we conciliate with bad arts are not ours, but someone else's, and often the adeption or the possession or the certain boasting of those is calamitous. On the contrary, however, in the honest and laborious profits of pious men, according to the Prophet's sentence, there is tranquility and great happiness: “For the labors of your hands, he says, because you will eat; blessed are you, and it will be well with you. Because we do not postulate multiple or delicate food, but rather that which satisfies the needs of nature; so that those who, disgusted with common food and potion, pursue the most exquisite types of bedsores and wines, may be ashamed in this place. Nor do those to whom Isaiah proposes those horrendous mines disapprove with this everyday voice: “Woe to those who join house to house, and field to field, copulate to the end of the place; Will you live alone in the middle of the earth? Because the cupidity of these men is incomprehensible, of whom it is written by Solomon: "The miser will not be filled with money." To whom also applies what the Apostle says: "Those who want to become rich fall into temptation and into the snare of the devil." Furthermore, daily bread is used because we feed on it to replenish the vital mood, which is consumed daily by the force of natural heat. Finally, there is that reason for this name: that it must be asked assiduously: so that in this habit of loving and cultivating God we are retained, and completely persuaded that, what is, our life and salvation depends on God.

Why should the rich, even though they abound in things, use these words? But what need is there for the rich, someone will say, to ask for daily bread, when they abound in all things? They have this need to pray in this way: not so that they are given those of which through the kindness of God they have a copy, but so that they do not lose those that abundantly assist them. Therefore, as the Apostle writes, from there let the rich learn not to know sublime things, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who abundantly lends us all things to fruition. But Saint Chrysostom provides this cause for this necessary request: not only so that we have plenty of food, but so that it is supplied by the hand of the Lord, who, by inserting salutary and even salutary strength into the daily bread, makes both the food benefit the body and the body serve the soul.

Why say Give us, not Give me. But what is it that we say Give us, in number of multitude, and not to me? Because it is characteristic of Christian charity that not only is each one caring for himself, but also that he works for his neighbor, and in the care of his usefulness he also remembers others. Added to this is that the muneres that are divinely paid to someone are not only paid so that only he or she possesses them or lives luxuriously in them, but also so that he or she communicates with others what is left over from the need. Because Saints Basil and Ambrose say: "It is the bread of the hungry that you withhold: it is the clothing of the naked that you enclose: the money that you deprive on earth is the redemption and absolution of the wretched."

What does the appositive vocula Hoy here imply? Today. This voice of common weakness admonishes us. For who is there who, if he least expects to be able by his own work to provide for a long time the necessary expenses of life, at least trusts that he will prepare the subsidies of sustenance for the day? But not even this trust is allowed to us by God, who commanded us to ask him also for the food of the singular days. Whose sentence has that necessary reason: because we all lack daily bread, it must also be used daily for Sunday precation. This of the bread that, perceived with the mouth, nourishes and sustains the body, that is imparted to all, common to the faithful and the unfaithful, the pious and the impious, by the admirable goodness of God: "Who makes his sun rise on the good and the evil, and rains on the just and the unjust."

What is to be understood here in the spiritual bread, which is also included in the scope of this petition. What remains is the spiritual Bread, which we also ask for in this place: with which are meant all that is required in this life for the salvation and safety of the spirit and the soul. Because as the food with which the body is nourished and sustained is multiple; Thus the esca that contains the life of the spirit and the soul is not of a single kind. Because the word of God is also food for the soul. For Wisdom says: "Come, eat my bread, and drink the wine that I mixed for you." But when God takes away from men the power of this word, which He usually does when He is most seriously offended by our scelerados, He is said to oppress the human race with hunger. Thus, in fact, it is in Amos: "I will send a famine on the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of the Lord." But just as it is a certain sign of approaching death when men cannot either take food or retain what they have taken: so it is a great argument for desperate salvation when they either do not seek the word of God, or, if it is present, they do not sustain it, and they utter in God that voice of impiety: "Depart from us, and we do not want the knowledge of your ways." In this fury of spirit and blindness of mind are those who, neglecting those who legitimately preside over them, Catholics, and the Bishops and Priests, and deserting the holy Roman Church, surrendered themselves to the discipline of the heretics corrupting the word of God.

Of the true supersubstantial bread, which is Christ the Lord. Now, however, it is bread of Christ the Lord, food for the soul. Because he himself says of himself: "I am the living bread, which came down from heaven." It is incredible with how much willingness and joy this bread perfuses the souls of the pious, then when they are most struggling with earthly annoyances and inconveniences.
