What can anger, what cupidity in us, how many are there who do not feel compelled to experience it to their great harm? Who is not lacessido with these stimuli? Who doesn't feel these aculeus? Who doesn't get burned with burning faces placed underneath? And certainly the blows are so varied, the requests so diverse, that it is extremely difficult not to receive some serious wound. And besides these enemies who dwell and live with us, there are also those staunch hosts of whom it is written: "It is not for us to collude against flesh and blood, but against the princes and powers, against the rulers of the world of this darkness, against the spiritual ones of foolishness in the heavenly ones."

How serious the insults of the Demons against us are, is explained according to the sentence of the divine Paul. Because the external impulses and impressions of the Demons, who openly ask of us, gain access to the intimate struggles, and influence our souls through cunicules, so that we can barely take care of them. The Apostle calls them both princes due to the excellence of nature (because by nature they precede men and other created things that fall under sense) and he calls them powers, because not only with the force of nature, but also with power they surpass; and appoint rulers of the world of darkness: because they do not govern the clear and illustrious world; that is, to the good and pious, but the dark and hallowed; namely, those who, blinded by the sordidness and darkness of the flagitious and criminal life, delight in the guide of darkness, the Devil. Also never blame the Spiritual Demons of foolishness: because there is foolishness of both the flesh and the spirit. What is called carnal nequicia, inflames the appetite for the libido and desires that are perceived with the senses. The spiritual follies are the bad studies and the prave cupidities that concern the higher part of the soul: which are so much worse than the rest, the more the mind and reason itself is higher and more powerful. Whose folly of Satan, because he seeks maximally to deprive us of the heavenly inheritance; That is why the Apostle said in the heavenly ones. From which it is lawful to understand that the forces of the hosts are great, their spirit undefeated, their hatred towards us immense and infinite; who also carry on perpetual war with us, so that no peace can be with them, no inducements can be made.

How much is the audacity and perversity of the Devil to tempt. But how much they dare, declares the voice of Satan in the Prophet: "I will ascend to heaven." He attacked the first men in Paradise, he worshiped the Prophets, he desired the Apostles, so that, as the Lord speaks in the Evangelist, he sifted them like wheat. Not even the face of Christ the Lord himself blushed: thus, his inexpressible cupidity and immense diligence was expressed by Saint Peter when he said: "Your adversary the Devil, like a roaring lion, circles around, seeking someone to devour." Although not only one Satan tempts men, but sometimes the Demons make an impetus in droves against the singular ones: which confessed that Demon who, asked by Christ the Lord what name he had, answered: "Legion is my name": namely, a multitude of Demons who had divided that wretch: and of another it is written: "He takes with him seven other spirits worse than him, and they enter and dwell there."

Why are the perverse less so, the pious more so, be infested by Demons. There are many who, as they minimally feel within themselves the impulses and impulses of the Demons, will judge that the whole thing is false: of whom it is not surprising that they are not challenged by the demons, to whom they spontaneously surrendered: there is in them no piety, no charity, not that virtue worthy of the Christian man: for which reason it happens that they are completely in the power of the devil; nor is it necessary any temptations to evert them, in whose minds he already, with them willingly, dwells. But those who dedicated themselves to God, stirring up the heavenly life on earth, those who are most sought after by the incursus of Satan, these he hates most bitterly, he plots schemes for these at every moment of time. The history is full of the divine letters of holy men whom, while also in the present mood, either by force or by fraud, he perverted. Adam, David, Solomon, and others, whom it would be difficult to enumerate, experienced the violent impulses and quiet cunning of demons, which cannot be resisted by the counsel or strength of men. Who, then, will consider himself sufficiently protected by his prison? Therefore, we must piously and chastely ask God not to allow us to be tempted beyond what we can: but also to make the temptation a success, so that we can sustain.

Demons cannot tempt men as much or as long as they want. But here the faithful must confirm themselves, if some, due to weakness of spirit or ignorance of the matter, ignore the power of demons, so that they themselves, agitated by the fluctuations of temptations, flee to this port of caution. Because Satan, in such power and pertinacity, in the capital hatred of our kind, cannot, nor how much or how long he wants, be able to tempt or vex us; but all his power is governed by the nutum and permission of God. The example of Job is very notable, of whom, if God had not said to the devil: "Behold, all that he has is in your hand," Satan would not have touched any of him: on the contrary, however, if the Lord had not added: "Only do not stretch out your hand on him," with a single blow from the devil he himself with his children and faculties would have fallen. Thus, however, the force of demons is involved, which not even those swine of which the Evangelists write could have invaded, not allowing God.

What the voice of tempting designates us, and with what reason we are tempted by God. But to understand the force of this request, it must be said what temptation means here, what item induces temptation. It is, however, tempting to endanger the one who is tempted, so that from him, by eliciting what we desire, we can squeeze out what is true. Whose way of tempting in no way falls on God: for what is there that God does not know? "All, however, says Paul, are naked and open to his eyes." There is another type of temptation, when progressing further one tends to look for something else, either for good or bad: for good, when someone's virtue is tempted with that thing, so that, seeing and knowing that, it is increased with comforts and honors, and its example is proposed to imitate others, and finally everyone for that very reason is excited to the praises of God: whose reason for tempting only suits God. An example of this temptation is that in Deuteronomy: "The Lord your God tempts you, so that it will become clear whether you pursue it or not." In what way is it also said to tempt God, when he oppresses with ignorance, morbidity and other kinds of calamities: which he does for the sake of testing his patience, and so that others may be a document of the Christian office. In this part we read that Abraham was tempted to sacrifice his son; With which fact he was a singular example of obedience and patience to the everlasting memory of men. In the same sentence it was said of Tobias: "Because you were acceptable to God, it was necessary that temptation test you."

How the devil tempts men. Men are tempted in a bad way when they are driven to sin or failure: which is the devil's own office. Because he tempts men with the intention of deceiving and precipitating them: which is why he is called tempter in the divine letters. But in those temptations, sometimes advocating intimate stimuli, he adsorbs by administering the affections and commotions of the soul; sometimes exaggerating us extrinsically, he uses external things, either prosperous to elevate us, or adverse to break us; Sometimes it has emissaries and cursors, lost men, and first of all heretics, who sitting in the chair of pestilence, disperse the deadly seeds of bad doctrines, so that those who have no delight or discrimination of virtue and vices, men themselves prone to evil, fluctuating and precipitating, can be driven.

An opportune example of the thing is Jerusalem, as Ezekiel attests, to which God would complete it with all kinds of ornaments, so that through the mouth of that Prophet God said: "You were perfect in my decorum, which I placed over you": and yet that city, accumulated of divine goods, is so far from being optimally deserving of itself and deserving God by having grace, it would use the heavenly benefits to obtain the beatitude, by whose grace it had received them, that, most ungrateful to the Father God, having thrown away the hope and cogitation of the heavenly fruits, she would only lustfully and madly fruit from the present abundance: which Ezekiel in the same chapter pursued with more words. Therefore, men who are ungrateful towards God are in the same place, who, with his permission, convert the supreme matter of righteous works to them by him divinely, converting them to vices. 11. In what ways is it said that someone is led into temptation. We say, however, that we are led into temptation when we succumb to temptations. But we are led into temptation in two ways: first, when, removed from the state, we fall into that evil to which someone has tempted us. But certainly no one is led by God into temptation in this way, because God is the author of sin to no one; indeed: "He hates all those who work iniquity." Thus, however, it is also in Saint James: "Let no one, when he is tempted, say that he is tempted by God: for God is not a tempter of evil." Then he is said to induce us into temptation who, although he himself does not tempt, nor does he cause us to be tempted, nevertheless he is called tempter, because, when he can prohibit that this does not happen, or that we are not overcome by temptations, he does not prevent. In this way God certainly allows the good and pious to be tempted, however, sustained by his grace, he does not desert them. Nor indeed do we sometimes, by the just and hidden judgment of God, postulated by our accelerated ones, left to ourselves, we fall. 12. God's benefits sometimes lead us into temptation. Furthermore, it is said that God leads us into temptation, when we abuse his benefits, which he gave us for salvation, for harm, and the substance of the father, like that Prodigal Son, we dissipate by living lustfully, indulging our cupidities. Therefore we can say what the Apostle said of the law: "The commandment, which was for life, was found for me to be for death."

In what way are the words of Scripture to be understood, which speak of God's permission through verbs that signify operation. But it is advisable to diligently attend to this custom of the divine Scripture, which sometimes means the permission of God with those words which, if properly received, mean action in God: for in the Exodus it is thus: "I will harden the heart of Pharaoh": and in Isaiah: "Blind the heart of this people": and to the Romans the Apostle wrote: "God gave them over to the passions of ignominy, and to a reprobate sense." In which places and other similar places it must be understood that that was not entirely acted by God, but rather permitted.

In this part of the precaution it is not postulated that we are completely immune from all temptation; but that we not be deserted by God in temptations. Having said these things, however, it will not be difficult to know what we postulate in this part of the precaution. Nor do we truly ask that we not be tempted at all: "For the life of men is a temptation on earth." It is, however, that thing useful and fruitful to the race of men: because in temptations we know ourselves, that is, our strength. Therefore we also humble ourselves under the powerful hand of God, and, deciphering manfully: we await the unfading crown of glory. Because "he who certifies in the arena is not crowned if he has not certified legitimately": and as Saint James says: "Blessed is the man who suffers temptation; for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life, which God promised to those who will look after him. That if we are sometimes urged by the temptations of our hosts, that cogitation will be of great relief to us: that we have as our helper a Pontiff who can sympathize with our weaknesses, having also been tempted in all things. So what are we asking for here? that, deserted from the divine prison, or deceived, we do not consent to temptations, or we give in afflicted: so that the grace of God is ready for us, that, when our own strength has failed us, it will recreate and heal us in evils. 15. In what way we should implore God's opem in our temptations. Therefore, in general, we must implore the opem of God in all temptations, as nominatim, when we are afflicted with singular ones, it is advisable to resort to caution. Which we read done by David in almost every type of temptation. Because in a lie he warns: "Do not take the word of truth out of my mouth until the end." In covetousness in this way: "Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to covetousness." But in the vain things of this life and in the ill-cebras of cupidities he used this prayer: "Avert my eyes, so that they do not see vanity." Then we postulate that we do not indulge cupidities, nor tire ourselves in sustaining temptations, nor decline from the way of the Lord, so that in both uncomfortable and prosperous things we may observe equity of spirit and perseverance, and that no part of us may be left empty of God's guardianship. We finally ask that Satan be brought under our feet.

In what way the victory of temptation is reported, and with what author it can be obtained. It remains for the parish priest to encourage the faithful people to whom in this precaution it is most convenient to consider and meditate: in which will be that optimal reason, if, understanding how much the weakness of men is, we distrust our strength, and, placing all the hope of our safety in the benignity of God, firm in that patronage, even in the greatest dangers we will have great courage, especially considering how many, endowed with this hope and this courage, God delivered from the raging jaws of Satan. Did he not elevate Joseph, surrounded on all sides by the burning faces of the insane woman, snatched from the utmost danger? Did he not preserve Susanna, obsessed by the ministers of Satan, when nothing was closer than being interfected with nefarious sentences? Nor to wonder: "For, he says, his heart was trusting in the Lord." The praise and glory of Job is famous, who triumphed over the world, over the flesh, over Satan. There are many examples of this kind, with which the parish priest must diligently coerce the pious people to that hope and trust.

The antesignan of our contest is Christ, partners of all the Saints, to whom those who do not follow are neighbors. Let the faithful also think about what dux they have in the temptations of the hosts, namely, Christ the Lord, who reported the victory of that contest. He defeated the Devil himself. He is the strongest, who by supervening surpassed the armed strong, whom he stripped of both weapons and spoils. Of his victory, which he reported from the world, it is in Saint John: "Be of good cheer, I have overcome the world." And in the Apocalypse it is said: "Behold, the lion conquers"; and "he came out conquering to conquer"; in whose victory he also gave his cultists the power to win. The Epistle of the Apostle to the Hebrews is full of the victories of holy men, who by faith conquered kingdoms... closed the mouths of lions, and what follows. But of these, which we read acted in this way, let us embrace with cogitation those victories that men willing in faith, hope and charity report daily from the intimate and external battles of the Demons; which are so many and so distinguished, that, if they fell under the appearance of the eyes, we would judge nothing that happens more frequently, nothing more gloriously; Of whose clades de los hostes Saint John wrote with these words: "I write to you, young people, because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you conquered the evil one."

How the Devil can be overcome by us. Satan is defeated, however, not with leisure, sleep, wine, eating, libidine, but with prayer, penance, vigil, abstinence, continence, chastity: "Watch and pray, he says, as we have already said, so that you do not enter into temptation": those who use these weapons for that struggle, convert their adversaries to flight: because those who resist the Devil, he will flee from them. In these, however, victories of the holy men that we mentioned, no one takes pleasure in himself, no one rises with insolence, so that he trusts that he can with his strength sustain the hostile temptations and impulses of the Demons: this is not our nature, not human imbecility.

How all the strength to win is given to us by God. These forces, with which we prostrate the satellites of Satan, are given by God, who places our arms like a bronze bow; for whose benefit the bow of the strong is surpassed, and the weak are girded with robbery; that gives us the protection of salvation; whose right hand raises us up; who teaches our hands to battle, and our fingers to war, so that we may give and have thanks for victory to one God, with whom only as author and helper can we conquer: which the Apostle did; because it says: "But thanks be to God, who gave us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ." The same author of victory preaches that heavenly voice in the Apocalypse: “There is salvation, and virtue, and the kingdom of our God, and the power of his Christ; for the accuser of our brothers has been projected, and they themselves defeated him by the blood of the Lamb. The same book testifies to the victory of Christ the Lord from the world and the flesh in that place: "These will fight with the Lamb, and the Lamb will overcome them." This about the cause and the way to overcome.

What are the prizes of the winners in that spiritual contest? Having explained these things, the parish priests will propose to the faithful people the crowns prepared by God and the everlasting breadth of prizes awarded to the winners; of which from the same Apocalypse they will utter divine testimonies: "He who overcomes will not be injured by the second death." And in another place: "He who overcomes, he will be clothed in white robes, and I will not blot out his name from the book of life, and I will confess his name before my Father and before his Angels": and shortly after, the same God and our Lord thus speaks to John: "He who overcomes, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God, and he will not go out again." Then he says: "Whoever conquers, I will give him to sit with me on my throne, just as I also conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne." Finally, when he had explained the glory of the Saints and that perpetual power of the goods they enjoy in heaven, he added: "He who conquers will possess these things." OF THE SEVENTH PETITION.

CHAPTER XVI

Nothing is contained in the higher petitions that is not included in this one. Because this request is like all the others, with which the Son of God concluded this divine prayer; Also showing his strength and weight, he used that clause of prayer when, upon migrating from life, he deprecated the Father God for the salvation of men: "In fact, I pray, he says, that you preserve them from evil." Then with this formula of precaution, which he both delivered by precept and confirmed by example, and with a certain epitome he summarily embraced the force and reason of the other requests. Because when we have prayed for what is contained in that prayer, nothing, with Saint Cyprian as author, remains that even more must be postulated, when once we ask for God's protection against evil: which once prayed for, against all those that the Devil and the world operate, we are safe and protected. Therefore, as much as this request is worth what we said, the parish priest must show great diligence in explaining it to the faithful. This and the next petition differ, however, in that with the former we postulate the avoidance of guilt, with this the liberation from punishment.

What urges us to spread this warning before the Lord. Therefore, the faithful people should no longer be warned about how much they labor for inconveniences and calamities, and lack heavenly support. Because how many and how great miseries the lives of men are exposed to, in addition to the fact that both sacred and profane writers copiously pursued this argument, there is almost no one who does not understand, both because of its danger and because of that of others. Because everyone is convinced of what the example of Job's patience brought to memory: "A man born of a woman, living a short time, is filled with many miseries: he comes out like a flower and shrinks, and flees like a shadow, and never remains in the same state." Nor is there truly any day that can pass that cannot be noted with some annoyance or inconvenience, as is witnessed by that voice of Christ the Lord: "The day's malice is enough." Although the condition of human life declares that instruction of the Lord himself, with which he taught that the cross must be taken up daily and followed. As, then, each one feels how laborious and dangerous this reason for living is, so the faithful people will easily be persuaded that they must implore God for deliverance from evils: especially when with nothing more are men induced to pray than with the cupidity and hope of deliverance from those inconveniences from which they are oppressed, or which they impede. Because there is this reason that insists on the minds of men: that in evils they immediately seek the help of God. Of which it is written that: "Fill their faces with ignominy, and they will seek your name, Lord."

With what reason should the depulsion of dangers and calamities be postulated from God. But if men do it almost spontaneously, let them invoke God in dangers and calamities; Certainly, how they can do it rightly, they must be taught maximally by those to whose faith and prudence their salvation is entrusted. Because there is no shortage of those who, against the command of Christ the Lord, use the order of precaution as a preposter. Because he who ordered us to go to him on the day of tribulation, he himself prescribed for us the order of prayer: because he wanted that before he freed us from evil, we should ask that the Name of God be sanctified, and his kingdom come, and we would postulate the rest, with which as with certain degrees we reach this place. But some, if the caput, if the side, if the foot hurt, if they boast of the familiar thing, if mines are attempted, if dangers from the enemies, in famine, in war, in pestilence, omitting the half degrees of Sunday precation, only ask to be freed from those evils. But this custom is repugnant to the command of Christ the Lord: "Seek first the kingdom of God." Thus, those who rightly make prayers, when they deprecate calamities, inconveniences, the depulsion of evils, refer it to the glory of God. So David, to that warning: "Lord, do not argue with me in your anger," subjugated the reason with which he shows himself to be the most precious of the glory of God: because he says: "because in death there is no one who remembers you: but in hell who will confess you?" And the same when he prayed to God to impart mercy to him, he subjoined that: "I will teach the wicked your ways, and the wicked will turn to you." To this salutary reason for praying, and to the example of the Prophet, the faithful listeners must be incited, and at the same time it must be taught how much interest there is between the prayers of unfaithful men and Christians. 4. Infidels ask to be freed from evil, and Christians do not in the same way. Those certainly vehemently pray to God that they can recover from illnesses and wounds, that they may be allowed to escape from urgent or imminent evils; but nevertheless they place the main hope of that liberation in remedies, compared by nature or by the industry of men: what is more, the medicine given to themselves by anyone, even if it has been made with songs, with benefits, with the work of demons, they adhere to it without any religion, as long as some hope of worthiness is shown. The reason of Christians is very different, who in morbidity and in all adverse things have God as their supreme refuge and refuge of salvation; He alone they recognize and venerate as the author of all good and as their liberator; But of the remedies, in which there is power to heal, they are certain that they were given them by God; and they estimate that they benefit the sick as much as God himself would have wanted: Because by God the medicine with which the morbidity could be cured was given to the race of men. Hence is that voice of the Ecclesiasticus: "The Most High created medicines from the earth, and the prudent man will not lack them."

Thus, those who gave the name to Jesus Christ do not restore the supreme hope of recovering their worth in those remedies, but rather they most trust in the author of the medicine himself, God. 5. How in morbidity one should trust only in God, who freed many from the very present dangers. For this reason also in the divine letters those who, with the confidence of medicine, do not require any help from God are rebuked: what is more, those who agitate life according to the divine laws, abstain from all remedies whatsoever that are proven not to have been ascribed by God to the cure. That if the hope of healing was also explored with the use of those medications, they nevertheless abhor them, as if they were songs and devices of demons. To this end, however, it is appropriate to encourage the faithful to trust in God. Because in that thing the most beneficent Father commanded us to postulate liberation from evils, so that in that same thing that he commanded we would also have the hope of impetration. There are many examples of this thing in sacred letters, so that those who least adduce with reasons to hope well, with the multitude of examples are compelled to trust. Abraham, Jacob, Lot, Joseph, David are before our eyes as very lofty witnesses of divine goodness. The sacred letters of the New Testament enumerate so many that the greatest discriminations were taken away with the weight of pious precaution, that the thing does not lack the commemoration of examples. Only, then, will we be content with that sentence of the Prophet, which can confirm even the weakest: "Indeed, he says, the righteous cried out, and the Lord heard them, and delivered them from all their tribulations."

What is meant here by the name evil, and what is the sentence of this petition. The force and reason of this request follows: let the faithful understand that in no way do we ask in this place that we be freed from all evils. Because there are certain things that are commonly considered evils, which nevertheless are fruitful to those who suffer them; like that encouragement that was attached to the Apostle, so that, by helping the grace of God, virtue could be perfected in weakness: these, if their strength is known, affect the pious with great will: so far are they from asking God to be removed. Therefore we only deprecate those evils that cannot bring any usefulness to the soul, the rest minimally, as long as there is some salutary fruit from there.

How many and how great are the kinds of evils from which we wish to free ourselves. Completely, then, that force is subject to this voice: that, freed from sin, we may also be snatched away from the danger of temptation, from intimate and external evils: so that we may be guardians of water, fire, lightning; lest the hail damage the fruits; lest we labor with the scarcity of annona, with seditions, with war; We ask God to deal with the morbidity, the plague, the vastness; that prohibits bonds, prison, exile, bans, snares and all other inconveniences with which men's lives are most often terrified and oppressed; finally remove all the causes of flagiciones and facínoras. We do not only deprecate these, which by everyone's consensus are evils; but also those that almost everyone confesses assets, riches, honors, bravery, theft, this very life; We ask, I say, that they not convert to evil and the destruction of our soul. We also pray to God that we may not be oppressed by sudden death: that we may not arouse within ourselves the wrath of God: that we may not increase the torments that await the wicked: that we may not be twisted with the fire of Purgatory; from which so that others may be freed, we preach piously and holyly. This request, both in the Mass and in the Litany, is interpreted as this by the Church: namely, that we deprecate those past, present and future evils.

God both overcomes impending evils and sometimes admirably removes them from us. Not in one way, however, does the goodness of God rescue us from evils: because it prohibits impending calamities, in the same way that we read that that great Jacob was freed from the enemies that the Siquimites had raised in him: because there is this: "The terror of God invaded all the cities around, and they did not dare to pursue those who retreated." And certainly all the Blessed, who reign with Christ the Lord in heaven, have been freed from all evils by the opem of God: but for us, who are versed in this pilgrimage, he in no way wants us to be freed from all inconveniences, but rather he takes us away from some; although those consolations that God sometimes gives to those who are oppressed by adverse things are in the manner of liberation from all evils. With these the Prophet consoled himself when he said: "According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations gladdened my soul." Furthermore, God frees men from evils, when those accused of being discriminated against are preserved whole and unscathed, which we read happened both to those boys conjected in the fiery furnace, and to Daniel, whom the lions did not harm at all, in the same way that the flame did not violate the boys either.

The Devil is called evil here, because he is the author of the guilt of evil, and the exacter of the punishment of evil. Evil, however, also according to the sentence of Saints Basil the Great, Chrysostom and Augustine, is mainly called the Devil, because he was the author of the guilt of men, that is, of the sceler and sin, of which God also uses as a minister in repeating the punishments of the sceleratos and criminals: "For God gives all evil to men, which they suffer because of sin." In which sentence the divine letters speak with those words: "Will there be evil in the city that the Lord has not done?" Item: "I am the Lord, and there is no other, forming light and creating darkness, making peace and creating evil." The Devil is also called evil for that reason: that, although we have not harmed him, he nevertheless inflicts perpetual war on us, and infests us with capital hatred. That if it cannot harm us, armed with faith and innocence, it nevertheless serves no purpose in tempting us with external evils, and in disputing us with any reason it can. Therefore we pray to God that he wants to free us from evil.

All the evils that our neighbors inflict on us come from the Devil. See St. Augustine, serm. 85 Temp. When we are not delivered from evils, we must be patiently carried away. Why with a singular voice, not a multitude, let us ask to be freed from evil. We say, however, of evil, not of evils, for this reason: that the evils that come from our neighbors, we assign to him as the author and promoter: for which reason we should not be angry with our neighbors; What's more, it is convenient to convert hatred and anger to Satan himself, from whom men are driven to inflict injury. Therefore, if your neighbor has injured you with something, when you make prayers to the Father God, ask that he not only free you from evil, that is, from those injuries that your neighbor imposes on you; but snatch that same neighbor from the hand of the devil, by whose impulse men are induced to fraud.

In what way we must be affected by evils, although we are not immediately freed. Finally, we must know this: that if in prayers and vows we are not freed from evils, we must patiently bear those that oppress us, understanding that it pleases the divine Numen that we suffer them tolerantly. Therefore it is in no way a reason for us to be indignant or hurt that God does not hear our prayers, but rather it is appropriate to refer all things to his nutum and will; considering that that is useful, that is salutary, that it pleases God that it be so, but not that which otherwise seems to us.

How many and how great comforts come to us from tribulations. Finally, the pious listeners must be taught that, while studying this curriculum of life, they must be prepared to bear, not only with an equo spirit, but also with joy, all kinds of inconveniences and calamities: "for all," he says, "who piously want to live in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution." Item: "Because of many tribulations it is necessary for us to enter the kingdom of God." Again: "Was it not necessary for Christ to suffer these things, and thus enter into his glory?" Because it is not fair for the servant to be greater than his Lord; as it is stupid, according to the sentence of St. Bernard, to be delicate members under the thorny head. Clear is that example of Uriah, proposed to be imitated, who, exhorting David to restrain himself at home, says: "The ark of God, and Israel and Judah live in pavilions... and I will enter my house...?" Educated with these reasons and meditations, if we come to pray, we will achieve that: that if nothing else, surrounded by evil everywhere and surrounded by evils, like those three boys intact from the fire, we will be preserved inviolate, certainly, like the Maccabees, we will constantly and strongly bear the adverse cases. In the contumelias and cruciados we will imitate the sacred Apostles, who, scourged with verbers, will vehemently rejoice that they have been worthy to suffer contumelias for Christ Jesus: Thus we, thus compared, will sing those with great will of spirit: "The princes persecuted me for free, and my heart was formed by their words: I will rejoice over your elocutions, like the one who found many spoils." From the extreme particle of the Sunday Prayer, which is Amen.

CHAPTER XVII

What is the use and fruit of this particle. This voice, So be it, Saint Jerome calls in the Commentaries on Matthew a signacle of the Sunday Prayer. Therefore, as we previously admonished the faithful of the preparation that must be given before attacking the divine precation, so now we consider what must be done so that they know the cause and reason of the clause and the purpose of the same precation. Because it is not of more value to diligently order divine prayers than to religiously absolve them. Let the faithful people, who are many, and those blessed, know the fruits that we perceive from the end of the Sunday Prayer; but of all the highest and easiest fruit is the impetration of those we postulate; of which sufficient has been said above. Not only, however, do we achieve with this last part of the precation that our prayers are heard, but also certain greater and more illustrious ones than can be explained in words.

How many good things come from prayer to men. Because when men colloquiate with God in prayer, as Saint Cyprian says, it happens in a certain inexplicable way that the divine majesty becomes more appropriate to the one who prays than to others: whom he also adorns with singular muneras; so that those who piously pray to God can in some way be compared to those who approach the fire: who if they are cold, become warm, if they are hot, they burn: thus those, assisting God, according to the way of piety and faith become more ardent: because their spirit is inflamed to the glory of God, their mind is enlightened in an admirable way, they are completely filled with divine munera. Because it is disclosed in the holy letters: "You provided for it in blessings of sweetness." An example to all is that great Moses, who, separating himself from the congress and colloquium of God, shone with a certain divine brilliance in such a way that the Israelites could not look at his eyes and his face. In all, those who with that vehement study make prayers, admirably enjoy the benignity and majesty of God: "Now I will attend, says the Prophet, and see: because you are not God that you want iniquity." The more men know these things, the more vehement worship and piety they venerate God: the more they also feel with more youth how gentle the Lord is, and how truly blessed are all those who hope in Him: then, however, surrounded by that most clear light, they consider how much is their humility, how much is the majesty of God. Because it is that rule of Saint Augustine: "Let him know you, let him know me." So it happens that, distrusting their own strength, they completely commit themselves to the kindness of God, without in any way doubting that He, embracing them with that paternal and admirable charity of His, abundantly supplies them with all the things that are necessary for life and salvation; from here they convert to giving thanks to God, as many maxims as the spirit can capture, as many as they embrace prayer; which we read that the great David did, that when he had thus instituted the precation: "Save me from all those who persecute me," he thus absolved it: "I will confess the Lord according to his justice, and I will praise the name of the Lord most high."

With what reason it happens that the prayers of the Saints, begun with fear, are concluded with joy. There are innumerable prayers of this type of Saints, whose exordium is full of fear, the clause full of good hope and joy: but it is admirable how much in that genre the precations of David himself shine. For when, disturbed with fear, he has thus begun to pray: "Many rise up against me, many say to my soul: there is no salvation for him in his God"; once confirmed and perfused with joy, he subjoined shortly after: "I will not fear thousands of the people who surround me." Also in another Psalm, when he has deplored his misery, to the extreme trusting in God he rejoices incredibly with the hope of eternal beatitude: "In peace in the same, he says, I will sleep and rest." What those words: "Lord, do not provoke me in your fury, nor punish me in your anger," with how much trembling and paleness are we to believe that the Prophet said them? On the contrary, those who later follow, with how confident and joyful a spirit? "Depart from me, he says, all you who work iniquity, for the Lord has heard the voice of my cry." When, however, he feared the wrath and fury of Saul, with what humility and devotion he implored God's help! "God, in your name save me, and in your virtue judge me": and yet joyfully and confidently in the same Psalm he subjoined: "Behold, indeed, God helps me: and the Lord is the susceptor of my soul." Therefore, he who commits himself to sacred prayers filled with faith and hope, approaches the Father God in such a way that he in no way distrusts that he can obtain what he needs.

With what meaning is that little voice Amen finally usurped here, and reserved for the Priest to pronounce it at Mass. There are, however, in this extreme word of the divine precation, Amen, many as if certain seeds of those reasons and cogitations that we said: and in truth was this Hebrew voice so frequent in the mouth of the Savior, that it pleased the Holy Spirit to be retained in the Church of God, to whose voice that sentence is in some way subject: "Know that your prayers have been heard": because it has the force of a responder, and of God who resigns with good grace to him who with the prayers he asked for what he wanted. This sentence confirmed the perpetual custom of the Church of God, which in the sacrifice of the Mass, when the Sunday prayer is pronounced, did not attribute to the ministers of the sacred thing, whose parts are to say that: But deliver us from evil, this voice Amen, but reserved it accommodated to the Priest himself, who, being an interpreter of God and men, answers to the people that God has been exorated.

There is not only one interpretation of the voice Amen. The Seventy translated γένοιτο, that is, let it be done, as in Psalm 40:14. Aquila truly πεπιστωμένως, that is, faithfully; Isaiah, however, 65, 16, where we have: He will swear in God Amen, the LXX read ὀμολογήσουσι τὸν Θεὸν τὸν ἀληθινόν. See Jerome, ep. 174 to Marcus in Isaiah.

In what way the diction Amen is variously expounded. And in fact, this word Amen was interpreted variously by many. The Seventy interpreters translated let there be; others truly redeemed; Aquila translated faithfully: but it matters little whether it was translated this way or that way; as long as we understand that it has that force that we said, of the Priest who confirms that what was requested has been granted; of which sentence the Apostle witnesses in the Epistle to the Corinthians: "For as many as the promises of God are, they are in Him: therefore also through Him the Amen to God for our glory." It is also this voice suited to us, in which there is a certain confirmation of those requests that we have hitherto accepted: which also makes those who carry out the sacred prayers attentive. Because it often happens that in caution, men distracted by various thoughts, they move elsewhere. Furthermore, with this same voice we ask with great study that all things be done, that is, granted, those that we previously asked for, or rather understanding that we already pray for all things, and feeling the present force of divine help, we sing that together with the Prophet: "Behold, in fact, God helps me, and the Lord is the susceptor of my soul." Nor is there any reason for anyone to doubt that, both by the name of his Son and by the word which he so frequently used, God is moved, who always, as the Apostle says: "He was heard because of his reverence."
